> 2. Explain what happens with a single threshold instead of a band, and construct a fault-rate sequence that oscillates.
> 3. Interview-style: "Would you alert on page-fault rate or on PSI memory pressure for a production service?" *Hint: consider which one changes meaning when you swap a hard disk for NVMe, and which one is measured in units of harm to the user.*

#### Memory-Mapped Files

**Theory**

Virtual memory's machinery — demand paging, page replacement, dirty tracking — is not only useful for anonymous memory. Applied to files, it produces an entirely different I/O interface.

**Memory mapping** associates a region of a process's virtual address space with a file. After `mmap`, the file's contents *are* the memory: reading a byte at the mapped address reads that byte of the file, and writing to it modifies the file. No `read`, no `write`, no explicit buffer.

The mechanism is exactly demand paging with the file as backing store. The mapping starts with no pages resident. The first access to any page faults; the kernel reads that page of the file into a frame and maps it. Subsequent accesses are plain memory accesses at hardware speed. Dirty pages are written back to the file by the same flusher that handles anonymous pages.

The advantages over `read`/`write`:

- **No copying.** `read()` copies from the kernel's page cache into your buffer. `mmap` maps the page-cache frame straight into your address space — the data exists once.
- **No system calls in the steady state.** After the mapping is established, access is ordinary loads and stores. A tight loop over a mapped file makes no syscalls at all.
- **Sharing is automatic.** Two processes mapping the same file `MAP_SHARED` map the same frames — the fastest IPC available (Chapter 2's shared memory, backed by a file).
- **Lazy and partial.** Mapping a 100 GB file costs nothing; only the pages touched are read.
- **Natural random access.** No `lseek`, just pointer arithmetic.

The costs and hazards are real and worth stating:

- **I/O errors become signals.** A `read()` returns `-1` with `errno`. A bad page in a mapping raises `SIGBUS`, which most programs do not handle.
- **Faults are invisible.** A pointer dereference that costs 8 ms does not look like I/O in the code, which makes latency profiling harder.
- **Truncation is dangerous.** If another process truncates the file, touching the mapped region beyond the new end raises `SIGBUS`.
- **Not always faster.** For a single sequential pass, `read()` with a large buffer can beat `mmap`, because it avoids per-page faults and TLB pressure. `mmap` wins for random access, repeated access, and sharing.

The flag that changes everything is `MAP_SHARED` versus `MAP_PRIVATE`: shared mappings write through to the file and are visible to others; private mappings are copy-on-write, so writes create private copies and never touch the file. That is how executables are mapped — text shared read-only, data private COW.

**Example**

```text
   read/write vs mmap

   READ                                  MMAP
   +-------------+                       +-------------+
   | user buffer | <-- COPY --+          | user vaddr  |--+
   +-------------+            |          +-------------+  |
                              |                           | mapped directly
   +-------------------------------+     +-------------------------------+
   |     page cache (kernel)       |     |     page cache (kernel)       |
   +-------------------------------+     +-------------------------------+
                  ^                                     ^
                  | disk read                           | demand-paged
             +---------+                           +---------+
             |  file   |                           |  file   |
             +---------+                           +---------+

   two copies, one syscall per call      one copy, ZERO syscalls after setup

   MAP_SHARED vs MAP_PRIVATE

     MAP_SHARED  : writes go to the FILE and are visible to other mappers
                   -> IPC, databases, writing through a mapping
     MAP_PRIVATE : writes trigger COW, creating a private copy
                   -> executable .data segments, read-mostly configuration

   HOW A PROGRAM IS LOADED -- IT IS ALL MMAP

     text   -> mmap(file, PROT_READ|PROT_EXEC,  MAP_PRIVATE)  shared frames
     data   -> mmap(file, PROT_READ|PROT_WRITE, MAP_PRIVATE)  COW
     bss    -> mmap(anonymous, zero-fill-on-demand)
     heap   -> mmap(anonymous) / brk
     -> exec() reads NO program bytes: every page arrives by demand fault

   WHEN TO USE WHICH

     access pattern            better choice   why
     -----------------------   -------------   ---------------------------
     one sequential pass       read()          no fault-per-page overhead
     random access             mmap            no lseek, only touched pages
     repeated access           mmap            page cache serves it directly
     shared between processes  mmap            same frames, zero copies
     very large file, sparse   mmap            lazily paged
     needs errno-style errors  read()          mmap gives you SIGBUS
```

```c
/* Memory-mapped file I/O: after mmap, file access is pointer arithmetic. */
#include <fcntl.h>
#include <stdio.h>
#include <sys/mman.h>
#include <sys/stat.h>
#include <unistd.h>

int main(void) {
    int fd = open("data.bin", O_RDWR);
    struct stat st;
    fstat(fd, &st);

    /* MAP_SHARED: writes go through to the file and to other mappers. */
    char *map = mmap(NULL, st.st_size, PROT_READ | PROT_WRITE,
                     MAP_SHARED, fd, 0);
    if (map == MAP_FAILED) { perror("mmap"); return 1; }
    close(fd);                      /* the mapping keeps its own reference */

    printf("%c\n", map[0]);         /* first touch -> PAGE FAULT -> disk read */
    printf("%c\n", map[1]);         /* same page   -> no fault, ~1 ns         */
    map[4096] = 'X';                /* second page -> fault, then marked DIRTY */

    msync(map, st.st_size, MS_SYNC);   /* force write-back NOW (durability)   */
    munmap(map, st.st_size);           /* unmap; dirty pages flushed later    */
    return 0;
}
```

```python
# mmap in Python: the same mechanism, and a demonstration that only
# touched pages become resident.
import mmap, os

with open("large.bin", "wb") as f:          # create a 256 MB file
    f.truncate(256 * 1024 * 1024)

def rss_mb():
    with open("/proc/self/statm") as f:
        return int(f.read().split()[1]) * os.sysconf("SC_PAGE_SIZE") / 2**20

with open("large.bin", "r+b") as f:
    mm = mmap.mmap(f.fileno(), 0)           # map the whole file
    print(f"after mmap 256 MB : {rss_mb():6.1f} MB")     # unchanged: lazy

    total = 0
    for off in range(0, len(mm), 4096 * 256):   # touch 1 page per MB
        total += mm[off]                        # each first touch = one fault
    print(f"after sparse touch: {rss_mb():6.1f} MB")     # only touched pages

    mm[0:5] = b"HELLO"                      # write through to the file
    mm.flush()                              # msync
    mm.close()

with open("large.bin", "rb") as f:
    print(f.read(5))                        # b'HELLO' -- the file changed
os.remove("large.bin")
```

**Key takeaways**

- `mmap` maps a file into the address space so file access becomes ordinary memory access, demand-paged by the same machinery.
- It avoids the copy that `read`/`write` performs and eliminates system calls in the steady state.
- `MAP_SHARED` writes through to the file and shares frames between processes; `MAP_PRIVATE` is copy-on-write.
- Program loading is entirely `mmap`: `exec` reads no bytes, and text pages are shared across all processes running the binary.
- Trade-offs: I/O errors arrive as `SIGBUS`, latency hides inside pointer dereferences, and a single sequential pass may be faster with `read`.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. Explain what happens, page by page, when a process maps a 10 GB file and reads bytes at offsets 0, 100, and 5,000,000,000. How many faults and how much resident memory?
> 2. Write the `mmap` flags for: a read-only configuration file, a shared counter between two processes, and a private scratch buffer. Justify each.
> 3. Interview-style: "When is `read()` the better choice over `mmap`?" *Hint: think about a single front-to-back pass over a huge file, and count the per-page costs `mmap` incurs that a large buffered read does not.*

#### Kernel Memory Allocation

**Theory**

Everything so far has described how the kernel manages *user* memory. The kernel's own allocations follow different rules, and understanding why explains the two specialised allocators in the next topic.

Four constraints separate kernel memory from user memory:

**1. Much of it must be physically contiguous.** A device performing DMA writes to *physical* addresses; it does not go through the MMU (or, with an IOMMU, goes through a different one). A driver's DMA buffer must therefore occupy consecutive physical frames. Page tables cannot paper over this, so external fragmentation of physical memory is a real problem for the kernel in a way it is not for user processes.

**2. Most of it cannot be paged out.** Kernel data structures are used in contexts where a page fault would be fatal — inside interrupt handlers, while holding a spinlock, in the page-fault path itself. A fault there could deadlock the system. So kernel memory is generally pinned, meaning it is a hard commitment against physical RAM.

**3. The allocations are small and repetitive.** The kernel constantly allocates and frees small, fixed-size objects: `task_struct` (a few KB), `inode`, `dentry`, socket buffers, file descriptors. Millions per second on a busy server. Rounding each to a page would waste enormously; a general-purpose allocator's per-allocation overhead would dominate.

**4. Failure is not an option in the same way.** A user allocation failure returns `NULL` and the program copes. A kernel allocation failure in a critical path may mean a panic, so the kernel keeps reserves and has emergency pools.

Linux exposes this in its API, and reading it tells you which constraint applies:

| Function | Contiguity | Use |
|---|---|---|
| `kmalloc(size, flags)` | **Physically** contiguous | Small allocations, DMA-capable |
| `vmalloc(size)` | Virtually contiguous only | Large buffers where physical contiguity is unnecessary |
| `alloc_pages(order)` | Whole physical pages, contiguous | Page-granular allocations |
| `kmem_cache_alloc(cache)` | From a slab of same-sized objects | Frequent fixed-size objects |

The `flags` argument carries the context: `GFP_KERNEL` may sleep (so it can reclaim), `GFP_ATOMIC` must not sleep (interrupt context — it dips into emergency reserves and fails fast), `GFP_DMA` restricts to memory a device can reach.

These constraints — physical contiguity, no paging, small repetitive objects — are precisely what the buddy system and slab allocator were designed for.

**Example**

```text
   WHY THE KERNEL IS DIFFERENT

   constraint               user memory            kernel memory
   ----------------------   --------------------   --------------------------
   physical contiguity      never needed (MMU)     REQUIRED for DMA
   pageable                 yes                    mostly NO (fault = deadlock)
   allocation sizes         KB to GB               tens of BYTES, millions/sec
   allocation failure       returns NULL           may PANIC
   fragmentation matters    external: solved       external: REAL PROBLEM again

   kmalloc vs vmalloc

   kmalloc(8192)                        vmalloc(8192)
   virtual : [ page A ][ page B ]       virtual : [ page A ][ page B ]
   physical: [ f100  ][ f101   ]        physical: [ f512  ][ f7     ]
             ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^                   ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
             CONTIGUOUS -> DMA-safe               scattered -> NOT DMA-safe
             limited by fragmentation             always succeeds if frames
                                                  exist anywhere

   ALLOCATION CONTEXT DECIDES THE FLAG

     process context, may block   -> GFP_KERNEL  (can reclaim, can sleep)
     interrupt handler            -> GFP_ATOMIC  (must not sleep; uses reserves)
     device-reachable memory      -> GFP_DMA     (address-range restricted)

     Using GFP_KERNEL in an interrupt handler is a classic kernel bug:
     it may sleep, and sleeping in interrupt context deadlocks the CPU.
```

```c
/* Kernel allocation, and what each choice commits you to.
   (Kernel-module code -- shown for the API, not to be compiled in user space.) */
#include <linux/slab.h>
#include <linux/vmalloc.h>
#include <linux/gfp.h>

struct my_dev {
    dma_addr_t dma_handle;
    void      *dma_buf;
    char      *big_scratch;
};

int setup(struct my_dev *d, struct device *dev) {
    /* DMA buffer: MUST be physically contiguous and device-reachable. */
    d->dma_buf = dma_alloc_coherent(dev, 64 * 1024, &d->dma_handle, GFP_KERNEL);
    if (!d->dma_buf)
        return -ENOMEM;

    /* A big scratch buffer no device will touch: physical contiguity is
       unnecessary, so vmalloc avoids stressing the buddy allocator. */
    d->big_scratch = vmalloc(4 * 1024 * 1024);
    if (!d->big_scratch) {
        dma_free_coherent(dev, 64 * 1024, d->dma_buf, d->dma_handle);
        return -ENOMEM;
    }
    return 0;
}

void interrupt_path(void) {
    /* In interrupt context: GFP_ATOMIC. It will NOT sleep, may use emergency
       reserves, and is more likely to fail -- so the caller must handle NULL. */
    char *buf = kmalloc(128, GFP_ATOMIC);
    if (!buf)
        return;                     /* fail fast; never block here */
    kfree(buf);
}
```

```bash
# What the kernel is actually holding.
grep -E 'Slab|SReclaimable|SUnreclaim|KernelStack|PageTables|VmallocUsed' /proc/meminfo
# Slab:            412880 kB     <- small object caches
# SReclaimable:    301224 kB     <- dentry/inode caches, reclaimable under pressure
# SUnreclaim:      111656 kB     <- genuinely pinned kernel data
# KernelStack:      18432 kB     <- one stack per thread, never paged
# PageTables:       88320 kB     <- the tables themselves cost memory

# Physical contiguity availability -- kmalloc of large sizes depends on this.
cat /proc/buddyinfo
# trailing zeros at high orders = large contiguous allocations will FAIL

# Which kernel object types dominate.
sudo slabtop -o | head -12
```

**Key takeaways**

- Kernel memory often must be physically contiguous (DMA) and mostly cannot be paged out (faults in critical sections would deadlock).
- Kernel allocations are dominated by small, fixed-size, extremely frequent objects — `task_struct`, `inode`, `dentry`, socket buffers.
- `kmalloc` gives physical contiguity for DMA; `vmalloc` gives only virtual contiguity but tolerates fragmentation.
- Allocation flags encode context: `GFP_KERNEL` may sleep, `GFP_ATOMIC` must not, `GFP_DMA` restricts the address range.
- These constraints motivate the buddy system (contiguous physical blocks) and the slab allocator (fast fixed-size objects).

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. For each, choose `kmalloc`, `vmalloc`, or a slab cache and justify: a 32-byte network header, a 4 MB decompression buffer, a DMA ring for a NIC, a per-process `task_struct`.
> 2. Read `/proc/meminfo` on your machine and compute what fraction of RAM the kernel holds in Slab, KernelStack, and PageTables combined.
> 3. Interview-style: "Why can't the kernel simply page out its own data structures like it does user memory?" *Hint: imagine the page-fault handler itself faulting, or a fault occurring while a spinlock is held with interrupts disabled.*

#### Buddy System and Slab Allocation

**Theory**

Two allocators, layered, solve the two kernel problems from the previous topic. The buddy system manages physically contiguous page blocks; the slab allocator sits on top and manages small objects.

**The buddy system** allocates in blocks of `2^k` pages ("order k"). To satisfy a request, it finds the smallest free block that fits; if that block is larger than needed, it splits it in half repeatedly until the right size is reached. The two halves of a split are called **buddies**. On free, if a block's buddy is also free, they merge back into a block of the next order, and the merge cascades upward.

The trick that makes it fast is address arithmetic. Two buddies differ in exactly one bit of their address — the one corresponding to their size — so finding a block's buddy is a single XOR:

```text
buddy_address = block_address XOR block_size
```

Coalescing is therefore O(1) per level, with no searching. That is why the buddy system is the kernel's answer to physical external fragmentation.

Its cost is internal fragmentation: rounding to a power of two wastes up to 50% in the worst case. A 33 KB request consumes a 64 KB block (order 4 at 4 KB pages). Acceptable for page-level allocations, ruinous for a 32-byte object — which is why a second layer exists.

**The slab allocator** solves the small-object problem. For each frequently used object type, it keeps a **cache**: pre-allocated slabs (contiguous page runs from the buddy allocator) divided into slots of exactly that object's size, with a free list threaded through them. Allocation pops a slot; free pushes it back. Both are O(1) with no splitting, no searching, and no rounding to powers of two.

Three further wins:

- **No internal fragmentation** — the slot is exactly the object size, so `inode` objects pack perfectly into their slabs.
- **Constructor reuse.** Freed objects retain their initialised state, so re-allocating one skips the constructor. Linux exploits this for lock and list-head initialisation.
- **Cache locality.** Objects of the same type sit adjacent in memory, so traversing them is cache-friendly, and per-CPU free lists remove lock contention on the fast path.

Slabs live in three states — full, partial, empty — and allocation prefers partial slabs to keep memory dense. Empty slabs are returned to the buddy allocator under memory pressure, which is why `SReclaimable` in `/proc/meminfo` counts as available memory.

Linux has had three implementations: SLAB (the original, with elaborate per-CPU queues), SLUB (the current default — simpler, less metadata, better on many-core machines), and SLOB (minimal, for tiny embedded systems). The idea is Jeff Bonwick's, from Solaris in 1994, and it is now near-universal — user-space allocators like `tcmalloc` and `jemalloc` use the same size-class-plus-free-list structure.

**Example**

```text
   BUDDY SYSTEM: SPLIT DOWN, MERGE UP
   Start: one free 1024 KB block. Request 100 KB -> rounds up to 128 KB.

   1024                    [------------ 1024 free ------------]
    split                  [---- 512 ----][---- 512 free ----]
    split                  [-256-][-256 -][---- 512 free ----]
    split                  [128][128][-256][---- 512 free ----]
    allocate               [USE][128][-256][---- 512 free ----]
                            ^^^ 128 KB block for a 100 KB request
                                (28 KB internal fragmentation)

   FREEING, WITH XOR COALESCING

     free the 128 KB block at address A
       buddy = A XOR 128K        <- one XOR, no search
       buddy free? -> merge into a 256 KB block
         its buddy free? -> merge into 512 KB
           its buddy free? -> merge into 1024 KB
     Cascading merge, O(1) per level.

   WORST-CASE INTERNAL FRAGMENTATION
     request 65 KB -> 128 KB block -> 49% wasted
     -> fine for pages, hopeless for a 32-byte inode. Hence slabs.

   SLAB ALLOCATOR: ONE CACHE PER OBJECT TYPE

   kmem_cache "inode_cache"  (object size 576 B, slab = 4 pages = 16 KB)

     FULL slabs      [XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX]  all 28 slots in use
     PARTIAL slabs   [XXXXXXXXXX....XXXX..........]  <- allocate from HERE
     EMPTY slabs     [............................]  <- return to buddy
                                                        under pressure

     alloc: pop the free list of a partial slab      O(1), no rounding
     free : push it back, keeping the constructed state

   THE TWO LAYERS TOGETHER

     kmem_cache_alloc(inode_cache)   <- 576 B, exact, O(1)
              |  needs a new slab?
              v
     alloc_pages(order=2)            <- 4 contiguous pages from the buddy system
              |
              v
     physical frames
```

```python
# Buddy system: splitting, and coalescing via XOR.

class BuddyAllocator:
    def __init__(self, total_pages):
        self.max_order = total_pages.bit_length() - 1
        # free_lists[k] holds addresses of free blocks of 2^k pages.
        self.free_lists = {k: set() for k in range(self.max_order + 1)}
        self.free_lists[self.max_order].add(0)
        self.allocated = {}

    def allocate(self, pages):
        order = max(0, (pages - 1).bit_length())        # round UP to 2^k
        for k in range(order, self.max_order + 1):
            if not self.free_lists[k]:
                continue
            addr = self.free_lists[k].pop()
            while k > order:                            # split down to size
                k -= 1
                buddy = addr + (1 << k)                 # the upper half
                self.free_lists[k].add(buddy)
            self.allocated[addr] = order
            waste = (1 << order) - pages
            return addr, order, waste
        return None, None, None

    def free(self, addr):
        order = self.allocated.pop(addr)
        while order < self.max_order:
            buddy = addr ^ (1 << order)                 # THE XOR TRICK
            if buddy not in self.free_lists[order]:
                break                                   # buddy busy: stop merging
            self.free_lists[order].remove(buddy)
            addr = min(addr, buddy)                     # merged block's address
            order += 1                                  # cascade upward
        self.free_lists[order].add(addr)

b = BuddyAllocator(1024)
a1, o1, w1 = b.allocate(100)      # 100 pages -> order 7 (128 pages)
a2, o2, w2 = b.allocate(30)       # 30 pages  -> order 5 (32 pages)
print(f"alloc 100 -> order {o1}, wasted {w1} pages")   # order 7, wasted 28
print(f"alloc  30 -> order {o2}, wasted {w2} pages")   # order 5, wasted  2
b.free(a1); b.free(a2)
print("largest free block after coalescing:",
      max(k for k, s in b.free_lists.items() if s))    # 10 -> fully merged
```

```python
# Slab allocator: exact-size slots, O(1) alloc/free, state preserved.

class SlabCache:
    def __init__(self, name, obj_size, slab_pages=4, page_size=4096):
        self.name, self.obj_size = name, obj_size
        self.per_slab = (slab_pages * page_size) // obj_size   # exact packing
        self.slabs = []                     # each: list of free slot indices
        self.stats = {"allocs": 0, "slabs_created": 0}

    def alloc(self):
        for slab in self.slabs:             # prefer a PARTIAL slab
            if slab["free"]:
                self.stats["allocs"] += 1
                return slab["free"].pop()
        slab = {"free": list(range(self.per_slab))}   # none partial: new slab
        self.slabs.append(slab)                       # from the buddy allocator
        self.stats["slabs_created"] += 1
        self.stats["allocs"] += 1
        return slab["free"].pop()

    def free(self, slot):
        # Object keeps its constructed state; re-allocation skips the constructor.
        self.slabs[0]["free"].append(slot)

inode_cache = SlabCache("inode_cache", obj_size=576)
print(f"objects per slab: {inode_cache.per_slab}")     # 28
for _ in range(100):
    inode_cache.alloc()
print(inode_cache.stats)      # {'allocs': 100, 'slabs_created': 4}
# 100 objects x 576 B = 57,600 B in 4 slabs of 16 KB = 65,536 B
# Internal fragmentation: only the slab tail, not per object.
```

```bash
# The buddy allocator's free lists, per order (order n = 2^n pages).
cat /proc/buddyinfo
# Node 0, zone Normal  4812 2201 980 310 88 12 3 0 0 0 0
#                       ^order 0 (4 KB)          ^order 10 (4 MB)
# Zeros at high orders: large contiguous kmalloc will fail.

# The slab caches, by memory used.
sudo slabtop -o | head -8
#  OBJS ACTIVE  USE OBJ SIZE  SLABS CACHE SIZE NAME
# 412k   398k  96%    0.19K   9821       78M  dentry
# 188k   181k  96%    0.57K   6714      107M  inode_cache
#  24k    23k  95%    7.06K   6021      172M  task_struct

cat /proc/slabinfo | head -5      # the raw per-cache statistics
```

**Key takeaways**

- The buddy system allocates power-of-two page blocks, splitting on demand and merging free buddies on release.
- Buddy addresses differ in one bit, so coalescing is a single XOR — O(1), no searching.
- Its cost is internal fragmentation of up to 50%, acceptable for pages and unacceptable for small objects.
- The slab allocator layers on top: per-type caches of exact-size slots with free lists, giving O(1) allocation, no rounding, and preserved constructor state.
- Slabs are full, partial, or empty; empty slabs return to the buddy allocator, which is why reclaimable slab counts as available memory.
- Linux ships SLUB by default; the same size-class design appears in `tcmalloc` and `jemalloc` in user space.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. A buddy allocator starts with 1 MB. Trace requests of 70 KB, 35 KB, and 80 KB: give the block size allocated, the internal fragmentation, and the free-list state after each.
> 2. Two 128 KB buddies sit at addresses `0x40000` and `0x60000`. Verify with the XOR rule whether they are buddies, and give the merged block's address and size.
> 3. Interview-style: "Why does the kernel need both a buddy allocator and a slab allocator?" *Hint: compute what a 192-byte `dentry` would cost if allocated directly from a power-of-two page allocator, then multiply by the hundreds of thousands live on a busy system.*

<a id="9-storage-systems"></a>
## 9. Storage Systems

Every abstraction built so far — processes, address spaces, pages evicted to a backing store — eventually rests on a device that remembers things after the power goes out, and that device is thousands to millions of times slower than RAM. This chapter opens up secondary storage: the physical structure of rotating disks and flash, the algorithms the kernel uses to order requests, and the redundancy schemes that turn unreliable devices into storage you can trust. It matters because storage is where most systems actually spend their time waiting, and because the right mental model for a hard disk is almost exactly the wrong one for an SSD.

<a id="91-secondary-storage-structure"></a>
### 9.1 Secondary Storage Structure

This section covers the hardware the operating system must drive: how a magnetic disk turns a linear block number into a mechanical operation, how flash differs so profoundly that it needs a translation layer of its own, how devices attach to the machine, and what "formatting" a disk actually writes.

#### Magnetic Disk Geometry

**Theory**

A hard disk drive is the last mechanical component in a modern computer, and nearly everything odd about disk performance follows from that single fact. Understanding its geometry is not nostalgia: it explains why disk scheduling algorithms exist, why file systems try to keep related blocks close together, and why the performance model of an SSD had to be rebuilt from scratch.

The physical construction is a stack of rigid **platters** coated in magnetic material, spinning together on one spindle at a constant rate — 5,400, 7,200, 10,000, or 15,000 revolutions per minute. Each platter surface is read by its own **head**, and all the heads are mounted on a single arm assembly that moves in and out as one unit. That last detail is important: the heads cannot be positioned independently, so at any instant all of them sit over the same radius.

The surface is organised into concentric rings called **tracks**, each divided into **sectors** — the smallest unit the device can read or write, historically 512 bytes and now typically 4,096 bytes. The set of tracks at the same radius across all surfaces forms a **cylinder**, which is the natural unit of locality: data in one cylinder is reachable by switching heads electronically, with no arm movement at all.

Three delays compose every disk access, and they differ by orders of magnitude:

1. **Seek time** — moving the arm to the correct cylinder. Mechanical, and the dominant cost: typically 3–12 ms average, with a short "track-to-track" seek near 0.5 ms.
2. **Rotational latency** — waiting for the desired sector to rotate under the head. On average, half a revolution. At 7,200 RPM a revolution takes 60/7200 s = 8.33 ms, so average latency is about 4.17 ms.
3. **Transfer time** — the actual data movement, once the head is in the right place. Fast: at 200 MB/s, a 4 KB sector takes about 20 microseconds.

Compare the numbers. Positioning costs milliseconds; transfer costs microseconds. A random 4 KB read spends roughly 99.8% of its time getting ready to read. This single asymmetry is the origin of nearly every storage optimisation ever devised: read ahead, batch, order requests to reduce arm motion, and above all prefer sequential access.

Because outer tracks are physically longer than inner ones, modern drives use **zone bit recording**: outer zones hold more sectors per track than inner zones. A consequence is that sequential throughput is genuinely higher at the start of a disk (outer edge) than at the end, often by a factor of two.

The old **CHS** addressing scheme (cylinder, head, sector) exposed this geometry to software. It is gone. Drives now present **logical block addressing (LBA)**: a flat array of blocks numbered 0 to N-1, which the drive maps internally to physical locations. LBA is a mercy — geometry varies by zone and bad sectors get remapped — but it also means the OS can only *approximate* physical locality. The one reliable heuristic that survives is that nearby LBAs are usually nearby physically.

The analogy is a vinyl record player where the needle must be lifted and repositioned by hand. Moving the arm to another groove is slow; waiting for the right part of the groove to come around is slow; reading once you are there is instant. If you had a hundred snippets to play, you would sort them by groove position rather than take them in the order requested — which is exactly what Section 9.2 is about.

**Example**

```text
   HARD DISK GEOMETRY (side view and top view)

   SIDE VIEW                              TOP VIEW OF ONE SURFACE
                                            ______________
    ====================  platter 0        /   ________   \
    --> head 0                            |   /  ____  \   |
    ====================  platter 1       |  |  / __ \  |  |   <- track
    --> head 1                            |  | | |  | | |  |
    ====================  platter 2       |  | | |()| | |  |   <- spindle
    --> head 2                            |  |  \ __ /  |  |
         |                                |   \  ____  /   |
     ARM ASSEMBLY (all heads move          \   ________   /
     together, one radius at a time)        \______________/

                                          A track is cut into SECTORS:
   CYLINDER = the same track number         [ s0 ][ s1 ][ s2 ][ s3 ]...
   on every surface. Reachable by
   switching heads: NO seek needed.

   THE THREE DELAYS, TO SCALE (7,200 RPM drive, 4 KB read)

   seek        |###################################|  ~4.0 ms   (mechanical)
   rotation    |#################################|    ~4.17 ms  (mechanical)
   transfer    |#|                                     ~0.02 ms  (electronic)
                                                       --------
                                              total    ~8.2 ms

   Positioning is ~99.8% of a random 4 KB read.
```

```python
# Modelling a disk access, and the sequential-vs-random gulf.

RPM              = 7200
AVG_SEEK_MS      = 4.0                    # average arm movement
TRACK_SEEK_MS    = 0.5                    # adjacent cylinder
TRANSFER_MB_S    = 200.0

rotation_ms      = 60_000 / RPM           # 8.33 ms for one full revolution
avg_rot_ms       = rotation_ms / 2        # on average, half a turn: 4.17 ms

def access_ms(bytes_read, seek_ms):
    transfer_ms = (bytes_read / (TRANSFER_MB_S * 1e6)) * 1000
    return seek_ms + avg_rot_ms + transfer_ms

# 1,000 random 4 KB reads: full seek + half rotation, every time.
random_total = 1000 * access_ms(4096, AVG_SEEK_MS)

# 1,000 sequential 4 KB blocks = one 4 MB read: pay positioning ONCE.
seq_total = access_ms(4096 * 1000, AVG_SEEK_MS)

print(f"random     : {random_total:8.1f} ms")   # random     :   8187.1 ms
print(f"sequential : {seq_total:8.1f} ms")      # sequential :     28.6 ms
print(f"ratio      : {random_total/seq_total:8.1f}x")  # ratio  :    285.8x

# Effective throughput tells the same story from the other side.
print(f"random  MB/s: {4096*1000/1e6 / (random_total/1000):.2f}")  # ~0.50 MB/s
print(f"seq     MB/s: {4096*1000/1e6 / (seq_total/1000):.2f}")     # ~143 MB/s
```

```bash
# Inspect real geometry and behaviour (Linux).
lsblk -o NAME,ROTA,SIZE,PHY-SEC,LOG-SEC,MODEL
# ROTA=1 means rotational (HDD); PHY-SEC 4096 with LOG-SEC 512 is "512e"

sudo hdparm -I /dev/sda | grep -Ei 'rotation|sector|model'
sudo smartctl -a /dev/sda | grep -Ei 'rotation rate|sector size'

# Sequential vs random, measured rather than assumed.
sudo hdparm -t /dev/sda                    # sequential read throughput
sudo fio --name=rand --filename=/dev/sda --rw=randread --bs=4k \
         --direct=1 --runtime=10 --time_based --readonly
# An HDD gives ~100-200 IOPS here; an SSD gives 100,000+. Same command.
```

**Key takeaways**

- A disk access costs seek time plus rotational latency plus transfer time; the first two are mechanical and dominate everything else.
- Average rotational latency is half a revolution: 60,000/RPM/2 milliseconds (4.17 ms at 7,200 RPM).
- A cylinder is the set of same-radius tracks across all surfaces; staying inside one cylinder avoids seeking entirely.
- Sequential access can beat random access by two orders of magnitude on the same drive — the difference is positioning, not bandwidth.
- Drives expose flat LBA rather than CHS, so software can only approximate physical locality; the surviving rule is that nearby LBAs are usually nearby.
- Zone bit recording puts more sectors on outer tracks, making the outer edge of a disk measurably faster.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. A 10,000 RPM drive has 5 ms average seek and transfers at 150 MB/s. Compute the average time for a random 4 KB read, and for a sequential 1 MB read.
> 2. A workload issues 200 random 8 KB reads per second to a 7,200 RPM drive with 4 ms average seek. Is the drive keeping up? Show the arithmetic, then state what has to change if it is not.
> 3. Interview-style: "Why does copying one 1 GB file take far less time than copying 250,000 4 KB files totalling 1 GB, on the same disk?" *Hint: count how many times positioning is paid in each case, and add metadata updates per file.*

#### Solid-State Drives

**Theory**

A solid-state drive stores bits as trapped charge in floating-gate transistors. There is nothing to move, so the seek and rotation terms of the previous topic simply vanish — a random read costs the same as a sequential one, roughly 50–100 microseconds on SATA and 20–80 microseconds on NVMe. If that were the whole story, SSDs would be "disks, but fast" and this topic would be one paragraph.

It is not the whole story, because NAND flash has three constraints that no rotating disk ever had.

**First: the read/write/erase asymmetry.** Flash is organised into **pages** (typically 4–16 KB) grouped into **blocks** (typically 128–512 pages, so a few megabytes). You can read a page. You can *program* (write) a page, but only if it is currently erased. You cannot overwrite a page in place — and erasure works only at whole-block granularity. So changing 4 KB inside a full block means: read the block elsewhere, erase it, rewrite it. This "read-modify-erase-write" asymmetry is the central awkwardness of flash, and it is what the Flash Translation Layer (next topic) exists to hide.

**Second: wear.** Each erase damages the oxide layer slightly. A block tolerates a finite number of program/erase (P/E) cycles before it stops holding charge reliably. The count depends on how many bits are packed into a cell:

| Type | Bits/cell | Voltage levels | Typical P/E cycles | Character |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **SLC** | 1 | 2 | 50,000–100,000 | Fast, durable, expensive |
| **MLC** | 2 | 4 | 3,000–10,000 | Balanced, now mostly enterprise |
| **TLC** | 3 | 8 | 1,000–3,000 | The consumer mainstream |
| **QLC** | 4 | 16 | 100–1,000 | Cheap, dense, slow writes, read-heavy use |

More bits per cell means more voltage levels to distinguish in the same physical window, which makes reads slower, writes much slower, and endurance worse. This is a density-versus-everything-else trade, and it is why a cheap large SSD can be slower at sustained writes than a hard disk once its cache is exhausted.

**Third: asymmetric and variable latency.** A read takes tens of microseconds; a program takes hundreds; an erase takes milliseconds. Because erases are triggered by background garbage collection, a write can occasionally be stuck behind one, which is why SSD latency distributions have a long tail even though their averages are excellent. Tail latency, not average latency, is what wakes people at night.

Against these constraints, flash offers something rotating media never could: **internal parallelism**. A drive contains many dies across several channels, all of which can be busy at once. A single outstanding request uses a small fraction of the device. Getting an SSD's advertised IOPS requires *many* concurrent requests — queue depth is a first-class performance parameter, which was never true of a single-armed disk.

The analogy is a whiteboard divided into panels, written in permanent marker. Reading any panel is instant. Writing on a blank area is quick. But changing one word means erasing an entire panel — and each panel survives only so many wipes before it goes grey and stops taking ink.

**Example**

```text
   NAND FLASH ORGANISATION AND THE THREE OPERATIONS

   DIE
    +--------------------------------------------------+
    |  BLOCK 0 (erase unit, ~4 MB)                      |
    |   +--------+--------+--------+ ... +--------+     |
    |   | page 0 | page 1 | page 2 |     | page N |     |  page = read/program
    |   | 16 KB  | 16 KB  | 16 KB  |     | 16 KB  |     |         unit
    |   +--------+--------+--------+ ... +--------+     |
    |  BLOCK 1 ...                                      |
    +--------------------------------------------------+

   OPERATION    GRANULARITY     TYPICAL TIME    NOTES
   read         page            25-100 us       cheap, repeatable
   program      page            200-1500 us     only onto an ERASED page
   erase        BLOCK           2-10 ms         resets a few MB at once

   WHY IN-PLACE OVERWRITE IS IMPOSSIBLE

   want: change 4 KB inside a full block
     naive:  read whole block -> erase block (ms!) -> rewrite whole block
             = megabytes of work and one P/E cycle for a 4 KB change
     real:   write the new data to a fresh erased page ELSEWHERE and
             remap the address. (This is the FTL -- see the next topic.)

   PARALLELISM: ONE REQUEST USES ALMOST NONE OF THE DEVICE

   channel 0 -> [die][die]      queue depth 1  : one die busy, ~7% utilised
   channel 1 -> [die][die]      queue depth 32 : most dies busy
   channel 2 -> [die][die]      => IOPS scale with CONCURRENCY, not clock
   channel 3 -> [die][die]
```

```python
# Endurance arithmetic: how long does a TLC drive actually last?

CAPACITY_GB      = 1000
PE_CYCLES        = 1500        # TLC
WRITE_AMP        = 2.5         # host writes vs actual flash writes (see FTL)
HOST_WRITES_GB_D = 40          # a fairly heavy desktop workload

total_flash_writes_gb = CAPACITY_GB * PE_CYCLES        # ideal, perfect wear levelling
effective_host_gb     = total_flash_writes_gb / WRITE_AMP
days                  = effective_host_gb / HOST_WRITES_GB_D

print(f"endurance (TBW): {effective_host_gb/1000:.0f} TB")   # 600 TB
print(f"lifetime       : {days/365:.1f} years")              # 41.1 years

# The same drive under a write-heavy database workload:
for gb_per_day in (40, 200, 1000):
    print(gb_per_day, "GB/day ->",
          round(effective_host_gb / gb_per_day / 365, 1), "years")
# 40 GB/day -> 41.1 years | 200 -> 8.2 years | 1000 -> 1.6 years
# Wear is a workload property, not a drive property.
```

```bash
# What the drive says about its own wear and geometry.
sudo smartctl -a /dev/nvme0n1 | grep -Ei 'percentage used|data units written|available spare'
# Percentage Used: 3%          <- fraction of rated P/E cycles consumed
# Data Units Written: 41,203,551  (x 512,000 bytes)

sudo nvme id-ns /dev/nvme0n1 -H | grep -i 'lba format'   # sector size in use

# Queue depth is the parameter that matters on flash. Same drive, two depths:
sudo fio --name=qd1  --filename=/dev/nvme0n1 --rw=randread --bs=4k \
         --iodepth=1  --direct=1 --runtime=10 --time_based --readonly
sudo fio --name=qd64 --filename=/dev/nvme0n1 --rw=randread --bs=4k \
         --iodepth=64 --direct=1 --runtime=10 --time_based --readonly
# Typical: ~15,000 IOPS at QD1 vs ~600,000 IOPS at QD64. The device did not
# get faster -- you finally used more than one die at a time.
```

**Key takeaways**

- SSDs have no seek or rotational delay, so random and sequential reads cost nearly the same; the disk-era intuition about locality mostly evaporates.
- Flash reads and programs at page granularity but erases only at block granularity, so in-place overwrite is impossible.
- Erase blocks wear out; endurance falls sharply as bits-per-cell rises (SLC to QLC), and QLC drives can be slower than an HDD at sustained writes.
- Latency is asymmetric — read microseconds, program hundreds of microseconds, erase milliseconds — which produces a long tail even with excellent averages.
- Performance comes from internal parallelism across channels and dies, so achieving rated IOPS requires deep queues, not faster individual requests.

>

> 2. Explain why a benchmark that issues one 4 KB read at a time reports roughly 5% of an NVMe drive's advertised IOPS, and what to change in the benchmark.
> 3. Interview-style: "A QLC SSD writes at 1.5 GB/s for twenty seconds and then collapses to 80 MB/s for the rest of a large copy. What is happening?" *Hint: think about what the fast region is made of, how big it is, and what has to happen before it can be reused.*

#### NVM and Flash Translation Layer

**Theory**

The previous topic ended with a problem: flash cannot be overwritten in place, but every operating system, file system, and application on earth assumes block N can be rewritten whenever they like. Something has to reconcile the two. That something is the **Flash Translation Layer (FTL)** — firmware running on the drive's own controller, with its own CPU and DRAM, which presents a perfect, infinitely-rewritable array of logical blocks on top of hardware that offers nothing of the sort.

The FTL's core trick is **indirection**. It keeps a mapping table from logical block address to physical flash page. A write never modifies the old page; it programs a *fresh, already-erased* page somewhere convenient, updates the map, and marks the old page **invalid**. This turns every random write into a sequential append into whatever erase block is currently open — which is precisely the access pattern flash likes.

That trick creates a new problem: invalid pages accumulate, and the drive eventually runs out of erased blocks. **Garbage collection** solves it. The FTL picks a victim block with many invalid pages, copies the still-valid pages out to a fresh block, and erases the victim. Note what just happened: writing user data caused *additional* internal writes. The ratio is **write amplification**:

```text
write amplification = bytes written to flash / bytes written by the host
```

Write amplification is the single most important number in SSD behaviour. It is near 1.0 for large sequential writes, and can exceed 5 for small random writes on a nearly full drive — which simultaneously multiplies wear and destroys sustained throughput. Two things reduce it: **over-provisioning** (hidden spare capacity, usually 7–28%, that guarantees erased blocks are always available) and keeping the drive from being filled to the brim, which is the same thing done voluntarily.

The FTL also handles **wear levelling**. Left alone, a filesystem that rewrites the same metadata block would destroy a handful of erase blocks while the rest stayed pristine. Wear levelling spreads erases evenly, migrating even cold, never-modified data occasionally so its blocks can take their turn. And it manages **bad block retirement**, pulling failed blocks out of service and replacing them from the spare pool.

One last piece is needed, and it must come from the OS. When a file is deleted, the file system stops caring about those blocks — but the drive has no idea. It will keep dutifully copying that dead data during garbage collection forever. The **TRIM** command (`DISCARD` in Linux, `DEALLOCATE` in NVMe) tells the drive "these LBAs no longer contain anything I want," letting the FTL mark those pages invalid immediately. Without TRIM, a drive's write amplification climbs steadily over its life and performance degrades permanently.

Alongside NAND sits a newer category: **non-volatile memory (NVM)** that is byte-addressable and sits on the memory bus rather than a storage bus. It blurs the storage/memory boundary — persistence at near-DRAM latency, accessed with load and store instructions rather than a block driver, which forces filesystems and databases to rethink durability primitives entirely (`clwb`, `sfence`, and persistent-memory-aware allocation instead of `write` and `fsync`). Intel's Optane was the commercial flagship and has been discontinued, but the programming model — DAX-mapped persistent memory — remains the reference design for the category, and CXL-attached memory is bringing the same questions back.

The analogy for the FTL is a librarian in a library where books cannot be edited. To "update" a book, she prints a corrected copy, shelves it in the next free slot, and rewrites the catalogue entry; the old copy is left to be recycled later. Occasionally she consolidates a shelf full of superseded copies to free it. The catalogue is the mapping table, the recycling is garbage collection, and if nobody ever tells her a book has been formally withdrawn, she will keep moving dead copies around forever — that is what TRIM prevents.

**Example**

```text
   FTL INDIRECTION: A WRITE NEVER OVERWRITES

   Host: write LBA 42 (new contents)

   BEFORE                                AFTER
   map: 42 -> P100                       map: 42 -> P307
   block A: [P100 valid  ]               block A: [P100 INVALID]  <- garbage
            [P101 valid  ]                        [P101 valid  ]
   block B: [P307 ERASED ]               block B: [P307 valid  ]  <- new data
            [P308 ERASED ]                        [P308 ERASED ]

   Random host writes become a SEQUENTIAL append into the open block.

   GARBAGE COLLECTION AND WRITE AMPLIFICATION

   victim block: [ V ][ I ][ V ][ I ][ I ][ V ][ I ][ I ]   V=valid I=invalid
                   3 valid pages, 5 invalid

   1. copy the 3 valid pages to a fresh block   -> 3 extra page writes
   2. erase the victim (one P/E cycle)          -> 8 pages now free
   net gain: 5 free pages, at a cost of 3 internal writes

   host wrote 5 pages worth of new data, flash wrote 5 + 3 = 8
   write amplification = 8 / 5 = 1.6

   HOW FULLNESS DESTROYS THIS

   drive 50% full : victims are mostly invalid -> WA ~1.1  (fast)
   drive 95% full : victims are mostly valid   -> WA ~5.0  (slow, wears out)

   WITHOUT TRIM, DELETED DATA IS STILL "VALID" TO THE DRIVE
   fs deletes file -> blocks free to the OS, still V to the FTL
   -> GC keeps copying dead pages forever -> WA climbs, perf never recovers
```

```python
# A minimal FTL: out-of-place writes, invalidation, garbage collection, and
# the write amplification that falls out of them.

PAGES_PER_BLOCK = 8

class FTL:
    def __init__(self, blocks):
        self.n     = blocks
        self.data  = [[None]  * PAGES_PER_BLOCK for _ in range(blocks)]
        self.valid = [[False] * PAGES_PER_BLOCK for _ in range(blocks)]
        self.free  = list(range(blocks))       # erased blocks, ready to program
        self.open, self.ptr = self.free.pop(), 0    # the currently open block
        self.map   = {}                        # LBA -> (block, page)
        self.host_writes = self.flash_writes = self.erases = 0

    def _program(self, lba):
        if self.ptr == PAGES_PER_BLOCK:        # open block is full
            while not self.free:               # no erased block? make one
                self._collect()
            self.open, self.ptr = self.free.pop(), 0
        b, p = self.open, self.ptr
        self.data[b][p], self.valid[b][p] = lba, True
        self.map[lba] = (b, p)
        self.flash_writes += 1                 # every PHYSICAL page write counts
        self.ptr += 1

    def write(self, lba):
        self.host_writes += 1
        if lba in self.map:                    # invalidate the OLD location --
            ob, op = self.map[lba]             # never overwrite it in place
            self.valid[ob][op] = False
        self._program(lba)                     # append to the open block

    def trim(self, lba):                       # the OS says: this is dead
        if lba in self.map:
            b, p = self.map.pop(lba)
            self.valid[b][p] = False           # GC will never relocate it again

    def _collect(self):
        # Greedy victim selection: the block with the fewest surviving pages.
        cands  = [b for b in range(self.n) if b != self.open and b not in self.free]
        victim = min(cands, key=lambda b: sum(self.valid[b]))
        surv   = [self.data[victim][p] for p in range(PAGES_PER_BLOCK)
                  if self.valid[victim][p]]
        self.data[victim]  = [None]  * PAGES_PER_BLOCK
        self.valid[victim] = [False] * PAGES_PER_BLOCK
        self.erases += 1
        self.free.append(victim)
        for lba in surv:                       # relocation: the cost of GC.
            self._program(lba)                 # THESE are the extra writes.

import random
for live in (40, 80, 100, 112):                # live LBAs out of 128 page slots
    random.seed(7)
    ftl = FTL(blocks=16)
    for _ in range(4000):
        ftl.write(random.randrange(live))      # uniform random overwrites
    print(f"{live/128:4.0%} full -> host {ftl.host_writes}, "
          f"flash {ftl.flash_writes:5}, erases {ftl.erases:4}, "
          f"WA {ftl.flash_writes/ftl.host_writes:.2f}")

# 31% full -> host 4000, flash  4028, erases  498, WA 1.01
# 62% full -> host 4000, flash  6763, erases  967, WA 1.69
# 78% full -> host 4000, flash  9699, erases 1265, WA 2.42
# 88% full -> host 4000, flash 14126, erases 1777, WA 3.53
#
# The host issued the SAME 4,000 writes every time. Only free space changed.
# On a roomy drive the victim block is nearly all invalid, so an erase is
# almost pure profit; on a full one the victim is mostly valid, so freeing a
# page costs several relocations. This is why leaving an SSD unpartitioned at
# the end -- or simply not filling it -- measurably improves both speed and
# lifetime, and why TRIM matters: every trimmed page is one GC never copies.
```

```bash
# Is TRIM actually reaching the device?
lsblk --discard                 # non-zero DISC-GRAN/DISC-MAX = discard supported
sudo fstrim -av                 # trim all mounted filesystems now
systemctl status fstrim.timer   # the weekly batch job most distros ship

# Continuous discard is the alternative, but it adds a command per delete:
grep discard /etc/fstab         # prefer the timer unless latency demands otherwise

# Over-provisioning by leaving a partition gap: give the FTL room to work.
sudo nvme id-ctrl /dev/nvme0 | grep -i tnvmcap   # total capacity vs usable

# Persistent memory, when present, appears as a DAX device rather than a disk:
ls /dev/pmem* 2>/dev/null
ndctl list -u 2>/dev/null       # namespaces, modes (fsdax, devdax, sector)
```

**Key takeaways**

- The FTL hides flash's no-overwrite rule behind a logical-to-physical map, turning every host write into an out-of-place append and invalidating the old page.
- Garbage collection reclaims blocks by relocating surviving pages, and the resulting extra writes are quantified as write amplification.
- Write amplification rises sharply as the drive fills; over-provisioning and free space are the direct remedies.
- Wear levelling spreads erases across all blocks, including migrating cold data so its blocks take a turn.
- TRIM/DISCARD is the OS's only way to tell the drive that deleted blocks are dead; without it, GC keeps relocating garbage and performance decays permanently.
- Byte-addressable persistent memory sits on the memory bus and replaces the block-device model with load/store plus explicit cache-flush instructions.
