<a id="11-inputoutput-systems"></a>
## 11. Input/Output Systems

A computer that cannot talk to the outside world computes nothing anyone can use, and the devices it must talk to differ from one another more than any other component of a system — a keyboard delivers bytes at human speed, an NVMe drive at gigabytes per second, a network card at unpredictable intervals decided by someone else's machine. This chapter covers how the hardware exposes those devices, how the kernel layers driver code beneath a uniform interface so applications never see the differences, and what the I/O subsystem does with the requests once it has them. It matters because I/O is where almost every real system spends its waiting time, and because the techniques here — interrupts, DMA, buffering, asynchrony — are the ones that decide whether that waiting overlaps with useful work or simply stops it.

<a id="111-io-hardware"></a>
### 11.1 I/O Hardware

This section covers what the machine physically offers: how a device is addressed and controlled, the buses that connect it, and the three escalating strategies — polling, interrupts, and DMA — for getting data across without wasting the processor.

#### Device Controllers and Ports

**Theory**

A CPU cannot drive a disk motor or modulate a radio. What it can do is read and write locations, so every device is presented to it as a small set of locations that happen to have side effects. The hardware that provides those locations is the **device controller** — a small special-purpose computer sitting between the bus and the physical device, translating "write 0x20 to this register" into whatever the device actually requires.

The analogy worth holding is a hotel's front desk. Guests do not walk into the kitchen; they leave a request at the desk, and the desk staff know how to turn "breakfast at seven" into actions in a part of the building the guest never sees. The controller is that desk, and its registers are the forms you fill in.

Nearly every controller exposes the same four kinds of register, whatever the device:

| Register | Direction | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| **Data-in** | Host reads | Bytes arriving from the device |
| **Data-out** | Host writes | Bytes going to the device |
| **Status** | Host reads | Busy, ready, error, data-available flags |
| **Control** | Host writes | Start a command, set a mode, enable interrupts |

Two mechanisms exist for reaching those registers, and the distinction still appears in driver code:

**Port-mapped I/O (PMIO).** The registers live in a separate address space reached only by special instructions — `IN` and `OUT` on x86. A device occupies a range of **port numbers** (the legacy serial port at 0x3F8, the PS/2 keyboard at 0x60). The address space is small (65,536 ports on x86) and the instructions are privileged, which gives protection for free: a user program simply cannot execute `OUT`.

**Memory-mapped I/O (MMIO).** The registers appear at ordinary physical memory addresses. The driver reads and writes them with ordinary load and store instructions, and protection comes from page tables — the kernel maps the region and user space does not. This is how essentially every modern device works, because it needs no special instructions, supports 64-bit address space, and allows large regions (a GPU exposes hundreds of megabytes of framebuffer this way).

MMIO carries one hazard that catches people: **these are not memory**. Reading a status register twice may give different answers, and writing a control register does something. So the CPU's normal freedoms — caching values, reordering accesses, merging writes — are all wrong here. Device regions must be mapped uncacheable, and drivers must use the platform's ordering primitives (`readl`/`writel` on Linux, which embed the necessary barriers) rather than raw pointer dereferences. A driver that uses a plain `volatile` pointer and no barriers works on one machine and fails on another.

Finding the registers is the remaining problem, and it is solved by **enumeration**. PCI Express devices expose a configuration space describing their vendor, device class, and the **Base Address Registers (BARs)** that declare how much space they need; firmware or the kernel assigns real addresses and writes them back. This is why modern systems have no fixed port numbers to memorise — the bus tells the kernel what is present and where.

**Example**

```text
   WHERE THE CPU MEETS THE DEVICE

   CPU ----- system bus -----+------------------+------------------+
                             |                  |                  |
                     +-------v-------+  +-------v-------+  +-------v-------+
                     | disk          |  | network       |  | USB           |
                     | CONTROLLER    |  | CONTROLLER    |  | CONTROLLER    |
                     +---------------+  +---------------+  +---------------+
                     | data-in reg   |          |                  |
                     | data-out reg  |          |                  |
                     | status reg    |      [ ethernet ]     [ keyboard ]
                     | control reg   |
                     +-------+-------+
                             |
                        [ actual disk ]

   TWO WAYS TO ADDRESS THOSE REGISTERS

   PORT-MAPPED                        MEMORY-MAPPED
   +------------------+               physical address space
   | memory 0..N      |               +-------------------------+
   +------------------+               | RAM        0x0000_0000  |
   | ports 0x0..0xFFFF|  <- separate  | ...                     |
   +------------------+     space     | RAM        0x7FFF_FFFF  |
                                      +-------------------------+
   outb(0x20, 0x3F8);                 | NIC regs   0xF000_0000  | <- device
   val = inb(0x3FD);                  | GPU BAR    0xE000_0000  |
                                      +-------------------------+
   special instructions,              writel(0x20, nic->ctrl);
   privileged by the ISA              val = readl(nic->status);
                                      protected by PAGE TABLES

   WHY MMIO REGIONS MUST NOT BE CACHED

   status = *reg;        // cached: CPU returns the OLD value forever
   while (status & BUSY) // loops until the heat death of the universe
       status = *reg;    // because nothing invalidates the cache line

   *ctrl = START;        // write-combined: may be merged, reordered,
   *ctrl = ABORT;        // or dropped. The device sees the wrong sequence.
```

```c
// A minimal PCIe driver's register access, the way Linux actually does it.
#include <linux/pci.h>
#include <linux/io.h>

#define REG_STATUS   0x08         // offsets into the device's BAR
#define REG_CONTROL  0x0C
#define REG_DATA     0x10
#define STATUS_READY (1u << 0)
#define CTRL_START   (1u << 1)

struct mydev {
    void __iomem *regs;           // __iomem: NOT an ordinary pointer
};

static int mydev_probe(struct pci_dev *pdev, const struct pci_device_id *id)
{
    struct mydev *dev = kzalloc(sizeof(*dev), GFP_KERNEL);

    pci_enable_device(pdev);                 // power it up, enable decoding
    pci_request_regions(pdev, "mydev");      // claim the BARs exclusively

    // Map BAR 0 uncached. The address came from the BUS, not from a constant.
    dev->regs = pci_iomap(pdev, 0, 0);
    if (!dev->regs)
        return -ENOMEM;

    pci_set_master(pdev);                    // allow the device to do DMA
    pci_set_drvdata(pdev, dev);
    return 0;
}

static int mydev_send(struct mydev *dev, u32 value)
{
    // readl/writel embed the compiler and CPU barriers this needs.
    // A plain *(volatile u32 *) would compile, and would be wrong.
    unsigned long deadline = jiffies + msecs_to_jiffies(100);

    while (!(readl(dev->regs + REG_STATUS) & STATUS_READY)) {
        if (time_after(jiffies, deadline))
            return -ETIMEDOUT;               // ALWAYS bound a hardware wait
        cpu_relax();                         // hint to the CPU: spin loop
    }

    writel(value, dev->regs + REG_DATA);     // load the data register first
    wmb();                                   // ordering: data BEFORE command
    writel(CTRL_START, dev->regs + REG_CONTROL);   // now tell it to go
    return 0;
}
```

```bash
# What the bus says is present, and where its registers landed.
lspci -v | head -20
#   00:1f.2 SATA controller: Intel Corporation ... (rev 05)
#       Flags: bus master, 66MHz, medium devsel, latency 0, IRQ 27
#       Memory at f7f00000 (32-bit, non-prefetchable) [size=8K]   <- BAR: MMIO
#       I/O ports at f070 [size=8]                                <- BAR: PMIO
#       Capabilities: [80] MSI: Enable+ Count=1/1

lspci -vvv -s 00:1f.2 | grep -A3 'Region'     # every BAR of one device
sudo lspci -xxx -s 00:1f.2 | head -4          # raw PCI configuration space

# The two address spaces, as the kernel sees them.
sudo cat /proc/iomem | head -20               # memory-mapped regions
#   f7f00000-f7f01fff : 0000:00:1f.2
#                        ^ the SATA controller's registers
sudo cat /proc/ioports | head -20             # port-mapped ranges
#   0060-0060 : keyboard
#   03f8-03ff : serial

# Which driver claimed which device.
lspci -k | head -12
ls -l /sys/bus/pci/devices/0000:00:1f.2/driver
```

**Key takeaways**

- A device controller is the hardware intermediary that turns register accesses into physical device actions; the CPU never touches the device itself.
- Almost every controller exposes the same four register types: data-in, data-out, status, and control.
- Port-mapped I/O uses a separate address space and privileged instructions; memory-mapped I/O uses ordinary addresses protected by page tables and is what modern devices use.
- MMIO regions are not memory: they must be mapped uncacheable, and drivers must use ordering-aware accessors (`readl`/`writel`) rather than raw pointers.
- PCIe devices declare their register requirements through Base Address Registers, and the kernel or firmware assigns the actual addresses at enumeration.
- Every wait on a hardware status bit must be bounded by a timeout, because a wedged device otherwise hangs the driver forever.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. List the four standard controller registers and, for a "read one sector" operation, state the order in which a driver would touch each.
> 2. Run `lspci -v` and `cat /proc/iomem` on your machine, and match one device's BAR to its entry in the memory map.
> 3. Interview-style: "A driver polls a status register in a loop and the loop never exits, though the device is working. What is the most likely cause?" *Hint: ask what the CPU is allowed to assume about a value it has already loaded, and what property the mapping needs to forbid that assumption.*

#### Buses and Interfaces

**Theory**

Controllers must be connected to the CPU and to memory, and the wiring that does it is the **bus**. The bus is not a neutral pipe: its topology and protocol decide how many devices can be attached, how much bandwidth each gets, and whether one slow device can hold up everybody else.

The historical arc is from **shared** to **switched**, and it mirrors what happened to Ethernet. Early buses (ISA, PCI, the original SCSI) were genuinely shared wires: every device saw every transaction, only one could transmit at a time, and arbitration decided who. That is simple and cheap, but total bandwidth is fixed no matter how many devices you attach, and electrical limits cap both the clock rate and the number of connections.

**PCI Express** replaced this with point-to-point serial **lanes** joined by switches. Each device gets its own link to a switch, so transfers to different devices proceed simultaneously; a link is negotiated as x1, x4, x8, or x16 lanes, so bandwidth is allocated per device rather than shared. Because each lane is a differential serial pair rather than a wide parallel bus, it clocks far higher — parallel buses died precisely because keeping 64 wires in skew at gigahertz rates is harder than running one pair very fast.

Bandwidth roughly doubles per PCIe generation:

| Generation | Per lane (each direction) | x4 link | x16 link |
|---|---|---|---|
| PCIe 3.0 | ~1 GB/s | ~4 GB/s | ~16 GB/s |
| PCIe 4.0 | ~2 GB/s | ~8 GB/s | ~32 GB/s |
| PCIe 5.0 | ~4 GB/s | ~16 GB/s | ~64 GB/s |

Above the bus sit **interfaces** — the command protocols devices speak. Here the important lesson is that a protocol designed for one device's physics can strangle another's. **AHCI/SATA** was designed for rotating disks: one command queue, 32 outstanding commands, an interrupt per completion. That is ample for a device doing 200 operations per second and absurd for flash capable of a million. **NVMe** was designed for the latter: up to 65,535 queues of 65,536 commands each, one queue per CPU core so there is no shared lock, doorbell registers instead of legacy handshakes, and a command set with a fraction of the overhead.

| Interface | Typical use | Queues | Queue depth | Latency overhead |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| SATA/AHCI | HDDs, budget SSDs | 1 | 32 | ~6 µs |
| SAS | Enterprise disks, expanders | 1 | 256 | ~5 µs |
| NVMe | Modern SSDs | up to 65,535 | up to 65,536 | ~2 µs |
| USB | Peripherals, external storage | polled schedule | varies | ~100 µs+ |
| Thunderbolt | External PCIe, displays | PCIe tunnelled | — | ~2 µs |

**USB** deserves separate mention because it is the opposite design point. It is a polled, host-scheduled, tiered-star bus: the host controller asks each device in turn whether it has data, on a fixed frame schedule. This makes devices cheap and hot-pluggable and gives predictable bandwidth allocation for isochronous transfers (audio, video), at the cost of latency that no amount of bandwidth fixes. It is also why a USB device cannot initiate a transfer — and why USB storage feels slower than its throughput number suggests.

Two practical consequences follow. First, **lane count matters as much as generation**: an NVMe drive in an x1 slot is capped regardless of its rating. Second, some slots are wired to the chipset rather than directly to the CPU, and everything behind the chipset shares one uplink — which is how two fast drives can each benchmark well alone and disappoint together.

**Example**

```text
   SHARED BUS vs SWITCHED FABRIC

   SHARED (PCI, ISA)                    SWITCHED (PCI Express)
   CPU --+---+---+---+                  CPU
         |   |   |   |                   |  x16
        [A] [B] [C] [D]              +---+----+
                                     | ROOT   |
   one transaction at a time;        | COMPLEX|
   total bandwidth FIXED and         +-+--+--++
   divided among all devices           |  |  | x4 each
                                      [A][B][ SWITCH ]
                                                |    |
                                               [C]  [D]
   A->CPU and B->CPU proceed SIMULTANEOUSLY.
   Adding devices adds bandwidth (until an uplink saturates).

   THE UPLINK TRAP

   CPU ==x16== [GPU]                       direct: full bandwidth
   CPU ==x4=== [CHIPSET] --x4-- [NVMe 1]   NVMe 1 + NVMe 2 + USB + NIC
                         --x4-- [NVMe 2]   ALL SHARE the single x4 uplink.
                         --x1-- [NIC]      Each benchmarks fine alone;
                         ------ [USB]      together they contend.

   WHY NVMe BEAT AHCI (the same SSD behind each)

   AHCI                                NVMe
   +-------------------+               core0 -> [SQ0][CQ0] -+
   | ONE queue, 32 deep|               core1 -> [SQ1][CQ1] -+--> device
   | shared lock       |               core2 -> [SQ2][CQ2] -+
   | all cores contend |               core3 -> [SQ3][CQ3] -+
   +-------------------+               no shared lock, no cross-core traffic
   ~100k IOPS ceiling                  millions of IOPS
   uncached register handshake         doorbell write per batch

   DEVICE SPEED SPANS SEVEN ORDERS OF MAGNITUDE
     keyboard        10 bytes/s      <- human-limited
     USB 2.0 mouse   ~1 KB/s
     gigabit NIC     125 MB/s
     SATA SSD        550 MB/s
     PCIe 4 NVMe     7 GB/s
     DDR5 memory     50 GB/s
   One interface cannot serve all of these well. Hence many buses.
```

```bash
# The PCIe topology of this machine, as a tree.
lspci -tv
#   -[0000:00]-+-00.0  Host bridge
#              +-01.0-[01]----00.0  NVIDIA GPU
#              +-1c.0-[02]----00.0  NVMe controller
#              \-1f.2  SATA controller

# Negotiated link speed and width -- the numbers that actually apply.
sudo lspci -vv -s 02:00.0 | grep -E 'LnkCap|LnkSta'
#   LnkCap: Speed 16GT/s, Width x4        <- what the device can do
#   LnkSta: Speed 8GT/s,  Width x4        <- what it NEGOTIATED
#   A mismatch here is the single most common "why is my drive slow" cause.

# Per-device theoretical bandwidth.
for d in $(lspci | awk '{print $1}'); do
  cap=$(sudo lspci -vv -s $d 2>/dev/null | grep -m1 LnkSta)
  [ -n "$cap" ] && echo "$d $cap"
done

# Storage interfaces present.
lsblk -o NAME,TRAN,ROTA,SIZE,MODEL
#   NAME     TRAN   ROTA  SIZE MODEL
#   sda      sata      1  1.8T ST2000DM008
#   nvme0n1  nvme      0  931G Samsung SSD 980 PRO

# NVMe queue structure: the reason it scales.
sudo nvme id-ctrl /dev/nvme0 | grep -iE 'sqes|cqes|mdts'
ls /sys/block/nvme0n1/mq/          # one directory per hardware queue
#   0  1  2  3  4  5  6  7          <- matches the core count
cat /sys/block/sda/mq/0/nr_tags    # AHCI: a single queue, 32 tags

# USB's tiered-star topology and its speed tiers.
lsusb -t
#   /:  Bus 02.Port 1: Dev 1, Class=root_hub, Driver=xhci_hcd/4p, 5000M
#       |__ Port 2: Dev 3, If 0, Class=Mass Storage, Driver=usb-storage, 5000M
```

```python
# Is the link or the device the bottleneck? Compute before benchmarking.
PCIE_PER_LANE_GBPS = {3: 0.985, 4: 1.969, 5: 3.938}   # GB/s per lane per direction

def link_bandwidth(gen, lanes):
    return PCIE_PER_LANE_GBPS[gen] * lanes

devices = [
    # name,                  gen, lanes, device's own rated GB/s
    ("NVMe Gen4 x4",           4,     4,  7.0),
    ("NVMe Gen4 drive in x1",  4,     1,  7.0),   # the classic misconfiguration
    ("NVMe Gen3 x4",           3,     4,  3.5),
    ("100 GbE NIC on x8 Gen3", 3,     8, 12.5),
    ("100 GbE NIC on x4 Gen3", 3,     4, 12.5),
]

print(f"{'device':<26}{'link GB/s':>11}{'device GB/s':>13}{'limited by':>13}")
for name, gen, lanes, rated in devices:
    link = link_bandwidth(gen, lanes)
    limiter = "LINK" if link < rated else "device"
    print(f"{name:<26}{link:>11.1f}{rated:>13.1f}{limiter:>13}")

# Shared uplink contention: what N devices behind one x4 link actually get.
UPLINK = link_bandwidth(3, 4)            # chipset uplink, ~3.9 GB/s
for n in (1, 2, 4):
    print(f"\n{n} device(s) behind a Gen3 x4 chipset uplink:")
    print(f"  each gets at most {UPLINK/n:.2f} GB/s "
          f"({'no contention' if n == 1 else 'contended'})")
```

**Key takeaways**

- Buses evolved from shared parallel wires to switched point-to-point serial links, so bandwidth now scales with device count instead of being divided among devices.
- PCIe bandwidth is per-lane and roughly doubles each generation; both generation and negotiated lane width must be checked, since either can throttle a device.
- Devices behind a chipset share one uplink, which is why two fast drives can each benchmark well alone and contend when used together.
- Interface protocols encode assumptions about device physics: AHCI's single 32-deep queue suited disks and strangled flash.
- NVMe gives each core its own submission and completion queue, removing shared-lock contention and enabling millions of IOPS.
- USB is a host-polled tiered star: cheap, hot-pluggable, and predictable for isochronous traffic, but with latency that bandwidth cannot fix.

> 2. Run `lspci -vv` on a storage or network device and compare `LnkCap` with `LnkSta`. Explain any difference you find.
> 3. Interview-style: "An NVMe drive rated for 7 GB/s benchmarks at 1.6 GB/s in one slot and 6.8 GB/s in another, on the same machine. Explain." *Hint: two independent properties of a PCIe link are negotiated at boot, and a motherboard's slots are not all wired to the same place.*

#### Polling

**Theory**

Once a driver has issued a command, it must find out when the device is done. The simplest possible answer is to keep asking. **Polling** — also called busy-waiting or programmed I/O — means the CPU reads the status register in a loop until the ready bit appears.

The handshake is a four-step protocol, and it is worth memorising because every device interaction is a variation of it:

1. The host reads the status register repeatedly until **busy** is clear.
2. The host sets the **command-ready** bit and writes the command and data.
3. The device notices the command, sets **busy**, and performs the operation.
4. The device clears **busy** and sets the **ready** or **error** bit; the host, still polling, observes this.

Polling's virtues are real. It is trivially simple, it has the **lowest possible latency** — the CPU learns of completion in the time it takes to execute one load instruction, with no interrupt delivery, no context switch, and no cache pollution — and it is completely deterministic, which matters in real-time systems where an interrupt's variable delivery time is itself the problem.

Its vice is equally clear: while polling, the CPU does nothing else. If a device takes 8 milliseconds, a 3 GHz processor burns roughly 24 million cycles' worth of potential work discovering that the device is not finished yet. For slow devices this is indefensible, and it is why interrupts were invented.

But the arithmetic reverses when devices get fast. An interrupt costs something — very roughly 1 to 5 microseconds once you count delivery, the handler, the context switch, and the cache and TLB damage. If the device completes in 100 microseconds, that overhead is 1-5% and interrupts are obviously right. If the device completes in 2 microseconds, the interrupt costs more than the operation. Polling wins.

This is why polling has returned in modern high-performance systems, not as a legacy technique but as the preferred one:

- **NAPI** in the Linux network stack: an interrupt signals the first packet, then interrupts are *disabled* and the driver polls until the queue drains. Under load this amortises one interrupt over hundreds of packets; when idle, it falls back to interrupts so nothing spins.
- **DPDK** and **SPDK** take it to the limit: user-space drivers that dedicate entire cores to polling, bypassing the kernel entirely. A core is consumed permanently in exchange for single-digit-microsecond latency.
- **io_uring** with `IORING_SETUP_IOPOLL`, and the block layer's **hybrid polling**, which sleeps for an estimated fraction of the expected completion time and then polls — capturing most of polling's latency benefit while returning most of the CPU.

The general rule: **poll when the wait is shorter than the cost of being interrupted, interrupt otherwise** — and hybrid approaches exist precisely because real workloads straddle the line.

**Example**

```text
   THE POLLING HANDSHAKE

   HOST                              DEVICE
   read status ---------------------> busy?
      | busy=1, loop                     |
      | busy=1, loop                     |
      | busy=0                           |
   write data to data-out reg -------->  |
   set command-ready in control ------>  | sees command
                                         | sets busy=1
      read status (busy=1) <-------------+  ... performing the operation ...
      read status (busy=1) <-------------+
      read status (busy=0, ready=1) <----+ done
   read data-in register -------------->

   WHERE THE CPU TIME GOES

   POLLING an 8 ms disk on a 3 GHz CPU
   |<--------------------- 8 ms = ~24,000,000 cycles ------------------->|
   [read status][read status][read status] ... 100% CPU, 0 useful work

   POLLING a 2 us NVMe completion
   |<-- 2 us = ~6,000 cycles -->|
   [poll][poll][poll]             vs INTERRUPT: ~1-5 us of OVERHEAD ALONE
                                  -> polling is FASTER *and* cheaper here

   THE CROSSOVER

   device latency  | interrupt overhead as % | better choice
   ----------------+-------------------------+---------------
     8 ms (HDD)    | 0.03%                   | interrupt
   100 us (SATA SSD)| 2%                     | interrupt
    10 us (NVMe)   | 20%                     | hybrid
     2 us (Optane) | 150%                    | POLL

   NAPI: THE HYBRID THAT RUNS EVERY LINUX MACHINE
     idle      -> interrupts ENABLED  (no CPU burned while nothing arrives)
     1st packet-> interrupt fires, driver DISABLES further interrupts
     busy      -> poll the ring until empty or the budget is spent
     drained   -> re-enable interrupts, go back to idle
   One interrupt can cover hundreds of packets under load.
```

```c
// Polling in a driver: correct, and with the two details people forget.
static int poll_wait_ready(struct mydev *dev, unsigned int timeout_us)
{
    ktime_t deadline = ktime_add_us(ktime_get(), timeout_us);
    u32 status;

    for (;;) {
        status = readl(dev->regs + REG_STATUS);   // uncached read: hits the device

        if (status & STATUS_ERROR)
            return -EIO;
        if (status & STATUS_READY)
            return 0;

        // (1) ALWAYS bound the wait. A wedged device must not hang the kernel.
        if (ktime_after(ktime_get(), deadline))
            return -ETIMEDOUT;

        // (2) Tell the CPU this is a spin loop: on x86 this is PAUSE, which
        //     saves power and avoids a memory-order violation penalty on exit.
        cpu_relax();
    }
}

// Hybrid: sleep for most of the expected wait, then poll for the tail.
static int hybrid_wait(struct mydev *dev, unsigned int expected_us)
{
    // Sleeping gives the CPU back; the final poll avoids the wake-up latency.
    usleep_range(expected_us / 2, expected_us * 3 / 4);
    return poll_wait_ready(dev, expected_us * 4);
}
```

```python
# When does polling beat interrupts? The arithmetic, and the CPU cost of each.
INTERRUPT_OVERHEAD_US = 3.0      # delivery + handler + context switch + cache damage
POLL_COST_PER_US      = 1.0      # polling burns one CPU-microsecond per microsecond

def compare(device_latency_us, ops_per_sec):
    # Interrupt-driven: CPU is free during the wait, but pays per completion.
    interrupt_cpu = ops_per_sec * INTERRUPT_OVERHEAD_US / 1e6      # CPU fraction
    interrupt_latency = device_latency_us + INTERRUPT_OVERHEAD_US

    # Polling: CPU is busy for the whole wait, but completion is seen instantly.
    poll_cpu = ops_per_sec * device_latency_us * POLL_COST_PER_US / 1e6
    poll_latency = device_latency_us

    return interrupt_cpu, interrupt_latency, poll_cpu, poll_latency

devices = [("HDD",        8000.0,     150),
           ("SATA SSD",    100.0,  80_000),
           ("NVMe",         10.0, 500_000),
           ("Optane/CXL",    2.0, 900_000)]

print(f"{'device':<12}{'IRQ cpu':>9}{'IRQ lat':>10}{'poll cpu':>10}{'poll lat':>10}  winner")
for name, lat, iops in devices:
    ic, il, pc, pl = compare(lat, iops)
    winner = "poll" if (pl < il and pc <= 1.0) else "interrupt"
    print(f"{name:<12}{ic:>8.1%}{il:>9.1f}us{min(pc,1.0):>9.1%}{pl:>9.1f}us  {winner}")
# Note the poll-CPU column saturates at 100%: that is a whole core consumed.
# DPDK and SPDK accept exactly that trade deliberately.
```

```bash
# Polling in production, on the block layer.
cat /sys/block/nvme0n1/queue/io_poll          # 1 = polling available
cat /sys/block/nvme0n1/queue/io_poll_delay
#   -1 = classic (pure) polling
#    0 = hybrid polling with an adaptive sleep
#   >0 = sleep this many nanoseconds, then poll

echo 0 | sudo tee /sys/block/nvme0n1/queue/io_poll_delay   # enable hybrid
fio --name=poll --ioengine=io_uring --hipri=1 --rw=randread \
    --bs=4k --iodepth=1 --filename=/dev/nvme0n1 --runtime=10 --time_based
# --hipri uses the polled path. Compare p50/p99 latency against the default.

# Network polling: NAPI budget and how often it is exhausted.
sysctl net.core.netdev_budget            # packets per poll cycle (default 300)
sysctl net.core.netdev_budget_usecs      # time bound per poll cycle
awk '{print $1, $2, $3}' /proc/net/softnet_stat | head -4
#   column 3 counts "time squeeze": budget exhausted with work remaining.
#   Persistently non-zero means raising the budget may help.

# Interrupt coalescing: the hardware's own version of the same trade.
sudo ethtool -c eth0
#   rx-usecs: 50          <- wait up to 50 us to batch completions
#   rx-frames: 64         <- or until 64 frames have arrived
sudo ethtool -C eth0 rx-usecs 0          # lowest latency, highest interrupt rate
sudo ethtool -C eth0 rx-usecs 100        # highest throughput, worst latency
```

**Key takeaways**

- Polling repeatedly reads a status register until the device signals completion, following a four-step busy/command-ready handshake.
- It has the lowest possible completion latency and is fully deterministic, which matters for real-time work.
- It consumes the CPU for the entire wait, which is indefensible for slow devices — the original motivation for interrupts.
- The trade reverses for very fast devices: when a completion takes less time than an interrupt costs to deliver, polling is both faster and cheaper.
- NAPI, DPDK, SPDK, and `io_uring`'s polled mode are all modern returns to polling, usually hybridised so idle systems do not spin.
- Every polling loop needs a timeout and a `cpu_relax()`-style pause hint; omitting either produces hangs or wasted power.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. A device completes in 40 µs and an interrupt costs 3 µs. Compute the overhead percentage, then repeat for a device completing in 3 µs, and state which method each favours.
> 2. Write the four-step polling handshake as pseudocode with a timeout, and mark the exact point at which a missing timeout would hang the system.
> 3. Interview-style: "Why does a high-performance packet processing framework deliberately burn a whole CPU core spinning?" *Hint: compare the cost of an interrupt against the time to process one packet at 10 million packets per second, and consider what else that core would have been doing.*

#### Interrupt-Driven I/O

**Theory**

Polling wastes the CPU because the CPU is asking. **Interrupts** invert the relationship: the device tells the CPU when it is ready, and until then the CPU runs other work. This single inversion is what makes multiprogramming possible — without it, every I/O would idle the machine.

The mechanism, in the order it happens:

1. The device raises an interrupt on its assigned line or sends an interrupt message.
2. The CPU finishes the current instruction, then saves enough state to resume.
3. It reads the interrupt number and indexes the **interrupt vector table** (the IDT on x86) to find the handler address.
4. It switches to kernel mode and, typically, to a dedicated interrupt stack, then jumps to the handler.
5. The handler services the device, acknowledges the interrupt at the controller, and returns.
6. State is restored and the interrupted work resumes — or the scheduler runs, if the handler woke something more important.

Two properties of that sequence drive everything else. First, an interrupt handler runs in **interrupt context**: there is no process to block, so it may not sleep, may not take a mutex that could sleep, and may not do anything slow. Second, interrupts have **priority levels**, so a high-priority device can preempt a lower-priority handler, and critical sections can mask lower levels while remaining responsive to higher ones. Non-maskable interrupts (NMI) sit above everything for hardware failures and watchdogs.

The "handlers must be fast" constraint creates the standard structure of every real driver: the **top half / bottom half** split. The top half is the actual interrupt handler — it does the minimum required to make the device stop shouting (acknowledge the interrupt, grab the status, copy the data out of a small buffer) and then schedules the rest. The bottom half — a softirq, tasklet, or workqueue on Linux; a DPC on Windows — runs later with interrupts enabled and, for workqueues, in a context that may sleep. Protocol processing, waking the waiting thread, and starting the next request all belong there.

Delivery has evolved along with buses. Legacy **pin-based** interrupts used physical lines (IRQ 0-15 originally), which were scarce and had to be **shared** — several devices on one line, so each handler had to check "was it me?" and return `IRQ_NONE` if not. **MSI** and **MSI-X** replaced this: the device signals an interrupt by *writing to a special memory address*, which needs no dedicated wire, allows thousands of distinct vectors, cannot be confused with another device's, and — crucially — eliminates a race in which a completion arrived before its interrupt did. MSI-X also lets one device have many vectors, which is what allows a NIC or NVMe drive to direct each queue's completions to a different CPU core.

Two pathologies are worth knowing by name. An **interrupt storm** occurs when a device raises interrupts faster than the system can retire them, so the machine spends all its time in handlers and makes no forward progress; the defences are coalescing (batch completions in hardware), NAPI-style interrupt disabling, and the kernel's own storm detection that disables a misbehaving line. And **interrupt affinity** matters on multi-core machines: if every completion is delivered to core 0, that core saturates while others idle, so the kernel (or `irqbalance`, or explicit pinning) spreads vectors across cores — ideally to the core that issued the request, so the data is already in its cache.

**Example**

```text
   THE INTERRUPT PATH

   CPU running user code
        |
        |  <=== device asserts interrupt / sends MSI write
        v
   finish current instruction
   save PC, flags, minimal registers
   read vector number --> IDT[vector] --> handler address
   switch to kernel mode + interrupt stack
        |
        v
   +--------------- TOP HALF (interrupt context) ---------------+
   | - acknowledge the device (stop it re-raising)              |
   | - read status, copy data out of the hardware buffer        |
   | - schedule the bottom half                                 |
   | - MAY NOT SLEEP, MAY NOT TAKE A SLEEPING LOCK              |
   +------------------------------------------------------------+
        |  return from interrupt
        v
   ... later, with interrupts enabled ...
   +------------- BOTTOM HALF (softirq / workqueue) ------------+
   | - protocol processing, checksum, wake the waiting thread   |
   | - start the next queued request                            |
   | - workqueues MAY sleep; softirqs may not                   |
   +------------------------------------------------------------+

   SHARED PIN-BASED vs MSI-X

   PIN-BASED (legacy)                  MSI-X
   [dev A] --+                         [dev A] -- writes 0xFEE00000, data=42
   [dev B] --+--- IRQ 11 --> CPU       [dev B] -- writes 0xFEE00000, data=57
   [dev C] --+                         [NIC q0] - vector 60 -> core 0
                                       [NIC q1] - vector 61 -> core 1
   every handler must ask "was it       [NIC q2] - vector 62 -> core 2
   me?"; one broken device can          no wires, no sharing, thousands of
   wedge the whole line                 vectors, per-queue CPU steering

   INTERRUPT STORM

   normal:  [work][irq][work][irq][work]      forward progress
   storm:   [irq][irq][irq][irq][irq][irq]    100% in handlers, 0 progress
   defences: coalescing (rx-usecs), NAPI (disable + poll), kernel's
             "nobody cared" auto-disable after 100,000 spurious interrupts

   AFFINITY: WHERE COMPLETIONS LAND
     all vectors -> core 0   : core 0 saturates, 15 cores idle
     one vector per core     : parallel, and the completion lands where the
                               request was issued, so its data is cache-hot
```

```c
// The canonical two-half driver structure.
#include <linux/interrupt.h>
#include <linux/workqueue.h>

struct mydev {
    void __iomem *regs;
    struct work_struct   slow_work;     // bottom half that may sleep
    struct tasklet_struct fast_work;    // bottom half that may not
    struct completion    done;
    u32 last_status;
};

// ---------- TOP HALF: runs in interrupt context, must be tiny ----------
static irqreturn_t mydev_isr(int irq, void *data)
{
    struct mydev *dev = data;
    u32 status = readl(dev->regs + REG_STATUS);

    // On a SHARED line this check is mandatory: the interrupt may be
    // another device's, and claiming it would break that device.
    if (!(status & STATUS_INTERRUPT_PENDING))
        return IRQ_NONE;

    writel(status, dev->regs + REG_INT_ACK);   // acknowledge FIRST, or it re-fires
    dev->last_status = status;

    if (status & STATUS_DATA_READY)
        tasklet_schedule(&dev->fast_work);     // defer: no processing here
    if (status & STATUS_ERROR)
        schedule_work(&dev->slow_work);        // error recovery may need to sleep

    return IRQ_HANDLED;
}

// ---------- BOTTOM HALF: interrupts enabled, real work happens ----------
static void mydev_tasklet(unsigned long data)
{
    struct mydev *dev = (struct mydev *)data;
    // Process the buffer, hand it upstream, start the next request.
    complete(&dev->done);                      // wake whoever was waiting
}

static void mydev_error_work(struct work_struct *w)
{
    struct mydev *dev = container_of(w, struct mydev, slow_work);
    // A workqueue runs in process context: msleep() and mutexes are legal here.
    msleep(10);
    mydev_reset(dev);
}

static int mydev_setup_irq(struct mydev *dev, struct pci_dev *pdev)
{
    int nvec, i;

    // Prefer MSI-X: no sharing, one vector per queue, steerable per CPU.
    nvec = pci_alloc_irq_vectors(pdev, 1, num_online_cpus(),
                                 PCI_IRQ_MSIX | PCI_IRQ_MSI | PCI_IRQ_LEGACY);
    if (nvec < 0)
        return nvec;

    for (i = 0; i < nvec; i++) {
        int irq = pci_irq_vector(pdev, i);
        int err = request_irq(irq, mydev_isr,
                              (nvec == 1) ? IRQF_SHARED : 0,   // sharing only on legacy
                              "mydev", dev);
        if (err)
            return err;
        // Steer each vector to its own CPU so completions land cache-hot.
        irq_set_affinity_hint(irq, cpumask_of(i % num_online_cpus()));
    }
    return 0;
}
```

```bash
# Which device uses which vector, and where its interrupts are landing.
cat /proc/interrupts | head -15
#            CPU0       CPU1       CPU2       CPU3
#   27:   1240912          0          0          0   PCI-MSI  nvme0q0
#   28:         0    8823401          0          0   PCI-MSI  nvme0q1
#            ^ one queue per core, each on its own CPU: correct.
#   19:     40122      39887      40003      39914   IO-APIC  ehci_hcd:usb1
#            ^ legacy shared line, spread by irqbalance

# Interrupt rate per second -- the number that reveals a storm.
watch -n1 "grep nvme /proc/interrupts"
sudo perf stat -e irq:irq_handler_entry -a sleep 5

# Affinity: read it, then pin it.
cat /proc/irq/28/smp_affinity_list      # 1  -> this vector goes to CPU 1
echo 2 | sudo tee /proc/irq/28/smp_affinity_list
systemctl status irqbalance             # the daemon that usually does this

# Reducing interrupt rate at the source: coalescing.
sudo ethtool -c eth0
sudo ethtool -C eth0 rx-usecs 50 rx-frames 64   # batch: fewer interrupts
sudo ethtool -C eth0 adaptive-rx on             # let the NIC decide

# Time spent in interrupt and softirq context -- the health check.
mpstat -P ALL 1
#   CPU  %usr %sys %irq %soft %idle
#     0   5.0 12.0  0.5  38.0   44.5     <- 38% softirq: network bottom halves
vmstat 1                                  # 'in' = interrupts/s, 'cs' = switches/s
cat /proc/softirqs | head -8              # NET_RX, NET_TX, BLOCK, TIMER counts
dmesg | grep -i 'nobody cared'            # the kernel disabling a storming line
```

**Key takeaways**

- Interrupts invert control: the device signals completion, so the CPU can do other work while waiting — the mechanism that makes multiprogramming possible.
- Delivery indexes an interrupt vector table to find the handler, switches to kernel mode, and runs in interrupt context where sleeping is forbidden.
- Drivers split into a top half (acknowledge, grab status, defer) and a bottom half (softirq, tasklet, or workqueue) so handlers stay short.
- Legacy pin-based interrupts are shared, requiring every handler to check whether the interrupt was its own; MSI/MSI-X are message writes with thousands of distinct vectors and no sharing.
- MSI-X lets one device use many vectors, enabling per-queue steering so completions land on the core that issued the request.
- Interrupt storms are defended against with hardware coalescing, NAPI-style disabling, and the kernel's spurious-interrupt detection; affinity settings decide whether one core saturates or the load spreads.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. List the steps from a device asserting an interrupt to the handler's first instruction, and mark the point at which the mode switch occurs.
> 2. Examine `/proc/interrupts` on your machine, identify one MSI device and one legacy line, and explain what the per-CPU distribution tells you.
> 3. Interview-style: "A driver's interrupt handler calls `kmalloc(GFP_KERNEL)` and the machine occasionally deadlocks. Why?" *Hint: consider what that allocation flag permits the allocator to do, and what is impossible in the context the handler runs in.*

#### DMA Transfers

**Theory**

Interrupts fixed the waiting problem but not the *moving* problem. With programmed I/O, the CPU still copies every byte between the device's data register and memory, one word per instruction. Transferring 4 KB means about 1,000 loads and 1,000 stores; transferring a gigabyte means the CPU does nothing else for a long time. **Direct Memory Access** removes the CPU from the data path entirely.

The idea: give the device (or a dedicated DMA engine) the ability to read and write main memory itself. The CPU's role shrinks to setting up and being told when it is over:

1. The driver allocates a buffer and obtains its **bus address** (below).
2. It programs the device with that address, the length, and the direction.
3. It issues the command and goes off to do something else entirely.
4. The device transfers the data directly to or from memory, over many bus cycles.
5. The device raises one interrupt — for the whole transfer, not per byte.

The saving is enormous: one interrupt and a few register writes instead of thousands of instructions. This is why every storage device, network card, and GPU is a **bus master** — capable of initiating its own memory transactions.

Three complications follow, and they are the substance of real DMA code.

**Addresses.** The device does not use virtual addresses, and on many systems it does not use physical addresses either. It uses **bus addresses**, which an **IOMMU** may translate. This is why drivers must call the DMA mapping API (`dma_map_single`, `dma_alloc_coherent`) rather than passing a pointer: the mapping call returns the address the *device* should use, establishes any IOMMU entry required, and bounces the buffer through an intermediate region if the device cannot address it (a 32-bit device on a machine with 64 GB of RAM). It also means DMA buffers must be physically contiguous, or described as a **scatter-gather list** of separate segments — which is what modern devices prefer, since it avoids the need for large contiguous allocations.

**Coherence.** If the CPU has cached part of the buffer and the device writes memory underneath it, the CPU may read stale data; if the CPU has dirty cache lines and the device reads memory, it may read stale data. On x86 the hardware keeps DMA coherent automatically; on many ARM systems it does not. The API handles both: `dma_alloc_coherent` returns memory that is consistent by construction (uncached or hardware-coherent), while `dma_map_single` plus `dma_sync_single_for_cpu`/`_for_device` explicitly flushes or invalidates around the transfer. Getting this wrong produces corruption that appears only on some architectures and only under load.

**Protection.** A device that can write any physical address can overwrite the kernel. This is not hypothetical — DMA attacks over Thunderbolt and FireWire are a real class of exploit. The **IOMMU** (Intel VT-d, AMD-Vi, ARM SMMU) is the answer: it sits between devices and memory as an MMU for I/O, so each device gets its own address space and can touch only the pages explicitly mapped for it. This is also what makes device passthrough to virtual machines safe.

Two refinements complete the picture. **Scatter-gather** lets one command describe many discrete memory segments, so a read into a user buffer spanning fifteen non-contiguous pages is still one operation. And **cycle stealing** describes how the DMA engine shares the memory bus with the CPU — taking cycles when available rather than seizing the bus, so the CPU is slowed somewhat but never stopped.

**Example**

```text
   PROGRAMMED I/O vs DMA (4 KB transfer)

   PROGRAMMED I/O
   CPU: [ld][st][ld][st][ld][st] ... x1024 ...  + 1 interrupt
        ~2,048 instructions of pure copying; CPU unavailable throughout

   DMA
   CPU: [setup: 4 register writes] ---- goes and does other work ----+
                                                                     |
   DEVICE: reads/writes memory directly over the bus                 |
           ... 4096 bytes moved without the CPU ...                  |
        <---------------- one interrupt: "done" --------------------+
        ~10 instructions of CPU involvement

   THE THREE ADDRESS SPACES A BUFFER LIVES IN

   driver's pointer   : 0xffff888012340000   (kernel VIRTUAL)
   physical address   : 0x0000000012340000   (what the MMU produces)
   bus/DMA address    : 0x00000000fffe0000   (what the DEVICE must use)
                         ^ produced by dma_map_*(); may differ because of
                           an IOMMU, a bounce buffer, or a bus offset.
   Passing a kernel pointer to a device is a bug, even when it happens to work.

   SCATTER-GATHER: ONE COMMAND, MANY SEGMENTS

   user buffer spans 4 non-contiguous pages:
     [page A][page B][page C][page D]   (physically scattered)

   SG list handed to the device:
     +--------------------+--------+
     | bus addr 0x1000000 | 4096   |
     | bus addr 0x8A2F000 | 4096   |
     | bus addr 0x0031000 | 4096   |
     | bus addr 0x77C1000 | 4096   |
     +--------------------+--------+
   ONE transfer, no contiguous allocation, no copying.

   THE IOMMU: AN MMU FOR DEVICES

   without IOMMU                     with IOMMU
   device --> ANY physical address   device --> [IOMMU] --> only MAPPED pages
              (can overwrite the                   |
               kernel; Thunderbolt                 +-- per-device page tables
               DMA attacks work)                   +-- unmapped access = fault

   COHERENCE, AND WHERE IT BITES

   x86: hardware-coherent. DMA snoops the caches. Nothing to do.
   ARM: not necessarily. Sequence for a DEVICE->CPU read:
        dma_map(..., DMA_FROM_DEVICE)     invalidate the cache lines
        ... device writes memory ...
        dma_sync_for_cpu(...)             invalidate again before reading
        Skip these and you read stale cache lines -- intermittently.
```

```c
// The three DMA patterns a driver actually uses.
#include <linux/dma-mapping.h>

// ---- 1. COHERENT (consistent) mapping: for long-lived shared structures ----
//     descriptor rings, doorbell areas -- things both sides touch constantly.
static int setup_ring(struct mydev *dev, struct device *d)
{
    dev->ring = dma_alloc_coherent(d, RING_BYTES, &dev->ring_dma, GFP_KERNEL);
    if (!dev->ring)
        return -ENOMEM;
    // dev->ring     : CPU pointer
    // dev->ring_dma : the address to program into the DEVICE
    writel(lower_32_bits(dev->ring_dma), dev->regs + REG_RING_LO);
    writel(upper_32_bits(dev->ring_dma), dev->regs + REG_RING_HI);
    return 0;
}

// ---- 2. STREAMING mapping: for one transfer, then unmapped ----
static int do_transfer(struct mydev *dev, struct device *d,
                       void *buf, size_t len)
{
    dma_addr_t dma;

    // Map for the device. This may flush caches and/or allocate a bounce buffer.
    dma = dma_map_single(d, buf, len, DMA_TO_DEVICE);
    if (dma_mapping_error(d, dma))
        return -EIO;                        // ALWAYS check: mapping can fail

    writel(lower_32_bits(dma), dev->regs + REG_ADDR_LO);
    writel(upper_32_bits(dma), dev->regs + REG_ADDR_HI);
    writel(len,                dev->regs + REG_LEN);
    wmb();                                  // descriptors visible before the doorbell
    writel(CTRL_START,         dev->regs + REG_CONTROL);

    wait_for_completion(&dev->done);        // CPU is free for other work meanwhile

    // Unmap: on non-coherent systems this performs the cache maintenance.
    // Touching `buf` before this point is undefined behaviour.
    dma_unmap_single(d, dma, len, DMA_TO_DEVICE);
    return 0;
}

// ---- 3. SCATTER-GATHER: one command over many discrete pages ----
static int do_sg_transfer(struct mydev *dev, struct device *d,
                          struct scatterlist *sgl, int nents)
{
    struct scatterlist *sg;
    int i, mapped;

    mapped = dma_map_sg(d, sgl, nents, DMA_FROM_DEVICE);
    if (!mapped)
        return -EIO;
    // The IOMMU may COALESCE segments, so 'mapped' can be < nents.

    for_each_sg(sgl, sg, mapped, i) {
        dev->desc[i].addr = cpu_to_le64(sg_dma_address(sg));  // bus address
        dev->desc[i].len  = cpu_to_le32(sg_dma_len(sg));
    }
    wmb();
    writel(mapped, dev->regs + REG_DESC_COUNT);
    writel(CTRL_START, dev->regs + REG_CONTROL);

    wait_for_completion(&dev->done);
    dma_unmap_sg(d, sgl, nents, DMA_FROM_DEVICE);
    return 0;
}

// Declare what the device can address, BEFORE any mapping call.
// A 32-bit device on a 64 GB machine needs bounce buffers; saying so lets
// the kernel arrange them instead of silently corrupting memory.
static int set_mask(struct device *d)
{
    if (dma_set_mask_and_coherent(d, DMA_BIT_MASK(64)) == 0)
        return 0;
    return dma_set_mask_and_coherent(d, DMA_BIT_MASK(32));
}
```

```bash
# Is the IOMMU on? (It should be, for both security and VM passthrough.)
dmesg | grep -iE 'DMAR|IOMMU|AMD-Vi'
#   DMAR: IOMMU enabled
#   DMAR: Intel(R) Virtualization Technology for Directed I/O
ls /sys/kernel/iommu_groups/ | wc -l         # 0 means no IOMMU
ls /sys/kernel/iommu_groups/12/devices/      # which devices share a group

# Enable it if absent (GRUB):
#   intel_iommu=on iommu=pt          (pt = passthrough for host devices: faster)
#   amd_iommu=on   iommu=pt

# Bounce buffers: the swiotlb pool, used when a device cannot reach a buffer.
dmesg | grep -i swiotlb
#   software IO TLB: mapped [mem 0x...] (64MB)
grep -i swiotlb /proc/vmstat
# Heavy swiotlb traffic means a device's DMA mask is too small: it is copying
# every transfer twice, and throughput will be poor.

# Which devices are bus masters (allowed to initiate DMA).
sudo lspci -vv | grep -B8 'BusMaster+' | grep -E '^[0-9a-f]{2}:'

# DMA-attack surface: Thunderbolt/PCIe hotplug without an IOMMU is an open door.
cat /sys/bus/thunderbolt/devices/*/authorized 2>/dev/null
boltctl list 2>/dev/null

# Watch DMA happen: zero CPU copying during a large read.
dd if=/dev/nvme0n1 of=/dev/null bs=1M count=4000 iflag=direct &
mpstat -P ALL 1 5
#   %sys stays low and %idle high while gigabytes move: that is DMA.
#   With programmed I/O, one core would be pinned at 100%.
```

**Key takeaways**

- DMA lets a device read and write main memory itself, reducing the CPU's role to setup plus one completion interrupt per transfer instead of per word.
- Devices use bus addresses, not kernel pointers: the DMA mapping API returns the correct address and sets up any IOMMU entry or bounce buffer needed.
- Cache coherence must be managed explicitly on architectures that lack hardware coherence, via coherent allocations or `dma_sync_*` around the transfer.
- Scatter-gather lists let one command cover many physically discrete segments, avoiding large contiguous allocations and extra copies.
- An IOMMU gives each device its own address space, containing buggy devices and defending against DMA attacks over hot-pluggable buses.
- A device's DMA mask must be declared accurately; an understated address range forces bounce-buffer copying and an overstated one corrupts memory.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. Compare the CPU instruction count for transferring 1 MB by programmed I/O (one 32-bit word per load/store pair) versus by DMA. State the ratio.
> 2. Explain why a driver may not pass a `kmalloc` pointer directly to a device, and name the three address spaces the buffer exists in.
> 3. Interview-style: "A driver works on x86 but corrupts data intermittently on ARM. What DMA-related mistake should you look for first?" *Hint: one architecture keeps DMA coherent with the CPU caches in hardware and the other does not, so a missing API call is invisible on the first and fatal on the second.*

<a id="112-io-software-layers"></a>
### 11.2 I/O Software Layers

Hardware gives every device a different interface; applications need one. This section covers the software that closes that gap: the drivers that know each device's specifics, the two abstractions the kernel presents them through, the three ways a program can wait for I/O, and the buffering that sits between them all.

#### Device Drivers

**Theory**

There are tens of thousands of device models and one kernel. The only way that works is if device-specific knowledge is confined to replaceable modules and everything above them sees a uniform interface. That module is the **device driver**, and it is the largest category of code in any modern kernel — the majority of Linux's source is drivers.

A driver's contract runs in two directions. Downward, it knows the device's registers, its command encoding, its quirks, and its errata. Upward, it implements a standard set of operations the kernel defined — `open`, `read`, `write`, `ioctl`, `release` for a character device; `queue_rq` for a block device; `ndo_start_xmit` for a network device. The kernel calls those operations through a table of function pointers, exactly as the VFS does for file systems (Section 10.2). The polymorphism is the point: `read()` works on a mouse, a disk, and a temperature sensor because each driver filled in the same slot with different code.

A driver's life cycle is worth understanding because it explains most driver bugs:

1. **Registration.** The module declares which devices it supports — a table of PCI vendor/device IDs, a USB ID table, or a device-tree `compatible` string on embedded systems.
2. **Probe.** When a matching device appears (at boot or on hot-plug), the bus calls the driver's `probe`. This is where the driver maps registers, allocates buffers, requests interrupts, and registers the device with the appropriate subsystem.
3. **Operation.** The kernel invokes the driver's operations on behalf of user requests.
4. **Remove.** On unplug or module unload, everything acquired in probe must be released, in reverse order. Failing to do so leaks memory, leaves interrupt handlers pointing at freed structures, or wedges the device.

Two structural ideas save enormous effort. First, the **subsystem** layer: a driver rarely implements a raw character device. It registers with a subsystem — the network stack, the block layer, V4L2 for video, ALSA for audio, input for keyboards — and gets protocol handling, queueing, and the user-facing interface for free. A new NIC driver implements transmit, receive, and configuration; it does not implement TCP.

Second, **bus-level generic drivers**. USB mass storage, HID, and CDC-ACM are class specifications, so one driver serves every conforming device. This is why a new USB flash drive needs no driver at all: it declares itself as mass storage and the existing driver handles it.

Where the driver *runs* is a genuine design axis. **Kernel-space** drivers are fast — no boundary crossings — but a bug takes the machine down and the security surface is the whole kernel. **User-space** drivers (FUSE for file systems, UIO and VFIO for devices, libusb, DPDK and SPDK for networking and storage) are isolated: a crash kills a process. Microkernels put nearly all drivers in user space by design, accepting message-passing overhead for robustness. The modern compromise is that mainstream kernels keep performance-critical drivers inside and increasingly host the rest outside.

**Example**

```text
   WHERE A DRIVER SITS

   application:  read(fd, buf, 4096)
        |
   +----v-------------------------------------------------+
   | system call interface                                 |
   +----+--------------------------------------------------+
   | SUBSYSTEM: block layer / network stack / input / ALSA |
   |   provides: queueing, protocol, user-facing interface |
   +----+--------------------------------------------------+
   | DRIVER: knows THIS device's registers and quirks      |
   |   implements the subsystem's operation table          |
   +----+--------------------------------------------------+
   | bus layer (PCI / USB / I2C / platform)                |
   +----+--------------------------------------------------+
        v  registers, interrupts, DMA
     DEVICE

   ONE INTERFACE, MANY IMPLEMENTATIONS

                       read(fd, ...)
                            |
        +---------+---------+---------+----------+
        |         |         |         |          |
     disk drv  mouse drv  tty drv  sensor drv  net drv
        |         |         |         |          |
      NVMe      USB HID   UART      I2C        PCIe

   DRIVER LIFE CYCLE (and the symmetry that must hold)

   probe():                          remove():
     pci_enable_device()               free_irq()
     pci_request_regions()             pci_iounmap()
     pci_iomap()            <------>   pci_release_regions()
     request_irq()                     pci_disable_device()
     register_with_subsystem()         unregister_from_subsystem()
   Anything acquired on the left MUST be released on the right, in
   reverse order. Most driver crashes are an asymmetry here.

   KERNEL-SPACE vs USER-SPACE DRIVERS

                    kernel-space          user-space (VFIO/UIO/FUSE)
   speed            no crossings          syscall or mmap per batch
   a bug            kernel panic          process dies, restart it
   security surface entire kernel         one process
   debugging        printk and crash dumps gdb, valgrind, normal tools
   examples         nvme, e1000, ext4     DPDK, SPDK, FUSE, libusb
```

```c
// A complete (minimal) character driver: the operation table is the contract.
#include <linux/module.h>
#include <linux/fs.h>
#include <linux/cdev.h>
#include <linux/uaccess.h>

#define DEVBUF 4096
static char   *buffer;
static size_t  data_len;
static dev_t   devno;
static struct cdev my_cdev;
static DEFINE_MUTEX(lock);          // process context: a sleeping lock is fine

static int my_open(struct inode *inode, struct file *f)
{
    return 0;                       // per-open state would be attached here
}

static ssize_t my_read(struct file *f, char __user *ubuf,
                       size_t count, loff_t *ppos)
{
    ssize_t ret;

    mutex_lock(&lock);
    if (*ppos >= data_len) { ret = 0; goto out; }        // 0 = EOF
    count = min(count, data_len - (size_t)*ppos);

    // NEVER dereference a user pointer directly: it may be invalid, swapped
    // out, or another process's. copy_to_user handles faults safely.
    if (copy_to_user(ubuf, buffer + *ppos, count)) { ret = -EFAULT; goto out; }

    *ppos += count;
    ret = count;                    // return BYTES TRANSFERRED, not success
out:
    mutex_unlock(&lock);
    return ret;
}

static ssize_t my_write(struct file *f, const char __user *ubuf,
                        size_t count, loff_t *ppos)
{
    ssize_t ret;

    if (count > DEVBUF) count = DEVBUF;
    mutex_lock(&lock);
    if (copy_from_user(buffer, ubuf, count)) { ret = -EFAULT; goto out; }
    data_len = count;
    ret = count;
out:
    mutex_unlock(&lock);
    return ret;
}

// ioctl: the escape hatch for operations read/write cannot express.
#define MY_IOC_RESET _IO('M', 1)
static long my_ioctl(struct file *f, unsigned int cmd, unsigned long arg)
{
    switch (cmd) {
    case MY_IOC_RESET:
        mutex_lock(&lock); data_len = 0; mutex_unlock(&lock);
        return 0;
    default:
        return -ENOTTY;             // the conventional "unknown ioctl" errno
    }
}

// THIS TABLE IS THE DRIVER'S ENTIRE UPWARD INTERFACE.
static const struct file_operations my_fops = {
    .owner          = THIS_MODULE,
    .open           = my_open,
    .read           = my_read,
    .write          = my_write,
    .unlocked_ioctl = my_ioctl,
};

static int __init my_init(void)
{
    int err;
    buffer = kzalloc(DEVBUF, GFP_KERNEL);
    if (!buffer) return -ENOMEM;

    err = alloc_chrdev_region(&devno, 0, 1, "mydev");   // ask for a major number
    if (err) goto free_buf;

    cdev_init(&my_cdev, &my_fops);
    err = cdev_add(&my_cdev, devno, 1);                 // device becomes live HERE
    if (err) goto unregister;

    pr_info("mydev: major=%d minor=%d\n", MAJOR(devno), MINOR(devno));
    return 0;

unregister:                          // unwind in exact reverse order
    unregister_chrdev_region(devno, 1);
free_buf:
    kfree(buffer);
    return err;
}

static void __exit my_exit(void)
{
    cdev_del(&my_cdev);
    unregister_chrdev_region(devno, 1);
    kfree(buffer);
}

module_init(my_init);
module_exit(my_exit);
MODULE_LICENSE("GPL");
```

```bash
# Which driver is bound to which device.
lspci -k | head -12
#   00:1f.2 SATA controller: Intel ...
#       Kernel driver in use: ahci
#       Kernel modules: ahci
ls -l /sys/bus/pci/devices/0000:00:1f.2/driver
ls /sys/bus/usb/drivers/                    # every USB driver registered

# Module management.
lsmod | head                                 # loaded modules and their users
modinfo nvme                                 # author, params, supported aliases
sudo modprobe -r nvme                        # unload (fails if in use)
sudo modprobe nvme poll_queues=4             # load with a parameter
cat /sys/module/nvme/parameters/poll_queues  # read a live parameter

# Rebinding a device to a different driver -- how VFIO passthrough is set up.
echo 0000:02:00.0 | sudo tee /sys/bus/pci/devices/0000:02:00.0/driver/unbind
echo 8086 1533    | sudo tee /sys/bus/pci/drivers/vfio-pci/new_id
# The device now belongs to a user-space driver (a VM, or DPDK).

# Driver messages and failures.
sudo dmesg -w | grep -i 'probe\|driver'
journalctl -k -b | grep -iE 'firmware|failed to probe'

# Hot-plug events, live.
sudo udevadm monitor --kernel --property
udevadm info -a -n /dev/sda | head -20      # attributes udev rules can match
```

**Key takeaways**

- A driver confines device-specific knowledge to one module and exposes a standard operation table upward, so the kernel's generic code works across every device.
- The life cycle is register, probe, operate, remove — and everything acquired in probe must be released in reverse order in remove.
- Drivers normally register with a subsystem (block, network, input, ALSA) and inherit its queueing, protocol handling, and user interface rather than implementing them.
- Class drivers (USB mass storage, HID, CDC) serve every conforming device, which is why most peripherals need no vendor driver.
- Kernel-space drivers are fastest but a bug panics the machine; user-space drivers (VFIO, UIO, FUSE, DPDK, SPDK) trade some overhead for isolation and ordinary debugging tools.
- Driver code must never dereference user pointers directly — `copy_to_user`/`copy_from_user` exist because those addresses can be invalid or unmapped.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. List the operations a character driver must supply and state which system call invokes each.
> 2. Use `lspci -k` and `lsmod` to identify the driver behind your network device, then read its parameters under `/sys/module/`.
> 3. Interview-style: "Why does a driver call `copy_to_user` instead of `memcpy` when returning data to a process?" *Hint: think about what guarantees the kernel has about a pointer that arrived from user space, and what must happen if that address is not currently valid.*

#### Block vs Character Devices

**Theory**

The kernel does not treat every device identically. It sorts them into two families whose access models differ so fundamentally that they get separate subsystems, separate caching strategies, and separate driver interfaces.

A **block device** is addressable storage: a numbered array of fixed-size blocks that can be read or written in any order. Disks, SSDs, USB sticks, RAM disks, and loop devices are block devices. Because any block can be reached at any time, the kernel can do interesting things on the path: cache blocks in the page cache, read ahead, merge adjacent requests, reorder the queue, and postpone writes. The block layer is where all the machinery of Chapter 9 and Chapter 10 attaches.

A **character device** is a byte stream: bytes arrive or depart in sequence, and there is generally no meaningful "seek to byte 5,000". Terminals, serial ports, mice, sound cards, `/dev/random`, and `/dev/null` are character devices. Because the stream is sequential and often generated on demand, most of the block layer's tricks are meaningless — you cannot read ahead on a keyboard — so character drivers talk almost directly to user space.

The distinction shows up concretely:

| Property | Block device | Character device |
|---|---|---|
| Addressing | Random, by block number | Sequential byte stream |
| Granularity | Fixed blocks (512 B / 4 KB) | Single bytes |
| Kernel caching | Page cache, read-ahead, writeback | Usually none (small internal buffers) |
| Request reordering | Yes — the I/O scheduler | No |
| `seek` meaningful | Yes | Usually not |
| `mmap` typical | Yes | Only for special cases (framebuffers) |
| `ls -l` type | `b` | `c` |
| Examples | `/dev/sda`, `/dev/nvme0n1` | `/dev/tty`, `/dev/null`, `/dev/random` |

Both are named in the file system by a **major** and **minor** number. The major identifies the driver; the minor identifies which device that driver is responsible for. `/dev/sda` and `/dev/sdb` share a major and differ in minor. This pair, not the filename, is what the kernel dispatches on — which is why `mknod` can create a working device node under any name, and why a device node on a mounted removable medium is a security problem (hence the `nodev` mount option from Section 10.1).

A third family exists in practice: **pseudo-devices** that have no hardware at all. `/dev/null` discards writes and returns EOF on read; `/dev/zero` produces zeros forever; `/dev/random` and `/dev/urandom` produce cryptographic randomness; `/dev/loop0` presents a file as a block device. These are pure kernel functions wearing a device interface, and they exist because the interface is useful even when there is nothing physical behind it.

Some devices can be reached both ways. Classic UNIX exposed a "raw" character interface to disks so databases could bypass the buffer cache; Linux dropped raw devices in favour of the `O_DIRECT` flag, which gets the same effect through the block interface. The underlying need — "let me manage my own caching" — is permanent even when the mechanism changes.

**Example**

```text
   THE TWO PATHS THROUGH THE KERNEL

   BLOCK DEVICE                          CHARACTER DEVICE
   read(fd, buf, 4096)                   read(fd, buf, 1)
        |                                     |
   +----v-----------------+              +----v-----------------+
   | page cache           | HIT -> done  | (little or no cache) |
   +----v-----------------+              +----v-----------------+
   | I/O scheduler        | merge/sort   | driver               |
   +----v-----------------+              +----v-----------------+
   | driver               |                   v
   +----v-----------------+               keyboard / serial line
        v
      disk

   Block: caching, read-ahead, merging, reordering all apply.
   Char : none of them make sense on a byte stream from a human.

   MAJOR AND MINOR: WHAT THE KERNEL ACTUALLY DISPATCHES ON

   $ ls -l /dev/sda /dev/sda1 /dev/null /dev/tty0
   brw-rw----  8,  0  /dev/sda      <- b = block,  major 8, minor 0
   brw-rw----  8,  1  /dev/sda1     <- same driver (8), different minor
   crw-rw-rw-  1,  3  /dev/null     <- c = char,   major 1, minor 3
   crw--w----  4,  0  /dev/tty0

   major -> WHICH DRIVER        minor -> WHICH DEVICE of that driver

   The NAME is irrelevant to the kernel:
     mknod /tmp/mydisk b 8 0      creates a second, working door to /dev/sda
   which is exactly why `nodev` exists as a mount option.

   PSEUDO-DEVICES: THE INTERFACE WITHOUT THE HARDWARE

   /dev/null    writes vanish, reads return EOF
   /dev/zero    an infinite supply of 0x00
   /dev/full    writes fail with ENOSPC  (for testing error paths)
   /dev/random  cryptographic randomness
   /dev/loop0   a FILE presented as a block device
```

```bash
# Identify the two families and their numbers.
ls -l /dev/sda /dev/nvme0n1 /dev/null /dev/tty /dev/random
#   brw-rw----  8,   0 /dev/sda
#   brw-rw---- 259,   0 /dev/nvme0n1
#   crw-rw-rw-  1,   3 /dev/null
stat -c '%n %F major=%t minor=%T' /dev/sda /dev/null   # %t/%T are hex

cat /proc/devices                   # every registered major, by family
#   Character devices:
#     1 mem
#     4 tty
#   Block devices:
#     8 sd
#   259 blkext

# Block-device behaviour: caching and read-ahead exist.
sudo blockdev --getra /dev/sda           # read-ahead, in 512-byte sectors
sudo blockdev --getbsz --getsize64 /dev/sda
sudo hdparm -t --direct /dev/sda         # --direct bypasses the page cache

# Character-device behaviour: no caching, byte at a time.
head -c 16 /dev/urandom | xxd
echo "test" > /dev/null                  # discarded
dd if=/dev/zero of=/dev/null bs=1M count=1000   # pure kernel, no hardware

# Proving major/minor is what matters, not the name.
sudo mknod /tmp/fakenull c 1 3 && echo "gone" > /tmp/fakenull   # works
sudo mknod /tmp/fakedisk b 8 0 && sudo head -c 64 /tmp/fakedisk | xxd | head -2

# A file made into a block device: the loop driver.
dd if=/dev/zero of=disk.img bs=1M count=100 status=none
sudo losetup -fP --show disk.img          # /dev/loop0
sudo mkfs.ext4 -q /dev/loop0 && sudo mount /dev/loop0 /mnt/loop
lsblk /dev/loop0
sudo umount /mnt/loop && sudo losetup -d /dev/loop0

# Who creates the nodes: udev, from kernel uevents.
sudo udevadm monitor --udev &
sudo modprobe loop
cat /etc/udev/rules.d/* 2>/dev/null | head
```

```python
import os, stat, time

def classify(path):
    st = os.stat(path)
    if stat.S_ISBLK(st.st_mode):
        kind = "block"
    elif stat.S_ISCHR(st.st_mode):
        kind = "char"
    else:
        kind = "not a device"
    return (f"{path:<16} {kind:<12} "
            f"major={os.major(st.st_rdev):>3} minor={os.minor(st.st_rdev):>3}")

for p in ["/dev/sda", "/dev/null", "/dev/zero", "/dev/tty", "/dev/urandom"]:
    try:
        print(classify(p))
    except FileNotFoundError:
        pass

# Seeking: meaningful on one family, not the other.
fd = os.open("/dev/zero", os.O_RDONLY)
print("\n/dev/zero seek to 1MB:", os.lseek(fd, 1_000_000, os.SEEK_SET))  # accepted,
os.close(fd)                                                # but meaningless

try:
    fd = os.open("/dev/tty", os.O_RDONLY)
    os.lseek(fd, 100, os.SEEK_SET)          # ESPIPE: a terminal cannot seek
except OSError as e:
    print("/dev/tty seek       :", e.strerror)
finally:
    try: os.close(fd)
    except Exception: pass

# The caching difference, measured on a block device.
os.system("sync; echo 3 | sudo tee /proc/sys/vm/drop_caches > /dev/null")
t0 = time.perf_counter()
with open("/dev/sda", "rb") as f: f.read(1 << 20)     # cold: reaches the device
cold = time.perf_counter() - t0
t0 = time.perf_counter()
with open("/dev/sda", "rb") as f: f.read(1 << 20)     # warm: page cache
warm = time.perf_counter() - t0
print(f"\nblock device 1 MB read: cold {cold*1000:.1f} ms, warm {warm*1000:.1f} ms")
# A character device shows no such gap: there is nothing to cache.
```

**Key takeaways**

- Block devices are randomly addressable fixed-size-block storage; character devices are sequential byte streams.
- The block layer adds page caching, read-ahead, request merging, and scheduling — all of which are meaningless on a byte stream, so character drivers talk almost directly to user space.
- Every device node carries a major number (which driver) and a minor number (which device); the filename is irrelevant to the kernel.
- Because any name can be given to any major/minor pair, device nodes on untrusted media are a privilege-escalation risk, which is what `nodev` prevents.
- Pseudo-devices like `/dev/null`, `/dev/zero`, and `/dev/loop0` use the device interface with no hardware behind them.
- The "let me bypass the cache" need that raw character devices once served is met today by `O_DIRECT` on the block interface.
