> 2. Create a loop device from a file, format and mount it, then explain which operations in that sequence only work because it is a block device.
> 3. Interview-style: "Why does read-ahead make sense for `/dev/sda` but not for `/dev/ttyS0`?" *Hint: read-ahead is a bet about what will be requested next; ask whether that bet is even well-defined when the data does not exist yet.*

#### Blocking and Non-Blocking I/O

**Theory**

When a program calls `read()` and the data is not there yet, something has to give. The three possible answers define the three I/O styles, and choosing among them is one of the most consequential decisions in any networked or interactive program.

**Blocking I/O** is the default and the simplest. The calling thread is put to sleep — moved out of the run queue entirely — until the data arrives, at which point the kernel wakes it and the call returns. The code reads exactly like the problem statement: request, then use the result. It costs the thread nothing while waiting (a blocked thread consumes no CPU), and it costs the programmer nothing in complexity.

Its limitation is that **one thread can wait for exactly one thing**. Serving 10,000 concurrent connections means 10,000 threads, each with its own stack (8 MB of reserved address space by default on Linux, typically 8-64 KB actually touched) and each contributing to scheduler and context-switch overhead. That is the "C10K problem", and it is why blocking I/O plus thread-per-connection stopped scaling in the 1990s.

**Non-blocking I/O** (`O_NONBLOCK`) changes the contract: if the operation cannot proceed immediately, it returns `EAGAIN`/`EWOULDBLOCK` instead of sleeping. The thread keeps control. Used naively — retrying in a loop — this is simply polling with all of polling's waste. Used correctly, it is half of the answer, and the other half is readiness notification.

**I/O multiplexing** provides that other half. `select`, `poll`, `epoll`, and `kqueue` let one thread ask "which of these hundreds of descriptors are ready?" and block until at least one is. Combined with non-blocking descriptors, a single thread can service thousands of connections: wait for readiness, then perform operations that are guaranteed not to block. This is the **event loop**, and it is the architecture of nginx, Redis, Node.js, and essentially every modern high-concurrency server.

The multiplexing calls are not equivalent, and the difference is asymptotic:

| Call | Interest set | Cost per call | Descriptor limit |
|---|---|---|---|
| `select` | Rebuilt and copied every call | O(n) scan | `FD_SETSIZE`, typically 1024 |
| `poll` | Rebuilt and copied every call | O(n) scan | None |
| `epoll` (Linux) | Registered once in the kernel | O(ready), not O(n) | None |
| `kqueue` (BSD/macOS) | Registered once | O(ready) | None |

`epoll` and `kqueue` win because the kernel keeps the interest set and returns only what is ready. With 10,000 idle connections and 5 active, `poll` copies and scans 10,000 entries per iteration; `epoll_wait` returns 5.

`epoll` additionally offers two trigger modes. **Level-triggered** reports readiness whenever data is available — forgiving, and the default. **Edge-triggered** reports only transitions, so the application must drain the descriptor until `EAGAIN` or lose the notification. Edge-triggered is faster and is where subtle bugs live.

The crucial caveat: **readiness is not the same as completion**. `epoll` tells you a `read()` will not block; you still perform the read, and the copy still costs CPU. For regular files it is worse — a disk file is always "ready", so multiplexing gives no benefit at all and the read blocks anyway. That gap is exactly what asynchronous I/O, the next topic, closes.

**Example**

```text
   THE THREE STYLES, SERVING THREE CONNECTIONS

   BLOCKING, THREAD PER CONNECTION
   thread1: read(c1) [=== blocked 40ms ===] process  |
   thread2: read(c2) [=== blocked 12ms ===] process  | concurrent, but
   thread3: read(c3) [=== blocked 90ms ===] process  | 3 stacks, 3 contexts
   10,000 connections -> 10,000 threads -> scheduler and memory pressure

   NON-BLOCKING WITHOUT MULTIPLEXING (the naive trap)
   loop: read(c1) EAGAIN, read(c2) EAGAIN, read(c3) EAGAIN, repeat...
   ONE thread, but 100% CPU discovering that nothing has happened.

   NON-BLOCKING + epoll (the event loop)
   epoll_wait() [== sleeps, 0% CPU ==] -> returns {c2 ready}
     read(c2) -> returns immediately, guaranteed
     process c2
   epoll_wait() [== sleeps ==] -> returns {c1, c3 ready}
   ONE thread, near-zero idle cost, thousands of connections.

   WHY epoll SCALES AND poll DOES NOT

   10,000 connections, 5 active
   poll : build 10,000-entry array -> copy to kernel -> kernel scans
          all 10,000 -> copy back -> app scans all 10,000 for revents
          => O(n) per iteration, EVERY iteration
   epoll: interest set already in the kernel; epoll_wait returns 5 entries
          => O(ready) per iteration

   LEVEL-TRIGGERED vs EDGE-TRIGGERED

   1000 bytes arrive; the app reads 400.
     LEVEL-triggered: next epoll_wait reports ready again (600 remain). Safe.
     EDGE-triggered : next epoll_wait reports NOTHING -- no new transition.
                      The remaining 600 bytes are stranded until more data
                      arrives. You MUST loop until EAGAIN.

   THE LIMIT OF READINESS
     socket : epoll says "ready" -> read() will not block.       Works.
     FILE   : epoll ALWAYS says "ready" -> read() blocks on disk anyway.
              Readiness models do not cover disk I/O. Use AIO / io_uring.
```

```python
import socket, selectors, os, errno

# ---------- 1. BLOCKING: simple, but one thread waits for one thing ----------
def blocking_server(port=9001):
    s = socket.socket(); s.bind(("", port)); s.listen()
    while True:
        conn, _ = s.accept()          # BLOCKS here: no other work possible
        data = conn.recv(4096)        # BLOCKS again, for this client only
        conn.sendall(data.upper())
        conn.close()
    # Serving N clients concurrently requires N threads.

# ---------- 2. NON-BLOCKING, naive: correct but burns a core ----------
def spinning_server(port=9002):
    s = socket.socket(); s.bind(("", port)); s.listen()
    s.setblocking(False)
    while True:
        try:
            conn, _ = s.accept()
        except BlockingIOError:       # EAGAIN: nothing pending
            continue                  # 100% CPU asking "anything yet?"
        conn.setblocking(False)

# ---------- 3. NON-BLOCKING + MULTIPLEXING: the event loop ----------
def event_loop_server(port=9003):
    sel = selectors.DefaultSelector()      # epoll on Linux, kqueue on BSD
    s = socket.socket()
    s.setsockopt(socket.SOL_SOCKET, socket.SO_REUSEADDR, 1)
    s.bind(("", port)); s.listen(); s.setblocking(False)
    sel.register(s, selectors.EVENT_READ, data=None)   # registered ONCE

    while True:
        # Sleeps at 0% CPU; returns ONLY the descriptors that are ready.
        for key, _ in sel.select(timeout=None):
            if key.data is None:                        # the listening socket
                conn, addr = key.fileobj.accept()       # guaranteed not to block
                conn.setblocking(False)
                sel.register(conn, selectors.EVENT_READ, data=bytearray())
            else:                                       # a client socket
                conn = key.fileobj
                try:
                    chunk = conn.recv(4096)             # guaranteed not to block
                except (BlockingIOError, InterruptedError):
                    continue
                if not chunk:                           # orderly close
                    sel.unregister(conn); conn.close(); continue
                conn.sendall(chunk.upper())
    # ONE thread, thousands of connections, near-zero cost while idle.

# ---------- edge-triggered: the drain-to-EAGAIN requirement ----------
def drain(conn):
    """With EPOLLET you MUST read until EAGAIN or lose the remaining data."""
    out = bytearray()
    while True:
        try:
            chunk = conn.recv(4096)
        except BlockingIOError:        # EAGAIN: NOW the socket is truly empty
            return out                 # only now is it safe to go back to wait
        if not chunk:
            return out                 # peer closed
        out += chunk
```

```c
// epoll directly, showing what the Python selector wraps.
#include <sys/epoll.h>
#include <fcntl.h>

static void set_nonblocking(int fd) {
    int flags = fcntl(fd, F_GETFL, 0);
    fcntl(fd, F_SETFL, flags | O_NONBLOCK);   // read/write now return EAGAIN
}

int run_loop(int listen_fd)
{
    struct epoll_event ev, events[64];
    int epfd = epoll_create1(0);

    set_nonblocking(listen_fd);
    ev.events  = EPOLLIN;                      // level-triggered (no EPOLLET)
    ev.data.fd = listen_fd;
    epoll_ctl(epfd, EPOLL_CTL_ADD, listen_fd, &ev);   // registered ONCE

    for (;;) {
        // Returns only READY descriptors: cost is O(ready), not O(registered).
        int n = epoll_wait(epfd, events, 64, -1);
        for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
            int fd = events[i].data.fd;
            if (fd == listen_fd) {
                int c = accept4(listen_fd, NULL, NULL, SOCK_NONBLOCK);
                ev.events  = EPOLLIN | EPOLLET;        // edge-triggered client
                ev.data.fd = c;
                epoll_ctl(epfd, EPOLL_CTL_ADD, c, &ev);
            } else {
                char buf[4096];
                ssize_t r;
                // EPOLLET: drain fully, or the rest is never reported again.
                while ((r = read(fd, buf, sizeof buf)) > 0)
                    write(fd, buf, r);
                if (r == 0 || (r < 0 && errno != EAGAIN)) {
                    epoll_ctl(epfd, EPOLL_CTL_DEL, fd, NULL);
                    close(fd);
                }
            }
        }
    }
}
```

**Key takeaways**

- Blocking I/O sleeps the calling thread until data arrives: simplest to write, and one thread can wait for only one thing.
- Thread-per-connection scales poorly because each thread costs stack memory and scheduler work — the C10K problem.
- Non-blocking descriptors return `EAGAIN` instead of sleeping, but retrying in a loop is just polling and wastes a core.
- Multiplexing (`select`, `poll`, `epoll`, `kqueue`) lets one thread wait on many descriptors and is what makes the event-loop architecture possible.
- `epoll` and `kqueue` keep the interest set in the kernel and cost O(ready) rather than O(registered), which is why they replaced `select` and `poll` at scale.
- Edge-triggered mode reports only transitions, so the application must drain to `EAGAIN` or strand data; level-triggered is the safer default.
- Readiness is not completion, and regular files are always "ready" — so multiplexing does not solve disk I/O at all.

> 3. Interview-style: "Why does `epoll` outperform `poll` at 10,000 connections but not at 10?" *Hint: compare what each call transfers and scans per invocation, and consider what fraction of descriptors are typically ready.*

#### Asynchronous I/O

**Theory**

Multiplexing solved "which descriptor is ready", but readiness has two limits: the application still performs the transfer itself, and regular files are always reported ready so disk I/O still blocks. **Asynchronous I/O** closes both gaps by changing what is submitted. Instead of asking "can I read?", the program says "perform this read and tell me when it is *done*".

The distinction is worth stating precisely, because the terms get used loosely:

- **Synchronous blocking**: `read()` returns when the data is in your buffer; your thread slept meanwhile.
- **Synchronous non-blocking**: `read()` returns immediately, with data or `EAGAIN`; you retry.
- **Readiness-based** (`epoll`): the kernel tells you when a subsequent `read()` will not block; you still do the read.
- **Completion-based** (true async): you submit the operation with its buffer; the kernel performs it and notifies you when the bytes are already in place.

Completion-based I/O is what Windows has offered since NT via **I/O Completion Ports (IOCP)**, and it is generally considered the cleaner model: the transfer overlaps with your computation, not just the waiting.

UNIX took longer to get there. **POSIX AIO** (`aio_read`, `aio_write`) exists but is widely regarded as a disappointment: on Linux, glibc implements it with a hidden thread pool, so it is not truly asynchronous, and the kernel's own `io_submit` interface only works reliably with `O_DIRECT`, silently falling back to blocking otherwise. The result was that for two decades, high-performance Linux applications used thread pools for disk I/O and `epoll` for sockets — two separate mechanisms for one problem.

**io_uring** (Linux 5.1, 2019) is the modern answer and worth understanding in some detail, because it changes the shape of the interface rather than just its speed. Two ring buffers are shared between the application and the kernel via `mmap`: a **submission queue (SQ)** the application writes into, and a **completion queue (CQ)** the kernel writes into. To perform I/O, the application fills in a submission queue entry and advances a tail pointer — *no system call at all*. A single `io_uring_enter` can submit hundreds of operations, and in polled mode (`SQPOLL`, where a kernel thread watches the ring) even that disappears.

What this buys:

- **Batching.** Hundreds of operations per crossing instead of one per call.
- **Uniformity.** Files, sockets, timers, `accept`, `fsync`, `openat`, `statx` — all through one interface, so an application needs one event mechanism rather than two.
- **Zero-copy paths** with registered buffers and registered files, which skip per-operation reference counting and mapping.
- **Chaining.** `IOSQE_IO_LINK` makes one operation depend on the previous one's success, so a read-then-write sequence needs no round trip through user space.

The costs are honest ones: the programming model is harder (completions arrive out of order and must be correlated by `user_data`), buffer lifetime rules are strict (the kernel owns the buffer until the completion arrives), and its rapid evolution has produced a real security-bug history, so some hardened environments disable it.

The general principle survives whichever mechanism is used: **asynchrony converts waiting into overlap**. Whether it is worth the complexity depends on whether there is other work to overlap with.

**Example**

```text
   READINESS vs COMPLETION

   READINESS (epoll)                     COMPLETION (io_uring, IOCP)
   app: "tell me when I can read"        app: "read 4 KB into THIS buffer"
   ...                                   ...
   kernel: "fd 7 is readable"            kernel: "done; the bytes are there"
   app: read(7, buf, 4096)   <- the      app: use buf directly
        copy happens HERE, in your            (the transfer already happened)
        thread, on your time

   Two crossings per operation           One submission, one completion,
   and the copy is yours.                and both can be batched.

   io_uring: TWO SHARED RING BUFFERS, MMAPPED

   user space                                   kernel
   +---------------------------+
   | SUBMISSION QUEUE (SQ)     |   app writes entries, advances TAIL
   | [op][op][op][op][  ][  ]  |-------------------------> kernel reads HEAD
   +---------------------------+                                  |
                                                                  | performs I/O
   +---------------------------+                                  |
   | COMPLETION QUEUE (CQ)     |   app reads entries, advances HEAD
   | [res][res][  ][  ][  ]    |<------------------------- kernel writes TAIL
   +---------------------------+

   SYSTEM CALLS PER 1,000 READS
     read()        : 1,000 crossings
     epoll + read  : ~1,000 reads + ~N epoll_wait calls
     io_uring      : 1 io_uring_enter (batched)
     io_uring+SQPOLL: 0  (a kernel thread polls the ring)

   ORDERING: COMPLETIONS ARE NOT IN SUBMISSION ORDER

   submit: [A: read block 900][B: read block 2][C: read block 450]
   complete:      B (2)            C (450)         A (900)
   Correlate with user_data. Assuming order is the classic async bug.

   CHAINING (IOSQE_IO_LINK): no user-space round trip between steps
     [openat] -> [read] -> [write] -> [close]
     submitted as one linked chain; a failure breaks the rest of the chain.
```

```python
# The conceptual model first: submit, do other work, collect completions.
import asyncio, time

async def fetch(name, delay):
    """Stands in for any awaitable I/O: the wait does not hold the thread."""
    await asyncio.sleep(delay)          # yields control; the loop runs others
    return f"{name} done after {delay}s"

async def sequential():
    t0 = time.perf_counter()
    for name, d in [("a", 0.3), ("b", 0.3), ("c", 0.3)]:
        await fetch(name, d)            # each wait is serialised
    return time.perf_counter() - t0

async def concurrent():
    t0 = time.perf_counter()
    # Submit all three, then collect: the waits OVERLAP.
    await asyncio.gather(fetch("a", 0.3), fetch("b", 0.3), fetch("c", 0.3))
    return time.perf_counter() - t0

async def main():
    print(f"sequential : {await sequential():.2f}s")   # ~0.90s: sum of waits
    print(f"concurrent : {await concurrent():.2f}s")   # ~0.30s: max of waits

asyncio.run(main())
# The CPU work is identical. Only the overlap changed -- which is the entire
# point of asynchrony, and also its limit: it helps only when you WAIT.
```

```c
// io_uring with liburing: submit a batch, collect completions out of order.
#include <liburing.h>
#include <fcntl.h>

#define QD 64

int read_many(const char *path, off_t *offsets, int n)
{
    struct io_uring ring;
    struct io_uring_sqe *sqe;
    struct io_uring_cqe *cqe;
    char *bufs[QD];
    int fd, i;

    io_uring_queue_init(QD, &ring, 0);          // create the SQ/CQ rings
    fd = open(path, O_RDONLY | O_DIRECT);

    // ---- SUBMIT: n operations, ZERO system calls so far ----
    for (i = 0; i < n && i < QD; i++) {
        posix_memalign((void **)&bufs[i], 4096, 4096);   // O_DIRECT: aligned
        sqe = io_uring_get_sqe(&ring);                   // a slot in the ring
        io_uring_prep_read(sqe, fd, bufs[i], 4096, offsets[i]);
        io_uring_sqe_set_data(sqe, (void *)(intptr_t)i); // CORRELATION TAG:
                                                         // completions are
                                                         // unordered
    }

    io_uring_submit(&ring);      // ONE crossing for all n operations
                                 // (with SQPOLL enabled, not even this)

    // ---- COLLECT: completions arrive in DEVICE order, not submission order ----
    for (i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        io_uring_wait_cqe(&ring, &cqe);
        int idx = (int)(intptr_t)io_uring_cqe_get_data(cqe);   // which request?

        if (cqe->res < 0)
            fprintf(stderr, "request %d failed: %s\n", idx, strerror(-cqe->res));
        else
            process(bufs[idx], cqe->res);       // bytes are ALREADY in place

        io_uring_cqe_seen(&ring, cqe);          // release the CQ slot
    }

    for (i = 0; i < n; i++) free(bufs[i]);
    close(fd);
    io_uring_queue_exit(&ring);
    return 0;
}

// Chaining: openat -> read -> close with no user-space round trips.
void linked_chain(struct io_uring *ring, const char *path, char *buf)
{
    struct io_uring_sqe *sqe;

    sqe = io_uring_get_sqe(ring);
    io_uring_prep_openat(sqe, AT_FDCWD, path, O_RDONLY, 0);
    sqe->flags |= IOSQE_IO_LINK;        // the NEXT entry waits for this one

    sqe = io_uring_get_sqe(ring);
    io_uring_prep_read(sqe, 0, buf, 4096, 0);   // fd comes from the linked open
    sqe->flags |= IOSQE_IO_LINK;

    sqe = io_uring_get_sqe(ring);
    io_uring_prep_close(sqe, 0);

    io_uring_submit(ring);              // three operations, one crossing
    // If the open fails, the linked read and close are cancelled automatically.
}
```

```bash
# Is io_uring available and permitted here?
uname -r                                   # 5.1+ for basic support, 5.10+ realistically
sysctl kernel.io_uring_disabled            # 0=on, 1=privileged only, 2=off entirely
# Some hardened distributions ship 2 because of io_uring's CVE history.

# Measure the three paths against each other on the same device.
fio --name=sync   --ioengine=sync     --rw=randread --bs=4k --iodepth=1 \
    --direct=1 --filename=/dev/nvme0n1 --runtime=10 --time_based
fio --name=libaio --ioengine=libaio   --rw=randread --bs=4k --iodepth=64 \
    --direct=1 --filename=/dev/nvme0n1 --runtime=10 --time_based
fio --name=uring  --ioengine=io_uring --rw=randread --bs=4k --iodepth=64 \
    --direct=1 --filename=/dev/nvme0n1 --runtime=10 --time_based
# Compare IOPS and the syscall count:
strace -c -f fio --name=x --ioengine=io_uring ... 2>&1 | tail -5

# Even fewer crossings: kernel-side submission polling.
fio --ioengine=io_uring --sqthread_poll=1 --hipri=1 ...   # SQPOLL + IOPOLL

# What POSIX AIO actually does on Linux (spoiler: threads).
strace -f -e trace=clone,io_submit ./posix_aio_program
#   clone(...)   clone(...)   <- glibc's hidden thread pool, not kernel async

# Applications already using it.
sudo ls -l /proc/*/fd 2>/dev/null | grep -c 'io_uring'
```

**Key takeaways**

- Asynchronous I/O is completion-based: you submit an operation with its buffer and are notified when the data is already in place, rather than when a transfer could begin.
- Readiness models (`epoll`) still perform the copy in your thread and do not work for regular files, which are always reported ready.
- POSIX AIO on Linux is largely a disappointment — glibc emulates it with threads, and the kernel path effectively requires `O_DIRECT`.
- `io_uring` uses two mmapped ring buffers so submissions need no system call, batches hundreds of operations per crossing, and covers files, sockets, timers, and metadata operations uniformly.
- Registered buffers and files cut per-operation overhead further, and `IOSQE_IO_LINK` chains dependent operations without returning to user space.
- Completions arrive out of order and must be correlated by a user tag; buffers belong to the kernel until the completion arrives.
- Asynchrony converts waiting into overlap, so it helps exactly as much as there is other work to overlap with.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. Explain the difference between readiness notification and completion notification, and give one case where only the latter helps.
> 2. Run the three `fio` engines above on the same device at the same queue depth and report IOPS and system-call counts for each.
> 3. Interview-style: "Why can `epoll` not solve the problem of a server that reads many small files from disk?" *Hint: ask what `epoll` reports for a regular file descriptor, and what the subsequent `read()` then does.*

#### Buffering and Caching

**Theory**

Buffers and caches both hold data in memory on the way to or from a device, and they are constantly conflated. The distinction is about *authority*:

- A **buffer** is a staging area. The data is in transit; the buffer exists because producer and consumer cannot be perfectly synchronised.
- A **cache** is a copy. The authoritative data lives elsewhere; the cache exists to avoid fetching it again.

Buffering solves three distinct problems, and it is worth separating them because they justify different buffer designs.

**Speed mismatch.** A producer and consumer rarely run at the same rate. A program generating log lines at bursty intervals and a disk that prefers large sequential writes need something between them to absorb the difference — a bucket under a tap that runs unevenly. The buffer smooths bursts and lets each side work at its own natural granularity.

**Size mismatch.** Devices have a preferred transfer size — 4 KB sectors, 1,500-byte network frames — and applications have their own. Buffering accumulates or fragments so each side sees its natural unit. A program writing one byte at a time would otherwise trigger a 4 KB read-modify-write per byte.

**Semantic requirements.** Some operations need the data to stay still. A DMA transfer must not have its source buffer modified mid-transfer, so the kernel copies into a stable buffer first. Network retransmission needs the original bytes available after `send()` returns. The copy is the price of the guarantee.

The classic arrangements:

| Scheme | Behaviour | Trade-off |
|---|---|---|
| Single buffer | Producer waits while the consumer drains | Simple, no overlap |
| Double buffer | Fill one while draining the other | Overlap; twice the memory |
| Circular buffer | N slots, producer and consumer chase each other | Smooths bursts; the standard design |

Double buffering is the classic overlap technique — the same idea as a graphics back buffer. Circular (ring) buffers are what real systems use, because they handle variable rates and, in the single-producer/single-consumer case, can be implemented lock-free with just two indices and a memory barrier.

Caching is the other half. The page cache (Section 10.4) makes most reads memory-speed, and the same principle appears at every level: the device's own DRAM cache, the block layer, the file system, the application, and — for network services — a separate cache tier. The recurring danger is **multiple layers caching the same data**, which wastes memory and, worse, produces inconsistency when one layer is invalidated and another is not. Databases typically use `O_DIRECT` precisely to eliminate the kernel's copy, because they manage a better-informed cache of their own.

Buffering is not free, and the cost is **copies**. A naive file-to-socket path copies four times: device to page cache, page cache to user buffer, user buffer to socket buffer, socket buffer to NIC. Each copy costs memory bandwidth and cache pollution. The zero-copy interfaces exist to remove them: `sendfile()` keeps the data in the kernel, `splice()` moves it between descriptors via a pipe, `mmap` removes the user-space copy, and `MSG_ZEROCOPY` and io_uring's registered buffers remove more. On a server pushing 10 GB/s, removing two copies of 10 GB/s is 20 GB/s of memory bandwidth returned.

**Example**

```text
   BUFFER vs CACHE

   BUFFER (data in transit)          CACHE (a copy of data that lives elsewhere)
   producer -> [buffer] -> consumer  device --> [cache] --> reader
   the data is HERE and nowhere      the AUTHORITATIVE copy is on the device;
   else until consumed               the cache can be dropped at any time

   SINGLE / DOUBLE / CIRCULAR

   SINGLE   producer: [fill......]      [fill......]
            consumer:             [drain]          [drain]
            -> strictly alternating, no overlap

   DOUBLE   producer: [fill A][fill B][fill A][fill B]
            consumer:        [drain A][drain B][drain A]
            -> full overlap; costs 2x memory

   CIRCULAR (ring)
            +---+---+---+---+---+---+---+---+
            | D | D | D |   |   |   | D | D |
            +---+---+---+---+---+---+---+---+
                      ^tail       ^head
            producer advances head, consumer advances tail
            absorbs BURSTS in both directions; the standard design

   THE COPY COUNT ON A FILE->SOCKET PATH

   NAIVE read()+write()           : 4 copies, 2 context switches
     disk --DMA--> page cache
     page cache --CPU--> user buffer      <- copy 1 (and a syscall)
     user buffer --CPU--> socket buffer   <- copy 2 (and a syscall)
     socket buffer --DMA--> NIC

   sendfile()                     : 2 copies (or 1 with scatter-gather DMA)
     disk --DMA--> page cache
     page cache --DMA--> NIC              <- never enters user space

   At 10 GB/s, removing two CPU copies returns ~20 GB/s of memory bandwidth
   and stops evicting the application's working set from L3.
```

```python
import os, time, socket

# ---------- buffering: the same bytes, different call counts ----------
N = 200_000
data = b"log line\n"

t0 = time.perf_counter()
fd = os.open("/tmp/unbuf.log", os.O_CREAT | os.O_WRONLY | os.O_TRUNC, 0o644)
for _ in range(N):
    os.write(fd, data)              # ONE system call per line
os.close(fd)
unbuffered = time.perf_counter() - t0

t0 = time.perf_counter()
with open("/tmp/buf.log", "wb", buffering=64 * 1024) as f:
    for _ in range(N):
        f.write(data)               # accumulates; ~28 system calls total
buffered = time.perf_counter() - t0

print(f"unbuffered {unbuffered:.3f}s   buffered {buffered:.3f}s   "
      f"{unbuffered/buffered:.1f}x")

# ---------- a lock-free SPSC ring buffer: the standard design ----------
class RingBuffer:
    """Single producer, single consumer. No lock needed: each index has
       exactly one writer, and one slot is left empty to distinguish
       'full' from 'empty'."""
    def __init__(self, capacity):
        self.buf  = [None] * capacity
        self.cap  = capacity
        self.head = 0                       # written ONLY by the producer
        self.tail = 0                       # written ONLY by the consumer

    def push(self, item):
        nxt = (self.head + 1) % self.cap
        if nxt == self.tail:
            return False                    # full: apply backpressure here
        self.buf[self.head] = item
        self.head = nxt                     # publish AFTER the store
        return True

    def pop(self):
        if self.tail == self.head:
            return None                     # empty
        item = self.buf[self.tail]
        self.tail = (self.tail + 1) % self.cap
        return item

rb = RingBuffer(8)
print("\npushed:", [rb.push(i) for i in range(9)])   # last one fails: full
print("popped:", [rb.pop() for _ in range(4)])

# ---------- zero-copy: the same transfer, without the user-space round trip ----------
def naive_send(path, sock):
    with open(path, "rb") as f:
        while chunk := f.read(65536):       # copy 1: kernel -> user
            sock.sendall(chunk)             # copy 2: user -> kernel

def zerocopy_send(path, sock):
    with open(path, "rb") as f:
        offset, size = 0, os.fstat(f.fileno()).st_size
        while offset < size:
            # The bytes never enter user space at all.
            sent = os.sendfile(sock.fileno(), f.fileno(), offset, size - offset)
            if sent == 0:
                break
            offset += sent
```

```bash
# Buffer memory, per subsystem.
free -h
#                total  used  free  shared  buff/cache  available
#   Mem:          31Gi  8Gi   2Gi   1Gi     21Gi        22Gi
#                                            ^ "buff/cache" is RECLAIMABLE
grep -E 'Buffers|Cached|Dirty' /proc/meminfo
#   Buffers:  block-device metadata buffers
#   Cached:   the page cache (file data)

# Network socket buffers: where bursts are absorbed.
sysctl net.core.rmem_max net.core.wmem_max
sysctl net.ipv4.tcp_rmem net.ipv4.tcp_wmem       # min / default / max
sudo sysctl -w net.core.rmem_max=134217728       # for long fat pipes
ss -tmi | head -6                                 # per-socket buffer usage

# NIC ring buffers: where packet bursts are absorbed before the driver runs.
sudo ethtool -g eth0
#   Pre-set maximums:  RX: 4096  TX: 4096
#   Current settings:  RX: 512   TX: 512
sudo ethtool -G eth0 rx 2048 tx 2048     # raise if drops are occurring
ip -s link show eth0 | grep -A2 RX       # 'dropped' rising = ring too small

# Zero-copy in practice.
strace -c -e trace=sendfile,splice,read,write nginx -g 'daemon off;' &
# nginx with sendfile on: few read/write pairs, many sendfile calls.
grep -r 'sendfile' /etc/nginx/nginx.conf

# Avoiding double caching: let the application own its cache.
#   PostgreSQL: shared_buffers + the OS page cache (deliberately both)
#   Oracle/MySQL InnoDB with O_DIRECT: skip the OS cache entirely
mysql -e "SHOW VARIABLES LIKE 'innodb_flush_method';"    # O_DIRECT
```

**Key takeaways**

- A buffer stages data in transit; a cache holds a copy whose authoritative version lives elsewhere. The difference is which copy is authoritative.
- Buffering exists to bridge speed mismatches, size mismatches, and semantic requirements such as keeping DMA source data stable.
- Double buffering overlaps production and consumption; circular buffers handle variable rates and can be lock-free for one producer and one consumer.
- Multiple layers caching the same data wastes memory and risks inconsistency, which is why databases often use `O_DIRECT` and manage their own cache.
- Every buffer boundary is a potential copy, and copies cost memory bandwidth and cache residency, not just time.
- Zero-copy paths (`sendfile`, `splice`, `mmap`, `MSG_ZEROCOPY`, registered buffers) remove those copies, which matters enormously at high throughput.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. Write the same 100,000 log lines with and without library buffering, and use `strace -c` to explain the timing difference by system-call count.
> 2. Implement a circular buffer with `push` and `pop`, and explain why leaving one slot empty distinguishes full from empty.
> 3. Interview-style: "A file server is CPU-bound at 40% of line rate, with most cycles in `memcpy`. What do you change and why?" *Hint: count the copies on the read-then-write path, then name the call that eliminates the ones that pass through user space.*

#### Spooling

**Theory**

Some devices cannot be shared by interleaving. If two processes write to a disk file alternately, the file system keeps their data separate. If two processes write to a printer alternately, you get one ruined document with lines from both jobs. The device has no notion of concurrent streams, and the output is physical and irreversible.

**Spooling** — Simultaneous Peripheral Operation On-Line — is the answer: instead of letting processes write to the device, give each one a *file*, and have a single dedicated daemon feed those files to the device one complete job at a time. The spool directory becomes a queue, and the device sees exactly one client.

This buys four things at once:

1. **Serialisation without blocking.** Ten users can print simultaneously from their own point of view; each writes a file and continues immediately. The jobs are serialised at the device, not at the application.
2. **Speed decoupling.** A program generating a 200-page document at memory speed does not run at printer speed. It writes the spool file and exits.
3. **Queue management.** Because jobs are now files with metadata, they can be listed, prioritised, held, reordered, cancelled, and retried — none of which is possible with a direct device write.
4. **Fault tolerance.** If the printer jams or the machine reboots, the spool files persist and the jobs resume. Nothing is lost mid-stream.

Spooling was historically the answer to slow card readers and line printers — in batch systems it was the entire reason a job's output did not hold the CPU hostage. But the pattern long outlived printers, and recognising it in modern form is the useful part:

- **Mail queues.** `sendmail` and Postfix spool outbound mail to disk, then retry delivery over hours or days. Accepting a message and delivering it are deliberately separated.
- **Print systems.** CUPS still does exactly the classic thing, in `/var/spool/cups`.
- **Batch and cron systems.** `at` and `cron` spool jobs in `/var/spool/`.
- **Message queues.** RabbitMQ, Kafka, SQS, and every task queue are spooling generalised: a durable intermediary so producers and consumers need not be simultaneously available or equally fast.
- **Log shipping and CI pipelines.** Write locally, ship asynchronously, retry on failure.

The general pattern is worth naming because it is a design tool: **when a resource cannot be shared concurrently, do not serialise the clients — serialise the work by putting a durable queue in front of it.** The costs are the ones any queue has: disk space for the backlog, added latency before the work actually happens, a queue that can grow without bound if the consumer is slower than the producer, and the need for a policy about what to do when the queue fills or a job repeatedly fails.

**Example**

```text
   WITHOUT SPOOLING: THE DEVICE CANNOT MULTIPLEX

   process A ---> [ PRINTER ] <--- process B
   output:  "Dear Sir,Invoice #42Yours faithfully,Total: $99"
            ^ two documents interleaved, paper wasted, both unusable
   The alternative -- an exclusive lock -- blocks B for A's entire job.

   WITH SPOOLING: ONE WRITER, MANY PRODUCERS

   process A --write--> /var/spool/cups/d00042-001 --+
   process B --write--> /var/spool/cups/d00043-001 --+--> [ SPOOLER ]
   process C --write--> /var/spool/cups/d00044-001 --+         |
        (each returns IMMEDIATELY)                             v
                                                         [ PRINTER ]
                                                   one COMPLETE job at a time

   THE SPOOL DIRECTORY IS A QUEUE, SO IT CAN BE MANAGED

   $ lpq
   Rank    Owner   Job  Files            Total Size
   active  ana     42   report.pdf       842000 bytes
   1st     ben     43   invoice.ps        12000 bytes
   2nd     cara    44   thesis.pdf      4200000 bytes

   operations a direct device write could never support:
     lprm 43            cancel
     lp -i 44 -H hold   hold
     lp -q 90 ...       prioritise
     (and after a crash, the files are still there)

   THE SAME PATTERN, MODERN NAMES

   printing   : app -> spool dir -> cupsd      -> printer
   mail       : app -> /var/spool/postfix      -> SMTP -> remote server
   batch      : at  -> /var/spool/cron/atjobs  -> atd
   messaging  : producer -> Kafka topic        -> consumer group
   CI         : job -> queue                   -> runner pool
   logs       : app -> local buffer file       -> shipper -> aggregator

   THE COSTS ANY QUEUE HAS
     - disk space for the backlog (a stuck printer fills /var)
     - latency: the work happens later, not now
     - unbounded growth if consumers are slower than producers
     - a policy is REQUIRED for: queue full, job poisoned, retries exhausted
```

```bash
# The classic case, still working exactly as described.
lpstat -p -d                              # printers and the default
lp -d office-printer report.pdf           # returns IMMEDIATELY
#   request id is office-printer-42 (1 file(s))
lpq                                       # the queue
sudo ls -l /var/spool/cups/               # the actual spool files
#   -rw-------  1 root lp  842000  d00042-001    <- the document data
#   -rw-r-----  1 root lp     512  c00042        <- the control file (metadata)
lprm 42                                   # cancel a queued job
lp -i 43 -H hold                          # hold it
cancel -a office-printer                  # drain the queue

# Mail: the same pattern, with retry over days.
mailq
postqueue -p
#   -Queue ID-  --Size-- ----Arrival Time---- -Sender/Recipient-------
#   3F2A1B4C21     2451  Thu Sep 11 09:14:02  sender@example.com
#            (connect to mx.example.net: Connection timed out)
sudo postqueue -f                         # flush: retry everything now
sudo postsuper -d 3F2A1B4C21              # delete one message
ls -l /var/spool/postfix/deferred/        # jobs waiting for a retry

# Batch jobs.
echo "backup.sh" | at 02:00
atq
ls -l /var/spool/cron/atjobs/

# What happens when the consumer stops: the queue is the failure mode.
df -h /var                                # a stuck spooler fills this
du -sh /var/spool/*
find /var/spool -type f -mtime +7         # jobs nobody is retrying successfully

# The modern generalisation.
kafka-consumer-groups.sh --bootstrap-server localhost:9092 \
  --describe --group workers
#   TOPIC  PARTITION  CURRENT-OFFSET  LOG-END-OFFSET  LAG
#   tasks  0          88213           91007           2794
#                                                     ^ the backlog, in messages
redis-cli LLEN task_queue                 # the same number, for a Redis queue
```

```python
import os, json, time, uuid, fcntl

# A spooler in miniature: producers write files, one consumer drains them.
SPOOL = "/tmp/myspool"
os.makedirs(SPOOL, exist_ok=True)

def submit(payload, priority=50):
    """Producer side: durable, atomic, and returns immediately."""
    job_id = f"{priority:03d}-{int(time.time())}-{uuid.uuid4().hex[:8]}"
    tmp   = os.path.join(SPOOL, f".{job_id}.tmp")
    final = os.path.join(SPOOL, f"{job_id}.job")

    with open(tmp, "w") as f:
        json.dump({"id": job_id, "payload": payload,
                   "submitted": time.time(), "attempts": 0}, f)
        f.flush()
        os.fsync(f.fileno())          # durable BEFORE it becomes visible
    os.rename(tmp, final)             # atomic publish: no partial job is ever seen
    return job_id

def drain(process_fn, max_attempts=3):
    """Consumer side: ONE worker touches the device, jobs run to completion."""
    # Sorting by name sorts by priority prefix, then by submission time.
    for name in sorted(os.listdir(SPOOL)):
        if not name.endswith(".job"):
            continue
        path = os.path.join(SPOOL, name)

        # Claim the job exclusively, so two spoolers cannot double-print it.
        try:
            fd = os.open(path, os.O_RDWR)
            fcntl.flock(fd, fcntl.LOCK_EX | fcntl.LOCK_NB)
        except (FileNotFoundError, BlockingIOError):
            continue                  # another worker has it, or it is gone

        try:
            job = json.load(os.fdopen(os.dup(fd), "r"))
            process_fn(job["payload"])        # the device sees ONE complete job
            os.unlink(path)                   # success: remove from the queue
        except Exception as e:
            job["attempts"] += 1
            if job["attempts"] >= max_attempts:
                os.rename(path, path + ".failed")   # dead-letter: do NOT retry
            else:                                    # retry policy is REQUIRED
                os.lseek(fd, 0, os.SEEK_SET); os.ftruncate(fd, 0)
                os.write(fd, json.dumps(job).encode())
        finally:
            os.close(fd)

for doc, pri in [("report.pdf", 50), ("urgent.pdf", 10), ("thesis.pdf", 90)]:
    print("queued:", submit(doc, pri))
drain(lambda p: print("printing:", p))
# Output order: urgent.pdf (010), report.pdf (050), thesis.pdf (090).
```

**Key takeaways**

- Spooling puts a durable queue in front of a device that cannot be shared by interleaving, so one daemon feeds the device complete jobs at a time.
- Producers write a file and return immediately, which decouples their speed from the device's and avoids blocking them for the whole job.
- Turning jobs into files makes listing, prioritising, holding, cancelling, and retrying possible — none of which a direct device write supports.
- Spool files persist across crashes, so a jam or reboot does not lose work mid-stream.
- The pattern generalises far beyond printers: mail queues, `at`/`cron`, message brokers, CI pipelines, and log shipping are all spooling.
- Every spool needs a policy for backlog growth, retry limits, and poisoned jobs, and a stuck consumer will eventually fill the disk.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. Explain what physically happens if two processes write to a printer device simultaneously, and how spooling prevents it without blocking either process.
> 2. Inspect `/var/spool/` on your machine and identify three subsystems using it. For one, find the metadata that accompanies each queued item.
> 3. Interview-style: "A task queue's backlog grows steadily during business hours and drains overnight. Is this a problem?" *Hint: consider whether the queue is absorbing bursts or hiding a capacity deficit, and what the latency of the oldest item implies in each case.*

<a id="113-kernel-io-subsystem"></a>
### 11.3 Kernel I/O Subsystem

Above the drivers sits the kernel code that serves every device alike: deciding what order requests go out in, coping when they fail, keeping one process's I/O away from another's, granting exclusive use where it is needed, and giving administrators the levers to tune all of it.

#### I/O Scheduling

**Theory**

Requests arrive at the block layer faster than a device can serve them, so a queue forms — and once there is a queue, the order in which it drains is a policy decision. **I/O scheduling** is that policy, and its correct answer changed completely when storage stopped having moving parts.

The classical objective was **minimising mechanical motion**. Chapter 9 covered the algorithms — FCFS, SSTF, SCAN, C-SCAN, LOOK, C-LOOK — all of which exist to keep a disk arm from thrashing back and forth. On a device where positioning costs 8 ms and transfer costs 20 µs, reordering a queue can improve throughput threefold, and it is worth considerable effort.

Two device-independent optimisations sit alongside that, and they survive the transition to flash:

- **Merging.** Two requests for adjacent blocks become one larger request. This reduces per-request overhead (each request costs a structure, a queue entry, and a completion) and is worth doing even when positioning is free.
- **Plugging.** The queue is deliberately held closed for a brief moment when it was empty, so that requests arriving together can be merged and sorted rather than dispatched one at a time.

Once the arm disappeared, the objectives changed. NVMe devices have internal parallelism across many flash dies, deep queues, and no positioning cost — so sorting by block number buys nothing and *costs* CPU and latency. Linux's answer was a new architecture, **blk-mq** (multi-queue block layer): per-CPU software queues feeding multiple hardware queues, so submission needs no shared lock and each core's completions come back to that core.

The schedulers that matter today:

| Scheduler | Designed for | Behaviour |
|---|---|---|
| `none` | NVMe, fast SSDs | No reordering; merge only. Lowest overhead. |
| `mq-deadline` | HDDs, SATA SSDs | Sorted queue plus per-request deadlines (500 ms reads, 5 s writes) so nothing starves |
| `bfq` | Desktops, interactive | Proportional-share fairness per process; best perceived responsiveness under load |
| `kyber` | Fast multi-queue devices | Targets latency directly by throttling queue depth to hit a configured p99 |

Two ideas deserve emphasis because they recur.

**Reads and writes are not symmetric.** A read usually has a thread blocked on it; a write usually went into the page cache and nobody is waiting. So deadline schedulers give reads much tighter deadlines than writes. Getting this backwards produces a system that benchmarks well and feels terrible.

**Fairness needs enforcement.** Without it, one process doing sequential streaming I/O can starve another doing small random reads, because the streaming requests keep arriving and keep merging. Deadlines bound the damage; **cgroup I/O controllers** (`io.max`, `io.weight`, `io.latency`) go further, capping IOPS and bandwidth per control group — which is how containers and multi-tenant systems avoid a noisy neighbour consuming the whole device.

The practical guidance is short: `none` for NVMe, `mq-deadline` for SATA SSDs and HDDs in servers, `bfq` for interactive desktops — and measure, because the wrong choice can cost a factor of two in either direction.

**Example**

```text
   WHAT A SCHEDULER DOES BETWEEN SUBMISSION AND THE DEVICE

   processes: A(blk 500) B(blk 12) C(blk 501) D(blk 13) E(blk 502)
        |
   +----v--------------------------------------------------+
   | per-CPU SOFTWARE queues (blk-mq): no shared lock       |
   +----v--------------------------------------------------+
   | SCHEDULER:  merge adjacent | sort | enforce deadlines  |
   |   merged: {500,501,502} -> ONE request                 |
   |   merged: {12,13}       -> ONE request                 |
   +----v--------------------------------------------------+
   | HARDWARE queues (one per core on NVMe)                 |
   +----v--------------------------------------------------+
        v
      device

   5 requests became 2. That saving applies to EVERY device type.

   REORDERING: WORTH IT ON A DISK, HARMFUL ON FLASH

   HDD, head at 53, queue {98,183,37,122,14,124,65,67}
     FCFS   : 53->98->183->37->122->14->124->65->67  = 640 cylinders
     C-LOOK : 53->65->67->98->122->124->183->14->37  = 322 cylinders
     ~2x less arm motion -> ~2x throughput.  REORDERING PAYS.

   NVMe, same queue of LBAs
     no arm, internal parallelism across dies, 2 us service time
     sorting costs CPU and ADDS latency; the device reorders better
     than the kernel can.  USE 'none'.

   READ vs WRITE ASYMMETRY (why deadline schedulers separate them)

   read  : a thread is BLOCKED right now, waiting    -> deadline 500 ms
   write : already in the page cache, nobody waits   -> deadline 5000 ms
   Treating them equally makes an interactive system feel broken while
   its throughput numbers look fine.

   CGROUP THROTTLING: THE NOISY-NEIGHBOUR FIX

   without:  [backup job] ############################  device saturated
             [database  ] #                             starved
   with io.max on the backup cgroup:
             [backup job] ########                      capped at 50 MB/s
             [database  ] ####################          responsive
```

```bash
# Which scheduler is active, and what is available.
cat /sys/block/nvme0n1/queue/scheduler
#   [none] mq-deadline kyber bfq          <- brackets mark the active one
cat /sys/block/sda/queue/scheduler
#   none [mq-deadline] kyber bfq

# Change it (immediately effective, no remount).
echo none        | sudo tee /sys/block/nvme0n1/queue/scheduler
echo mq-deadline | sudo tee /sys/block/sda/queue/scheduler
echo bfq         | sudo tee /sys/block/sda/queue/scheduler    # desktop

# Persist with a udev rule, because sysfs resets at boot.
cat <<'EOF' | sudo tee /etc/udev/rules.d/60-ioschedulers.rules
ACTION=="add|change", KERNEL=="nvme[0-9]n[0-9]", ATTR{queue/scheduler}="none"
ACTION=="add|change", KERNEL=="sd[a-z]", ATTR{queue/rotational}=="1", ATTR{queue/scheduler}="bfq"
ACTION=="add|change", KERNEL=="sd[a-z]", ATTR{queue/rotational}=="0", ATTR{queue/scheduler}="mq-deadline"
EOF

# Deadline tuning: the read/write asymmetry, in milliseconds.
cat /sys/block/sda/queue/iosched/read_expire     # 500
cat /sys/block/sda/queue/iosched/write_expire    # 5000
cat /sys/block/sda/queue/iosched/writes_starved  # 2 reads batches per write batch

# The queue's own parameters.
cat /sys/block/nvme0n1/queue/nr_requests         # queue depth
cat /sys/block/nvme0n1/queue/rotational          # 0 = flash (affects defaults)
cat /sys/block/nvme0n1/queue/nomerges            # 0 = merge, 2 = never merge
ls /sys/block/nvme0n1/mq/                        # one dir per hardware queue

# Compare schedulers on YOUR workload -- the only way to choose correctly.
for s in none mq-deadline kyber bfq; do
  echo $s | sudo tee /sys/block/sda/queue/scheduler > /dev/null
  echo "=== $s ==="
  fio --name=t --filename=/dev/sda --rw=randread --bs=4k --iodepth=32 \
      --numjobs=4 --direct=1 --runtime=20 --time_based --group_reporting \
      --output-format=terse | awk -F';' '{print "  IOPS="$8" p99us="$28}'
done

# Per-cgroup limits: the multi-tenant answer.
sudo mkdir -p /sys/fs/cgroup/backup
echo "259:0 rbps=52428800 wbps=52428800" | \
  sudo tee /sys/fs/cgroup/backup/io.max          # 50 MB/s each way
echo "259:0 target=10000" | sudo tee /sys/fs/cgroup/db/io.latency   # protect 10ms
echo $$ | sudo tee /sys/fs/cgroup/backup/cgroup.procs
cat /sys/fs/cgroup/backup/io.stat

# Observing the queue in flight.
iostat -x 1
#   Device  r/s   w/s  rareq-sz  aqu-sz  r_await  w_await  %util
#   nvme0n1 8420  120  4.0       12.3    1.42     0.31     94.2
#           ^ aqu-sz = average queue depth; r_await = read latency (ms)
sudo biolatency-bpfcc 10 1          # latency histogram
sudo biotop-bpfcc                    # which processes are generating the I/O
```

```python
# Why merging matters regardless of device type, and why sorting does not.
PER_REQUEST_OVERHEAD_US = 2.0        # request struct, queue entry, completion
TRANSFER_US_PER_KB      = 0.5

def cost(requests_kb):
    """requests_kb: list of request sizes."""
    return sum(PER_REQUEST_OVERHEAD_US + TRANSFER_US_PER_KB * kb
               for kb in requests_kb)

unmerged = [4] * 256                  # 256 separate 4 KB requests
merged   = [1024]                     # one 1 MB request, same bytes
print(f"256 x 4 KB unmerged : {cost(unmerged):8.1f} us")
print(f"1 x 1 MB merged     : {cost(merged):8.1f} us")
print(f"overhead removed    : {cost(unmerged)-cost(merged):8.1f} us\n")

# Reordering: valuable on a disk, pure cost on flash.
queue = [98, 183, 37, 122, 14, 124, 65, 67]
head  = 53

def seek_total(order, start):
    pos, total = start, 0
    for c in order:
        total += abs(c - pos); pos = c
    return total

clook = sorted([c for c in queue if c >= head]) + sorted([c for c in queue if c < head])
print(f"HDD FCFS  : {seek_total(queue, head):>4} cylinders of arm motion")
print(f"HDD C-LOOK: {seek_total(clook, head):>4} cylinders "
      f"({seek_total(queue,head)/seek_total(clook,head):.1f}x better)")

SORT_CPU_US, NVME_SERVICE_US = 0.8, 2.0
print(f"\nNVMe: service {NVME_SERVICE_US} us, sorting costs {SORT_CPU_US} us/request")
print(f"  -> sorting adds {SORT_CPU_US/NVME_SERVICE_US:.0%} latency and saves nothing.")
print("  -> scheduler 'none': merge, do not sort.")
```

**Key takeaways**

- Once requests queue, their order is a policy decision; the right policy depends entirely on whether the device has moving parts.
- Merging adjacent requests and plugging an empty queue briefly are worthwhile on every device, because per-request overhead is real even without positioning cost.
- Sorting by block number pays on disks (up to several times less arm motion) and actively hurts on NVMe, where it adds CPU and latency for no benefit.
- blk-mq gives each CPU its own software queue feeding multiple hardware queues, removing the shared-lock bottleneck of the old single-queue design.
- Reads have a thread waiting and writes usually do not, so deadline schedulers give reads far tighter deadlines — reversing this ruins interactivity.
- Use `none` for NVMe, `mq-deadline` for SATA and HDD servers, `bfq` for interactive desktops, and cgroup `io.max`/`io.latency` to contain noisy neighbours.

> 2. Check the active scheduler for every block device on your machine and say whether each choice matches the device type.
> 3. Interview-style: "Setting the scheduler to `none` on an NVMe drive improved p99 latency. Why would removing scheduling make things better?" *Hint: consider what the scheduler was spending time doing, and whether the device's own controller already does it more effectively.*

#### Error Handling

**Theory**

I/O is where things go wrong. Memory rarely fails silently in a way software must handle; devices do it constantly — cables come loose, sectors go bad, networks partition, drives overheat, firmware has bugs. The kernel's job is to distinguish what it can fix from what it cannot, and to report the latter honestly rather than pretending.

The first distinction is **transient versus permanent**. A transient error may succeed if simply tried again: a bus timeout under load, a read that failed once because of vibration, a network packet that was dropped. A permanent error will never succeed: a sector whose magnetic domain is dead, a removed device, a write to read-only media. Retrying a permanent error wastes time and, on a failing disk, actively accelerates its death. Retrying a transient error is usually free. Getting the classification wrong in either direction is the main failure mode of error-handling code.

Layers handle errors at different levels, and the higher you go, the more context there is:

1. **The device** corrects internally. Every disk sector carries ECC; a single-bit flip is fixed and never reported. SSDs relocate wearing blocks silently.
2. **The driver** retries a small number of times and may reset the device.
3. **The block layer or protocol stack** retries, fails over to another path (multipath I/O), or reconstructs from redundancy (RAID).
4. **The file system** may remount read-only, replay its journal, or repair from a checksum-verified copy.
5. **The application** gets an error code and must decide — and this is where most software is weakest.

The errors a program actually sees are a small vocabulary worth knowing:

| Code | Meaning | Usual response |
|---|---|---|
| `EIO` | Low-level I/O failure | Often permanent; do not blindly retry |
| `EAGAIN` | Would block | Retry when ready (not an error) |
| `EINTR` | Interrupted by a signal | Retry the call |
| `ENOSPC` | No space | Free space; retrying without doing so is pointless |
| `EDQUOT` | Quota exceeded | Same, but per-user |
| `ENODEV` / `ENXIO` | Device gone | Fail; do not retry |
| `EROFS` | Read-only file system | Often the aftermath of an earlier error |
| `ETIMEDOUT` | Operation timed out | Usually transient |

Three application-level mistakes recur so often they are worth naming.

**Unchecked writes.** `write()` returns the number of bytes written, which may be less than requested, and `close()` can fail — returning the error from a deferred writeback. A program that ignores both can lose data with no indication. The correct pattern is to loop on partial writes and check `close()` as well as `fsync()`.

**Retrying without backoff.** Immediate retries on a struggling device or network add load precisely when the system is least able to take it, converting a transient problem into a sustained outage. **Exponential backoff with jitter** is the standard remedy; the jitter matters because synchronised retries from many clients produce a thundering herd.

**Silent corruption.** The hardest class, because nothing reports an error at all. A drive returns wrong bytes, a cable flips a bit, firmware misdirects a write. Only end-to-end checksums (Section 10.4) detect this — which is the strongest argument for ZFS, Btrfs, or application-level verification.

Finally, errors must be **visible**. A system that retries silently forever looks healthy until it collapses. SMART attributes, `dmesg`, kernel error counters, and per-device I/O error metrics should be collected and alerted on, because rising reallocated-sector counts and occasional bus resets are warnings that arrive well before the failure does.

**Example**

```text
   WHERE AN ERROR IS HANDLED, AND WHAT EACH LAYER CAN DO

   application    "EIO on read of report.pdf"     <- most context, least info
        ^                                            about the cause
   file system    remount read-only; repair from checksum+redundancy
        ^
   block/RAID     retry; failover to another path; reconstruct from parity
        ^
   driver         retry N times; reset the device
        ^
   device         ECC corrects the bit; remap the sector; report if it cannot
                  <- least context, most information about the cause

   Most errors never reach the top. The ones that do have already
   defeated every layer below.

   TRANSIENT vs PERMANENT: THE CLASSIFICATION THAT MATTERS

   transient (retry helps)          permanent (retry harms)
     bus timeout under load           medium error on a dead sector
     dropped network packet           device unplugged
     temporary queue-full             write to read-only media
     ETIMEDOUT, EAGAIN, EINTR         ENODEV, EROFS, repeated EIO

   Retrying a permanent error on a failing disk makes it fail FASTER
   and delays the failover that would have saved the service.

   EXPONENTIAL BACKOFF WITH JITTER

   no backoff : |||||||||||||||||||||||   retries pile onto a sick device
   backoff    : |  |    |        |        load falls as failures persist
   + jitter   : | |      |   |            clients de-synchronise

   attempt: 1     2     3     4      5
   delay  : 0.1s  0.2s  0.4s  0.8s   1.6s   (x random 0.5-1.5)

   THE ERROR NOBODY REPORTS

   write(fd, buf, 4096)  -> 4096      "success"
   close(fd)             -> -1 EIO    <- the writeback failed; the data is GONE
   Programs that ignore close() lose data with NO indication whatsoever.
```

```python
import os, time, random, errno

# ---------- 1. A correct write: partial writes and close() both checked ----------
def write_all(fd, data: bytes):
    """write() may transfer FEWER bytes than requested. Looping is mandatory."""
    view, total = memoryview(data), 0
    while total < len(data):
        try:
            n = os.write(fd, view[total:])
        except InterruptedError:              # EINTR: a signal arrived
            continue                          # not an error; just retry
        except BlockingIOError:               # EAGAIN on a non-blocking fd
            time.sleep(0.001); continue
        if n == 0:
            raise IOError("write returned 0")
        total += n
    return total

def durable_write(path, data: bytes):
    fd = os.open(path, os.O_CREAT | os.O_WRONLY | os.O_TRUNC, 0o644)
    try:
        write_all(fd, data)
        os.fsync(fd)                          # errors surface HERE...
    finally:
        os.close(fd)                          # ...or HERE. Both must be checked;
                                              # a bare close() in a finally can
                                              # swallow the error, so in real code
                                              # close explicitly and check it.

# ---------- 2. Retry: only for transient errors, always with backoff ----------
TRANSIENT = {errno.EAGAIN, errno.EINTR, errno.ETIMEDOUT, errno.EBUSY, errno.ENOBUFS}
PERMANENT = {errno.ENODEV, errno.ENXIO, errno.EROFS, errno.ENOSPC, errno.EACCES}

def with_retry(op, attempts=5, base=0.1, cap=10.0):
    for attempt in range(attempts):
        try:
            return op()
        except OSError as e:
            if e.errno in PERMANENT:
                raise                          # retrying CANNOT help
            if e.errno not in TRANSIENT and e.errno != errno.EIO:
                raise
            if attempt == attempts - 1:
                raise
            # Exponential backoff with full jitter: de-synchronises clients.
            delay = min(cap, base * (2 ** attempt)) * random.uniform(0.5, 1.5)
            print(f"  attempt {attempt+1} failed ({e.strerror}); "
                  f"retrying in {delay:.2f}s")
            time.sleep(delay)

# ---------- 3. Detecting what no layer reports: silent corruption ----------
import hashlib

def write_verified(path, data: bytes):
    durable_write(path, data)
    digest = hashlib.blake2b(data, digest_size=16).hexdigest()
    durable_write(path + ".sum", digest.encode())
    return digest

def read_verified(path):
    with open(path, "rb") as f:
        data = f.read()
    with open(path + ".sum") as f:
        expected = f.read().strip()
    actual = hashlib.blake2b(data, digest_size=16).hexdigest()
    if actual != expected:
        # No errno was ever returned. Only the checksum knows.
        raise IOError(f"SILENT CORRUPTION in {path}: {expected} != {actual}")
    return data
```

```bash
# The kernel's own record of I/O trouble -- check this first, always.
dmesg -T | grep -iE 'i/o error|medium error|reset|ata[0-9]|nvme.*error|failed command'
#   [Thu Sep 11 09:14:02] blk_update_request: I/O error, dev sda, sector 1234567
#   [Thu Sep 11 09:14:02] ata1.00: failed command: READ FPDMA QUEUED
journalctl -k -p err -b

# Per-device error counters.
cat /sys/block/sda/device/ioerr_cnt
sudo nvme error-log /dev/nvme0 | head -20
sudo nvme smart-log /dev/nvme0 | grep -iE 'critical|media_errors|num_err'

# The pre-failure warning nobody reads until it is too late.
sudo smartctl -a /dev/sda | grep -iE 'Reallocated|Pending|Uncorrectable|Offline'
#   5  Reallocated_Sector_Ct   0x0033  100  100  010  Pre-fail  -  128
#   197 Current_Pending_Sector 0x0012  100  100  000  Old_age    -  8
#       ^ pending sectors are failing reads RIGHT NOW
sudo smartctl -t short /dev/sda && sleep 120 && sudo smartctl -l selftest /dev/sda
sudo systemctl enable --now smartd        # continuous monitoring + alerts

# Multipath: the failover that makes a path error survivable.
multipath -ll
#   mpatha (3600508b4000...) dm-0
#   |-+- policy='service-time 0' prio=50 status=active
#   | `- 2:0:0:1 sdb 8:16 active ready running
#   `-+- policy='service-time 0' prio=10 status=enabled
#     `- 3:0:0:1 sdc 8:32 active ghost running     <- standby path

# Timeouts: how long before the kernel gives up on a request.
cat /sys/block/sda/device/timeout            # 30 seconds by default
echo 10 | sudo tee /sys/block/sda/device/timeout   # fail over sooner

# Testing error paths deliberately, rather than discovering them in production.
sudo dmsetup create flaky --table "0 $(blockdev --getsz /dev/sdb) \
  flakey /dev/sdb 0 8 4"                     # 8s up, 4s returning errors
dd if=/dev/zero of=/dev/full bs=1M count=1   # a device that always gives ENOSPC
```

**Key takeaways**

- The essential classification is transient versus permanent: retrying the first is nearly free, retrying the second wastes time and can accelerate a failing device's death.
- Errors are handled at every layer — device ECC, driver retries, RAID or multipath recovery, file system repair — and only what defeats all of them reaches the application.
- `write()` can transfer fewer bytes than requested and `close()` can report a deferred writeback failure; ignoring either loses data silently.
- Retries need exponential backoff with jitter, or synchronised clients turn a transient fault into a sustained outage.
- Silent corruption produces no error code at all and is detectable only with end-to-end checksums.
- Error visibility matters as much as error handling: SMART attributes, kernel logs, and per-device counters warn well before a failure becomes an outage.

#### I/O Protection

**Theory**

Every device is a capability. A program that can write raw blocks to `/dev/sda` can rewrite the file system, including the password file, regardless of file permissions. A program that can put a network interface in promiscuous mode can read other people's traffic. A program that can program a DMA-capable device can write anywhere in physical memory. So I/O is a protection problem before it is a performance problem, and the defences are layered.

**Layer 1: privileged instructions.** The I/O instructions themselves (`IN`, `OUT` on x86) are available only in kernel mode, and MMIO regions are simply not mapped into user address spaces. A user program cannot touch a device register, so all device access must go through system calls — which is the whole reason dual-mode operation exists.

**Layer 2: device file permissions.** Once access is mediated by the file system, ordinary permissions apply. `/dev/sda` is `brw-rw----  root disk`, so only root and members of `disk` can open it — and membership of `disk` is effectively equivalent to root, a fact that surprises people. `/dev/null` is world-writable because it is harmless; `/dev/mem` is root-only and usually disabled entirely (`CONFIG_STRICT_DEVMEM`) because it would otherwise expose all of physical memory.

**Layer 3: capabilities.** Coarse root-or-not is too blunt. Linux splits root's powers into capabilities so a program can be given exactly one: `CAP_NET_RAW` for raw sockets (what `ping` needs), `CAP_NET_ADMIN` for interface configuration, `CAP_SYS_RAWIO` for raw device access, `CAP_SYS_ADMIN` for a regrettably large grab-bag. Granting `CAP_NET_RAW` to a binary is vastly safer than making it setuid-root.

**Layer 4: mount options.** Section 10.1's `nodev`, `nosuid`, and `noexec` prevent a device node on removable or user-writable media from being a path to privilege. Without `nodev`, a user who can mount a USB stick containing a `/dev/sda` node owns the machine.

**Layer 5: the IOMMU.** All of the above are useless against a device that does DMA to arbitrary physical addresses. The IOMMU confines each device to explicitly mapped pages, which is what makes Thunderbolt hot-plug and VM device passthrough safe.

**Layer 6: sandboxing.** `seccomp` filters which system calls a process may make at all — a process that cannot call `ioctl` cannot misuse a device even if it holds a descriptor. Namespaces give containers their own `/dev` with only the entries they need. SELinux and AppArmor add mandatory policy on top of discretionary permissions.

Two mechanisms deserve special mention because they sit at the boundary. **`ioctl` is a hole in the type system**: it takes an arbitrary command number and an arbitrary pointer, so every driver's `ioctl` handler is attack surface, and historically a rich source of privilege-escalation bugs. Drivers must validate command numbers, validate sizes, and copy user data properly. And **device passthrough** to a VM hands a guest direct control of real hardware; it is safe only with an IOMMU, and only at the granularity of an IOMMU group, since devices sharing a group can reach each other.

**Example**

```text
   THE LAYERS, AND WHAT EACH STOPS

   user process
        |  (1) cannot execute IN/OUT; device registers are not mapped
        v
   system call boundary
        |  (2) /dev node permissions: who may open this device at all
        |  (3) capabilities: CAP_NET_RAW, CAP_SYS_RAWIO -- root, subdivided
        |  (6) seccomp: may this process even CALL ioctl?
        v
   kernel driver
        |  (4) mount options: nodev stops device nodes on foreign media
        v
   device
        |  (5) IOMMU: the device may touch ONLY its mapped pages
        v
   physical memory

   WHY /dev/sda PERMISSIONS ARE A PRIVILEGE BOUNDARY

   $ ls -l /dev/sda
   brw-rw---- 1 root disk 8, 0 /dev/sda
                    ^^^^ membership of 'disk' == the ability to rewrite
                         /etc/shadow directly, bypassing every file
                         permission on the system. It IS root.

   THE nodev ESCALATION, IN THREE STEPS

   1. attacker creates a USB image containing:  /dev/sda  (b 8 0), mode 0666
   2. mounts it WITHOUT nodev
   3. writes to /media/usb/dev/sda -> raw disk write as an unprivileged user
   Mount options exist to close exactly this.

   ioctl: WHY IT IS THE CLASSIC ATTACK SURFACE

   ioctl(fd, SOME_CMD, user_pointer)
          ^      ^          ^
          |      |          +-- arbitrary, driver-interpreted, often a struct
          |      +------------- arbitrary number the driver switches on
          +-------------------- any device the process can open
   The kernel cannot type-check this. Every driver must validate it itself.

   CAPABILITIES vs setuid-root

   setuid root binary : holds ALL of root's powers for its whole lifetime
   CAP_NET_RAW only   : may open raw sockets; may NOT read /etc/shadow,
                        load modules, or write raw devices
```

```bash
# Layer 2: device permissions, and what they actually grant.
ls -l /dev/sda /dev/null /dev/mem /dev/kmsg
#   brw-rw----  root disk    /dev/sda    <- 'disk' group == root, effectively
#   crw-rw-rw-  root root    /dev/null   <- harmless, so world-writable
#   crw-r-----  root kmem    /dev/mem    <- all physical memory; usually disabled
grep CONFIG_STRICT_DEVMEM /boot/config-$(uname -r)    # =y means /dev/mem is limited
getent group disk kmem video                          # audit who is in these

# Layer 3: capabilities instead of setuid.
getcap /usr/bin/ping
#   /usr/bin/ping cap_net_raw=ep          <- NOT setuid root any more
sudo setcap cap_net_bind_service=+ep /usr/local/bin/myserver   # bind port 80 only
getpcaps $$                               # this shell's capabilities
capsh --print | head -5
find / -perm -4000 -type f 2>/dev/null    # audit remaining setuid binaries

# Layer 4: mount options on anything a user can supply.
mount | grep -E 'nodev|nosuid|noexec'
# /etc/fstab for removable media:
#   /dev/sdb1  /media/usb  auto  rw,nosuid,nodev,noexec,noauto,user  0  0
findmnt -o TARGET,OPTIONS /tmp /home /media

# Layer 5: the IOMMU.
dmesg | grep -iE 'DMAR: IOMMU enabled|AMD-Vi: .*initialized'
ls /sys/kernel/iommu_groups/ | wc -l
# Passthrough is only as isolated as the GROUP:
for g in /sys/kernel/iommu_groups/*/devices/*; do
  echo "group ${g#*groups/} -> $(lspci -s $(basename $g) | cut -c1-60)"
done | sort | head
# Two devices in one group cannot be separated: pass through both, or neither.

# Layer 6: sandboxing.
systemd-analyze security sshd              # per-unit exposure score
# Hardening directives in a unit file:
#   PrivateDevices=yes      -> a minimal private /dev
#   DeviceAllow=/dev/null rw
#   RestrictAddressFamilies=AF_INET AF_INET6
#   SystemCallFilter=@system-service
#   NoNewPrivileges=yes

# Containers get their own /dev by default.
docker run --rm alpine ls /dev             # a short, safe list
docker run --rm --privileged alpine ls /dev | wc -l   # everything: avoid
docker run --rm --device=/dev/snd alpine ls /dev/snd  # grant ONE device

# udev decides ownership and mode as devices appear.
cat <<'EOF' | sudo tee /etc/udev/rules.d/99-mydev.rules
SUBSYSTEM=="usb", ATTR{idVendor}=="1234", MODE="0660", GROUP="plugdev"
EOF
sudo udevadm control --reload && sudo udevadm trigger
```

```c
// Validating an ioctl: what every driver must do, and what attackers rely on
// drivers forgetting.
static long my_ioctl(struct file *f, unsigned int cmd, unsigned long arg)
{
    struct my_request req;

    // (1) Validate the command's magic number: reject anything not ours.
    if (_IOC_TYPE(cmd) != MY_IOC_MAGIC)
        return -ENOTTY;
    if (_IOC_NR(cmd) > MY_IOC_MAXNR)
        return -ENOTTY;

    // (2) Validate the size encoded in the command against our struct.
    if (_IOC_SIZE(cmd) != sizeof(req))
        return -EINVAL;

    // (3) Check privilege PER OPERATION, not once at open().
    //     An fd can be passed to another process over a UNIX socket.
    if (cmd == MY_IOC_RAW_ACCESS && !capable(CAP_SYS_RAWIO))
        return -EPERM;

    // (4) Copy in safely -- never dereference the user pointer directly.
    if (copy_from_user(&req, (void __user *)arg, sizeof(req)))
        return -EFAULT;

    // (5) Validate EVERY field AFTER copying. Checking before the copy is
    //     a time-of-check-to-time-of-use bug: user space can change it.
    if (req.offset > DEVICE_SIZE || req.length > DEVICE_SIZE - req.offset)
        return -EINVAL;                     // this check stops the classic
                                            // integer-overflow out-of-bounds
    return do_operation(&req);
}
```

**Key takeaways**

- Device access is a privilege boundary: raw block access bypasses every file permission, and DMA-capable devices can reach all of physical memory.
- Privileged I/O instructions and unmapped MMIO regions mean user code can only reach devices through system calls.
- Device node permissions matter enormously — membership of the `disk` group is effectively root — and `nodev` stops device nodes on user-supplied media becoming an escalation path.
- Capabilities subdivide root's powers so a program can hold exactly `CAP_NET_RAW` or `CAP_SYS_RAWIO` rather than everything.
- The IOMMU is the only defence against a malicious or buggy device doing arbitrary DMA, and it is what makes passthrough and hot-plug safe.
- `ioctl` is untyped by construction, so every driver must validate the command number, the size, the caller's privilege, and every field after copying it in.
