> 1. Explain why adding a user to the `disk` group is equivalent to giving them root, with a concrete sequence of commands they could run.
> 2. Compare a setuid-root binary with one holding only `CAP_NET_RAW`, listing two things the former can do that the latter cannot.
> 3. Interview-style: "Why is device passthrough to a VM unsafe without an IOMMU?" *Hint: think about what address space the device uses for DMA and who controls the values the guest programs into it.*

#### Device Reservation

**Theory**

Most devices multiplex happily: the kernel interleaves requests from many processes and each sees a coherent view. Some cannot. A tape drive has one physical position, so two processes writing alternately produce a useless tape. A CD burner in the middle of a session cannot serve anybody else. A serial port tied to an instrument needs one owner for the duration of the conversation. For these, the kernel or the application must arrange **exclusive access**.

The simplest mechanism is exclusive open. `open(O_EXCL)` on a block device fails if the device is already open by anybody, which is why you cannot `mkfs` a mounted file system. Windows has the same idea in `CreateFile`'s share mode. This is enforced by the kernel and cannot be ignored, unlike the advisory file locks of Section 10.1.

Advisory mechanisms cover the rest. **Lock files** in `/var/lock` are the traditional UNIX convention for serial ports and similar devices, with the format `LCK..ttyS0` containing the owner's PID. They only work if every program participates — which, by convention, they mostly do. `flock` on the device node is the modern equivalent and is automatically released when the holder dies, which avoids the stale-lock problem that plagues PID files.

Once processes wait for exclusive devices, **deadlock becomes possible**, and this is Chapter 6 applied to hardware. A process holding the tape drive and requesting the scanner, while another holds the scanner and requests the tape drive, is the textbook circular wait — with the added difficulty that preemption is often impossible (you cannot take a tape drive away mid-write) and rollback is meaningless (you cannot un-burn a CD). The practical defences are the familiar ones: impose a global ordering on device acquisition, acquire everything at once or nothing, and always use timeouts so a wedged holder does not block the system forever.

Three practical issues complete the picture.

**Stale locks.** A process holding an exclusive device that dies without cleaning up leaves the device unusable. Kernel-enforced mechanisms (`O_EXCL`, `flock`) release automatically on process exit; PID files do not, so any PID-file scheme needs a liveness check — and a PID can be reused, so the check must be more than "does this PID exist".

**Timeouts.** Every acquisition should be bounded. A batch job that blocks forever on a device somebody forgot to release is an outage, not a wait.

**Virtualisation.** In containers and VMs the question becomes which guest gets the device. Passthrough (VFIO) gives one guest exclusive control at IOMMU-group granularity; SR-IOV lets a capable device present multiple virtual functions so several guests each get a real, isolated slice; and mediated devices (vGPU) let a driver time-slice one physical device among several guests. These are the modern forms of the same reservation problem.

**Example**

```text
   WHY SOME DEVICES CANNOT BE INTERLEAVED

   SHAREABLE (disk)                   NON-SHAREABLE (tape)
   P1: write block 100                P1: write record   -> tape advances
   P2: write block 500                P2: write record   -> tape advances
   P1: write block 101                P1: write record   -> tape advances
   the file system keeps them          one physical position; the records
   separate; both are correct          interleave and BOTH streams are ruined

   THE MECHANISMS, FROM STRONGEST TO WEAKEST

   O_EXCL on a block device : KERNEL-ENFORCED. Cannot be bypassed.
                              Released automatically on process exit.
   flock on the device node : advisory, but kernel-tracked and
                              auto-released on exit. The sane default.
   /var/lock/LCK..ttyS0     : pure convention. Works only if everyone
                              participates. Goes STALE if the holder dies.

   DEADLOCK WITH DEVICES (Chapter 6, in hardware)

   P1: holds TAPE     waits for SCANNER
   P2: holds SCANNER  waits for TAPE
        +--------+                +----------+
        |   P1   |--- wants ----->| SCANNER  |
        +--------+                +----------+
             ^                         |
          holds                      holds
             |                         v
        +----------+             +--------+
        |   TAPE   |<-- wants ---|   P2   |
        +----------+             +--------+

   Worse than software deadlock: you cannot PREEMPT a tape drive
   mid-write, and you cannot ROLL BACK a burned disc.
   Defences: global acquisition ORDER, all-or-nothing acquisition, TIMEOUTS.

   THE STALE-LOCK PROBLEM

   PID file    : holder is SIGKILLed -> file remains -> device unusable
                 forever, and the PID may be REUSED by an unrelated process
   flock/O_EXCL: holder dies -> kernel releases the lock -> next waiter
                 proceeds. This is why kernel-tracked locks are preferred.

   VIRTUALISATION: THE SAME QUESTION, NEW FORMS

   passthrough (VFIO) : one guest owns the device; granularity is the
                        entire IOMMU GROUP, not one function
   SR-IOV             : the device presents N virtual functions; each
                        guest gets a real, isolated slice
   mediated (vGPU)    : a host driver time-slices one device among guests
```

```python
import os, fcntl, errno, time, contextlib

# ---------- 1. Kernel-enforced exclusivity on a block device ----------
def open_block_exclusive(path):
    """O_EXCL on a block device fails if ANYONE has it open -- including
       the kernel, if it is mounted. This is why mkfs refuses."""
    try:
        return os.open(path, os.O_RDWR | os.O_EXCL)
    except OSError as e:
        if e.errno == errno.EBUSY:
            raise RuntimeError(f"{path} is mounted or already held") from e
        raise

# ---------- 2. flock: advisory, but auto-released on process death ----------
@contextlib.contextmanager
def device_lock(path, timeout=10.0):
    f = open(path, "r+b")
    deadline = time.monotonic() + timeout
    while True:
        try:
            fcntl.flock(f, fcntl.LOCK_EX | fcntl.LOCK_NB)
            break
        except BlockingIOError:
            if time.monotonic() > deadline:        # ALWAYS bound the wait
                f.close()
                raise TimeoutError(f"{path} held by another process")
            time.sleep(0.05)
    try:
        yield f
    finally:
        fcntl.flock(f, fcntl.LOCK_UN)
        f.close()
    # If this process is SIGKILLed mid-block, the kernel releases the lock.
    # A PID file would have been left behind, stale, forever.

# ---------- 3. Multiple devices: a global order prevents deadlock ----------
DEVICE_ORDER = {"/dev/st0": 1, "/dev/sg1": 2, "/dev/ttyUSB0": 3}

@contextlib.contextmanager
def acquire_all(paths, timeout=10.0):
    """Acquire in a FIXED GLOBAL ORDER, so a cycle cannot form."""
    ordered = sorted(paths, key=lambda p: DEVICE_ORDER.get(p, 999))
    held = []
    try:
        for p in ordered:
            cm = device_lock(p, timeout)
            held.append((p, cm, cm.__enter__()))
        yield [h[2] for h in held]
    finally:
        for _, cm, _ in reversed(held):            # release in reverse order
            with contextlib.suppress(Exception):
                cm.__exit__(None, None, None)

# P1 asking for {tape, scanner} and P2 asking for {scanner, tape} now BOTH
# acquire tape first. One waits; neither deadlocks.

# ---------- 4. Why PID files need a liveness check, and why it is not enough ----
def stale_lock_check(lockfile):
    try:
        with open(lockfile) as f:
            pid = int(f.read().strip())
    except (FileNotFoundError, ValueError):
        return "no lock"
    try:
        os.kill(pid, 0)                    # signal 0: existence test only
    except ProcessLookupError:
        return "STALE: holder is gone (safe to remove)"
    except PermissionError:
        return "held by another user's process"
    return "held (but the PID may have been REUSED by an unrelated process)"
```

```bash
# Kernel-enforced exclusivity, demonstrated.
sudo mount /dev/sdb1 /mnt/x
sudo mkfs.ext4 /dev/sdb1
#   /dev/sdb1 is mounted; will not make a filesystem here!
#   (mkfs opens with O_EXCL, and the mount holds it)
sudo umount /mnt/sdb1 && sudo mkfs.ext4 /dev/sdb1   # now it succeeds

# Who is holding a device open.
sudo fuser -v /dev/sdb1
sudo lsof /dev/ttyUSB0
#   COMMAND   PID  USER  FD  TYPE  DEVICE  NAME
#   minicom  4821   ana   3u  CHR  188,0   /dev/ttyUSB0

# The traditional serial-port convention, still in use.
ls -l /var/lock/
#   -rw-r--r-- 1 ana dialout 11 Sep 11 09:14 LCK..ttyUSB0
cat /var/lock/LCK..ttyUSB0        # the holder's PID, in ASCII
# Stale after a crash: nothing removes it. This is the scheme's weakness.

# The modern equivalent: kernel-tracked, self-releasing.
flock -x /dev/ttyUSB0 -c 'stty -F /dev/ttyUSB0 115200; cat /dev/ttyUSB0'
flock -n /dev/st0 -c 'tar cf /dev/st0 /data' || echo "tape drive busy"
cat /proc/locks | grep FLOCK

# Tape drives: the canonical non-shareable device.
mt -f /dev/st0 status
mt -f /dev/st0 rewind
tar cf /dev/nst0 /data            # 'n' = no-rewind: position is STATE

# Virtualisation: reserving a device for one guest.
lspci -nn | grep -i nvidia
echo 0000:01:00.0 | sudo tee /sys/bus/pci/devices/0000:01:00.0/driver/unbind
echo 10de 1b80    | sudo tee /sys/bus/pci/drivers/vfio-pci/new_id
ls /sys/kernel/iommu_groups/13/devices/    # ALL of these move together

# SR-IOV: one card, several isolated slices.
cat /sys/class/net/eth0/device/sriov_totalvfs
echo 4 | sudo tee /sys/class/net/eth0/device/sriov_numvfs
lspci | grep 'Virtual Function'
```

**Key takeaways**

- Some devices cannot be interleaved because they carry physical state — tape position, burn session, instrument conversation — so they need exclusive access.
- `O_EXCL` on a block device is kernel-enforced and cannot be bypassed, which is why `mkfs` refuses to format a mounted volume.
- `flock` on a device node is advisory but kernel-tracked and released automatically on process death, making it far safer than a PID lock file.
- Traditional `/var/lock/LCK..*` files work only by convention and go stale when the holder is killed; any PID scheme needs a liveness check, and even that is imperfect because PIDs are reused.
- Waiting for exclusive devices reintroduces deadlock, made worse because devices usually cannot be preempted or rolled back — so use a global acquisition order and always time out.
- In virtualised environments the same problem appears as passthrough (whole IOMMU group), SR-IOV (hardware-isolated slices), or mediated devices (time-sliced).

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. Explain why `mkfs` refuses to run on a mounted device and name the exact mechanism that prevents it.
> 2. Two programs need both a tape drive and a scanner. Show the acquisition order that makes deadlock impossible, and explain why it works.
> 3. Interview-style: "A serial-port application leaves `/var/lock/LCK..ttyUSB0` behind after a crash, and the device stays unusable. Fix it properly." *Hint: the problem is that nothing is tracking liveness; ask which locking mechanism the kernel cleans up on its own when a process dies.*

#### STREAMS

**Theory**

STREAMS is a framework from UNIX System V for building character-device and network I/O paths out of **stackable, reusable modules**. Its practical importance today is limited — Linux never adopted it and Solaris was its main home — but it is worth understanding because the idea it embodies is everywhere, and because it makes a clean case study in a design trade-off.

The problem it addressed: a terminal driver, a network protocol stack, and a pseudo-terminal all need similar processing steps — line editing, character translation, flow control, protocol framing — and in a monolithic driver each one reimplements them. STREAMS proposed making each step a **module** with a standard interface, so a path could be assembled by pushing modules onto a stack at runtime.

A stream has three parts:

1. The **stream head**, at the top, interfacing with user system calls.
2. Zero or more **modules** in the middle, each with a read queue and a write queue, doing one transformation.
3. The **driver end**, at the bottom, talking to the device.

Modules communicate by passing **messages** up and down the queues, never by calling each other directly, and each queue has high and low water marks for flow control. Because the interface is uniform, `ioctl(fd, I_PUSH, "ldterm")` can insert a line-discipline module onto a live stream, and `I_POP` removes it. The composability is genuine: a TCP connection over a tunnel over a compression module is just three modules stacked.

The costs are what kept it from dominating. Every message crosses every module, so each layer adds allocation, queueing, and scheduling overhead on a path that is extremely hot. The message-based flow-control model is subtle and hard to reason about. And the flexibility is rarely needed at runtime — most stacks are known at compile time, so paying a runtime-composition cost forever to enable reconfiguration that almost nobody performs is a poor trade. Linux chose specialised, tightly-coupled paths (the tty layer with its line disciplines, `netfilter` hooks in the network stack) and got better performance with less generality.

The idea, however, won everywhere that performance is not the binding constraint. Linux **line disciplines** are STREAMS modules in all but name — `N_TTY` for terminals, `N_PPP`, `N_SLIP` — pushed onto a tty to change how bytes are processed. **Netfilter** hooks let modules inspect and transform packets at defined points. **eBPF** attaches programs at hook points throughout the kernel. Outside the kernel, the same shape appears in Unix pipelines, servlet filters, HTTP middleware chains, audio and video plugin graphs, and every service mesh sidecar.

The transferable lesson: **stackable modules with a uniform message interface buy composability and cost per-layer overhead.** That trade is right when paths change or vary and wrong on a path where every nanosecond is counted.

**Example**

```text
   A STREAM: HEAD, MODULES, DRIVER

   user process
        |  read() / write() / ioctl()
   +----v--------------------+
   |     STREAM HEAD         |  the system-call interface
   +----+--------------------+
        |  messages down  ^  messages up
   +----v-----------------+--+
   |  MODULE: ldterm      |     line discipline: echo, erase, line buffering
   |  [write q] [read q]  |
   +----+-----------------+--+
        |                 ^
   +----v-----------------+--+
   |  MODULE: compress    |     pushed at RUNTIME with I_PUSH
   |  [write q] [read q]  |
   +----+-----------------+--+
        |                 ^
   +----v-----------------+--+
   |  DRIVER END          |     the actual hardware
   +----+--------------------+
        v
     serial port

   Each module has TWO queues and does ONE transformation.
   Modules never call each other: they pass MESSAGES.

   RUNTIME COMPOSITION -- the feature that justified the design

   ioctl(fd, I_PUSH, "ldterm");     insert line editing
   ioctl(fd, I_PUSH, "compress");   insert compression underneath it
   ioctl(fd, I_POP,  0);            remove the topmost module
   ioctl(fd, I_LIST, &list);        what is currently stacked

   THE COST

   monolithic tty driver : one function call chain, one buffer
   STREAMS               : message alloc + enqueue + scheduling PER MODULE
                           on a path handling millions of bytes per second
   Generality is not free, and this path is extremely hot.

   THE SAME IDEA, WHERE IT ACTUALLY WON

   Linux line disciplines : N_TTY, N_PPP, N_SLIP pushed onto a tty
   netfilter              : PREROUTING -> FORWARD -> POSTROUTING hooks
   eBPF                   : programs attached at defined kernel hook points
   shell pipelines        : cmd | filter | filter | sink
   HTTP middleware        : auth -> log -> compress -> handler
   audio/video graphs     : GStreamer, JACK, Web Audio nodes
```

```c
// STREAMS as it was actually used (System V / Solaris).
#include <stropts.h>

int build_stream(const char *path)
{
    int fd = open(path, O_RDWR);
    struct str_list list;
    char names[8][FMNAMESZ + 1];
    int i;

    // Push modules onto the stream. Order matters: the LAST pushed is
    // the TOPMOST, i.e. closest to the user process.
    ioctl(fd, I_PUSH, "ldterm");      // line discipline: erase, kill, echo
    ioctl(fd, I_PUSH, "ttcompat");    // BSD tty compatibility translation

    // Inspect the current stack.
    list.sl_nmods    = 8;
    list.sl_modlist  = (struct str_mlist *)names;
    if (ioctl(fd, I_LIST, &list) >= 0)
        for (i = 0; i < list.sl_nmods; i++)
            printf("module %d: %s\n", i, names[i]);   // ttcompat, ldterm, driver

    ioctl(fd, I_POP, 0);              // remove ttcompat, leaving ldterm

    // Messages, not byte streams: control and data are separate bands.
    struct strbuf ctl  = { .len = sizeof(cmd),  .buf = (char *)&cmd  };
    struct strbuf data = { .len = payload_len,  .buf = payload       };
    putmsg(fd, &ctl, &data, 0);       // send a control + data message down

    int flags = 0;
    getmsg(fd, &ctl, &data, &flags);  // receive one from above
    return fd;
}
```

```bash
# Linux's line disciplines: the surviving form of the same idea.
cat /proc/tty/ldiscs
#   n_tty  0        <- the default: cooked mode, line editing, signals
#   n_ppp  3
#   n_hdlc 13
cat /proc/tty/drivers

# Pushing a different discipline onto a live tty -- STREAMS' I_PUSH, in effect.
sudo ldattach PPP /dev/ttyS0          # attach the PPP discipline
sudo ldattach -d GPS /dev/ttyUSB0     # NMEA GPS discipline

# The line discipline's transformations, switched off and on.
stty -a -F /dev/pts/0
#   speed 38400 baud; line = 0;
#   -icanon -echo    <- raw: no line editing, no echo (what vim sets)
#   icanon echo      <- cooked: the discipline does erase/kill/echo for you
stty raw -echo; stty sane             # toggle, then restore

# Netfilter: modules at defined hook points in the packet path.
sudo nft list ruleset | head -20
sudo iptables -L -v -n --line-numbers
# PREROUTING -> [modules] -> FORWARD -> [modules] -> POSTROUTING

# eBPF: the modern, verified, JIT-compiled version of "push a module".
sudo bpftool prog list | head
sudo bpftool net list                 # programs attached at network hooks
sudo tc filter add dev eth0 ingress bpf obj filter.o sec ingress

# The userspace expression of exactly the same pattern.
cat access.log | grep ' 500 ' | awk '{print $1}' | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn
#      ^ source    ^ filter    ^ transform    ^ aggregate    ^ sink
# Each stage does one thing, communicates only through the stream between
# them, and can be reordered or replaced independently.
```

**Key takeaways**

- STREAMS builds an I/O path from stackable modules, each with a read and a write queue, communicating only by passing messages.
- A stream is a head (system-call interface), zero or more modules, and a driver end; modules are pushed and popped at runtime with `I_PUSH` and `I_POP`.
- The benefit is genuine composability and reuse — one line-discipline module serves every terminal-like device.
- The cost is per-module message allocation, queueing, and scheduling on a very hot path, which is why Linux chose specialised paths instead.
- The idea survives as line disciplines, netfilter hooks, and eBPF attachment points in the kernel, and as pipelines, middleware chains, and media graphs outside it.
- The transferable lesson is the trade itself: uniform stackable interfaces buy flexibility and cost per-layer overhead, which is right when paths vary and wrong when nanoseconds are counted.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. Name the three parts of a stream and state what each is responsible for.
> 2. Run `cat /proc/tty/ldiscs` and `stty -a`, then explain which transformations the current line discipline is applying to your terminal.
> 3. Interview-style: "Why did Linux reject STREAMS but adopt netfilter hooks, which look like the same idea?" *Hint: compare how often each path is traversed, and how much processing happens per traversal, then ask where a fixed per-module overhead actually hurts.*

#### I/O Performance Tuning

**Theory**

I/O is where most systems spend their waiting time, so tuning it has outsized effect — and it is also where guessing does the most damage, because the layers interact and a change that helps one workload devastates another. The discipline is therefore: measure, identify the actual bottleneck, change one thing, measure again.

The first question is always **which resource is saturated**. There are only a few candidates, and each has a distinctive signature:

| Bottleneck | Signature | Where to look |
|---|---|---|
| Device throughput | `%util` near 100, queue depth high, `await` rising | `iostat -x` |
| Device latency | `await` high, `%util` moderate, queue shallow | `iostat`, `biolatency` |
| CPU in the I/O path | High `%sys` or `%soft`, low `%util` | `mpstat`, `perf top` |
| Interrupt handling | One core at 100% `%soft`, others idle | `/proc/interrupts`, `mpstat -P ALL` |
| Memory / cache | High page-cache miss rate, heavy `swap` | `/proc/meminfo`, `vmstat` |
| Application | Device idle, low CPU, poor throughput | `strace -c`, flame graphs |

Two derived numbers are worth internalising. **Little's Law** — concurrency = throughput × latency — tells you how many operations must be in flight to reach a target rate: 100,000 IOPS at 100 µs latency requires 10 operations outstanding at all times. If the application submits one at a time, the queue depth is 1 and no amount of device speed helps. This single relation explains most "the hardware is fast but the application is slow" situations.

And **the latency curve is not linear**. Utilisation of 90% is not "10% of headroom left"; queueing theory puts average wait at `service_time × u/(1-u)`, so going from 80% to 90% utilisation doubles the wait, and 95% doubles it again. Systems should be sized so that normal load sits well below the knee.

The levers, roughly in order of typical payoff:

1. **Fix the application's access pattern.** Sequential instead of random, batched instead of per-item, larger requests, and enough concurrency to fill the device. This usually dwarfs every kernel tunable.
2. **Match the request size.** Too small wastes per-request overhead; too large adds latency. Align to the device's preferred size, and align partitions and file system blocks to physical sectors.
3. **Increase queue depth** if the device is idle and the application is serialised — via threads, async I/O, or `io_uring`.
4. **Choose the right scheduler**: `none` for NVMe, `mq-deadline` or `bfq` otherwise.
5. **Tune caching and writeback**: `dirty_ratio`, `dirty_background_ratio`, read-ahead size, and `vm.swappiness`.
6. **Spread interrupts** across cores and enable coalescing where latency permits.
7. **Remove copies** with `sendfile`, `splice`, or registered buffers if the profile shows `memcpy` dominating.
8. **Consider `O_DIRECT`** only when the application has a better-informed cache of its own.

Three warnings. Benchmark the **real workload** — synthetic sequential reads predict nothing about a random-read database. Change **one variable at a time**, or the result is uninterpretable. And know your **target metric**: throughput and latency tuning pull in opposite directions, and the settings that maximise one (large batches, deep queues, aggressive coalescing) systematically harm the other.

**Example**

```text
   THE DIAGNOSTIC LADDER -- work top to bottom, do not skip

   1. Is the DEVICE busy?           iostat -x 1   -> %util
        no  -> the bottleneck is above it (app, CPU, locks, serialisation)
        yes -> continue
   2. Is it LATENCY or THROUGHPUT?  r_await / w_await vs r/s + rMB/s
        latency high, queue shallow -> per-request cost; check alignment/size
        queue deep, bandwidth at spec -> genuinely saturated; add devices
   3. Is CPU the limit?             mpstat -P ALL 1
        one core 100% %soft  -> interrupt affinity / coalescing
        high %sys everywhere -> copies, syscall rate; check strace -c
   4. Is MEMORY the limit?          free -h ; vmstat 1
        cache too small, or swapping

   LITTLE'S LAW: THE MOST USEFUL LINE OF ARITHMETIC IN I/O

     concurrency = throughput x latency

     target 100,000 IOPS, device latency 100 us
       => need 100,000 x 0.0001 = 10 requests IN FLIGHT at all times
     an application doing synchronous one-at-a-time I/O has depth 1
       => achieves 1 / 0.0001 = 10,000 IOPS, and NO device upgrade helps

   THE UTILISATION KNEE (wait = service x u/(1-u))

   u     | relative wait     100% |                        *
   ------+---------------         |                       *
   0.50  |  1.0x                  |                     *
   0.80  |  4.0x             wait |                  *
   0.90  |  9.0x                  |              *
   0.95  | 19.0x                  |        *
   0.99  | 99.0x                  |  *  *
                              0%  +------------------------- utilisation
                                  0%                      100%
   "90% utilised" is not "10% of headroom": it is already 9x the wait.

   THROUGHPUT AND LATENCY PULL IN OPPOSITE DIRECTIONS

   for THROUGHPUT           for LATENCY
     deep queues              shallow queues
     large requests           small requests
     interrupt coalescing     coalescing off (rx-usecs 0)
     aggressive read-ahead    read-ahead off for random access
     batched commits          fsync per operation
   Decide WHICH ONE you are optimising before changing anything.
```

```bash
# ---------- STEP 1: where is the time going? ----------
iostat -x 1 5
#   Device   r/s    w/s   rMB/s  rareq-sz  aqu-sz  r_await  w_await  %util
#   nvme0n1  8420   120   32.9   4.0       12.3    1.42     0.31     94.2
#            ^IOPS        ^BW    ^avg size ^depth  ^latency(ms)      ^busy
# %util ~100 + deep queue + rising await = the device is the bottleneck.
# %util low + poor throughput            = look UP the stack, not down.

mpstat -P ALL 1 5          # %soft pinned on one core = interrupt affinity issue
vmstat 1 5                 # 'b' = blocked on I/O; 'wa' = iowait; 'si/so' = swap
free -h                    # is the page cache being squeezed?

# ---------- STEP 2: what is the latency distribution, not the average? ----------
sudo biolatency-bpfcc -m 10 1      # histogram: averages hide the p99 tail
sudo biosnoop-bpfcc | head -20     # per-I/O: process, sector, size, latency
sudo biotop-bpfcc                  # which process is generating the load
sudo funclatency-bpfcc vfs_read

# ---------- STEP 3: is the application the problem? ----------
strace -c -p $(pgrep -n myapp)
#   % time  calls    syscall
#    62.1   482911   read          <- 482,911 reads: what size were they?
strace -e trace=read -p $(pgrep -n myapp) 2>&1 | head -5
#   read(7, "...", 512) = 512      <- 512-byte reads on a 4 KB device:
#                                     8x the necessary request count
sudo perf top -p $(pgrep -n myapp)
sudo perf record -g -p $(pgrep -n myapp) -- sleep 10 && sudo perf report

# ---------- STEP 4: the tunables, one at a time ----------
# scheduler
echo none | sudo tee /sys/block/nvme0n1/queue/scheduler

# read-ahead: raise for sequential, drop to 0 for random
sudo blockdev --setra 512 /dev/sda        # 256 KB
sudo blockdev --setra 0   /dev/nvme0n1    # random workload: prefetch is waste

# writeback: keep the dirty pool small so flushes never stall the system
sudo sysctl -w vm.dirty_background_bytes=134217728    # 128 MB
sudo sysctl -w vm.dirty_bytes=536870912               # 512 MB
sudo sysctl -w vm.swappiness=10                       # protect the page cache

# queue depth
cat /sys/block/nvme0n1/queue/nr_requests
echo 1024 | sudo tee /sys/block/nvme0n1/queue/nr_requests

# interrupts: spread them, and coalesce if latency permits
systemctl status irqbalance
sudo ethtool -C eth0 rx-usecs 50 rx-frames 64    # throughput
sudo ethtool -C eth0 rx-usecs 0                  # latency
sudo ethtool -G eth0 rx 2048                     # bigger NIC ring

# ---------- STEP 5: measure the REAL workload, not a synthetic one ----------
fio --name=realistic --filename=/dev/nvme0n1 --direct=1 \
    --rw=randrw --rwmixread=70 --bs=8k --iodepth=32 --numjobs=4 \
    --runtime=60 --time_based --group_reporting --percentile_list=50:95:99:99.9
#   read: IOPS=284k, BW=2.2GiB/s
#   clat percentiles (usec): 50.00th=[95], 99.00th=[412], 99.90th=[1729]
#                                                          ^ the number users feel
```

```python
# Little's Law and the utilisation knee: the two calculations to do FIRST.
def required_concurrency(target_iops, latency_us):
    return target_iops * (latency_us / 1e6)

def achievable_iops(queue_depth, latency_us):
    return queue_depth / (latency_us / 1e6)

print("TARGET 100,000 IOPS on a device with 100 us latency")
print(f"  requests that must be in flight: "
      f"{required_concurrency(100_000, 100):.0f}\n")

print(f"{'queue depth':>12}{'achievable IOPS':>18}")
for qd in (1, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64):
    print(f"{qd:>12}{achievable_iops(qd, 100):>18,.0f}")
print("  -> a synchronous, one-at-a-time application is capped at 10,000 IOPS")
print("     regardless of how fast the device is.\n")

# The queueing knee: why 90% utilisation is not '10% of headroom left'.
def wait_multiplier(u):
    return u / (1 - u)

print(f"{'utilisation':>12}{'wait vs service time':>24}")
for u in (0.5, 0.7, 0.8, 0.9, 0.95, 0.99):
    print(f"{u:>11.0%}{wait_multiplier(u):>22.1f}x")

# Request size: the trade between per-request overhead and per-request latency.
OVERHEAD_US, US_PER_KB = 5.0, 0.4
print(f"\n{'req size':>10}{'reqs for 1 MB':>15}{'total us':>11}{'per-req lat':>13}")
for kb in (4, 16, 64, 256, 1024):
    reqs  = 1024 // kb
    per   = OVERHEAD_US + US_PER_KB * kb
    print(f"{kb:>8} KB{reqs:>15}{reqs*per:>11.0f}{per:>12.1f}us")
# Bigger requests: better throughput, worse per-request latency. Pick one.
```

**Key takeaways**

- Tuning starts with identifying which resource is saturated; each bottleneck has a distinctive signature across `iostat`, `mpstat`, `vmstat`, and profiling tools.
- Little's Law (concurrency = throughput × latency) shows why a synchronous application cannot reach a fast device's rated IOPS regardless of hardware.
- Wait time grows as `u/(1-u)`, so 90% utilisation already means nine times the service time in queueing — size systems well below the knee.
- The application's access pattern and request size usually matter far more than any kernel tunable.
- Throughput and latency tuning pull in opposite directions: deep queues, large requests, and coalescing help the first and harm the second.
- Benchmark the real workload, change one variable at a time, and look at percentile latency rather than averages, because averages hide the tail users actually experience.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. A device has 80 µs average latency. Compute the queue depth needed to sustain 50,000 IOPS, and the IOPS achievable at queue depth 1.
> 2. Run `iostat -x 1` during a heavy copy and interpret `%util`, `aqu-sz`, and `r_await`. State which resource is the bottleneck and how you concluded it.
> 3. Interview-style: "A service's average I/O latency is 2 ms and users complain constantly about slowness. The dashboards look fine. What is happening?" *Hint: ask which statistic a user actually experiences during a request, and what an average conceals about the shape of a distribution.*

<a id="12-protection-and-security"></a>
## 12. Protection and Security

Every abstraction in this book — processes, address spaces, files, devices — is also a boundary, and a boundary is only meaningful if something enforces it. This chapter covers the mechanisms operating systems use to decide who may do what (protection), the threats those mechanisms exist to resist (security), and the defensive techniques that have accumulated as attackers defeated each earlier generation of them. It matters because every other guarantee in the system rests on these: a scheduler's fairness, a file system's permissions, and a hypervisor's isolation are all worth exactly as much as the protection machinery underneath them.

Two terms are used precisely throughout. **Protection** is the internal mechanism: how the system controls access by programs and users to its own resources. **Security** is the broader question of whether the system's data and behaviour can be trusted in the presence of an adversary — which includes protection, but also authentication, cryptography, physical access, and the humans involved. Protection is a mechanism; security is a property.

<a id="121-protection-mechanisms"></a>
### 12.1 Protection Mechanisms

This section covers the models operating systems use to express and enforce access decisions: the guiding principle, the abstraction of a protection domain, the matrix that describes all permissions, its two practical implementations, and the two policy models that scale it to real organisations.

#### Principle of Least Privilege

**Theory**

The most useful idea in this entire chapter is also the simplest: **every program, user, and process should have exactly the privileges required for its task, and no more.** It is the principle of least privilege, and nearly every other mechanism in this section is a way of implementing it.

The reasoning is about damage limitation, not prevention. Assume — correctly — that some component will be compromised: a bug will be exploited, a credential will leak, an administrator will be careless. The question then becomes not "how do we make that impossible" but "how much can the attacker do afterwards". If a PDF viewer runs with full user privileges, a bug in its font parser reads every file the user owns. If it runs in a sandbox that can read one file and write nothing, the same bug yields almost nothing.

The classic illustration is the hotel key. A guest gets a key to one room, housekeeping gets a floor, the manager gets everything. Losing a guest key costs one room. If every key opened every door, losing any key would cost the whole hotel. Least privilege is the observation that the number of doors a key opens is a choice, and usually a badly made one.

Three related principles are usually stated alongside it, and they interlock:

- **Fail-safe defaults.** Deny by default; permit by explicit grant. A firewall rule set that ends in `DROP` is safe when someone forgets a rule; one that ends in `ACCEPT` is not.
- **Separation of privilege.** Require more than one condition for a sensitive action — two-person authorisation, or splitting a daemon so that only a small part runs privileged.
- **Complete mediation.** Check every access, not just the first. Caching an authorisation decision means that revoking a right may not take effect.

The obstacle is not understanding the principle but applying it, because privilege is convenient and least privilege requires knowing exactly what a program needs. Systems therefore make it as easy as possible:

- **Privilege separation** splits a program so that only a tiny, auditable part runs with privilege. OpenSSH's design is the canonical example: the process handling untrusted network data runs unprivileged in a chroot, and hands narrow requests to a small monitor process.
- **Privilege dropping** acquires a privilege, uses it, and permanently discards it. A web server binds port 80 as root and then `setuid`s to `www-data` before serving a single request.
- **Capabilities** (next topics) subdivide root, so a program needing to bind a low port gets `CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE` rather than everything.
- **Sandboxing** restricts even the unprivileged case, which is Section 12.3.

The measure of success is a counterfactual: if this component were fully compromised right now, what could the attacker reach? That question, asked of each component in turn, is what least privilege operationalises.

**Example**

```text
   THE BLAST RADIUS OF ONE BUG

   WITHOUT least privilege          WITH least privilege
   +---------------------------+    +---------------------------+
   | web server runs as root   |    | root: binds :80, then     |
   |                           |    |       DROPS to www-data   |
   | bug in image parser       |    | bug in image parser       |
   |   -> read /etc/shadow     |    |   -> read only files      |
   |   -> write /etc/cron.d    |    |      www-data can read    |
   |   -> load a kernel module |    |   -> no writes outside    |
   |   -> FULL SYSTEM          |    |      /var/www/cache       |
   +---------------------------+    +---------------------------+
   one bug = total compromise       one bug = limited disclosure

   PRIVILEGE SEPARATION (the OpenSSH pattern)

           network (untrusted input)
                  |
       +----------v-----------+     narrow, typed requests
       | UNPRIVILEGED child   |------------------------+
       | - parses the protocol|                        |
       | - chroot, no creds   |                        v
       | - this is where bugs |          +-------------------------+
       |   will be found      |          | PRIVILEGED monitor      |
       +----------------------+          | - a few hundred lines   |
                                         | - "is this password ok?"|
       compromising the child gets       | - "make me a pty"       |
       the attacker a chrooted, +--------+ - audited exhaustively  |
       credential-less process           +-------------------------+

   THE THREE COMPANION PRINCIPLES

   fail-safe defaults    : default DENY; a forgotten rule fails closed
   separation of privilege: two conditions required for one sensitive act
   complete mediation    : check EVERY access, not only the first
                           (a cached decision survives a revocation)

   THE QUESTION TO ASK OF EVERY COMPONENT
     "If this were fully compromised right now, what could it reach?"
```

```python
import os, pwd, grp, resource

def drop_privileges(user="www-data", group="www-data"):
    """Acquire what you need as root, then discard root PERMANENTLY.
       Order matters: get the ids first, drop the group before the user,
       and verify afterwards."""
    if os.getuid() != 0:
        return                                   # nothing to drop

    pw = pwd.getpwnam(user)
    gid = grp.getgrnam(group).gr_gid

    # (1) Drop supplementary groups FIRST -- otherwise root's groups persist.
    os.setgroups([])

    # (2) Group before user: after setuid we no longer have the right to setgid.
    os.setgid(gid)

    # (3) setuid (not seteuid) makes the change PERMANENT and unrecoverable.
    os.setuid(pw.pw_uid)

    # (4) VERIFY. A failed drop that goes unnoticed is worse than no drop,
    #     because the code now believes it is unprivileged.
    if os.getuid() == 0 or os.geteuid() == 0:
        raise RuntimeError("privilege drop failed -- refusing to continue")

    # (5) Prove it is irreversible.
    try:
        os.setuid(0)
        raise RuntimeError("privileges were recoverable -- drop was ineffective")
    except PermissionError:
        pass                                     # correct: root is gone for good

def bind_then_drop(port=80):
    import socket
    s = socket.socket()
    s.setsockopt(socket.SOL_SOCKET, socket.SO_REUSEADDR, 1)
    s.bind(("", port))          # requires root (or CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE)
    s.listen(128)
    drop_privileges()           # ... and root is needed for nothing after this
    return s                    # the socket stays valid: the fd was already open

def restrict_self():
    """Belt and braces: shrink what this process can do even as a normal user."""
    resource.setrlimit(resource.RLIMIT_NOFILE, (256, 256))       # fd exhaustion
    resource.setrlimit(resource.RLIMIT_NPROC,  (64, 64))         # fork bombs
    resource.setrlimit(resource.RLIMIT_CORE,   (0, 0))           # no core dumps
    resource.setrlimit(resource.RLIMIT_AS, (512 << 20, 512 << 20))  # 512 MB
```

```bash
# Audit: what currently runs with more privilege than it needs?
ps -eo user,pid,comm --sort=user | awk '$1=="root"' | head -20
find / -perm -4000 -type f 2>/dev/null          # setuid binaries: each is a risk
find / -perm -2000 -type f 2>/dev/null          # setgid

# Replace setuid-root with one capability.
getcap /usr/bin/ping
#   /usr/bin/ping cap_net_raw=ep                <- not setuid root any more
sudo setcap cap_net_bind_service=+ep /usr/local/bin/myserver
sudo chmod u-s /usr/local/bin/myserver          # and remove the setuid bit

# systemd: least privilege declaratively, per service.
systemd-analyze security                        # rank every unit by exposure
systemd-analyze security nginx.service
#   NAME                    DESCRIPTION                    EXPOSURE
#   PrivateUsers=           Service has access to user db  0.3
#   ...
#   -> Overall exposure level for nginx.service: 6.8 MEDIUM

cat <<'EOF' | sudo tee /etc/systemd/system/myapp.service.d/hardening.conf
[Service]
User=myapp
Group=myapp
NoNewPrivileges=yes            # cannot gain privilege via setuid, ever
PrivateTmp=yes                 # its own /tmp, invisible to others
PrivateDevices=yes             # a minimal /dev
ProtectSystem=strict           # the entire filesystem is read-only...
ReadWritePaths=/var/lib/myapp  # ...except this
ProtectHome=yes                # /home, /root, /run/user are invisible
ProtectKernelTunables=yes
ProtectKernelModules=yes
RestrictAddressFamilies=AF_INET AF_INET6 AF_UNIX
SystemCallFilter=@system-service
SystemCallArchitectures=native
CapabilityBoundingSet=CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE
EOF
sudo systemctl daemon-reload && sudo systemctl restart myapp

# sudo: grant specific commands, not a shell.
sudo visudo
#   BAD : alice ALL=(ALL) NOPASSWD: ALL
#   BAD : alice ALL=(ALL) /bin/vi          <- vi can spawn a root shell (:!sh)
#   GOOD: alice ALL=(root) /usr/bin/systemctl restart nginx
sudo -l                                          # what may I actually run?
```

**Key takeaways**

- Least privilege means granting exactly the rights a task requires, and its purpose is to bound the damage from a compromise rather than prevent one.
- The operative question is counterfactual: if this component were fully compromised now, what could it reach?
- Fail-safe defaults (deny unless permitted), separation of privilege, and complete mediation are its companions.
- Privilege separation isolates untrusted input handling in an unprivileged process that makes narrow requests of a small privileged monitor.
- Privilege dropping acquires a right, uses it, and discards it permanently — and the drop must be verified, because a silently failed drop is worse than none.
- Capabilities, sandboxing, and systemd's per-service restrictions are the practical tooling that makes least privilege cheap enough to actually apply.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. List three privileges a typical web server needs at startup but not afterwards, and say how each can be dropped.
> 2. Run `find / -perm -4000 -type f` on your machine, pick one result, and explain what an attacker would gain by exploiting a bug in it.
> 3. Interview-style: "Why is `alice ALL=(ALL) /usr/bin/vi` in a sudoers file effectively equivalent to giving alice full root?" *Hint: think about what a text editor can do besides editing text, and whether the privilege ends when the file is saved.*

#### Protection Domains

**Theory**

Before you can decide whether an access is allowed, you need to know *who* is asking. The abstraction for that is the **protection domain**: a set of `(object, rights)` pairs defining exactly what its occupant may do. A process always executes within some domain, and every access it attempts is checked against that domain's rights.

The idea generalises several familiar things at once. In UNIX, a domain is essentially a `(uid, gid, supplementary groups)` triple — which is why changing user changes what you can touch. In a system with rings, the domain is the current privilege level: ring 0 may execute privileged instructions and ring 3 may not. In a capability system, the domain is literally the set of capabilities the process holds.

Domains may **overlap**, and this is the normal case rather than an exception: two users both having read access to `/etc/passwd` means their domains share that right. What matters is that overlap is deliberate — every shared right is a potential path between domains.

The interesting question is **domain switching**: how does a process change domains, and who controls it? Every switch is a privilege boundary, and every privilege boundary is attack surface.

- **System calls** switch from the user's domain to the kernel's, but only at defined entry points with validated arguments. The kernel does the work and returns; the user never executes in ring 0.
- **setuid execution** is UNIX's user-space domain switch: running a setuid binary changes the effective uid to the file's owner, so `passwd` can write `/etc/shadow` on behalf of an unprivileged user. This is genuinely necessary and genuinely dangerous — the binary now runs with the owner's rights while processing the caller's input, which is the classic setup for privilege escalation.
- **Explicit transitions** in mandatory access control systems (SELinux domain transitions) change the security context on `exec`, governed by policy rather than by a file bit.

The crucial design property is that a domain switch must be **controlled by the system, not the caller**. The caller decides *that* a switch happens (by running the program) but never *what rights result*. A setuid binary's rights come from its owner, not from whoever invoked it.

UNIX complicates the picture with three user IDs per process, and the distinction matters:

| ID | Purpose |
|---|---|
| **Real uid** | Who the user actually is; used for signals and accounting |
| **Effective uid** | What is checked for access decisions — the operative domain |
| **Saved uid** | A parked copy, letting a process drop privilege temporarily and regain it |

A setuid-root program starts with real uid = the caller, effective uid = 0, saved uid = 0. It may `seteuid(real)` to drop temporarily and `seteuid(saved)` to come back — useful, and a frequent source of bugs when code believes it has dropped privilege and has not.

**Example**

```text
   A DOMAIN IS A SET OF (OBJECT, RIGHTS) PAIRS

   D1 (user: alice)          D2 (user: www-data)      D3 (kernel)
   +---------------------+   +---------------------+  +------------------+
   | /home/alice: rwx    |   | /var/www:      r-x  |  | ALL memory: rw   |
   | /etc/passwd: r--    |   | /var/log/nginx: -w- |  | ALL devices: rw  |
   | /tmp:        rwx    |   | /etc/passwd:    r-- |  | priv. instrs: x  |
   +---------------------+   +---------------------+  +------------------+
              \                        /
               \______________________/
                  OVERLAP: both may read /etc/passwd.
                  Every overlap is a deliberate decision -- and a path
                  between domains if one of them is compromised.

   DOMAIN SWITCHING: THE THREE MECHANISMS

   (1) SYSTEM CALL          user domain --[defined entry, validated args]--> kernel
                            returns to the user domain when done

   (2) setuid EXEC          alice's domain --exec(/usr/bin/passwd)--> passwd's
                            domain (euid=root), because the FILE is owned by
                            root and has the setuid bit. Alice chose to run it;
                            alice did NOT choose the resulting rights.

   (3) POLICY TRANSITION    unconfined_t --exec(httpd)--> httpd_t
                            (SELinux: the POLICY decides, not a file bit)

   THE THREE UNIX USER IDs, IN A setuid-root PROGRAM

   alice runs /usr/bin/passwd (owner root, mode 4755)

       real uid      = 1000 (alice)   <- who you ARE; signals, accounting
       effective uid = 0    (root)    <- what is CHECKED for access
       saved uid     = 0    (root)    <- parked copy, so you can come back

   seteuid(1000)  -> euid 1000: privileges dropped TEMPORARILY
   seteuid(0)     -> euid 0:    regained from the SAVED id
   setuid(1000)   -> all three become 1000: PERMANENT, unrecoverable

   The bug pattern: code calls seteuid(), believes it is unprivileged,
   then an attacker triggers a path that calls seteuid(0) again.

   WHY setuid IS DANGEROUS
     the binary runs with the OWNER's rights
     while processing the CALLER's input:
       argv, environ, fds, cwd, umask, rlimits, signal dispositions
     ALL of these are attacker-controlled. Every one has been an exploit.
```

```c
// The three IDs, and the difference between temporary and permanent drops.
#include <unistd.h>
#include <stdio.h>

void show_ids(const char *label)
{
    uid_t r, e, s;
    getresuid(&r, &e, &s);                 // Linux: read all three at once
    printf("%-22s real=%d effective=%d saved=%d\n", label, r, e, s);
}

int main(void)
{
    show_ids("at start:");                 // real=1000 effective=0 saved=0

    // TEMPORARY drop: euid changes, saved uid still holds root.
    seteuid(getuid());
    show_ids("after seteuid(real):");      // real=1000 effective=1000 saved=0
    //                                                                 ^^^^^^
    // Privilege is NOT gone. Anything that calls seteuid(0) gets it back.

    seteuid(0);
    show_ids("after seteuid(0):");         // real=1000 effective=0 saved=0

    // PERMANENT drop: sets all three. This is what you almost always want.
    if (setresuid(getuid(), getuid(), getuid()) != 0)
        return 1;                          // ALWAYS check: a failed drop is
                                           // the classic escalation bug
    show_ids("after setresuid:");          // real=1000 effective=1000 saved=1000

    // Verify the drop is irreversible.
    if (seteuid(0) == 0) {
        fprintf(stderr, "FATAL: privileges were recoverable\n");
        return 1;
    }
    return 0;
}
```

```bash
# Which domain is this process in?
id
#   uid=1000(alice) gid=1000(alice) groups=1000(alice),27(sudo)
id -u; id -g; groups                         # the components of the domain
grep -E '^(Uid|Gid|Groups|CapEff):' /proc/self/status
#   Uid:  1000  1000  1000  1000             <- real, effective, saved, fs
#   CapEff: 0000000000000000                 <- capability component

# Watch a domain switch happen.
ls -l /usr/bin/passwd
#   -rwsr-xr-x 1 root root ... /usr/bin/passwd
#      ^ the 's' is the setuid bit: exec switches euid to the FILE'S OWNER
passwd &
grep Uid /proc/$!/status                     # Uid: 1000 0 0 0 -- euid is root

# SELinux domains: transitions decided by policy, not by a file bit.
id -Z                                        # unconfined_u:unconfined_r:unconfined_t
ps -eZ | grep httpd                          # system_u:system_r:httpd_t
sudo sesearch -T -s unconfined_t -t httpd_exec_t
#   type_transition unconfined_t httpd_exec_t : process httpd_t;

# Audit every setuid binary: each is a domain-switch point.
find / -perm -4000 -type f -exec ls -l {} \; 2>/dev/null
# Remove the bit where the program no longer needs it.
sudo chmod u-s /usr/bin/some-legacy-tool

# NoNewPrivileges: forbid domain elevation for a process and all its children.
systemd-run --uid=1000 -p NoNewPrivileges=yes --pty /bin/bash
# Inside: setuid binaries no longer elevate, at all.
grep NoNewPrivs /proc/self/status            # NoNewPrivs: 1
```

**Key takeaways**

- A protection domain is a set of `(object, rights)` pairs; a process always executes in one, and every access is checked against it.
- In UNIX the domain is essentially the uid/gid set; with rings it is the privilege level; in capability systems it is the held capability set.
- Domains commonly overlap, and each shared right is a deliberate connection between them.
- A domain switch must be controlled by the system: the caller decides that a switch occurs, never what rights result from it.
- `setuid` execution is UNIX's user-space domain switch and is inherently risky, because the program runs with the owner's rights while processing the caller's fully controlled input.
- The real/effective/saved uid triple allows temporary drops, and code that confuses a temporary drop with a permanent one is a recurring source of escalation bugs.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. Define a protection domain for a backup service, listing the objects it needs and the rights on each.
> 2. Explain the difference between `seteuid(1000)` and `setresuid(1000,1000,1000)` for a setuid-root process, and why the second is usually correct.
> 3. Interview-style: "Why is `NoNewPrivileges=yes` a strong hardening option even for a service that already runs unprivileged?" *Hint: consider what a compromised unprivileged process could otherwise execute, and what property of that execution the flag removes.*

#### Access Matrix

**Theory**

Once domains and objects exist, the complete protection state of a system is just a table: rows are domains, columns are objects, and each cell holds the rights that domain has on that object. This is the **access matrix**, and it is the reference model that every real mechanism approximates.

Its value is conceptual rather than implementational. It gives a precise vocabulary for questions like "what can this domain do?" (read a row), "who can touch this object?" (read a column), and "is this access permitted?" (look up one cell). Almost every access-control discussion becomes clearer when reduced to this form.

|  | file1 | file2 | printer | domain D2 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **D1** | read, write | read | — | switch |
| **D2** | — | read, write | print | — |
| **D3** | read | — | print | — |

Note the last column: **domains are themselves objects**, so the matrix can express the right to switch into another domain. That is what makes it a complete model rather than just a file-permission table.

The matrix also expresses how rights *change*, which is the part people usually forget. Special rights govern the matrix itself:

- **Owner**: the holder may add or remove any right in that object's column.
- **Copy** (often written `r*`): the holder may give this right to another domain. A copy right may be transferred (moving it) or copied (duplicating it), and the distinction matters for how far a right can propagate.
- **Control**: the holder may remove rights from another *domain's* row — a right over a domain, not over an object.

Once rights can propagate, **confinement** becomes the hard problem: can you grant a right while guaranteeing it goes no further? In general, no. Harrison, Ruzzo, and Ullman proved in 1976 that for a general access-control model with rights that can be created and copied, the **safety question** — "can this right ever leak to that domain?" — is *undecidable*. This is not a practical difficulty; it is a theoretical impossibility. Real systems escape it by restricting the model: take-grant systems, type-enforcement systems like SELinux, and systems that simply forbid arbitrary right propagation all make safety decidable by being less general.

The matrix's problem in practice is that it is enormous and almost entirely empty. A system with 10,000 users and 10 million files has a matrix of 100 billion cells, nearly all blank. Nobody stores it. Instead it is stored **by column** (access control lists, attached to objects) or **by row** (capabilities, held by domains) — which are the next two topics, and which are best understood as two ways of compressing the same table.

**Example**

```text
   THE ACCESS MATRIX (domains x objects, including domains AS objects)

                  | file1  | file2  | printer | D1     | D2     | D3
   ---------------+--------+--------+---------+--------+--------+--------
   D1 (alice)     | rw,own | r      |         |        | switch |
   D2 (www-data)  |        | rw,own | print   |        |        |
   D3 (backup)    | r      | r      |         |        |        |
                    ^                            ^
                    a CELL is the rights         domains are OBJECTS too,
                    D_i has on O_j               so 'switch' is expressible

   READING IT THREE WAYS

   ROW    (D1)     -> everything alice can do          = a CAPABILITY LIST
   COLUMN (file1)  -> everyone who can touch file1     = an ACCESS CONTROL LIST
   CELL   (D1,f1)  -> is this specific access allowed? = the authorisation check

   RIGHTS THAT CHANGE THE MATRIX ITSELF

   own      : may add/remove any right in that object's COLUMN
   copy (*) : may pass this right to another domain
              r*  = "read, and may grant read to others"
              transfer = the right MOVES; copy = it is DUPLICATED
   control  : may remove rights from another domain's ROW

   Before:  D1: file2 = r*          After D1 grants read to D3:
            D3: file2 = (none)       D1: file2 = r*
                                     D3: file2 = r      <- propagated

   THE SAFETY PROBLEM (Harrison-Ruzzo-Ullman, 1976)

   "Given this matrix and these rules, can right R ever reach domain D?"
                    -> UNDECIDABLE in the general model.

   Real systems regain decidability by being LESS GENERAL:
     - no arbitrary copy rights (classic UNIX)
     - type enforcement with a fixed policy (SELinux)
     - take-grant models with restricted propagation

   WHY NOBODY STORES THE MATRIX

   10,000 users x 10,000,000 files = 10^11 cells, ~99.99% EMPTY
   store by COLUMN -> ACL   (with the object: "who may touch me")
   store by ROW    -> CAPABILITIES ("what may I touch")
```

```python
from collections import defaultdict

class AccessMatrix:
    """The reference model, implemented sparsely -- as every real system does."""

    def __init__(self):
        self.cells = defaultdict(set)         # (domain, object) -> {rights}
        self.domains, self.objects = set(), set()

    def grant(self, domain, obj, *rights):
        self.cells[(domain, obj)].update(rights)
        self.domains.add(domain); self.objects.add(obj)

    def check(self, domain, obj, right):
        """One cell lookup: the authorisation decision."""
        return right in self.cells[(domain, obj)]

    def row(self, domain):
        """A domain's capability list: everything it may touch."""
        return {o: r for (d, o), r in self.cells.items() if d == domain and r}

    def column(self, obj):
        """An object's ACL: everyone who may touch it."""
        return {d: r for (d, o), r in self.cells.items() if o == obj and r}

    def copy_right(self, holder, receiver, obj, right):
        """Propagation requires the COPY right (written r*), not just r."""
        if f"{right}*" not in self.cells[(holder, obj)]:
            raise PermissionError(f"{holder} may not propagate '{right}' on {obj}")
        self.cells[(receiver, obj)].add(right)   # granted WITHOUT the star:
        self.domains.add(receiver)               # the receiver cannot re-grant

    def transfer_ownership(self, owner, obj, receiver, *rights):
        if "own" not in self.cells[(owner, obj)]:
            raise PermissionError(f"{owner} does not own {obj}")
        self.cells[(receiver, obj)].update(rights)

m = AccessMatrix()
m.grant("alice",    "file1", "read", "write", "own")
m.grant("alice",    "file2", "read*")          # read, AND may grant read
m.grant("www-data", "file2", "read", "write", "own")
m.grant("backup",   "file1", "read")
m.grant("alice",    "D2",    "switch")         # a domain used as an object

print("alice's capabilities :", m.row("alice"))
print("file1's ACL          :", m.column("file1"))
print("alice read file1?    :", m.check("alice", "file1", "read"))    # True
print("backup write file1?  :", m.check("backup", "file1", "write"))  # False

m.copy_right("alice", "backup", "file2", "read")      # allowed: alice holds read*
print("backup read file2?   :", m.check("backup", "file2", "read"))   # True
try:
    m.copy_right("backup", "eve", "file2", "read")    # backup got read, not read*
except PermissionError as e:
    print("propagation blocked  :", e)

# Sparsity: why the full table is never materialised.
full = len(m.domains) * len(m.objects)
print(f"\ncells stored {len([c for c in m.cells.values() if c])} of {full} possible "
      f"({len([c for c in m.cells.values() if c])/full:.0%} occupied)")
```

```bash
# The column view: an object's ACL.
getfacl /var/www/html/index.html
#   # owner: root
#   user::rw-
#   user:www-data:r--          <- one cell of the matrix
#   group::r--
#   other::---

# The row view: what one domain can reach.
sudo -u www-data -s <<'EOF'
  find / -writable -type d 2>/dev/null | head       # the writable part of the row
EOF
namei -l /var/www/html/index.html      # every permission check on the path

# 'own' as a right: only the owner may change the column.
touch /tmp/f && chmod 600 /tmp/f
sudo -u nobody chmod 666 /tmp/f        # chmod: Operation not permitted

# Domain-as-object: the right to switch INTO another domain.
sudo -l -U alice
#   User alice may run the following commands:
#       (root) /usr/bin/systemctl restart nginx    <- a controlled switch
sudo sesearch -T -s unconfined_t | head -3         # SELinux domain transitions
```

**Key takeaways**

- The access matrix is the reference model: rows are domains, columns are objects, and each cell holds the rights that domain has on that object.
- Domains are themselves objects in the matrix, which is what lets it express the right to switch domains.
- Reading a row gives a capability list, reading a column gives an ACL, and reading a cell is the authorisation decision.
- Rights such as `own`, `copy`/`*`, and `control` change the matrix itself, and copy rights make propagation possible.
- The safety question — can a right ever leak to a given domain — is undecidable in the general model, so real systems restrict the model to regain decidability.
- The matrix is never stored directly because it is huge and almost entirely empty; ACLs and capabilities are its column-wise and row-wise compressions.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. Draw an access matrix for two users and three files, including one `own` right and one domain-switch right, then read out one row and one column in words.
> 2. Explain the difference between the `read` and `read*` rights, and trace what happens when a domain holding only `read` tries to grant it onward.
> 3. Interview-style: "Why do real systems not implement the general access matrix with arbitrary copy rights?" *Hint: consider what question an administrator most wants answered about a permission change, and what was proved about answering it in 1976.*

#### Access Control Lists

**Theory**

An **access control list** stores the access matrix by column: each object carries the list of who may do what to it. This is the dominant model in practice — UNIX permissions, POSIX ACLs, NTFS ACLs, S3 bucket policies, and database `GRANT` statements are all ACLs.

Its appeal is that it matches how people reason about resources. "Who can read this document?" is answered by looking at the document. Revoking access is equally direct: remove the entry, and the change is immediate and complete, because every access consults the list.

UNIX uses a deliberately compressed ACL: three entries (owner, group, other) times three rights (read, write, execute), stored as nine bits plus three special ones. The compression made sense when inodes were precious, and its economy is remarkable — but the limitation is severe: you cannot express "alice and bob may read, carol may write, everyone else nothing" without creating a group, and group creation is usually an administrator's privilege. This is the "one group per sharing relationship" problem, and it is why POSIX ACLs were added.

The bit layout is worth knowing exactly, including the three special bits that behave differently on files and directories:

| Bit | On a file | On a directory |
|---|---|---|
| `r` | Read contents | List entries |
| `w` | Modify contents | Create/delete entries |
| `x` | Execute | Traverse (use in a path) |
| setuid (4000) | Run as the file's owner | (no effect) |
| setgid (2000) | Run as the file's group | New entries inherit the directory's group |
| sticky (1000) | (no effect) | Only the owner may delete an entry — this is what makes `/tmp` safe |

**POSIX ACLs** extend this with named user and group entries, plus a **mask** that caps the rights of all named entries and the group class. The mask trips people constantly: a file may list `user:alice:rwx` while the mask is `r--`, and alice gets only read. `ls -l` shows a `+` to indicate extended ACLs are present, and the group bits it displays are actually the mask.

Two design points recur across every ACL system:

**Evaluation order.** When entries conflict, which wins? POSIX ACLs use a specificity order: owner, then named users, then group entries, then other — first match wins, and later entries are not consulted. NTFS evaluates *deny* entries before *allow*, so an explicit deny always overrides. AWS IAM likewise makes explicit deny final. Knowing the order is essential, because "alice is in a denied group but has an individual allow" resolves differently on different systems.

**Inheritance.** New objects need sensible permissions. POSIX handles this with **default ACLs** on a directory, which are copied onto anything created inside it. NTFS has inheritance flags propagating down the tree. Without inheritance, every new file needs manual configuration, and in practice that means most of them are wrong.

The weaknesses of ACLs are structural. They scale by object, so answering "what can alice reach?" requires scanning every object in the system — the row question is expensive in a column-wise store. And they are subject to the **confused deputy** problem: a privileged program checks the ACL using *its own* identity rather than the requester's, and can be tricked into acting on the attacker's behalf. That is precisely what capabilities, the next topic, address.

**Example**

```text
   ACL = THE MATRIX STORED BY COLUMN (with the object)

   /var/www/index.html
   +----------------------------------+
   | owner : root       rw-           |
   | user  : www-data   r--           |   <- a named entry (POSIX ACL)
   | user  : deploy     rw-           |
   | group : webadmin   r-x           |
   | mask  :            r-x           |   <- CAPS every named/group entry
   | other :            ---           |
   +----------------------------------+
   "Who can touch this?" -> read the list. Direct.
   "What can deploy touch?" -> scan EVERY object on the system. Expensive.

   CLASSIC UNIX MODE BITS: 12 BITS TOTAL

     4  7  5  5
     |  |  |  +--- other:  r-x
     |  |  +------ group:  r-x
     |  +--------- owner:  rwx
     +------------ special: setuid(4) setgid(2) sticky(1)

   THE SPECIAL BITS MEAN DIFFERENT THINGS BY TYPE

   setuid on a FILE      : run as the file's OWNER      (passwd)
   setgid on a FILE      : run as the file's GROUP
   setgid on a DIRECTORY : new entries inherit the DIRECTORY's group
                           (the standard shared-project-folder setup)
   sticky on a DIRECTORY : only the OWNER of an entry may delete it
                           drwxrwxrwt /tmp
                                    ^ this 't' is why /tmp is usable at all:
                                      world-writable, but you cannot delete
                                      other people's files

   THE POSIX ACL MASK: THE MOST COMMON SOURCE OF CONFUSION

   $ getfacl report.txt
   user::rw-
   user:alice:rwx          <- alice appears to have rwx ...
   group::r--
   mask::r--               <- ... but the MASK caps her at r--
   other::---
                           EFFECTIVE rights for alice: r--

   And in `ls -l`, the GROUP triplet shown is actually the MASK:
   -rw-r-----+ 1 root root  report.txt
       ^^^      ^ the '+' means extended ACLs exist -- ls is not the whole story

   CONFLICT RESOLUTION DIFFERS BY SYSTEM

   POSIX  : owner -> named user -> group entries -> other. FIRST MATCH wins.
   NTFS   : explicit DENY -> explicit ALLOW -> inherited DENY -> inherited ALLOW
   AWS IAM: any explicit Deny is FINAL, regardless of any Allow

   "alice is in a denied group but has an individual allow" resolves
   DIFFERENTLY on each of the three. Know which one you are in.
```

```bash
# Classic mode bits.
ls -l /etc/shadow /usr/bin/passwd /tmp
#   -rw-r----- 1 root shadow   /etc/shadow      <- other: nothing at all
#   -rwsr-xr-x 1 root root     /usr/bin/passwd  <- 's': setuid
#   drwxrwxrwt 1 root root     /tmp             <- 't': sticky
stat -c '%A %a %U:%G %n' /etc/shadow /tmp

chmod 640 report.txt                       # rw- r-- ---
chmod u=rw,g=r,o= report.txt               # the same, symbolically
chmod g+s /srv/project                     # new files inherit the group
chmod +t /srv/shared                       # only owners may delete

# POSIX ACLs: named entries beyond owner/group/other.
setfacl -m u:alice:rw report.txt           # a named user entry
setfacl -m g:auditors:r report.txt         # a named group entry
setfacl -x u:alice report.txt              # remove one entry
setfacl -b report.txt                      # strip all extended entries

getfacl report.txt
#   user::rw-
#   user:alice:rw-
#   group::r--
#   mask::rw-
#   other::---

# The mask trap, demonstrated.
setfacl -m u:alice:rwx report.txt
setfacl -m m::r report.txt                 # set the mask to r--
getfacl report.txt | grep -A1 alice
#   user:alice:rwx              #effective:r--     <- getfacl tells you
chmod g=rw report.txt                      # NOTE: chmod on an ACL file sets
getfacl report.txt | grep mask             # the MASK, not the group entry

# Default ACLs: inheritance for new files.
setfacl -d -m u:deploy:rwx /srv/app        # 'd' = default, applied to new entries
setfacl -d -m o::--- /srv/app
touch /srv/app/newfile && getfacl /srv/app/newfile   # inherited automatically

# Recursive application, correctly (X = execute only where already executable).
setfacl -R -m u:deploy:rX /srv/app
chmod -R u=rwX,g=rX,o= /srv/app            # capital X: directories yes, files no

# Answering the ROW question with a COLUMN store -- note how expensive it is.
sudo -u alice find / -writable -type f 2>/dev/null | head
# There is no index for "what can alice reach"; the whole tree must be walked.

# Windows: deny beats allow, and inheritance is explicit.
#   icacls C:\data /grant "Analysts:(OI)(CI)R"
#   icacls C:\data /deny  "Interns:(OI)(CI)W"     <- wins over any allow
#   icacls C:\data /inheritance:r                 <- stop inheriting
```

```python
import os, stat, subprocess

def explain_mode(path):
    """Decode a mode into the decisions it encodes."""
    m = os.stat(path).st_mode
    print(f"{path}: {stat.filemode(m)}  ({oct(m & 0o7777)})")
    is_dir = stat.S_ISDIR(m)
    for who, bits in (("owner", 6), ("group", 3), ("other", 0)):
        r = "r" if m >> bits & 4 else "-"
        w = "w" if m >> bits & 2 else "-"
        x = "x" if m >> bits & 1 else "-"
        meaning = ("list / create-delete / traverse" if is_dir
                   else "read / write / execute")
        print(f"  {who:<6} {r}{w}{x}   ({meaning})")
    if m & stat.S_ISUID: print("  setuid: runs as the file's OWNER")
    if m & stat.S_ISGID: print("  setgid: " + ("new entries inherit this group"
                                               if is_dir else "runs as the group"))
    if m & stat.S_ISVTX: print("  sticky: only an entry's owner may delete it")

for p in ("/etc/shadow", "/tmp", "/usr/bin/passwd"):
    explain_mode(p); print()

# The umask: what is REMOVED from the requested mode at creation time.
old = os.umask(0o077)                  # 0o077: owner only
os.close(os.open("/tmp/private.txt", os.O_CREAT | os.O_WRONLY, 0o666))
print("with umask 077:", oct(os.stat("/tmp/private.txt").st_mode & 0o777))  # 0o600
os.umask(0o022)                        # the common default
os.close(os.open("/tmp/shared.txt", os.O_CREAT | os.O_WRONLY, 0o666))
print("with umask 022:", oct(os.stat("/tmp/shared.txt").st_mode & 0o777))   # 0o644
os.umask(old)
# The requested mode is a MAXIMUM; umask can only clear bits, never set them.
```

**Key takeaways**

- An ACL stores the access matrix by column, attaching to each object the list of who may do what — which matches how people reason about resources and makes revocation immediate.
- UNIX mode bits are a compressed nine-bit ACL plus setuid, setgid, and sticky; the special bits mean different things on files and directories.
- The sticky bit on a directory restricts deletion to each entry's owner, which is what makes a world-writable `/tmp` safe.
- POSIX ACLs add named user and group entries plus a mask that caps them; `ls -l` shows the mask in the group position and a `+` to signal extended entries.
- Conflict resolution differs by system — POSIX takes the first match by specificity, while NTFS and AWS IAM let an explicit deny override any allow.
- Default ACLs and inheritance flags exist because without them new objects get wrong permissions by default.
- ACLs answer "who can access this object" cheaply and "what can this subject reach" expensively, and they are vulnerable to the confused deputy problem.
