<a id="13-virtualization"></a>
## 13. Virtualization

Every chapter so far has described an operating system multiplexing hardware among processes; this one describes software multiplexing hardware among entire operating systems. Virtualization takes the interposition trick that makes a process think it owns the CPU and memory and applies it one level down, so a kernel can be given the same convincing illusion — and then examines the lighter-weight alternative, containers, which reuses the kernel's own isolation primitives instead of simulating hardware. It matters because essentially all server computing now runs on one of these two substrates, and the differences between them determine performance, density, and, critically, where the security boundary actually lies.

One distinction is worth fixing before anything else. A **virtual machine** duplicates the hardware interface, so the thing running inside it is a complete guest kernel with its own drivers, scheduler, and page tables. A **container** duplicates the system-call interface, so the thing running inside it is a set of processes sharing the host kernel. Both produce something that "looks like its own machine" from the inside; they differ in what is being simulated, and therefore in what an escape requires.

<a id="131-virtualization-concepts"></a>
### 13.1 Virtualization Concepts

This section builds the conceptual apparatus: what a virtual machine formally is, the two places a hypervisor can sit, and the three strategies — trap-and-emulate, cooperative guests, and translation — for making guest code run correctly on hardware it does not exclusively own.

#### Virtual Machine Abstraction

**Theory**

Start with the problem virtualization was invented to solve. In the 1960s an IBM mainframe was enormously expensive and could run one operating system at a time, while different departments wanted different operating systems. Buying more mainframes was absurd; so IBM's CP-67 instead created the illusion of many mainframes on one, each running its own OS. Sixty years later the economics are the same in a different currency: a data-centre server has 128 cores and a terabyte of RAM, no single tenant's workload uses that, and you cannot safely put several tenants' workloads in one operating system.

A **virtual machine** is an efficient, isolated duplicate of a real machine. The software that creates it is the **virtual machine monitor** (VMM) or **hypervisor**. The essential move is one you have already seen: the OS gives a process the illusion of owning the CPU by intercepting its attempts to do anything privileged; the hypervisor gives a whole *kernel* the same illusion by the same mechanism. The guest kernel runs deprivileged — it believes it is in kernel mode, but it is not — and every instruction it executes that would actually touch hardware traps into the hypervisor, which emulates the effect against virtual state.

This is **trap-and-emulate**, and Popek and Goldberg formalised it in 1974 with three requirements a VMM must satisfy:

| Requirement | Meaning | Why it is hard |
|---|---|---|
| **Fidelity** (equivalence) | A program runs in the VM exactly as it would on bare metal, except for timing and resource availability | The guest must not be able to tell, except through timing |
| **Performance** (efficiency) | The overwhelming majority of guest instructions execute directly on the real CPU, unmediated | Interpreting every instruction would be correct but useless |
| **Safety** (resource control) | The VMM has complete control of resources; the guest can never escape its allocation | One guest must not be able to affect another, or the host |

From these they derived the classic theorem. Divide the instruction set into **privileged** instructions (those that trap when executed in user mode) and **sensitive** instructions (those that either change the machine's configuration — *control-sensitive* — or whose behaviour depends on it — *behaviour-sensitive*). Then:

> A VMM using trap-and-emulate can be constructed if the set of sensitive instructions is a subset of the set of privileged instructions.

The intuition is simple: the hypervisor can only intervene where it gets control, and it only gets control on a trap. Any instruction that matters but does *not* trap is an instruction the guest executes behind the hypervisor's back, producing either wrong results or an escape.

Classic x86 famously failed this test. It had 17 sensitive-but-unprivileged instructions — the notorious example being `POPF`, which pops flags from the stack. In kernel mode it updates the interrupt-enable flag `IF`; in user mode it *silently ignores* that part rather than faulting. A deprivileged guest kernel executing `cli`-then-`popf` sequences would think it had disabled interrupts while nothing had happened, and no trap would ever tell the hypervisor to fix it. This single architectural detail is why x86 virtualization took the detour through binary translation (covered later in this section) before hardware support arrived.

Terminology worth keeping straight: the hypervisor's own environment is the **host**; each virtual machine is a **guest**; and the guest's illusion is maintained in three dimensions — CPU (vCPUs time-shared onto physical cores), memory (guest-physical addresses translated to host-physical), and I/O (virtual devices backed by real ones, or by files).

**Example**

```text
   THE SAME TRICK, APPLIED ONE LEVEL DOWN

   Ordinary OS                          Hypervisor
   ------------------------------       ------------------------------
   [ proc ][ proc ][ proc ]             [ guest OS ][ guest OS ]
        |  syscall / fault                    |  sensitive instruction
        v                                     v
   [    kernel     ]                     [  hypervisor  ]
   [   hardware    ]                     [   hardware   ]

   The kernel gives a PROCESS the illusion of owning the machine.
   The hypervisor gives a KERNEL the same illusion, by the same means:
   intercept anything privileged, emulate it against virtual state.


   TRAP-AND-EMULATE, ONE INSTRUCTION AT A TIME

   guest kernel (running deprivileged, in user mode)
     |
     |  mov  eax, [mem]      <- ordinary instruction: runs DIRECTLY on
     |  add  eax, 1             the real CPU at full speed. No trap.
     |
     |  mov  cr3, eax        <- SENSITIVE + PRIVILEGED: reloading the page
     |                          table would hijack the real MMU
     +--> TRAP ------------------> hypervisor
                                     decode the instruction
                                     update the VM's VIRTUAL cr3
                                     rebuild the real mapping
                                     advance the guest's PC
                                   <-- resume guest

   Fidelity : the guest observes exactly what real hardware would.
   Performance: only the rare privileged instruction pays the trap cost.
   Safety  : the real cr3 was never written by the guest.


   WHY CLASSIC x86 BROKE THE THEOREM

   sensitive instructions           privileged instructions
   +----------------------+         +----------------------+
   |  popf, pushf, sgdt,  |         |  mov cr3, hlt,       |
   |  sidt, sldt, smsw,   |         |  invlpg, lgdt, ...   |
   |  lar, lsl, verr, ... |         |                      |
   +----------------------+         +----------------------+
            |                                  ^
            |  these 17 are sensitive but NOT privileged
            +---- they do NOT trap in user mode -----------X

   popf in kernel mode : updates the interrupt-enable flag IF
   popf in user mode   : silently ignores the IF bit, does NOT fault

   A deprivileged guest "disables interrupts", nothing happens, and the
   hypervisor is never told. The illusion is broken silently -- the worst
   possible failure mode. Requirement: sensitive (subset of) privileged.
```

```python
# A miniature trap-and-emulate VMM. The "CPU" executes guest instructions
# directly unless they are sensitive, in which case control transfers to
# the monitor, which emulates them against per-VM virtual state.

class VirtualCPU:
    """Per-VM state the guest THINKS is real hardware."""
    def __init__(self):
        self.registers = {"eax": 0}
        self.cr3 = 0x0          # guest's idea of the page-table base
        self.interrupts_on = True

SENSITIVE = {"mov_cr3", "cli", "sti", "hlt", "in", "out"}

class Hypervisor:
    def __init__(self):
        self.vms = {}
        self.exits = 0          # every exit is measurable overhead
        self.direct = 0         # instructions run natively: the fast path

    def run(self, vm_id, instruction, operand=None):
        vcpu = self.vms.setdefault(vm_id, VirtualCPU())
        if instruction not in SENSITIVE:
            self.direct += 1                    # executes on the real CPU
            return "native"
        self.exits += 1                         # TRAP: control leaves the guest
        return self._emulate(vcpu, instruction, operand)

    def _emulate(self, vcpu, instruction, operand):
        if instruction == "mov_cr3":
            vcpu.cr3 = operand                  # virtual cr3 only; the REAL
            return f"virtual cr3 <- {operand:#x}"   # cr3 is never touched
        if instruction == "cli":
            vcpu.interrupts_on = False          # guest believes interrupts are
            return "guest IF cleared (host unaffected)"   # off; the host's are not
        if instruction == "sti":
            vcpu.interrupts_on = True
            return "guest IF set"
        if instruction == "hlt":
            return "vCPU descheduled (host keeps running)"  # NOT a real halt
        if instruction in ("in", "out"):
            return f"device emulation for port {operand:#x}"
        raise NotImplementedError(instruction)

hv = Hypervisor()
program = [("mov_eax", None), ("add", None), ("cli", None),
           ("mov_cr3", 0x7F000), ("add", None), ("sti", None), ("hlt", None)]

for instr, arg in program:
    result = hv.run("vm1", instr, arg)
    print(f"{instr:<10} -> {result}")

total = hv.direct + hv.exits
print(f"\ndirect: {hv.direct}/{total}  exits: {hv.exits}/{total}")
# Real workloads sit near 99.9% direct execution. Performance is entirely
# a question of how often you leave the guest, not how fast emulation is.
```

**Key takeaways**

- A virtual machine is an efficient, isolated duplicate of a real machine; the hypervisor creates it by applying to a kernel the same interposition the kernel applies to a process.
- Popek and Goldberg require fidelity, performance, and safety — and performance specifically demands that most guest instructions run natively rather than being interpreted.
- Trap-and-emulate is constructible when every sensitive instruction is also privileged, because the hypervisor can only act where a trap gives it control.
- Sensitive means control-sensitive (changes machine configuration) or behaviour-sensitive (behaves differently depending on it); privileged means it faults in user mode.
- Classic x86 had 17 sensitive-but-unprivileged instructions, `POPF` chief among them, which silently did the wrong thing instead of trapping — making pure trap-and-emulate impossible.
- The guest illusion has three dimensions — CPU, memory, and I/O — and each needs its own mechanism, covered in section 13.2.
- Virtualization overhead is dominated by the *frequency* of exits from the guest, not by the cost of any single emulation.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. Classify each of `add`, `hlt`, `mov cr3`, `pushf`, and `rdtsc` as sensitive, privileged, both, or neither, and say which of them breaks pure trap-and-emulate.
> 2. A guest measures elapsed time with `rdtsc` and notices gaps where the hypervisor descheduled its vCPU. Which Popek–Goldberg requirement does this bear on, and why is it considered acceptable in practice?
> 3. Extend the `Hypervisor` class above so that `in`/`out` on port `0x3F8` (the serial port) appends a byte to a per-VM output buffer, and print the buffer at the end. Note how many exits a one-line message costs.
> 4. Interview-style: "Why can't you virtualize a CPU by simply running the guest kernel in kernel mode and hoping for the best?" *Hint: think about what the guest's `mov cr3` would do to the host's page tables, and what a guest's `hlt` would do to the other tenants.*

#### Type 1 and Type 2 Hypervisors

**Theory**

Given that a hypervisor must interpose on privileged operations, there are exactly two places to put it: underneath every operating system, or inside one. That choice is the Type 1 / Type 2 distinction, and almost every practical difference between virtualization products follows from it.

A **Type 1 hypervisor** — also called *bare-metal* or *native* — runs directly on the hardware. It *is* the lowest-level software on the machine; there is no host operating system beneath it. It owns the physical CPUs, memory, and devices, and schedules guests onto them. VMware ESXi, Xen, Microsoft Hyper-V, and Nutanix AHV are Type 1. Because nothing sits between it and the hardware, it has the shortest path to devices, the smallest trusted computing base, and the most control over scheduling — which is why every serious cloud provider runs one.

A **Type 2 hypervisor** — *hosted* — runs as an application on a conventional operating system. It uses the host OS for device drivers, memory allocation, and process scheduling, and its virtual machines appear to the host as ordinary processes. VMware Workstation, VirtualBox, and Parallels are Type 2. The convenience is enormous: you install it like any other program, it inherits driver support for every piece of laptop hardware, and you can run a VM alongside your browser. The cost is a second scheduler and a second memory manager between the guest and the hardware.

The clean two-way split is somewhat dated, because the most important modern hypervisors are deliberately hybrid:

- **KVM** (Linux) turns the Linux kernel *itself* into a hypervisor via a loadable module. Linux keeps doing everything it did — scheduling, memory management, drivers — and a VM becomes a Linux process whose threads are vCPUs. Argue whichever way you like: it has a full OS beneath it (Type 2) but that OS is executing as the hypervisor with direct hardware access (Type 1). The practical answer is that KVM gets Type 1 performance with Type 2 driver support, which is why it underpins most of the public cloud.
- **Xen** uses a privileged guest, **dom0**, which runs a normal Linux kernel and owns the physical device drivers on behalf of the tiny Type 1 hypervisor beneath it. The hypervisor is minimal; the driver mass lives in a VM.
- **Hyper-V** similarly demotes the "host" Windows install into a privileged *root partition* once the role is enabled.

| Dimension | Type 1 (bare-metal) | Type 2 (hosted) |
|---|---|---|
| Runs on | Hardware directly | A host operating system |
| Guest I/O path | Hypervisor to device | Guest to hypervisor to host OS to device |
| Scheduling | Hypervisor schedules vCPUs onto cores | Host OS schedules the VMM's threads |
| Trusted computing base | Small (thin hypervisor) | Large (entire host OS plus its applications) |
| Device driver support | Limited to a certified list | Everything the host OS supports |
| Typical overhead | Low (single-digit percent) | Higher, and less predictable |
| Boot requirement | Dedicated machine | Installs like an application |
| Examples | ESXi, Xen, Hyper-V | VMware Workstation, VirtualBox, Parallels |
| Best suited to | Servers, cloud, consolidation | Desktops, development, testing |

The security consequence deserves emphasis. The attack surface of a hypervisor is everything a guest can reach: the instruction emulator, the virtual devices, the hypercall interface. For a Type 1 hypervisor that is a few hundred thousand lines. For a Type 2 hypervisor it is that *plus the entire host kernel*, because the VMM makes host system calls on the guest's behalf — and plus every other program running on the host, any of which might be compromised and then attack the VMM's memory. This is why "run the malware sample in VirtualBox on my laptop" is a meaningfully weaker containment story than "run it on a dedicated ESXi host".

**Example**

```text
   WHERE THE HYPERVISOR SITS

   TYPE 1 (bare-metal)              TYPE 2 (hosted)
   +----------+  +----------+       +----------+  +---------+ +--------+
   | Guest OS |  | Guest OS |       | Guest OS |  | Guest OS| | Browser|
   +----------+  +----------+       +----------+  +---------+ |  etc.  |
   +------------------------+       +------------------------+ +-------+
   |      HYPERVISOR        |       |    Hypervisor (an app)  |        |
   +------------------------+       +---------------------------------+
   |       HARDWARE         |       |          HOST OS                |
   +------------------------+       +---------------------------------+
                                    |          HARDWARE               |
                                    +---------------------------------+

   Note what the guest's I/O has to cross in each case.


   KVM: THE HYBRID THAT WON

   +----------+  +----------+   +---------+  +---------+
   | Guest OS |  | Guest OS |   | sshd    |  | nginx   |   ordinary
   +----------+  +----------+   +---------+  +---------+   processes
   |  QEMU    |  |  QEMU    |   <- userspace: device models, VM lifecycle
   +----------+--+----------+---+---------+--+---------+
   |        LINUX KERNEL + kvm.ko  (this IS the hypervisor)          |
   +-----------------------------------------------------------------+
   |                        HARDWARE                                 |
   +-----------------------------------------------------------------+

   A VM is a Linux PROCESS. Each vCPU is a Linux THREAD.
   Consequences that follow directly from that one design decision:
     - `top` shows VMs; `nice` and cgroups work on them
     - the CFS/EEVDF scheduler schedules vCPUs
     - the OOM killer can kill a virtual machine
     - every Linux driver is available to the host


   XEN: A THIN HYPERVISOR PLUS A DRIVER VM

   +--------+  +--------+  +--------+
   | dom0   |  | domU   |  | domU   |     dom0 is privileged: it owns
   | Linux  |  | guest  |  | guest  |     the real drivers and the
   | DRIVERS|  |        |  |        |     control tools (xl, toolstack)
   +--------+  +--------+  +--------+
   +--------------------------------+
   |   XEN HYPERVISOR (~150k LOC)   |  <- small, so it is auditable
   +--------------------------------+
   |           HARDWARE             |
   +--------------------------------+

   The trusted computing base is small; the driver mass is in a VM that
   can crash and be restarted without taking the hypervisor down.


   THE I/O PATH, COUNTED IN BOUNDARY CROSSINGS

   Type 1:  guest driver -> VM exit -> hypervisor -> device        (2)
   Type 2:  guest driver -> VM exit -> VMM -> host syscall
                         -> host driver -> device                  (4+)

   Each crossing is a context switch and a cache disturbance. This is
   the entire performance story, and it is why Type 1 dominates servers.
```

```bash
# ---------- What is actually running on this machine? ----------

# Am I inside a VM, and if so, under what?
systemd-detect-virt              # kvm | vmware | xen | oracle | microsoft | none
lscpu | grep -i hypervisor       # "Hypervisor vendor: KVM"

# The CPUID hypervisor-present bit: set by any well-behaved hypervisor.
grep -o hypervisor /proc/cpuinfo | head -1

# Does this hardware support acceleration at all?
grep -Eoc '(vmx|svm)' /proc/cpuinfo   # vmx = Intel VT-x, svm = AMD-V; 0 = none
lsmod | grep -E '^kvm'                # kvm_intel / kvm_amd loaded?

# ---------- KVM: a VM really is just a process ----------
# Start a guest (Type 2-looking command line, Type 1-class performance):
#   qemu-system-x86_64 -enable-kvm -m 4G -smp 4 -drive file=disk.qcow2
#
# Then observe it with ordinary process tools:
ps -eo pid,comm,nlwp | grep qemu       # nlwp = threads; one per vCPU plus I/O
#   PID   COMMAND            NLWP
#   4821  qemu-system-x86     7        <- 4 vCPU threads + iothreads + main

# Which thread is which vCPU, and where is it running?
ps -T -p 4821 -o spid,comm,psr
#   SPID   COMMAND     PSR
#   4823   CPU 0/KVM    2           <- vCPU 0, currently on physical core 2
#   4824   CPU 1/KVM    7

# Because it is a process, every Linux resource control applies to it:
systemd-run --scope -p CPUQuota=200% -p MemoryMax=8G qemu-system-x86_64 ...
taskset -cp 8-15 4823                  # pin vCPU 0 to a NUMA-local core set

# Count VM exits -- the single most useful virtualization metric:
sudo perf kvm stat live                # live histogram of exit reasons
sudo perf stat -e kvm:kvm_exit -p 4821 sleep 5
#   Frequent EPT_VIOLATION  -> memory mapping churn
#   Frequent IO_INSTRUCTION -> emulated device; switch it to virtio
#   Frequent HLT            -> idle guest; usually harmless
```

**Key takeaways**

- A hypervisor sits either directly on hardware (Type 1, bare-metal) or as an application on a host OS (Type 2, hosted); everything else follows from that placement.
- Type 1 gives a shorter I/O path, direct control of scheduling, and a small trusted computing base — the reasons it runs servers and clouds.
- Type 2 inherits the host OS's entire driver ecosystem and installs like any program, at the cost of an extra scheduler, an extra memory manager, and a far larger attack surface.
- KVM blurs the categories by making Linux itself the hypervisor: a VM is a process and each vCPU is a thread, so all existing Linux tooling applies to virtual machines.
- Xen keeps the hypervisor tiny and puts the physical drivers in a privileged guest (dom0), trading an extra hop for auditability and driver-crash isolation.
- The security boundary of a Type 2 setup includes the entire host OS and every other process on it, which makes it a weaker containment story than a dedicated Type 1 host.
- `systemd-detect-virt` and the CPUID hypervisor bit answer "am I virtualized?"; `perf kvm stat` answers "why is it slow?" by showing exit reasons.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. Run `systemd-detect-virt` and `grep -Eoc '(vmx|svm)' /proc/cpuinfo` on your machine and explain what each result tells you about where your code is executing.
> 2. Draw the boundary crossings for a single 4 KiB disk read issued by a guest under (a) ESXi and (b) VirtualBox on Windows, and explain which of the two has more variable latency.
> 3. Argue both sides of "KVM is a Type 2 hypervisor", then state which properties of Type 1 and Type 2 it actually exhibits.
> 4. Interview-style: "A security team wants to detonate untrusted binaries. They propose VirtualBox on an analyst's laptop. What is your objection, and what would you propose instead?" *Hint: enumerate the code an escaping guest would then be adjacent to, and count how much of it is privileged.*

#### Full Virtualization

**Theory**

**Full virtualization** means the guest operating system runs *completely unmodified* — the same binary kernel that boots on bare metal boots in the VM, with no awareness that it is virtualized. This is the property that made virtualization commercially viable: you could take a running Windows NT server, image it, and boot it in a VM without source code, recompilation, or a vendor's cooperation.

Achieving it on an architecture that satisfies Popek–Goldberg is straightforward trap-and-emulate. Achieving it on classic x86, which did not, required an ingenious workaround that VMware shipped in 1999 and which is worth understanding even though hardware has since made it unnecessary.

The technique is **binary translation**, applied selectively. The insight is that the problem is confined to *kernel* code: user-mode guest applications contain no sensitive instructions that matter, so they can run directly on the CPU at full native speed. Only the guest kernel needs treatment. So the VMM:

1. Runs all guest **user** code directly on the CPU, unmodified. This is the overwhelming majority of cycles in a typical workload, and it costs nothing.
2. Intercepts guest **kernel** code and translates it, one basic block at a time, before execution. The translation is x86-to-x86 and is nearly the identity function — most instructions are copied verbatim.
3. Replaces each problematic instruction in that block with a call into the VMM. `popf` becomes a sequence that updates the *virtual* interrupt flag. `cli`/`sti` become updates to virtual state. Control-flow at the end of the block is patched to chain to the next translated block.
4. **Caches** translated blocks in a *translation cache*, so a loop is translated once and executed thousands of times. This is what makes the approach viable rather than merely correct.

Guest kernel code, therefore, never executes as written — but it also never notices, because the translation preserves semantics exactly with respect to the virtual machine state.

Two more pieces complete the illusion. **Memory** is handled with shadow page tables (section 13.2): the guest builds page tables mapping guest-virtual to guest-physical, and the VMM maintains a shadow set mapping guest-virtual directly to host-physical, which is what the real MMU walks. **Devices** are handled by emulating well-known legacy hardware — an Intel E1000 network card, an LSI SCSI controller, a PS/2 keyboard — precisely because every OS already ships drivers for them. The guest loads its ordinary E1000 driver, writes to what it believes are the card's registers, and each write traps to the VMM, which translates it into real I/O.

That last point is also where full virtualization is slowest, and it explains the natural next step. Emulating an E1000 faithfully costs several VM exits per packet. If you are willing to give up the "completely unmodified guest" property just for the device drivers, you can do much better — which is paravirtualization, the next topic. In practice, modern systems are hybrids: hardware-assisted full virtualization for the CPU and MMU, paravirtual drivers for I/O.

**Example**

```text
   FULL VIRTUALIZATION: WHO RUNS WHAT

   guest user code   ------------------> runs DIRECTLY on the CPU
   (~99% of cycles)                       full native speed, no work

   guest kernel code ---> BINARY TRANSLATOR ---> translation cache
                          rewrite the 17 bad         |
                          instructions; copy         v
                          everything else       execute translated block
                                                (subsequent hits: no
                                                 translation, just run)

   guest devices     ---> emulate an E1000 / LSI / PS/2, because every
                          OS already has a driver for those


   BINARY TRANSLATION, ONE BASIC BLOCK

   guest kernel source block            translated block in the cache
   -------------------------            -----------------------------
   mov  eax, [ebx]                      mov  eax, [ebx]        <- copied
   add  eax, 4                          add  eax, 4            <- copied
   cli                                  mov  [VCPU_IF], 0      <- REWRITTEN
   mov  cr3, eax                        call VMM_SET_CR3       <- REWRITTEN
   sti                                  mov  [VCPU_IF], 1      <- REWRITTEN
   jmp  target                          call VMM_CHAIN(target) <- patched,
                                                                  then linked
                                                                  directly on
                                                                  the 2nd hit

   Nearly the identity translation. Only the instructions that would
   touch real machine state are replaced -- with code that touches
   VIRTUAL machine state instead.


   WHY CACHING IS THE WHOLE GAME

   a kernel loop executed 10,000 times:
     without a cache : 10,000 translations + 10,000 executions   (hopeless)
     with a cache    :      1 translation  + 10,000 executions   (viable)

   steady state: the translation cache hit rate exceeds 99.9%, so the
   translator itself stops appearing in profiles entirely.


   FULL vs PARAVIRTUAL: WHAT THE GUEST KNOWS

                       full virtualization      paravirtualization
   guest kernel        unmodified               modified / PV-aware
   guest knows?        no                       yes
   privileged ops      trapped or translated    explicit hypercalls
   device model        emulated legacy HW       ring buffers (virtio)
   can run Windows?    yes, off the shelf       only with PV drivers
                                                installed

   Modern reality is the diagonal: HARDWARE-ASSISTED full virtualization
   for CPU and MMU + PARAVIRTUAL drivers for disk and network.
```

```python
# A binary translator's core loop, reduced to its essentials: translate a
# basic block once, cache it, and execute the cached form thereafter.

SENSITIVE_REWRITES = {
    # instruction -> replacement that manipulates VIRTUAL state instead
    "cli":        "mov [VCPU.if], 0",
    "sti":        "mov [VCPU.if], 1",
    "popf":       "call VMM_EMULATE_POPF",     # the instruction that broke x86
    "mov cr3":    "call VMM_SET_CR3",
    "hlt":        "call VMM_YIELD_VCPU",
    "in":         "call VMM_PORT_IN",
    "out":        "call VMM_PORT_OUT",
}

class BinaryTranslator:
    def __init__(self):
        self.cache = {}              # guest PC -> translated block
        self.translations = 0
        self.cache_hits = 0

    def translate_block(self, block):
        out = []
        for instr in block:
            key = next((k for k in SENSITIVE_REWRITES if instr.startswith(k)), None)
            # The identity case dominates: most instructions are simply copied.
            out.append(SENSITIVE_REWRITES[key] if key else instr)
        return out

    def execute(self, pc, block):
        if pc in self.cache:
            self.cache_hits += 1                  # the steady-state path
        else:
            self.translations += 1
            self.cache[pc] = self.translate_block(block)
        return self.cache[pc]

kernel_loop = ["mov eax, [ebx]", "add eax, 4", "cli",
               "mov cr3, eax", "sti", "jmp 0x1000"]

bt = BinaryTranslator()
translated = bt.execute(0x1000, kernel_loop)
for src, dst in zip(kernel_loop, translated):
    mark = "  <- rewritten" if src != dst else ""
    print(f"{src:<18} => {dst}{mark}")

for _ in range(9999):                             # the loop runs again and again
    bt.execute(0x1000, kernel_loop)

total = bt.translations + bt.cache_hits
print(f"\ntranslations: {bt.translations}   cache hits: {bt.cache_hits}")
print(f"hit rate: {bt.cache_hits / total:.4%}")
# Translation cost amortises to nothing. Only the rewritten instructions
# still cost anything, and only when they actually execute.
```

**Key takeaways**

- Full virtualization runs a completely unmodified guest kernel, which is what allowed existing OS installations to be moved into VMs without vendor cooperation.
- On architectures satisfying Popek–Goldberg this is plain trap-and-emulate; on classic x86 it required binary translation of guest kernel code.
- Binary translation is applied only to kernel code — guest user code runs directly on the CPU at native speed, which is where nearly all cycles are.
- The translation is x86-to-x86 and almost the identity function: only sensitive instructions are rewritten into calls that update virtual state.
- Caching translated blocks is what makes the technique practical; steady-state hit rates above 99.9% make the translator invisible in profiles.
- Devices are emulated as well-known legacy hardware (E1000, LSI, PS/2) precisely because every guest OS already ships those drivers.
- Emulated device I/O is the main remaining cost, which is exactly the gap paravirtual drivers were created to close.

Why did VMware keep its binary translator for years afterwards?" *Hint: early VT-x made every privileged operation a full VM exit; compare the cost of one exit against a rewritten instruction that never leaves the guest.*

#### Paravirtualization

**Theory**

Full virtualization is defined by what the guest does *not* know. Paravirtualization takes the opposite position: tell the guest it is virtualized, modify it accordingly, and collect the performance that honesty buys.

The motivation is the cost of maintaining an illusion nobody actually needs. A guest kernel disabling interrupts around a short critical section does not truly require interrupts to be disabled on a physical core — it requires that *its own* virtual CPU not be interrupted. A guest's network driver does not truly need to poke an E1000's registers — it needs to hand a packet to the outside world. Emulating the hardware faithfully is an expensive way to achieve an outcome that could be requested directly.

So in a paravirtualized system, the guest kernel is ported: privileged operations are replaced with explicit **hypercalls** to the hypervisor. A hypercall is precisely analogous to a system call, one level down — a deliberate, structured request across a known interface, rather than a trap the hypervisor has to decode and interpret. The differences compound:

- One hypercall can batch many operations. Xen's `mmu_update` applies a whole list of page-table changes in a single crossing, where trap-and-emulate would cost one exit per write.
- No instruction decoding is required. The hypervisor is handed structured arguments rather than having to fetch, decode, and emulate an instruction.
- The guest can be given *useful truths* that no real hardware exposes: which of its vCPUs are currently scheduled, how much time was stolen from it, that a spinlock's holder is not running and spinning is pointless.

The historically important implementation is **Xen**, which around 2003 delivered near-native performance on pre-VT-x x86 by requiring ported guests. The cost was exactly the property full virtualization was prized for: a paravirtualized guest kernel must be modified, so Linux and the BSDs could participate and Windows could not.

The compromise that actually won is the **hybrid**, and it is what essentially everything runs today. Use hardware-assisted full virtualization for the CPU and MMU, so the guest kernel is unmodified and any OS can boot; then load **paravirtual drivers** inside that unmodified guest for the parts where emulation hurts most — disk, network, console, memory ballooning, clock. The guest is fully virtualized where that is cheap and paravirtualized where that pays.

**virtio** is the standard interface for this, and its design is the reason it is ubiquitous. Rather than modelling a device, virtio defines a transport: shared-memory **virtqueues**, in which the guest places descriptors pointing at its own buffers and then "kicks" the host, and the host places completions back. Notifications can be suppressed in both directions when a queue is busy, so a saturated link approaches *zero* exits per packet — the guest and host simply poll shared memory. There is no register-level device to emulate at all.

| Aspect | Full virtualization | Paravirtualization |
|---|---|---|
| Guest kernel | Unmodified | Ported, or PV drivers installed |
| Privileged operations | Trapped and emulated, or translated | Explicit hypercalls |
| Batching | One exit per operation | Many operations per hypercall |
| Device model | Emulated legacy hardware | Shared-memory ring buffers |
| Exits per network packet | Several | Approaching zero under load |
| Runs closed-source guests | Yes | Only with vendor-provided drivers |
| Guest can be told the truth | No | Yes (steal time, vCPU state) |

The "useful truths" point is worth its own emphasis, because it fixes a genuine pathology. A guest spinlock assumes the lock holder is running and will release shortly — an assumption that is simply false when the hypervisor has descheduled the holder's vCPU. The waiter then spins uselessly through its whole timeslice, a phenomenon called **lock-holder preemption**, and it can cost an order of magnitude in a spinlock-heavy workload. Paravirtual spinlocks fix it: the guest asks the hypervisor to block the waiting vCPU and wake it when the lock is released. That fix is impossible without the guest knowing it is a guest.

**Example**

```text
   THE SAME OPERATION, THREE WAYS

   Guest wants to update 64 page-table entries.

   (a) TRAP-AND-EMULATE (full virtualization)
       write PTE -> trap -> emulate -> resume     ] x 64
       cost: 64 VM exits, ~1500 cycles each  = ~96,000 cycles

   (b) HYPERCALL (paravirtualization)
       build a 64-entry list in guest memory
       hypercall(MMU_UPDATE, list, 64) -> one crossing
       cost: 1 crossing + 64 cheap in-hypervisor updates = ~3,000 cycles

   (c) NESTED PAGING (hardware, section 13.2)
       write PTE directly; the hardware walks both levels
       cost: 0 exits -- but every TLB miss walks two page tables


   VIRTIO: A DEVICE WITH NO REGISTERS TO EMULATE

            GUEST                     |          HOST
                                      |
    driver fills a buffer             |
         |                            |
         v                            |
    +-----------------------------+   |
    | AVAILABLE ring  (guest -> host) |    shared memory: BOTH sides
    |  [desc 3][desc 7][desc 9]   |   |    map the same physical pages.
    +-----------------------------+   |    No copying, no emulation.
    | DESCRIPTOR table            |   |
    |  3 -> {addr, len, flags}    |<--+--- host reads the guest's buffer
    +-----------------------------+   |    in place
    | USED ring       (host -> guest) |
    |  [desc 3 done, 1514 bytes]  |   |
    +-----------------------------+   |
         ^                            |
         |  "kick" (one exit) -- and SUPPRESSED while the queue is busy
         +----------------------------+

   idle link : 1 exit per packet (a kick is needed to wake the host)
   busy link : ~0 exits per packet (host is already polling; guest sets
               NO_NOTIFY and just writes into the ring)

   Throughput therefore IMPROVES the busier it gets -- the opposite of
   emulated devices, where every packet costs the same several exits.


   LOCK-HOLDER PREEMPTION: THE BUG ONLY AN HONEST GUEST CAN FIX

   bare metal          : holder runs, releases in ~100 ns, waiter spins 100 ns
   naive virtualization: holder's vCPU is DESCHEDULED mid-critical-section
                         waiter spins for a FULL TIMESLICE (~ms) for nothing
                         ...and may itself be holding another lock

   paravirtual spinlock:
     waiter spins briefly, then  hypercall(VCPU_BLOCK)
     releaser              does  hypercall(VCPU_KICK, waiter)
     -> the wasted timeslice becomes useful work for another guest
```

```c
/* Paravirtual interfaces as they appear in a real guest kernel.
 * The pattern is always: replace an instruction that would be trapped
 * and emulated with a structured request the hypervisor can act on
 * directly -- and, where possible, batch. */

/* --- 1. A hypercall: a syscall to the layer below --- */
struct mmu_update {
    uint64_t ptr;   /* machine address of the PTE to update */
    uint64_t val;   /* the new entry */
};

struct mmu_update updates[64];
for (int i = 0; i < 64; i++) {
    updates[i].ptr = pte_machine_addr(i);
    updates[i].val = make_pte(frames[i], PTE_PRESENT | PTE_RW);
}
/* ONE crossing applies all 64 changes. Trap-and-emulate would cost 64. */
HYPERVISOR_mmu_update(updates, 64, NULL, DOMID_SELF);

/* --- 2. Information no real hardware can provide --- */
uint64_t steal = paravirt_steal_clock(cpu);
/* Nanoseconds this vCPU was RUNNABLE but not scheduled by the hypervisor.
 * This is why a guest can show 100% "idle" while running slowly: the time
 * was taken by another tenant. Visible as %st in top / vmstat. */

/* --- 3. Paravirtual spinlock: stop spinning against a descheduled holder --- */
static void pv_wait_for_lock(struct spinlock *lock, int want)
{
    for (int spins = 0; spins < SPIN_THRESHOLD; spins++) {
        if (try_acquire(lock))          /* fast path: holder is running */
            return;
        cpu_relax();
    }
    /* Slow path: the holder is probably not on a physical CPU at all.
     * Give the core back instead of burning a timeslice. */
    HYPERVISOR_vcpu_op(VCPUOP_poll, smp_processor_id(), &lock->waitq);
}

static void pv_unlock(struct spinlock *lock)
{
    store_release(&lock->locked, 0);
    if (lock->has_waiters)               /* explicitly wake the blocked vCPU */
        HYPERVISOR_vcpu_op(VCPUOP_send_nmi, lock->waiter_cpu, NULL);
}

/* --- 4. virtio transmit: notification suppression is the point --- */
static int virtio_xmit(struct virtqueue *vq, struct sk_buff *skb)
{
    add_buf(vq, skb->data, skb->len);    /* write a descriptor into shared memory */

    if (vq->used->flags & VRING_USED_F_NO_NOTIFY)
        return 0;                        /* host is polling: NO exit at all */

    virtqueue_kick(vq);                  /* otherwise one exit to wake the host */
    return 0;
}
```

```bash
# Is this guest using paravirtual devices, and is it being starved of CPU?

lspci | grep -i virtio
#   00:03.0 Ethernet controller: Red Hat, Inc. Virtio network device
#   00:05.0 SCSI storage controller: Red Hat, Inc. Virtio block device
# If you see "Intel 82540EM" instead, you are on an EMULATED E1000 --
# typically a several-fold throughput loss. Switch the device model.

# Which paravirtual features did the hypervisor negotiate?
dmesg | grep -iE 'kvm|xen|paravirt'
#   kvm-clock: using sched offset
#   kvm-guest: KVM setup pv remote TLB flush
#   kvm-guest: setup PV sched yield
#   kvm-guest: KVM setup pv IPIs

# Steal time: the truth an honest guest is told.
vmstat 1 5
#   procs -----------cpu------------
#    r  b   us  sy  id  wa  st
#    8  0   45   8   2   0  45      <- 45% st: nearly half your CPU is
#                                      going to other tenants. No amount
#                                      of guest-side tuning fixes this.
cat /proc/stat | head -1   # the 8th field is steal, in USER_HZ
```

**Key takeaways**

- Paravirtualization tells the guest it is virtualized and modifies it to cooperate, trading the unmodified-guest property for performance.
- Hypercalls are system calls one level down: structured, batchable requests that avoid instruction decoding and collapse many operations into one crossing.
- Xen proved the approach on pre-VT-x x86 but could not support guests whose source it could not modify, notably Windows.
- The arrangement that actually won is hybrid: hardware-assisted full virtualization for CPU and MMU, plus paravirtual drivers for disk, network, clock, and ballooning.
- virtio is not a device model but a shared-memory transport; notification suppression means a busy queue approaches zero exits per packet, so throughput improves under load.
- Paravirtualization uniquely allows the hypervisor to tell the guest things no real hardware could — steal time, vCPU scheduling state — which is what makes fixes like paravirtual spinlocks possible.
- Lock-holder preemption, where a guest spins against a descheduled lock holder, is a real and severe pathology that only an honest guest can avoid.
- Seeing an emulated `Intel 82540EM` rather than a `Virtio network device` in `lspci` is a concrete, fixable performance bug.
