What is happening?" *Hint: ask what the hypervisor might have done to the vCPU holding the lock, and what the waiter has no way of knowing.*

#### Emulation and Binary Translation

**Theory**

Everything so far has assumed the guest and host share an instruction set — that guest instructions *can* run directly on the physical CPU, and the hypervisor's job is only to intercept the dangerous ones. **Emulation** abandons that assumption. It implements a target machine entirely in software, so an ARM binary can run on an x86 host, or a 6502 program from 1982 can run on anything.

The naive approach is an **interpreter**: a loop that fetches the next guest instruction, decodes it, and executes a host function implementing its semantics. It is simple, portable, and trivially correct — and roughly 10 to 100 times slower than native, because each guest instruction costs dozens of host instructions of dispatch overhead before any useful work happens.

**Dynamic binary translation** (DBT) eliminates that overhead in the same way the previous topic's translation cache did, but working across architectures. Instead of interpreting instruction by instruction, the emulator:

1. Identifies a **basic block** — a straight-line run of guest instructions ending in a branch.
2. Translates the whole block into host machine code, once.
3. **Caches** the result, keyed by guest address.
4. Executes the cached host code directly on subsequent visits, and **chains** blocks so that a hot loop stops returning to the dispatcher entirely.

Because real programs spend nearly all their time in a small fraction of their code, hit rates are extremely high and the cost of translation amortises away. Good DBT lands within 1.5 to 4 times native speed instead of 10 to 100. QEMU's **TCG** (Tiny Code Generator) works this way, translating guest instructions into an intermediate representation and then into host code, which is how one codebase emulates a dozen architectures on a dozen others.

Real systems add more layers. **Tiered translation** applies a fast, low-quality translator first and re-optimises only the blocks that prove hot, exactly as JavaScript engines do. Apple's **Rosetta 2** goes further with **ahead-of-time translation**: it translates an entire x86-64 binary to ARM64 at install time, so most code never needs runtime translation at all, and falls back to DBT only for JIT-generated code. Its remarkable performance also owes something to hardware — Apple Silicon implements x86's stricter *total store order* memory model in hardware, removing what is otherwise DBT's single worst cost.

That memory-model point generalises into the hardest problem in emulation. Correct translation must preserve not only instruction semantics but the target's **memory ordering** and its **exact exception behaviour**. Emulating a strongly-ordered guest (x86) on a weakly-ordered host (ARM) requires inserting memory barriers that can dominate the cost; getting the precise fault state right at every instruction that might trap forces the translator to be conservative about what it can optimise. And **self-modifying code** invalidates cached translations, so the emulator must write-protect translated guest pages to detect it.

| Technique | Guest ISA | Speed vs native | Example |
|---|---|---|---|
| Interpretation | Any | 10–100x slower | QEMU without TCG; classic console emulators |
| Dynamic binary translation | Any | 1.5–4x slower | QEMU TCG, Rosetta 2 runtime path |
| Ahead-of-time translation | Any | 1.1–1.5x slower | Rosetta 2 install-time path |
| Same-ISA binary translation | Same | ~1.05x slower | Classic VMware, pre-VT-x |
| Hardware-assisted virtualization | Same | ~1.01x slower | KVM, VT-x/AMD-V |

The decision rule is clean: if guest and host share an ISA, use hardware virtualization, because nothing else comes close. Use emulation only when you genuinely need a *different* machine — cross-architecture development, running legacy or foreign binaries, firmware and embedded development before silicon exists, or malware analysis where full instruction-level introspection is worth an order of magnitude in speed.

**Example**

```text
   THE THREE EXECUTION STRATEGIES, SIDE BY SIDE

   INTERPRETATION                 per guest instruction:
     fetch -> decode -> switch -> execute -> update PC
     ~50-200 host instructions to perform ONE guest instruction
     cost is paid EVERY time, even in a loop's ten-thousandth iteration

   DYNAMIC BINARY TRANSLATION
     first visit to a block:  translate whole block -> host code -> cache
     every later visit:       jump straight into cached host code
     hot loops: blocks are CHAINED, so the dispatcher is never re-entered

   HARDWARE VIRTUALIZATION (same ISA only)
     guest instructions ARE host instructions. Nothing to translate.


   QEMU TCG: ONE IR, MANY FRONT ENDS AND BACK ENDS

     ARM code  --\                                   /-- x86-64 host
     RISC-V    ---\   +----------------+   +-----+  /--- ARM64 host
     MIPS      ----+->|  TCG frontend  |-->| IR  |-+---- RISC-V host
     PowerPC   ---/   +----------------+   +-----+  \--- PowerPC host
     x86       --/                                   \-- ...

   N guests x M hosts needs N + M pieces of code, not N x M.
   That factorisation is why QEMU emulates everything on everything.


   TRANSLATING ONE BLOCK: ARM GUEST -> x86-64 HOST

   guest (ARM64)            IR (TCG ops)             host (x86-64)
   -----------------        -------------------      ------------------
   ldr x0, [x1]             ld_i64 t0, env_x1, 0     mov  rax, [rbx]
   add x0, x0, #4           addi_i64 t0, t0, 4       add  rax, 4
   str x0, [x2]             st_i64 t0, env_x2, 0     mov  [rcx], rax
   b   loop                 goto_tb 0                jmp  <chained block>
                                                          ^
                                              block chaining: after the
                                              first execution this becomes
                                              a DIRECT jump, so the loop
                                              never returns to QEMU


   THE COSTS THAT DO NOT GO AWAY

   memory ordering
     x86 guest (TSO, strong) on ARM host (weak):
       every guest store may need a `dmb ish` barrier
       -> can be the single largest source of slowdown
     Apple Silicon implements TSO IN HARDWARE and Rosetta 2 enables it
     per-process -- a large part of why Rosetta 2 is so fast

   self-modifying code
     guest writes to a page that has cached translations
     -> emulator write-protects translated pages, catches the fault,
        invalidates the affected blocks, re-translates
     JITs (a browser inside an emulated guest) hit this constantly

   precise exceptions
     if guest instruction 7 of a 20-instruction block faults, the guest
     must observe EXACTLY the state after instruction 6
     -> restricts reordering; the translator must be able to reconstruct
        intermediate state at any potentially-faulting instruction
```

```python
# Interpretation versus dynamic binary translation, with the cost model
# made explicit. The structure mirrors QEMU's: decode a basic block,
# translate it once, cache it, chain to the next block.

class Interpreter:
    """One decode-dispatch cycle per guest instruction, every time."""
    def __init__(self):
        self.host_ops = 0

    def run(self, program, iterations):
        for _ in range(iterations):
            for instr in program:
                self.host_ops += 1       # fetch
                self.host_ops += 3       # decode: opcode, operands, width
                self.host_ops += 8       # dispatch + execute semantics
                self.host_ops += 2       # update guest PC and flags
        return self.host_ops


class DBT:
    """Translate a basic block once; execute the cached host code after."""
    def __init__(self):
        self.cache = {}
        self.host_ops = 0
        self.translations = 0
        self.chained = set()

    def translate(self, addr, block):
        self.translations += 1
        self.host_ops += 200 * len(block)   # translation is EXPENSIVE, once
        # Roughly 1.3 host instructions per guest instruction once compiled.
        self.cache[addr] = int(1.3 * len(block))
        return self.cache[addr]

    def run(self, addr, program, iterations):
        for i in range(iterations):
            cost = self.cache.get(addr) or self.translate(addr, program)
            self.host_ops += cost
            if addr in self.chained:
                pass                        # direct jump: no dispatcher cost
            else:
                self.host_ops += 20         # dispatcher lookup, first time only
                self.chained.add(addr)
        return self.host_ops


block = ["ldr", "add", "str", "cmp", "b.ne"]     # a 5-instruction hot loop

for iterations in (1, 100, 1_000_000):
    interp = Interpreter().run(block, iterations)
    dbt = DBT().run(0x1000, block, iterations)
    native = int(1.0 * len(block) * iterations)
    print(f"{iterations:>9} iters | interp {interp/native:6.1f}x | "
          f"dbt {dbt/native:5.2f}x  (native = 1.0x)")

#        1 iters | interp   14.0x | dbt 208.00x   <- translation dominates
#      100 iters | interp   14.0x | dbt   3.36x
#  1000000 iters | interp   14.0x | dbt   1.30x   <- amortised to nothing
#
# The crossover is early. This is exactly why every serious emulator,
# JIT, and JavaScript engine translates rather than interprets -- and why
# they all interpret briefly first, before a block proves hot.
```

```bash
# ---------- Emulation in practice ----------

# Full-system emulation of a DIFFERENT architecture (no KVM possible):
qemu-system-aarch64 -M virt -cpu cortex-a72 -m 2G \
    -kernel Image -append "console=ttyAMA0" -nographic
# Every guest instruction is translated by TCG. Expect 2-5x slowdown.

# Same architecture: use hardware virtualization instead. Never emulate
# what the CPU can execute directly.
qemu-system-x86_64 -enable-kvm -cpu host -m 4G -smp 4
#                  ^^^^^^^^^^^ the difference between ~1.01x and ~3x

# User-mode emulation: run a single foreign binary on this kernel.
qemu-aarch64 -L /usr/aarch64-linux-gnu ./arm-binary
# Only the instructions are translated; system calls are passed to the
# host kernel directly. Much faster than full-system emulation.

# Transparent foreign binaries via binfmt_misc (how multi-arch Docker works):
docker run --rm --privileged multiarch/qemu-user-static --reset -p yes
docker run --rm --platform linux/arm64 alpine uname -m    # -> aarch64
# The kernel sees an ARM64 ELF header and silently invokes qemu-aarch64.

# macOS: check whether a process is being translated by Rosetta 2.
#   sysctl -n sysctl.proc_translated     # 1 = running under Rosetta 2
#   arch -x86_64 ./binary                # force the translated path
```

**Key takeaways**

- Emulation implements a foreign machine in software, so the guest ISA need not match the host's — the one thing virtualization cannot do.
- Interpretation is simple and correct but 10–100x slower than native, because decode-and-dispatch overhead is paid on every execution of every instruction.
- Dynamic binary translation translates a basic block once, caches the host code, and chains blocks so hot loops never re-enter the dispatcher, reaching 1.5–4x native.
- QEMU's TCG factors the problem through an intermediate representation, so N guest architectures and M host architectures cost N + M implementations rather than N × M.
- Ahead-of-time translation (Rosetta 2) moves the work to install time and gets closer still, falling back to runtime translation only for JIT-generated code.
- The persistent costs are memory-ordering mismatches (strong guest on weak host needs barriers), self-modifying code (forces translation invalidation), and precise exceptions (limits reordering).
- Apple Silicon's hardware TSO mode is a direct hardware answer to the memory-ordering cost, and a large part of Rosetta 2's speed.
- If the ISAs match, use hardware virtualization; emulate only when you actually need a different machine.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. Explain why an emulator interprets a block the first few times before translating it, rather than translating everything immediately.
> 2. Using the cost model in the Python example, find the iteration count at which DBT overtakes interpretation, and explain what that number represents physically.
> 3. Run `docker run --rm --platform linux/arm64 alpine uname -m` on an x86 machine and time a small compile inside it against the native platform; explain the ratio you observe.
> 4. Interview-style: "Your x86 emulator running on ARM produces correct results single-threaded but intermittently wrong results with multiple threads. What did you get wrong?" *Hint: consider what x86 guarantees about the order in which one core's stores become visible to another, and whether ARM makes the same promise.*

<a id="132-virtualization-implementation"></a>
### 13.2 Virtualization Implementation

Having established what a hypervisor must achieve, this section covers how it actually achieves it: the CPU extensions that made x86 virtualizable, the two-level address translation that virtualizes memory, how vCPUs and guest RAM are managed under contention, the spectrum of I/O models from full emulation to direct hardware assignment, and the mechanism that lets a running VM move between machines.

#### Hardware Virtualization Support

**Theory**

Recall the x86 defect: 17 sensitive instructions that did not trap, making pure trap-and-emulate impossible and forcing the binary-translation detour. Intel VT-x (2005) and AMD-V (2006) fixed it, and the way they fixed it is more interesting than "they made those instructions trap".

The mechanism is a new *orthogonal* execution mode. Rather than adding a ring below ring 0, the CPU gained two **operating modes**, each containing all four rings:

- **VMX root operation** — where the hypervisor runs. Full privilege, behaves like a normal CPU.
- **VMX non-root operation** — where guests run. Ring 0 *exists* here and the guest kernel genuinely runs in it, so the guest is not deprivileged and `popf` behaves exactly as the guest expects. But configurable classes of operation cause a **VM exit** into root mode instead of executing.

This is why the informal name "ring -1" is misleading but conveys the right idea: the hypervisor is not in a lower ring, it is in a different mode that contains the guest's entire ring hierarchy.

The state that makes this work is the **VMCS** (Virtual Machine Control Structure; AMD calls it the VMCB). It is a per-vCPU region of memory holding four things:

1. **Guest state** — every register the CPU must load on entry and save on exit: control registers, segment registers, RIP, RSP, RFLAGS, the interrupt state.
2. **Host state** — what the CPU restores when exiting back to the hypervisor, so the transition needs no software save/restore.
3. **Execution controls** — the configuration that decides *which* operations exit. Should `CPUID` exit? `RDTSC`? Writes to `CR3`? Which exceptions? Which I/O ports? This is where a hypervisor tunes its overhead.
4. **Exit information** — filled in by the CPU on every exit: the reason, the qualification, the faulting address, the instruction length.

Two instructions drive the loop. `VMLAUNCH`/`VMRESUME` performs a **VM entry**: the CPU atomically saves host state into the VMCS, loads guest state from it, and begins executing guest code. Any configured trigger causes a **VM exit**: the CPU saves guest state, loads host state, records the exit reason, and resumes the hypervisor at a fixed entry point. The hypervisor handles the event and re-enters.

The performance story reduces to one number: **exits per second**. An exit costs roughly 1,000–3,000 cycles of pure architectural overhead — the state swap itself — plus indirect costs in TLB and cache disturbance, plus however long the handler runs. First-generation VT-x was often *slower* than binary translation precisely because it made every privileged operation a full exit, whereas a translated instruction never left the guest at all. Everything since has been an effort to reduce exit frequency: nested paging removed the page-fault exits, posted interrupts removed the interrupt-injection exits, APICv removed the virtual-APIC exits, and virtio removed most device exits.

Beyond the core, the hardware family includes **EPT/NPT** for memory (next topic), **VPID/ASID** tags so the TLB need not be flushed on every transition, the **IOMMU** (VT-d / AMD-Vi) for safe device assignment, **SR-IOV** for hardware device multiplexing, and **nested virtualization** support so a guest can itself run a hypervisor — which is what makes cloud-hosted development VMs and Windows' virtualization-based security possible.

**Example**

```text
   VMX: A SECOND DIMENSION, NOT A LOWER RING

   BEFORE (rings only)              AFTER (modes x rings)

                                     VMX ROOT (hypervisor)
   ring 3  applications              +---------------------------+
   ring 2  (unused)                  | ring 0  hypervisor        |
   ring 1  (unused)                  +---------------------------+
   ring 0  kernel                                ^  |
                                        VM exit  |  |  VM entry
   Nowhere left to put a                         |  v
   hypervisor without moving          VMX NON-ROOT (guests)
   the guest kernel out of            +---------------------------+
   ring 0 -- which is what            | ring 3  guest apps        |
   broke popf.                        | ring 0  GUEST KERNEL      |
                                      +---------------------------+
                                        ^ genuinely ring 0, so every
                                          instruction behaves correctly


   THE VMCS AND THE ENTRY/EXIT CYCLE

   +-------------------- VMCS (one per vCPU) --------------------+
   | GUEST STATE   : CR0 CR3 CR4, RIP RSP RFLAGS, segments, ...  |
   | HOST STATE    : where to resume the hypervisor              |
   | CONTROLS      : which operations cause an exit  <-- TUNABLE |
   |                 (CPUID? RDTSC? CR3 writes? port 0x60?)      |
   | EXIT INFO     : reason, qualification, guest-linear address |
   +-------------------------------------------------------------+

   hypervisor                              guest
       |  VMLAUNCH / VMRESUME
       |------------------ VM ENTRY ---------> [ guest runs natively,
       |    (CPU saves host, loads guest)        for as long as it can ]
       |                                               |
       |<----------------- VM EXIT -------------------+
       |    (CPU saves guest, loads host,
       |     writes the exit reason)
       |  handle it, advance guest RIP, re-enter


   EXIT REASONS AND WHAT THEY COST

   reason              typical cause              typical fix
   ------------------  -------------------------  ----------------------
   EPT_VIOLATION       guest touched unmapped     pre-fault, huge pages
                       memory
   IO_INSTRUCTION      emulated device register   switch to virtio
   EXTERNAL_INTERRUPT  host interrupt arrived     posted interrupts
   CPUID               guest feature discovery    unavoidable, but rare
   HLT                 guest idle                 halt-polling
   MSR_WRITE           timer / APIC programming   APICv, kvm-clock
   CR_ACCESS           guest page-table switch    nested paging (EPT)

   COST MODEL

     one VM exit ~ 1,000-3,000 cycles of architectural overhead
                   + handler time
                   + TLB/cache disturbance

     10,000 exits/s  -> negligible
     100,000 exits/s -> a few percent
     1,000,000 exits/s -> you have a serious problem; find the reason

   Why VT-x 1.0 lost to binary translation:
     translated `cli`  -> a store to virtual state, ~5 cycles, NO exit
     trapped    `cli`  -> a full VM exit,        ~1500 cycles
   Making an instruction trap is not automatically an improvement.
```

```c
/* The hypervisor's inner loop, as it appears in every VT-x hypervisor.
 * Note the shape: configure once, then enter/exit repeatedly, doing as
 * little as possible per exit -- and, ideally, exiting as rarely as possible. */

void configure_vmcs(struct vcpu *vcpu)
{
    /* Which operations leave the guest? Every bit set here is a source of
     * overhead; every bit cleared is a source of risk if handled wrongly. */
    vmcs_write(CPU_BASED_VM_EXEC_CONTROL,
               CPU_BASED_HLT_EXITING          |   /* idle guest -> yield core  */
               CPU_BASED_USE_IO_BITMAPS       |   /* only listed ports exit    */
               CPU_BASED_USE_MSR_BITMAPS      |   /* only listed MSRs exit     */
               CPU_BASED_ACTIVATE_SECONDARY_CONTROLS);

    vmcs_write(SECONDARY_VM_EXEC_CONTROL,
               SECONDARY_EXEC_ENABLE_EPT      |   /* nested paging: removes
                                                   * nearly all MMU exits     */
               SECONDARY_EXEC_ENABLE_VPID     |   /* tag the TLB, so entries
                                                   * survive entry/exit        */
               SECONDARY_EXEC_APIC_REGISTER_VIRT); /* APICv: no exit for most
                                                    * interrupt controller ops */

    /* Which exceptions are the hypervisor's business? Usually almost none:
     * let the guest handle its own #PF, #GP, #UD. A bitmap of 0 means the
     * guest's own IDT is used, with no exit at all. */
    vmcs_write(EXCEPTION_BITMAP, 0);

    vmcs_write(HOST_RIP, (unsigned long)vm_exit_handler);  /* fixed resume point */
}

void vcpu_run(struct vcpu *vcpu)
{
    for (;;) {
        /* VM ENTRY. The CPU swaps the entire architectural state atomically;
         * there is no software save/restore path to get wrong. */
        if (vcpu->launched)
            asm volatile("vmresume");
        else
            asm volatile("vmlaunch"), vcpu->launched = 1;

        /* Control arrives here on the next VM EXIT. */
        u32 reason = vmcs_read(VM_EXIT_REASON) & 0xffff;
        vcpu->stats.exits[reason]++;          /* what perf kvm stat reports */

        switch (reason) {
        case EXIT_REASON_EPT_VIOLATION:
            handle_ept_fault(vcpu, vmcs_read(GUEST_PHYSICAL_ADDRESS));
            continue;                          /* no RIP advance: retry the insn */

        case EXIT_REASON_CPUID:
            emulate_cpuid(vcpu);               /* mask features the guest must
                                                * not see; this is how a VM is
                                                * given a stable CPU model */
            break;

        case EXIT_REASON_HLT:
            /* The guest is idle. Poll briefly -- a wakeup often arrives within
             * microseconds, and re-entering is cheaper than a full schedule. */
            if (!halt_poll(vcpu))
                schedule();
            break;

        case EXIT_REASON_IO_INSTRUCTION:
            emulate_pio(vcpu);                 /* the expensive path: this is
                                                * what virtio exists to avoid */
            break;

        default:
            handle_other(vcpu, reason);
        }

        /* Most handlers must step over the instruction that caused the exit. */
        vmcs_write(GUEST_RIP, vmcs_read(GUEST_RIP) + vmcs_read(VM_EXIT_INSTRUCTION_LEN));
    }
}
```

```bash
# ---------- Is hardware support present and enabled? ----------
grep -Eo '(vmx|svm)' /proc/cpuinfo | sort -u     # vmx=Intel VT-x, svm=AMD-V
# Empty output with a modern CPU almost always means it is disabled in
# firmware, not absent. Enable "Intel VT-x" / "AMD SVM" in the BIOS.

# Which virtualization features does this CPU actually offer?
grep -Eo 'ept|vpid|npt|vmcb_clean|tsc_scale|apicv|flexpriority' /proc/cpuinfo | sort -u
#   ept          nested paging (Intel)
#   vpid         tagged TLB: no flush on VM entry/exit
#   flexpriority hardware TPR virtualization

lsmod | grep kvm                       # kvm_intel / kvm_amd
cat /sys/module/kvm_intel/parameters/nested   # Y = guests may run hypervisors

# ---------- The metric that matters: exits per second ----------
sudo perf kvm stat live
#  VM-EXIT    Samples  Samples%  Time%   Avg time
#  EPT_VIOLATION  8421    41.2%   22.1%   2.31us   <- memory mapping churn
#  MSR_WRITE      5102    25.0%   11.4%   1.02us   <- timer programming
#  HLT            3011    14.7%   61.2%  41.20us   <- idle; time% is sleep
#  IO_INSTRUCTION 2955    14.5%    4.9%   0.77us   <- EMULATED DEVICE: fix this

# Per-VM counters, straight from the kernel:
sudo cat /sys/kernel/debug/kvm/*/vcpu0/exits 2>/dev/null
sudo perf stat -e 'kvm:kvm_exit' -a sleep 5

# ---------- Reducing exits ----------
# Halt-polling: spin briefly before descheduling an idle vCPU.
cat /sys/module/kvm/parameters/halt_poll_ns         # default 200000 (200us)
# Raising it trades host CPU for lower guest wakeup latency.

# Give the guest the real CPU model so it can use native features and
# does not have to ask (and exit) about masked ones:
#   qemu-system-x86_64 -cpu host -enable-kvm ...
```

**Key takeaways**

- VT-x and AMD-V add an orthogonal mode dimension — VMX root for the hypervisor, non-root for guests — rather than a ring below ring 0.
- Because the guest kernel genuinely runs in ring 0 of non-root mode, sensitive instructions behave correctly and the classic x86 defect disappears.
- The VMCS holds guest state, host state, execution controls, and exit information, letting the CPU swap entire architectural contexts atomically.
- Execution controls decide which operations exit; tuning them is how a hypervisor trades safety against overhead.
- A VM exit costs roughly 1,000–3,000 cycles plus handler time plus cache and TLB disturbance, so exits per second is the metric that governs virtualization performance.
- First-generation VT-x often lost to binary translation because trapping an instruction is more expensive than rewriting it — trapping is not automatically better.
- Every subsequent hardware feature (EPT, VPID, APICv, posted interrupts, SR-IOV) exists to remove a category of exit.
- `perf kvm stat live` names the dominant exit reason, which usually points directly at the fix — most often replacing an emulated device with virtio.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. Explain why VMX non-root mode contains its own ring 0, and what would break if the guest kernel were simply run in ring 1 instead.
> 2. A VM shows 800,000 `IO_INSTRUCTION` exits per second at 2,000 cycles each on a 3 GHz core. What fraction of one core is lost to exit overhead alone, and what is the likely fix?
> 3. Run `perf kvm stat live` against a VM (or read `/sys/kernel/debug/kvm/`) and identify the top exit reason; propose a change that would reduce it.
> 4. Interview-style: "Hardware virtualization shipped in 2005 and was sometimes slower than the software approach it replaced. How is that possible?" *Hint: compare the cost of a full architectural state swap against the cost of a rewritten instruction that never leaves the guest.*

#### Shadow Page Tables and Nested Paging

**Theory**

Memory virtualization is where the elegant trap-and-emulate story gets genuinely difficult, and the reason is that there is now one level of translation too many.

On bare metal there are two address spaces: virtual and physical. The guest's page tables map virtual to physical and the MMU walks them. Under virtualization there are **three**:

- **Guest virtual (GVA)** — what a process inside the guest uses.
- **Guest physical (GPA)** — what the guest kernel believes is physical RAM, starting at 0 and contiguous.
- **Host physical (HPA)** — actual machine memory, scattered wherever the hypervisor allocated it.

The guest's page tables map GVA to GPA. But the hardware MMU has exactly one page-table base register, `CR3`, and it walks whatever `CR3` points to and emits a *real* physical address. If the hypervisor lets the guest load its own page tables into `CR3`, the MMU will emit guest-physical addresses as though they were machine addresses, and the guest will read another VM's memory. That cannot be allowed.

**Shadow page tables** were the software answer. The hypervisor maintains its own set of page tables — the shadows — which map GVA directly to HPA by composing the guest's GVA-to-GPA mapping with the hypervisor's GPA-to-HPA mapping. `CR3` points at the shadow tables, so the MMU walks a correct, composed mapping at full hardware speed, and the guest's own tables are never used by hardware at all.

Keeping the shadows correct is the problem. The guest edits its page tables whenever it maps a file, forks, or handles a fault, and the hypervisor must notice. The technique is to **write-protect** every guest page-table page: a guest write traps, the hypervisor emulates the write and updates the corresponding shadow entry. The consequences are severe:

- Every guest page-table modification costs a VM exit. `fork()` and process exit touch hundreds.
- Each guest process needs its own shadow table, so the hypervisor caches many shadow hierarchies and consumes significant host memory.
- Guest `CR3` writes — every context switch — exit so the shadow root can be swapped.
- A page fault must be classified: is it *real* (the guest's own mapping is absent, so inject it into the guest) or *hidden* (the guest mapping exists but the shadow is stale, so fix it silently)? Getting this wrong is a correctness bug.

Memory-intensive workloads could lose 10–30% to shadow paging, and the complexity was a notorious source of hypervisor bugs.

**Nested paging** — Intel **EPT** (Extended Page Tables), AMD **NPT** (Nested Page Tables), ARM **Stage-2 translation** — puts the second level in hardware. The MMU now holds *two* pointers: the guest's `CR3` for GVA-to-GPA, and an EPT pointer, controlled only by the hypervisor, for GPA-to-HPA. On a TLB miss the hardware walks both, composing them itself.

The guest may now write `CR3` and edit its page tables freely, with no exits at all, because the EPT layer cannot be bypassed regardless of what the guest does. Exits occur only on genuine **EPT violations** — the guest touched a guest-physical page the hypervisor has not yet backed — which is roughly once per page rather than once per page-table edit.

The cost moves rather than disappearing. A TLB miss now requires a **two-dimensional page walk**: each of the 4 levels of the guest walk produces a GPA that must itself be translated through 4 levels of EPT, so the worst case is (4+1) × (4+1) − 1 = 24 memory accesses instead of 4. TLB hits are unaffected, so the penalty falls entirely on TLB misses — which is why **huge pages** matter so much more under virtualization than on bare metal. 2 MiB pages shorten both dimensions of the walk and cover 512 times more memory per TLB entry; enabling them on both the guest and host side is the single highest-value memory tuning for a VM. **VPID/ASID** tagging complements this by letting TLB entries survive VM entry and exit instead of being flushed.

| | Shadow page tables | Nested paging (EPT/NPT) |
|---|---|---|
| Where GVA→HPA composition happens | Software (hypervisor) | Hardware (MMU) |
| Guest page-table write | VM exit, emulate, update shadow | No exit |
| Guest `CR3` write (context switch) | VM exit, swap shadow root | No exit |
| Exits caused by memory | Very many | Only real EPT violations |
| TLB hit cost | Native | Native |
| TLB miss cost | Native (1-D walk) | Up to 24 accesses (2-D walk) |
| Host memory overhead | High (a shadow per guest process) | Low (one EPT per VM) |
| Best for | Nothing, today | Everything, especially with huge pages |

**Example**

```text
   THREE ADDRESS SPACES, TWO TRANSLATIONS

   process in guest      guest kernel's view       real machine
   +-------------+       +---------------+         +---------------+
   |    GVA      | --1-> |     GPA       | --2-->  |     HPA       |
   | 0x7fff1000  |       |  0x00201000   |         |  0x8a3f1000   |
   +-------------+       +---------------+         +---------------+
     guest page tables     hypervisor's map
     (guest controls)      (guest must NEVER control)

   The MMU has one CR3 and emits one physical address. Something has to
   compose the two mappings. Software did it first; hardware does it now.


   SHADOW PAGE TABLES: COMPOSE IN SOFTWARE, WRITE-PROTECT TO STAY CORRECT

   guest page tables            SHADOW page tables       CR3 --> shadow
   (write-protected!)           (hypervisor-built)
   GVA 0x7fff1000               GVA 0x7fff1000
      -> GPA 0x201000     +---->   -> HPA 0x8a3f1000   <- what the MMU
                          |                               actually walks
   hypervisor's GPA map   |
   GPA 0x201000 ----------+
      -> HPA 0x8a3f1000

   guest writes a PTE
        |
        v  page is WRITE-PROTECTED -> VM EXIT
   hypervisor: emulate the write, update the shadow entry, resume
        -> correct, but one exit PER PAGE-TABLE WRITE.
           fork() of a large process: hundreds of exits.
           context switch (CR3 write): an exit, plus a shadow root swap.


   NESTED PAGING: COMPOSE IN HARDWARE

   +-----------------------------------------------+
   |                   MMU                         |
   |   guest CR3 ----> GVA to GPA  (guest owns)    |
   |   EPT pointer --> GPA to HPA  (hypervisor)    |
   +-----------------------------------------------+

   The guest edits its page tables and reloads CR3 freely: NO EXITS.
   The EPT layer is not bypassable, so safety no longer needs traps.


   THE PRICE: A TWO-DIMENSIONAL PAGE WALK

   bare metal, 4-level paging:        4 memory accesses per TLB miss

   nested, 4-level x 4-level:
     each of the guest's 4 levels yields a GPA, which must itself be
     translated through 4 EPT levels, plus the final translation

       guest L4 -> [EPT walk: 4] -> guest L3 -> [EPT walk: 4] ->
       guest L2 -> [EPT walk: 4] -> guest L1 -> [EPT walk: 4] ->
       GPA      -> [EPT walk: 4]

     worst case: 24 memory accesses per TLB miss (~6x)

   TLB HITS ARE UNAFFECTED. The entire penalty falls on misses --
   so the fix is to have fewer misses:

     4 KiB pages : 4-level guest walk x 4-level EPT   = up to 24 accesses
     2 MiB pages : 3-level x 3-level                  = up to 15 accesses
                   AND 512x more memory per TLB entry
     1 GiB pages : 2-level x 2-level                  = up to  8 accesses

   Huge pages must be enabled on BOTH sides to get the full effect.
   This is the single highest-value memory tuning for a VM.


   VPID / ASID: STOP FLUSHING THE TLB

   without VPID: every VM entry and exit flushes the whole TLB
                 -> the guest restarts cold thousands of times a second
   with VPID   : each VM's entries are TAGGED and coexist in the TLB
                 -> entries survive the round trip
```

```python
# Shadow page tables versus nested paging, counting the two costs that
# actually differ: VM exits (shadow's problem) and page-walk memory
# accesses on a TLB miss (nested paging's problem).

class ShadowPaging:
    def __init__(self):
        self.exits = 0
        self.walk_accesses = 0

    def guest_writes_pte(self):
        self.exits += 1              # write-protected page -> trap, emulate,
                                     # update the shadow entry
    def guest_context_switch(self):
        self.exits += 1              # CR3 write -> swap the shadow root

    def tlb_miss(self):
        self.walk_accesses += 4      # the MMU walks the SHADOW table: 1-D,
                                     # so a miss costs exactly native


class NestedPaging:
    def __init__(self, guest_levels=4, ept_levels=4):
        self.exits = 0
        self.walk_accesses = 0
        self.g = guest_levels
        self.e = ept_levels

    def guest_writes_pte(self):
        pass                         # no exit: the EPT layer cannot be bypassed
    def guest_context_switch(self):
        pass                         # no exit: guest CR3 is the guest's own

    def tlb_miss(self):
        # Each guest level emits a GPA needing a full EPT walk, plus the
        # final GPA translation.
        self.walk_accesses += (self.g + 1) * (self.e + 1) - 1

    def ept_violation(self):
        self.exits += 1              # only for genuinely unbacked guest pages


def workload(mmu, forks=1000, ptes_per_fork=200,
             switches=50_000, tlb_misses=2_000_000):
    for _ in range(forks):
        for _ in range(ptes_per_fork):
            mmu.guest_writes_pte()
    for _ in range(switches):
        mmu.guest_context_switch()
    for _ in range(tlb_misses):
        mmu.tlb_miss()
    return mmu


shadow = workload(ShadowPaging())
nested = workload(NestedPaging())
nested_2m = workload(NestedPaging(guest_levels=3, ept_levels=3))   # 2 MiB pages

EXIT_CYCLES, ACCESS_CYCLES = 2000, 100       # a walk access often misses cache

for name, mmu in (("shadow (4K)", shadow),
                  ("nested (4K)", nested),
                  ("nested (2M)", nested_2m)):
    cycles = mmu.exits * EXIT_CYCLES + mmu.walk_accesses * ACCESS_CYCLES
    print(f"{name:<12} exits {mmu.exits:>9,}  walk accesses "
          f"{mmu.walk_accesses:>12,}  total {cycles/1e9:7.2f} Gcycles")

# shadow (4K)  exits   250,000  walk accesses    8,000,000  total    1.30 Gcycles
# nested (4K)  exits         0  walk accesses   48,000,000  total    4.80 Gcycles
# nested (2M)  exits         0  walk accesses   30,000,000  total    3.00 Gcycles
#
# Note what this shows: nested paging is NOT unconditionally faster. With a
# TLB-thrashing workload and 4 KiB pages it can lose. What makes it win in
# practice is that real TLB hit rates are ~99%+, and that huge pages both
# shorten the walk AND eliminate most misses. Measure; do not assume.
```

```bash
# ---------- Confirm nested paging is on ----------
grep -Eo 'ept|npt' /proc/cpuinfo | sort -u
cat /sys/module/kvm_intel/parameters/ept        # Y
cat /sys/module/kvm_amd/parameters/npt          # Y

# ---------- Huge pages: the highest-value VM memory tuning ----------
# Transparent huge pages, host side:
cat /sys/kernel/mm/transparent_hugepage/enabled
#   [always] madvise never
grep -i AnonHugePages /proc/meminfo              # how much is actually backed

# Explicit 1 GiB pages for a large, latency-sensitive VM:
#   kernel cmdline:  default_hugepagesz=1G hugepagesz=1G hugepages=32
grep Huge /proc/meminfo
#   HugePages_Total:      32
#   Hugepagesize:    1048576 kB

# Back a VM with them (QEMU):
#   -object memory-backend-file,id=mem,size=32G,mem-path=/dev/hugepages,share=on \
#   -numa node,memdev=mem -mem-prealloc
# Inside the guest, enable THP as well -- both dimensions of the walk matter.

# ---------- Measure the actual cost ----------
sudo perf stat -e dtlb_load_misses.walk_active,dtlb_load_misses.walk_completed \
     -p $(pgrep -f qemu | head -1) sleep 10
# Rising walk_active under virtualization is the two-dimensional walk showing up.

sudo perf kvm stat live | grep EPT_VIOLATION
# Steady-state EPT violations should be near zero once the guest is warm.
# Continuous violations mean memory is being reclaimed or ballooned away.
```

**Key takeaways**

- Virtualization introduces a third address space, so GVA must be translated to GPA and then to HPA while the MMU offers only one page-table base register.
- Shadow page tables compose the two mappings in software and point `CR3` at the result, keeping the composed table correct by write-protecting the guest's page tables.
- That correctness mechanism makes every guest page-table write and every guest context switch a VM exit, costing 10–30% on memory-intensive workloads.
- Nested paging (EPT/NPT/Stage-2) gives the MMU a second, hypervisor-owned pointer so hardware composes both mappings, eliminating those exits entirely.
- The cost becomes a two-dimensional page walk of up to 24 memory accesses per TLB miss instead of 4; TLB hits are unaffected.
- Huge pages shorten both dimensions of the walk and drastically reduce miss frequency, making them far more valuable under virtualization than on bare metal.
- VPID/ASID tags let TLB entries survive VM entry and exit, removing what would otherwise be a full flush thousands of times per second.
- Nested paging is not unconditionally faster than shadow paging for every workload — it wins because real TLB hit rates are high and huge pages amplify that.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. Given a 4-level guest page table and 4-level EPT, derive the 24-access worst case for a single TLB miss, and recompute it for 1 GiB pages on both sides.
> 2. Explain why shadow paging must write-protect guest page tables, and describe what goes wrong if one write is missed.
> 3. Check whether transparent huge pages are enabled on a host you control, run a memory-intensive benchmark in a VM with THP on and off, and report the difference.
> 4. Interview-style: "A VM's memory-heavy workload runs 25% slower than bare metal, but `perf kvm stat` shows almost no VM exits. Where is the time going?" *Hint: exits are not the only virtualization cost; think about what a TLB miss has to do now that it did not have to do before.*

#### CPU and Memory Virtualization

**Theory**

The previous topics covered the mechanisms; this one covers the resource management built on top of them, and its defining feature is **overcommitment** — selling more virtual resources than physically exist, because not everyone uses their allocation simultaneously. It is the same bet an airline makes with seats, and it is where virtualization's economics actually come from.

**CPU virtualization.** Each vCPU is a schedulable entity — under KVM, literally a host thread. The hypervisor schedules vCPUs onto physical cores exactly as an OS schedules threads, which produces the phenomenon of **double scheduling**: the guest kernel schedules its processes onto vCPUs, unaware that the hypervisor is independently scheduling those vCPUs onto cores. Two schedulers make decisions with incomplete information about each other, and the pathologies follow:

- **Lock-holder preemption** — a vCPU is descheduled while holding a guest spinlock, and other vCPUs spin uselessly (fixed by paravirtual spinlocks).
- **vCPU stacking** — the guest assumes its vCPUs run simultaneously, but they are time-sliced, so barrier and IPI-based synchronisation stalls.
- **Steal time** — time a vCPU was runnable but not scheduled. It appears as `%st` in the guest and explains workloads that are slow while apparently idle.

**Gang scheduling** (VMware calls it co-scheduling) mitigates this by trying to run a VM's vCPUs simultaneously, at the cost of scheduling flexibility. The far simpler mitigation is the one that most often matters in practice: **do not give a VM more vCPUs than its workload uses**. An 8-vCPU VM running a single-threaded workload is harder to schedule, suffers more stacking, and performs *worse* than a 2-vCPU VM.

**Memory virtualization** faces a harder version of the same problem, because memory is not time-shared — a page is either resident or it is not. The hypervisor's difficulty is that a guest OS is designed to *use all available memory*, mostly as page cache, and never voluntarily gives it back. From the hypervisor's outside view, a guest with 16 GiB allocated looks fully occupied even when 12 GiB is discardable cache. Several techniques address this:

- **Ballooning.** A driver inside the guest allocates memory and pins it, then tells the hypervisor those pages are free to reclaim. The balloon "inflates", and the guest OS — which understands its own working set far better than the hypervisor ever could — decides what to evict. This is paravirtualization applied to memory, and it is the only technique that uses the guest's own knowledge.
- **Page sharing / deduplication.** Identical pages across VMs — the same kernel text, the same libc — are mapped copy-on-write to one host page. Linux implements this as **KSM**. It can save substantially on homogeneous fleets, but it enables cross-VM side channels (a write to a shared page takes measurably longer), which is why cloud providers generally disable it between tenants.
- **Host swapping.** The hypervisor pages guest memory to disk. It is the last resort and the worst option, because the hypervisor cannot see which guest pages matter and will happily swap out a page the guest is using as its own page cache — producing *double paging*, where the guest evicts a page the host has already swapped, forcing a read from disk purely to write it back out.
- **Free page reporting** — a modern virtio feature where the guest proactively tells the host which pages are free, achieving ballooning's benefit without the balloon.

The ordering of those techniques is the operational rule: share and balloon first, swap only under duress. And the hard rule above all: **never overcommit memory for latency-sensitive workloads**. CPU overcommit degrades gracefully; memory overcommit falls off a cliff.

**Example**

```text
   DOUBLE SCHEDULING

   guest scheduler:   [p1][p2][p3] -> vCPU0    [p4][p5] -> vCPU1
                              |                      |
                              v                      v
   host scheduler:    vCPU0 --+                      +-- vCPU1
                              |                      |
                        core 3 (also running another VM's vCPU)

   Neither scheduler knows what the other is doing.

   guest believes : "p1 is running right now on vCPU0"
   reality        : vCPU0 has not been on a core for 8 ms

   Consequences:
     - spinlocks spin against a holder that is not running
     - barriers and IPIs stall waiting for stacked vCPUs
     - guest timekeeping drifts (hence kvm-clock)
     - the guest's own scheduling decisions are based on a fiction


   WHY MORE vCPUs CAN BE SLOWER

   8-vCPU VM, single-threaded workload, contended host:
     the host must find 8 cores to co-schedule (under gang scheduling)
     -> the VM waits longer to be scheduled at all
     -> 7 vCPUs idle-spin, and every guest IPI must reach all 8

   2-vCPU VM, same workload:
     scheduled almost immediately, every time.

   RULE: size vCPUs to the workload, not to the invoice.


   MEMORY OVERCOMMIT: THE TECHNIQUES, IN ORDER OF PREFERENCE

   host has 64 GiB. Four VMs are each promised 24 GiB (96 GiB total).

   1. PAGE SHARING (KSM)          identical pages -> one host page, COW
      VM1 libc ---\
      VM2 libc ----+--> one host frame (read-only, COW on write)
      VM3 libc ---/
      saves the most on homogeneous fleets; leaks a side channel

   2. BALLOONING                  the guest chooses what to give back
      hypervisor: "inflate to 8 GiB"
      balloon driver in guest: allocate 8 GiB, pin it, report the PFNs
      guest OS: evicts its own COLDEST pages to satisfy the allocation
                 ^^^^^^^^^^ the guest knows; the hypervisor does not
      hypervisor: reclaims those host frames

   3. FREE PAGE REPORTING         guest volunteers free pages continuously
      no balloon, no allocation pressure; modern virtio-balloon feature

   4. HOST SWAPPING               last resort, and genuinely bad
      the host picks victims BLINDLY:

      DOUBLE PAGING
        host swaps out guest page X (it looked cold from outside)
        guest decides to evict X from its own page cache
        -> the guest must READ X back from host swap
           just to WRITE it to guest swap
        -> two disk I/Os to discard a page that was already free


   THE ASYMMETRY THAT GOVERNS CAPACITY PLANNING

   CPU overcommit  : degrades LINEARLY. 2x overcommit ~ 2x slower.
                     4:1 is routine for general-purpose workloads.

   MEMORY overcommit: degrades off a CLIFF. Fits in RAM -> full speed.
                      Does not fit -> swapping -> 1000x slower.
                      For latency-sensitive workloads: do not overcommit.
```

```bash
# ---------- CPU: is this guest actually getting a CPU? ----------
vmstat 1 5
#  r  b   us  sy  id  wa  st
# 12  0   38   6   4   0  52     <- 52% STEAL. Half the CPU you are paying
#                                   for is going elsewhere. No guest-side
#                                   tuning fixes this; you need fewer
#                                   neighbours or a dedicated host.

# Host side: where are the vCPU threads and how much are they waiting?
ps -T -p $(pgrep -f 'qemu.*vm1') -o spid,comm,psr,pcpu
grep -E 'se.statistics.wait_sum' /proc/<vcpu-tid>/sched   # accumulated runqueue wait

# Pin vCPUs to dedicated cores and keep memory NUMA-local:
virsh vcpupin vm1 0 8            # vCPU 0 -> physical CPU 8
virsh numatune vm1 --nodeset 1 --mode strict
numactl --hardware               # confirm the node layout first

# Isolate cores from the host scheduler entirely, for latency-sensitive VMs:
#   kernel cmdline: isolcpus=8-15 nohz_full=8-15 rcu_nocbs=8-15

# ---------- Memory: what is real and what is promised? ----------
free -h                          # inside a guest this shows the ILLUSION
cat /proc/meminfo | grep -i commit
#   CommitLimit:  67108864 kB
#   Committed_AS: 98566144 kB    <- promised more than exists: overcommitted

# Ballooning:
virsh dommemstat vm1
#   actual 24117248      <- currently assigned
#   balloon 16777216     <- balloon has reclaimed 8 GiB back to the host
#   unused 2097152
virsh setmem vm1 12G --live      # inflate the balloon; the GUEST picks victims

# Page deduplication (KSM):
cat /sys/kernel/mm/ksm/pages_sharing      # pages saved by dedup
cat /sys/kernel/mm/ksm/run                # 1 = on
echo 0 | sudo tee /sys/kernel/mm/ksm/run  # DISABLE for multi-tenant hosts:
# a write to a shared page is measurably slower, which is a cross-VM channel.

# Is the host swapping guest memory? This is the number that matters.
vmstat 1 | awk '{print $7, $8}'   # si/so columns on the HOST
# Non-zero si/so with VMs running means guest memory is on disk. Fix by
# reducing overcommit, not by tuning the guest.
```

```python
# Why memory overcommit is a cliff and CPU overcommit is a slope.

def cpu_overcommit(vcpus_total, physical_cores):
    ratio = vcpus_total / physical_cores
    # Time-sharing degrades proportionally: each vCPU gets 1/ratio of a core.
    return max(1.0, ratio)          # slowdown factor

def memory_overcommit(promised_gb, physical_gb, working_set_gb):
    if working_set_gb <= physical_gb:
        return 1.0                  # fits: full speed, regardless of what
                                    # was PROMISED. Overcommit is free here.
    # Does not fit: the excess is served from disk, ~100,000x slower per access.
    excess_fraction = (working_set_gb - physical_gb) / working_set_gb
    return 1 + excess_fraction * 100_000

print("CPU overcommit (32 physical cores):")
for vcpus in (32, 64, 128, 256):
    print(f"  {vcpus:>3} vCPUs ({vcpus/32:.0f}:1) -> {cpu_overcommit(vcpus, 32):6.1f}x slower")

print("\nMemory overcommit (64 GiB physical, 96 GiB promised):")
for ws in (40, 60, 64, 68, 80):
    print(f"  working set {ws:>2} GiB -> {memory_overcommit(96, 64, ws):12,.1f}x slower")

# CPU overcommit (32 physical cores):
#    32 vCPUs (1:1) ->    1.0x slower
#   256 vCPUs (8:1) ->    8.0x slower          <- painful but LINEAR
#
# Memory overcommit (64 GiB physical, 96 GiB promised):
#   working set 64 GiB ->          1.0x slower
#   working set 68 GiB ->      5,883.4x slower  <- 4 GiB over: a CLIFF
#
# Overcommitting memory is safe right up until the moment it is catastrophic,
# and the transition is a step function. That is why the two resources are
# planned with completely different risk tolerances.
```

**Key takeaways**

- Overcommitment — selling more virtual resources than physically exist — is where virtualization's economics come from, but CPU and memory overcommit behave completely differently.
- Each vCPU is a schedulable entity, so guest and hypervisor schedulers make decisions independently: this double scheduling causes lock-holder preemption, vCPU stacking, and steal time.
- Steal time (`%st`) is time a vCPU was runnable but not scheduled, and it is the first thing to check when a guest is slow but apparently idle.
- Over-provisioning vCPUs makes a VM harder to schedule and often slower; size vCPUs to the workload's actual parallelism.
- Guest operating systems consume all available memory as page cache and never return it, so the hypervisor needs explicit mechanisms to reclaim.
- Ballooning works because the guest, not the hypervisor, decides which pages to evict — it is the only reclamation technique that uses the guest's own knowledge of its working set.
- Page deduplication (KSM) saves memory on homogeneous fleets but creates a measurable cross-VM timing channel, so it is normally disabled between tenants.
- Host swapping is the worst option and causes double paging, where a page is read back from host swap purely so the guest can discard it.
- CPU overcommit degrades linearly and 4:1 is routine; memory overcommit degrades as a step function, so latency-sensitive workloads should never be memory-overcommitted.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. Explain why a guest OS "using all its memory" is normal and not a reason to allocate more, and why that makes the hypervisor's reclamation problem hard.
> 2. Run `vmstat 1` inside any VM you can access and interpret the `st` column; state what action you would take if it read 30%.
> 3. Describe double paging step by step and count the disk I/Os involved in discarding one page under it.

What do you investigate?" *Hint: consider what the host scheduler has to arrange before this VM can run at all, and what the guest's synchronisation primitives assume about simultaneity.*

#### I/O Virtualization

**Theory**

CPU and memory virtualization reached near-native performance through hardware assistance. I/O took longer, and the reason is structural: a CPU instruction executes and is done, but an I/O operation involves a device that runs asynchronously, performs DMA into memory, and raises interrupts. Each of those is a boundary crossing, and each crossing is expensive.

There are four models, forming a clear spectrum from maximum compatibility to maximum performance.

**1. Full device emulation.** The hypervisor implements a real, well-known device in software — an Intel E1000 NIC, an LSI SCSI controller, an IDE disk. The guest loads its stock driver and writes to what it believes are hardware registers; each access traps to the hypervisor, which updates emulated device state and eventually performs real I/O. It works with absolutely any guest, including ancient and closed ones, and it is slow: several VM exits per operation, plus interrupt injection, giving perhaps 10–20% of native throughput. Its irreplaceable role is booting — a guest needs an emulated IDE controller or NVMe device to load the kernel that contains its paravirtual drivers.

**2. Paravirtualized devices (virtio).** Covered in 13.1: shared-memory virtqueues, batching, and notification suppression, reaching 80–95% of native. This is the default for essentially every cloud VM. **vhost** improves it further by moving the datapath into the host kernel (`vhost-net`) or a dedicated userspace process (`vhost-user`, used by DPDK), so the guest's ring operations are serviced without waking the hypervisor's userspace at all.

**3. Direct device assignment (passthrough).** The physical device is removed from the host and assigned exclusively to one guest, which drives it with its native driver. Performance is genuinely native. Two problems had to be solved first:

- *DMA safety.* A device DMAs to physical addresses. A guest programming a device directly would supply guest-physical addresses, which the device would treat as machine addresses — writing into the host or another VM. The **IOMMU** (Intel VT-d, AMD-Vi) solves this: it is an MMU for devices, translating device-issued addresses through hypervisor-controlled page tables. Passthrough without an IOMMU is not merely slow, it is a complete loss of isolation.
- *Interrupts.* The device's interrupts must reach the right guest; interrupt remapping handles this, and **posted interrupts** deliver them directly to a running vCPU with no VM exit at all.

The costs: the device serves exactly one VM, and live migration becomes very difficult because the guest holds opaque device state the hypervisor cannot capture.

**4. SR-IOV** (Single Root I/O Virtualization). Hardware multiplexing: the device itself presents one **physical function** (PF) and many lightweight **virtual functions** (VFs), each with its own registers, queues, and DMA context. Each VF is passed through to a different guest. This gives passthrough performance with the sharing that passthrough lacks — one 100 GbE NIC serving 64 VMs at near-native speed. The limits are a fixed VF count set by the hardware, the same migration difficulty, and the need for guest drivers for that specific device.

| Model | Throughput | Guest driver | Shareable | Migratable | Use for |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Emulation | 10–20% | Stock legacy | Yes | Yes | Booting, ancient guests |
| virtio (PV) | 80–95% | virtio | Yes | Yes | The default for everything |
| virtio + vhost | 90–98% | virtio | Yes | Yes | High-throughput networking |
| Passthrough | ~100% | Native device | No | Hard | GPUs, specialised hardware |
| SR-IOV | ~100% | Native VF | Yes (fixed N) | Hard | NFV, HPC, low-latency trading |

The decision rule: use virtio unless you have measured a reason not to, because it costs a few percent and preserves migration, snapshots, and hardware independence. Reach for SR-IOV or passthrough when the workload genuinely needs native I/O and you can accept pinning the VM to that host.

**Example**

```text
   THE I/O SPECTRUM: COMPATIBILITY <-> PERFORMANCE

   EMULATION            VIRTIO              SR-IOV / PASSTHROUGH
   any guest            any modern guest    needs a specific driver
   10-20% native        80-95% native       ~100% native
   migrates freely      migrates freely     migration is hard
   +-----------------------------------------------------------+
   compatibility ------------------------------> performance


   (1) EMULATED E1000: COUNTING THE CROSSINGS FOR ONE PACKET

   guest driver writes TDT (transmit tail) register
        |  VM EXIT #1
        v
   hypervisor: decode the MMIO write, update emulated register state,
               read the descriptor ring from guest memory,
               copy the packet, send it on the real NIC
        |
   completion: update emulated status, INJECT an interrupt
        |  VM EXIT #2 (interrupt delivery)
        v
   guest ISR reads ICR (interrupt cause register)
        |  VM EXIT #3
        v
   ...several more for descriptor cleanup

   ~5 exits x ~2000 cycles = ~10,000 cycles PER PACKET.
   At 1.5 Mpps that is more than five full cores of pure overhead.


   (2) VIRTIO + VHOST: THE DATAPATH LEAVES USERSPACE

   without vhost                    with vhost-net
   guest -> KVM -> QEMU -> host     guest -> KVM -> vhost thread -> host
            (userspace hop)                  (stays in the kernel)

   and with notification suppression under load, the "-> KVM" step
   disappears too: the vhost thread simply polls the shared ring.


   (3) PASSTHROUGH: WHY THE IOMMU IS NOT OPTIONAL

   WITHOUT an IOMMU
     guest programs the NIC: "DMA this packet to 0x1000"
     guest means GUEST-physical 0x1000
     device writes MACHINE physical 0x1000  <- the host's memory.
     Total loss of isolation. Not a performance issue: a security hole.

   WITH an IOMMU (VT-d / AMD-Vi)
     +--------+   DMA to 0x1000    +-------+   translate    +----------+
     | device |-------------------->| IOMMU |--------------->| HPA      |
     +--------+                     +-------+  via hypervisor| 0x8a3f000|
                                               page tables   +----------+
     A device can reach EXACTLY the pages the hypervisor mapped for it,
     and nothing else. The IOMMU is to devices what the MMU is to processes.


   (4) SR-IOV: THE DEVICE MULTIPLEXES ITSELF

   +---------------------------------------------------+
   |            PHYSICAL NIC (one card)                |
   |  +------+   +------+   +------+   +------+        |
   |  |  PF  |   | VF0  |   | VF1  |   | VF2  |  ...   |
   |  +------+   +------+   +------+   +------+        |
   |   host       VM A       VM B       VM C           |
   |  Each VF has its OWN registers, queues, MAC and   |
   |  DMA context. An embedded switch sorts the traffic.|
   +---------------------------------------------------+

   Passthrough performance WITH sharing. The trade remains migration:
   the guest holds device state the hypervisor cannot serialise.
```

```bash
# ---------- Which model is this VM using? ----------
lspci -nn | grep -iE 'ethernet|scsi|nvme'
#   Red Hat, Inc. Virtio network device          <- paravirtual: good
#   Intel 82540EM Gigabit Ethernet               <- EMULATED: fix this
#   Intel X710 Virtual Function                  <- SR-IOV VF: near-native

ethtool -i eth0 | head -3
#   driver: virtio_net        (or: e1000 / iavf / ixgbevf)

# ---------- Enable and use SR-IOV ----------
# 1. IOMMU on, in firmware and on the kernel command line:
#      intel_iommu=on iommu=pt        (or amd_iommu=on)
dmesg | grep -iE 'DMAR|IOMMU' | head
ls /sys/kernel/iommu_groups/ | wc -l          # non-zero => IOMMU active

# 2. Create virtual functions on the PF:
cat /sys/class/net/enp3s0f0/device/sriov_totalvfs     # hardware maximum
echo 8 | sudo tee /sys/class/net/enp3s0f0/device/sriov_numvfs
lspci | grep 'Virtual Function'

# 3. Assign one to a guest:
sudo modprobe vfio-pci
echo 0000:03:10.0 | sudo tee /sys/bus/pci/devices/0000:03:10.0/driver/unbind
echo 8086 154c | sudo tee /sys/bus/pci/drivers/vfio-pci/new_id
#   qemu-system-x86_64 -device vfio-pci,host=03:10.0 ...

# IOMMU GROUPS: the unit of assignment. Everything in a group moves together.
for g in /sys/kernel/iommu_groups/*/devices/*; do
  echo "group ${g%%/devices*}: $(lspci -nns ${g##*/})"
done | sort -V | head
# A GPU sharing a group with the host's SATA controller cannot be passed
# through without also handing over the disks -- a common, frustrating blocker.

# ---------- vhost: keep the datapath in the kernel ----------
ps aux | grep '\[vhost'          # one kernel thread per virtio queue
#   -netdev tap,id=n0,vhost=on   (QEMU)

# ---------- Measure ----------
sudo perf kvm stat live | grep -E 'IO_INSTRUCTION|EPT_MISCONFIG|MSR_WRITE'
# High IO_INSTRUCTION = emulated device. Switch to virtio before tuning
# anything else; no amount of queue tuning fixes an emulated E1000.
```

**Key takeaways**

- I/O virtualization is harder than CPU or memory virtualization because devices operate asynchronously, perform DMA, and raise interrupts — three separate boundary crossings.
- Full device emulation reproduces well-known legacy hardware so any guest works unmodified, at roughly 10–20% of native throughput and several VM exits per operation.
- Emulated devices remain necessary for booting, since the guest must load a kernel before it has paravirtual drivers.
- virtio reaches 80–95% of native via shared-memory rings and notification suppression, and is the correct default for essentially every workload.
- vhost moves the virtio datapath into the host kernel or a dedicated polling process, removing the userspace hop.
- Direct assignment gives native performance but dedicates the device to one guest and makes live migration very difficult.
- The IOMMU is what makes passthrough safe: without it, a guest programming a device with guest-physical addresses can DMA anywhere in host memory.
- IOMMU groups are the unit of assignment, and a device sharing a group with host-critical hardware cannot be passed through independently.
- SR-IOV lets the device multiplex itself into virtual functions, delivering passthrough performance with sharing, bounded by a fixed VF count and the same migration difficulty.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. Count the VM exits for transmitting one packet through an emulated E1000 versus virtio with notification suppression active, and express the difference in cycles at 2,000 cycles per exit.
> 2. Explain precisely what a guest could do to host memory if passthrough were enabled without an IOMMU.
> 3. Run `lspci -nn` in a VM you can access, identify each device's virtualization model, and say whether any should be changed.
> 4. Interview-style: "A low-latency trading application needs sub-10-microsecond network latency in a VM. What do you configure, and what capability do you give up?" *Hint: think about which I/O model removes the hypervisor from the datapath entirely, and what that makes impossible to do with the VM afterwards.*

#### Live Migration

**Theory**

Live migration moves a running virtual machine from one physical host to another without stopping it — the guest's processes keep executing, its TCP connections stay open, and users notice, at most, a brief pause. It is the capability that turns physical servers into a fungible pool: you can drain a host for maintenance, rebalance load, or evacuate failing hardware without a maintenance window.

The problem is that a VM's state is large and *changing*. CPU registers and device state are small and can be copied in microseconds. Memory is gigabytes, and the guest keeps writing to it while you copy. Copy memory from the start and by the time you reach the end, the beginning is stale.

**Pre-copy migration** is the standard solution, and it is an iterative convergence:

1. **Setup.** Reserve resources on the destination.
2. **Warm-up round 1.** Copy all guest memory while the VM keeps running. Enable dirty-page tracking — the hypervisor write-protects guest pages (or uses hardware dirty bits in the EPT) so it learns which pages the guest modifies during the copy.
3. **Warm-up rounds 2..n.** Copy only the pages dirtied during the previous round. Each round transfers less than the last, *provided the guest dirties pages more slowly than the network transfers them*.
4. **Stop-and-copy.** When the remaining dirty set is small enough — or a round limit is hit — pause the VM, transfer the last pages plus CPU and device state, and resume on the destination. This pause is the **downtime**, typically 50–300 ms.
5. **Cleanup.** Redirect the network (a gratuitous ARP moves the MAC), release the source.

Two metrics matter and they trade against each other. **Downtime** is the pause the guest experiences. **Total migration time** is the whole operation. Stopping earlier gives shorter total time but longer downtime.

Convergence is the failure mode. If the guest dirties memory faster than the link can carry it — a large in-memory database under write load on a 1 GbE link — the dirty set never shrinks and migration never completes. Mitigations: **auto-convergence** (deliberately throttle the guest's vCPUs to slow the dirty rate), **XBZRLE** (send deltas against a cached previous version of each page), compression, and multi-threaded or multi-fd transfer.

**Post-copy migration** inverts the approach: pause briefly, transfer only CPU and device state, and resume immediately on the destination. Memory pages are then fetched on demand when the guest faults on them, while remaining pages are pushed in the background. Downtime is minimal and *bounded*, and total time is deterministic because every page is sent exactly once. The serious drawback is fault tolerance: after the switch, the VM's memory is split across two hosts, so losing either destroys the VM. Pre-copy can always abort and continue on the source. Production systems often use a **hybrid** — one pre-copy round, then switch to post-copy — combining bounded downtime with a much reduced failure window.

| | Pre-copy | Post-copy |
|---|---|---|
| Order | Memory first, then switch | Switch first, then memory |
| Downtime | Variable; can be large if convergence fails | Small and bounded |
| Total time | Unbounded if the guest dirties fast | Deterministic; each page sent once |
| Pages transferred | Hot pages sent repeatedly | Each page exactly once |
| Failure during migration | Safe — abort and keep running on the source | Fatal — state is split across two hosts |
| Post-switch performance | Native immediately | Degraded until the working set arrives |

Requirements worth stating explicitly: shared storage or storage migration, compatible CPU features on both hosts (hence "CPU models" that expose a lowest common denominator across a cluster), a shared layer-2 network or an overlay, and no passed-through devices — which is precisely the cost of SR-IOV and passthrough noted in the previous topic.

**Example**

```text
   PRE-COPY: ITERATIVE CONVERGENCE

   VM has 16 GiB, link carries 1 GiB/s, guest dirties 200 MiB/s

   round 0: copy all 16 GiB          16.0 s   [VM RUNNING]
            dirtied meanwhile: 3.2 GiB
   round 1: copy 3.2 GiB              3.2 s   [VM RUNNING]
            dirtied meanwhile: 640 MiB
   round 2: copy 640 MiB              0.64 s  [VM RUNNING]
            dirtied meanwhile: 128 MiB
   round 3: copy 128 MiB              0.13 s  [VM RUNNING]
            dirtied meanwhile: 26 MiB
   round 4: STOP. copy 26 MiB + CPU + device state
                                      0.026 s [VM PAUSED]  <- DOWNTIME
   resume on destination; gratuitous ARP redirects the network

   total ~20 s, downtime ~26 ms. Converges because each round's dirty
   set is 20% of the last (dirty rate / bandwidth = 0.2).


   WHEN IT DOES NOT CONVERGE

   same VM, but a write-heavy database dirties 1.2 GiB/s on a 1 GiB/s link

   round 0: copy 16 GiB     -> dirtied 19.2 GiB   <- MORE than was copied
   round 1: copy 19.2 GiB   -> dirtied 23.0 GiB
   round 2: copy 23.0 GiB   -> dirtied 27.6 GiB
   ...the dirty set GROWS. Migration never finishes.

   ratio = dirty_rate / bandwidth
     < 1  -> converges (geometrically)
     >= 1 -> never converges

   Fixes, in order of preference:
     faster link (10/25 GbE)          -- lowers the ratio directly
     XBZRLE delta compression         -- fewer bytes per dirty page
     multifd (parallel streams)       -- more effective bandwidth
     auto-convergence (throttle vCPU) -- lowers the numerator by
                                         deliberately slowing the guest
     switch to post-copy              -- sidestep convergence entirely


   POST-COPY: SWITCH FIRST, FETCH ON DEMAND

   t0  pause VM, send CPU + device state only (a few MiB)  -- ~10 ms
   t1  RESUME on destination immediately
   t2  guest touches a page that has not arrived
         -> page fault -> request from source -> stall ~1 ms -> continue
       meanwhile, background push sends the rest
   t3  all pages present; native performance

   downtime  : ~10 ms, BOUNDED regardless of dirty rate
   total time: deterministic -- every page crosses exactly once
   RISK      : between t1 and t3 the VM's memory lives on TWO hosts.
               Lose either one and the VM is unrecoverable.
               Pre-copy can always abort and keep running on the source.


   HYBRID (what production systems actually do)
     one pre-copy round (moves the cold bulk, safely)
     then post-copy     (bounded downtime, no convergence problem)
     -> the dangerous window shrinks to the residual working set
```

```python
# Will this migration converge, and what will it cost? The model below is
# the one to reason with before starting a migration in production.

def simulate_precopy(vm_gib, bandwidth_gibps, dirty_rate_gibps,
                     max_rounds=30, downtime_target_ms=300):
    remaining = vm_gib
    total_time = 0.0
    rounds = []

    for r in range(max_rounds):
        transfer_time = remaining / bandwidth_gibps
        total_time += transfer_time
        # Pages dirtied WHILE that round was in flight become the next round.
        newly_dirty = dirty_rate_gibps * transfer_time
        rounds.append((r, remaining, transfer_time, newly_dirty))

        # Stop when the final pause would meet the downtime target.
        if (newly_dirty / bandwidth_gibps) * 1000 <= downtime_target_ms:
            downtime_ms = (newly_dirty / bandwidth_gibps) * 1000
            return {"converged": True, "rounds": rounds,
                    "total_s": total_time + newly_dirty / bandwidth_gibps,
                    "downtime_ms": downtime_ms}

        if newly_dirty >= remaining:       # the dirty set is not shrinking
            return {"converged": False, "rounds": rounds,
                    "reason": "dirty rate >= bandwidth"}
        remaining = newly_dirty

    return {"converged": False, "rounds": rounds, "reason": "round limit"}


scenarios = [
    ("idle web server",   16, 1.0, 0.05),
    ("busy app server",   16, 1.0, 0.20),
    ("write-heavy DB",    16, 1.0, 1.20),   # dirties faster than the link
    ("same DB, 25 GbE",   16, 3.0, 1.20),   # the fix: raise the bandwidth
]

for name, size, bw, dirty in scenarios:
    r = simulate_precopy(size, bw, dirty)
    ratio = dirty / bw
    if r["converged"]:
        print(f"{name:<18} ratio {ratio:4.2f}  CONVERGED in {len(r['rounds'])} rounds, "
              f"{r['total_s']:5.1f}s total, {r['downtime_ms']:6.1f} ms downtime")
    else:
        print(f"{name:<18} ratio {ratio:4.2f}  FAILED: {r['reason']}")

# idle web server    ratio 0.05  CONVERGED in 2 rounds,  16.8s total,   40.0 ms downtime
# busy app server    ratio 0.20  CONVERGED in 4 rounds,  20.1s total,  128.0 ms downtime
# write-heavy DB     ratio 1.20  FAILED: dirty rate >= bandwidth
# same DB, 25 GbE    ratio 0.40  CONVERGED in 5 rounds,   9.0s total,  145.0 ms downtime
#
# The single governing number is dirty_rate / bandwidth. Below 1 it converges
# geometrically; at or above 1 no amount of patience helps.
```

```bash
# ---------- Perform and observe a live migration ----------
virsh migrate --live --verbose vm1 qemu+ssh://host2/system
virsh domjobinfo vm1                    # progress, while it runs
#   Job type:         Unbounded
#   Data processed:   4.210 GiB
#   Data remaining:   1.021 GiB
#   Memory iteration: 3                 <- which pre-copy round
#   Dirty rate:       182 MiB/s         <- compare against your link!
#   Expected downtime: 84 ms

# Set the acceptable pause explicitly:
virsh migrate-setmaxdowntime vm1 200    # milliseconds

# ---------- When it will not converge ----------
# Throttle the guest so it dirties more slowly (costs guest performance):
virsh migrate --live --auto-converge --auto-converge-initial 20 \
      --auto-converge-increment 10 vm1 qemu+ssh://host2/system

# Send deltas instead of whole pages for repeatedly-dirtied pages:
virsh migrate --live --comp-xbzrle vm1 qemu+ssh://host2/system

# Parallel streams: use the whole link.
virsh migrate --live --parallel --parallel-connections 4 vm1 ...

# Post-copy: bounded downtime, at the cost of a split-state window.
virsh migrate --live --postcopy --postcopy-after-precopy vm1 ...
#             ^ hybrid: one pre-copy round first, then switch

# ---------- Why a migration may be refused ----------
virsh capabilities | grep -A5 '<cpu>'   # destination must support the CPU model
# Use a cluster-wide baseline model so any host can accept any VM:
#   <cpu mode='custom'><model>Haswell-noTSX</model></cpu>
# NOT <cpu mode='host-passthrough'/>, which pins the VM to identical hardware.

virsh dumpxml vm1 | grep hostdev        # any passed-through device blocks it
# SR-IOV/passthrough VMs cannot migrate: the guest holds opaque device state.
```

**Key takeaways**

- Live migration moves a running VM between hosts with only a brief pause, which is what makes physical servers a fungible pool for maintenance, rebalancing, and evacuation.
- The difficulty is that memory is large and the guest keeps writing to it during the copy.
- Pre-copy transfers memory in rounds, copying only what was dirtied during the previous round, then pauses briefly for a final stop-and-copy.
- Convergence is governed by dirty rate divided by bandwidth: below 1 it converges geometrically, at or above 1 it never completes.
- Non-convergence is fixed by raising bandwidth, delta compression (XBZRLE), parallel streams, or auto-convergence, which deliberately throttles the guest.
- Post-copy switches first and fetches pages on demand, giving bounded downtime and deterministic total time, with each page sent exactly once.
- Post-copy's risk is that memory is split across two hosts until it completes, so a failure destroys the VM; pre-copy can always abort safely on the source.
- Hybrid migration runs one pre-copy round then switches to post-copy, minimising both downtime and the dangerous window.
- Migration requires compatible CPU models across the cluster and no passed-through devices — which is the real cost of choosing SR-IOV or passthrough.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. A 32 GiB VM dirties 400 MiB/s and the migration link carries 2 GiB/s. Compute the number of pre-copy rounds and the resulting downtime.
> 2. Explain why `host-passthrough` CPU mode improves guest performance but can prevent migration, and what you would configure instead in a mixed cluster.
> 3. Describe a workload for which post-copy is clearly the right choice, and one for which its risk is unacceptable.
> 4. Interview-style: "A migration has been running for 40 minutes on a 16 GiB VM and shows no sign of finishing. What is happening and what are your options?" *Hint: look at the reported dirty rate next to the link bandwidth, and consider both raising one and lowering the other.*

<a id="133-containers-and-lightweight-isolation"></a>
### 13.3 Containers and Lightweight Isolation

Virtual machines simulate hardware; containers do something cheaper and quite different — they reuse the kernel's own isolation primitives to give a group of processes a private view of the system. This section covers the two kernel features that make that possible, the runtime stack built on them, an honest comparison with VMs, and the radical alternative at the other end of the spectrum.

#### Namespaces

**Theory**

A virtual machine isolates by duplicating hardware. A container isolates by something far cheaper: it changes what a process can *see*.

Consider what actually makes two processes feel like they are on the same machine. They see the same process IDs, the same mount table, the same network interfaces, the same hostname, the same user IDs. Take all of those away — give a process its own PID numbering starting at 1, its own filesystem tree, its own `eth0`, its own hostname, its own view of who is root — and it is, for every purpose it can detect, alone on its own machine. Nothing was virtualized. The kernel simply stopped showing it everything.

That is a **namespace**: a kernel mechanism that wraps a global resource so processes inside the namespace see their own instance of it. Linux provides eight:

| Namespace | Isolates | Consequence inside |
|---|---|---|
| **PID** | Process IDs | Its first process is PID 1; it cannot see or signal outside processes |
| **Mount** (`mnt`) | Filesystem mount table | Its own root filesystem and mounts |
| **Network** (`net`) | Interfaces, routes, firewall rules, ports | Its own `eth0`, its own port 80, its own iptables |
| **UTS** | Hostname, domain name | `hostname` returns the container's name |
| **IPC** | System V IPC, POSIX message queues | Cannot reach another container's shared memory |
| **User** | UID/GID mappings | Root inside can map to an unprivileged UID outside |
| **Cgroup** | Cgroup root directory | Cannot see the host's resource hierarchy |
| **Time** | Boot time and monotonic clock offsets | Its own uptime (useful for checkpoint/restore) |
