Three system calls manage them. `clone()` creates a process in new namespaces (`CLONE_NEWPID`, `CLONE_NEWNET`, …). `unshare()` moves the *calling* process into new namespaces. `setns()` joins an existing namespace — which is exactly what `docker exec` and `nsenter` do.

The **user namespace** deserves special attention, because it is what makes unprivileged containers possible. It maps UIDs: UID 0 inside the namespace can correspond to UID 100000 outside. A process can be fully root inside its container — able to mount filesystems, configure its own network, install packages — while the host kernel treats it as an ordinary unprivileged user. If it escapes, it escapes as nobody in particular. This is the single most valuable container hardening measure, and the reason rootless Podman exists.

Namespaces are also independent, which is a genuinely important design property. A container is not an object the kernel knows about; it is a *combination* chosen by userspace. You can share some namespaces and not others, and real systems do:

- A Kubernetes **pod** shares network and IPC namespaces between its containers, so they reach each other on `localhost`, but keeps mount namespaces separate.
- `docker run --network host` gives a container its own PID and mount namespaces but the host's network stack.
- A debug sidecar shares the target's PID namespace so it can see and inspect its processes.

There is no `struct container` in the Linux kernel. "Container" is a userspace convention for a process running with a particular set of namespaces, cgroups, capabilities, and a seccomp filter. Understanding that is what makes container security reasoning possible: you are not asking "is the container secure", you are asking "which of these mechanisms is applied, and what does each one actually cover".

**Example**

```text
   NAMESPACES: A PRIVATE VIEW, NOT A PRIVATE MACHINE

   HOST VIEW                         CONTAINER'S VIEW (PID ns)
   PID  1  systemd                   PID  1  nginx     <- same process!
   PID  842 sshd                     PID  7  worker
   PID  1503 dockerd                 (nothing else exists)
   PID  1876 nginx     <---------------------+
   PID  1882 worker    <---------------------+

   One process, two PIDs. The kernel is running it exactly once; the
   NUMBER it reports depends on who is asking. Nothing was simulated.


   THE EIGHT NAMESPACES, AND WHAT EACH HIDES

   +-- PID     -> its own process tree, its own PID 1
   +-- mount   -> its own root filesystem and mount table
   +-- network -> its own interfaces, routes, ports, firewall rules
   +-- UTS     -> its own hostname
   +-- IPC     -> its own shared memory and message queues
   +-- user    -> its own UID map: root inside != root outside
   +-- cgroup  -> its own view of the resource hierarchy
   +-- time    -> its own boot time and uptime

   A "container" is just a process with a chosen COMBINATION of these.
   The kernel has no container object at all.


   USER NAMESPACES: ROOT THAT IS NOT ROOT

   inside the container          host kernel's view
   uid 0     (root)      <---->  uid 100000  (unprivileged)
   uid 1     (daemon)    <---->  uid 100001
   uid 1000  (app)       <---->  uid 101000

   The process can apt-get install, mount, and bind port 80 inside.
   If it escapes, it is uid 100000 on the host: it owns nothing,
   can signal nothing, can read no other user's files.

   This is the highest-value single hardening measure for containers.


   NAMESPACES ARE INDEPENDENT -- SHARE THEM SELECTIVELY

   Kubernetes POD:
     +------------------------------------------+
     |  shared: network ns, IPC ns              |
     |  +----------------+  +----------------+  |
     |  | container A    |  | container B    |  |
     |  | own mount ns   |  | own mount ns   |  |
     |  | own PID ns     |  | own PID ns     |  |
     |  +----------------+  +----------------+  |
     |  A reaches B at 127.0.0.1 -- same netns  |
     +------------------------------------------+

   docker run --network host  : own PID+mount, HOST network
   docker run --pid container:X : share X's process view (debug sidecars)
   nsenter -t <pid> -n -m      : join an existing container's ns from outside
```

```bash
# ---------- Build a container by hand, one namespace at a time ----------
# This is what a runtime does; doing it manually shows there is no magic.

# 1. UTS namespace: an isolated hostname.
sudo unshare --uts sh -c 'hostname isolated; hostname; ls /'
hostname                       # unchanged on the host

# 2. PID namespace: a fresh process tree. --fork and --mount-proc are
#    required because PID 1 semantics apply to the CHILD, and /proc must
#    be remounted to reflect the new numbering.
sudo unshare --pid --fork --mount-proc sh -c 'ps aux'
#   USER  PID  COMMAND
#   root    1  sh          <- our shell is PID 1
#   root    5  ps
#   The host's hundreds of processes are simply not visible.

# 3. Network namespace: its own, empty network stack.
sudo unshare --net sh -c 'ip link show'
#   1: lo: <LOOPBACK> state DOWN      <- only loopback, and it is down

# 4. Mount namespace: mounts here do not affect the host.
sudo unshare --mount sh -c 'mount -t tmpfs none /mnt && df -h /mnt'
df -h /mnt                     # host: unaffected

# 5. User namespace: root inside, nobody outside. Note: NO sudo.
unshare --user --map-root-user sh -c 'id; cat /proc/self/uid_map'
#   uid=0(root) gid=0(root)
#            0       1000          1     <- inside 0 == outside 1000

# 6. All at once -- this is essentially `docker run`:
sudo unshare --pid --fork --mount-proc --uts --ipc --net --mount \
     sh -c 'hostname mybox; ps aux; ip link'

# ---------- Inspect the namespaces of a running container ----------
CPID=$(docker inspect -f '{{.State.Pid}}' mycontainer)
sudo ls -l /proc/$CPID/ns/
#   net -> 'net:[4026532281]'      <- the inode IS the namespace identity
#   pid -> 'pid:[4026532283]'
#   uts -> 'uts:[4026532279]'
ls -l /proc/1/ns/net             # different inode => different namespace
# Matching inodes mean the namespace is SHARED (e.g. within a pod).

lsns                             # every namespace on the system, with owners
lsns -t net                      # just network namespaces

# ---------- Enter one from outside (this is `docker exec`) ----------
sudo nsenter -t $CPID -n ip addr        # join only the network namespace
sudo nsenter -t $CPID -a /bin/sh        # join all of them

# ---------- Rootless containers: user namespaces in production ----------
podman run --rm -it alpine id           # no daemon, no root on the host
cat /etc/subuid                         # the UID ranges delegated to you
#   youruser:100000:65536
```

```c
/* What a container runtime actually calls. The whole mechanism is one
 * clone() with the right flags -- everything else is setup. */
#define _GNU_SOURCE
#include <sched.h>
#include <sys/mount.h>
#include <sys/wait.h>
#include <unistd.h>
#include <stdio.h>

static char child_stack[1024 * 1024];

static int child_main(void *arg)
{
    /* We are PID 1 inside the new PID namespace. */
    sethostname("container", 9);                 /* UTS ns: ours alone */

    /* Mount ns: give this process its own root. pivot_root is what a real
     * runtime uses; chroot is shown here for brevity and is weaker. */
    mount("none", "/", NULL, MS_REC | MS_PRIVATE, NULL);  /* do not leak
                                                           * mounts back */
    chroot("/var/lib/containers/rootfs");
    chdir("/");
    mount("proc", "/proc", "proc", 0, NULL);     /* /proc must reflect the
                                                  * NEW pid namespace */
    printf("inside: pid=%d\n", getpid());        /* prints 1 */
    execlp("/bin/sh", "sh", NULL);
    return 1;
}

int main(void)
{
    int flags = CLONE_NEWPID     /* own process tree            */
              | CLONE_NEWNS      /* own mount table             */
              | CLONE_NEWNET     /* own network stack           */
              | CLONE_NEWUTS     /* own hostname                */
              | CLONE_NEWIPC     /* own SysV IPC                */
              | CLONE_NEWUSER    /* own UID map: root != root   */
              | CLONE_NEWCGROUP  /* own cgroup root             */
              | SIGCHLD;

    pid_t pid = clone(child_main, child_stack + sizeof(child_stack), flags, NULL);
    printf("outside: child is pid=%d\n", pid);   /* a normal host PID */

    /* With CLONE_NEWUSER the parent must write the UID/GID maps before the
     * child can use its privileges -- this is what makes root-inside safe. */
    /* write "0 100000 65536" to /proc/<pid>/uid_map and gid_map */

    waitpid(pid, NULL, 0);
    return 0;
}
```

**Key takeaways**

- A namespace isolates by changing what a process can see, not by duplicating hardware, which is why containers cost almost nothing to create.
- Linux provides eight namespaces — PID, mount, network, UTS, IPC, user, cgroup, and time — each wrapping one global resource.
- `clone()` creates a process in new namespaces, `unshare()` moves the caller into new ones, and `setns()` joins existing ones (what `docker exec` and `nsenter` do).
- The user namespace maps UIDs so a process can be root inside while being unprivileged on the host; it is the highest-value container hardening measure.
- Namespaces are independent and can be shared selectively, which is how a Kubernetes pod gives its containers a shared network but separate filesystems.
- There is no container object in the Linux kernel — a container is a userspace convention combining namespaces, cgroups, capabilities, and seccomp.
- Because the combination is chosen, container security must be assessed mechanism by mechanism rather than as a single property.
- `lsns` and `/proc/<pid>/ns/` expose namespace membership directly, and identical inode numbers mean two processes share a namespace.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. Run `sudo unshare --pid --fork --mount-proc sh -c 'ps aux'` and explain why both `--fork` and `--mount-proc` are required.
> 2. Compare `ls -l /proc/1/ns/` with the same listing for a container's PID and explain what matching or differing inode numbers indicate.
> 3. Create two network namespaces with `ip netns add`, connect them with a veth pair, and demonstrate that they can ping each other but the host cannot see their addresses.
> 4. Interview-style: "A container runs as root. Is that dangerous?" *Hint: the answer depends on one namespace in particular; ask what UID the host kernel actually sees, and what changes if the answer is 0.*

#### Control Groups

**Theory**

Namespaces control *visibility*; they say nothing about *consumption*. A process in a perfectly isolated set of namespaces can still allocate all the host's memory, spin every core, and saturate the disk — taking down every other container on the machine. This is the **noisy neighbour** problem, and **control groups** (cgroups) are the answer.

A cgroup is a hierarchical grouping of processes with resource controllers attached. Each controller accounts for and limits one resource type:

| Controller | Limits | Key knobs (cgroup v2) |
|---|---|---|
| `cpu` | CPU time | `cpu.max` (quota/period), `cpu.weight` (relative share) |
| `memory` | RAM and swap | `memory.max` (hard), `memory.high` (throttle), `memory.low` (protect) |
| `io` | Block I/O | `io.max` (IOPS and bandwidth caps), `io.weight` |
| `pids` | Process count | `pids.max` — the fork-bomb defence |
| `cpuset` | Which cores and NUMA nodes | `cpuset.cpus`, `cpuset.mems` |
| `hugetlb` | Huge page usage | `hugetlb.*.max` |

Two distinctions matter more than the individual knobs.

**Limits versus weights.** A limit (`cpu.max = 50000 100000`, i.e. 0.5 CPU) is absolute: the cgroup is throttled at that ceiling even if the machine is idle. A weight (`cpu.weight = 100`) is proportional: it only takes effect under contention, and an idle machine lets the cgroup use everything. Weights give better utilisation; limits give predictability and are what you need to prevent one tenant affecting another's latency. Kubernetes exposes exactly this pair as *requests* (weights and scheduling) and *limits* (hard ceilings).

**CPU versus memory enforcement.** This asymmetry catches people constantly. Exceeding a CPU limit means being **throttled** — the cgroup is descheduled until its next quota period, so it just runs slower. Exceeding a memory limit means the **OOM killer** terminates a process in the cgroup, because memory cannot be time-sliced. A container that exceeds CPU is slow; a container that exceeds memory is dead. This is why a Kubernetes pod shows `OOMKilled` with exit code 137 (128 + SIGKILL) rather than simply slowing down.

CPU throttling has a notorious subtlety. The quota is enforced per *period* (100 ms by default), and a multi-threaded application can exhaust its entire quota in the first few milliseconds of a period and then sit idle for the remaining 90+ ms. The result is that an application shows severe latency spikes while reporting average CPU usage well below its limit. Diagnosing this means reading `nr_throttled` and `throttled_time` in `cpu.stat`, not average utilisation.

**cgroup v2** replaced v1's separate per-controller hierarchies with a single unified tree, which fixed genuine coordination problems — v1 could not sensibly account for page cache written by one cgroup on behalf of another, because memory and I/O lived in different hierarchies. v2 also adds pressure stall information (**PSI**), which reports the fraction of time tasks were stalled waiting for CPU, memory, or I/O. PSI is a far better saturation signal than utilisation: 100% CPU utilisation with zero pressure means the work fits, while 70% utilisation with high pressure means tasks are waiting.

**Example**

```text
   NAMESPACES AND CGROUPS ARE ORTHOGONAL, AND YOU NEED BOTH

   namespaces only        : perfect isolation of VIEW,
                            zero isolation of CONSUMPTION
                            -> one container can starve every other
   cgroups only           : resource limits, but everything is visible
                            -> processes can see and signal each other
   namespaces + cgroups   : a container

   "What can I see?"  -> namespaces
   "How much can I use?" -> cgroups


   CGROUP v2: ONE UNIFIED TREE

   /sys/fs/cgroup/                          cpu.max = max (unlimited)
   |
   +-- system.slice/                        cpu.weight = 100
   |    +-- sshd.service/
   |    +-- docker.service/
   |
   +-- kubepods.slice/                      memory.max = 48G
        +-- burstable/
        |    +-- pod-a/                     cpu.max = 200000 100000 (2 CPUs)
        |         +-- container-1/          memory.max = 2G
        +-- guaranteed/
             +-- pod-b/                     cpuset.cpus = 8-11 (pinned)

   Limits are HIERARCHICAL: a child can never exceed its ancestors'.


   LIMIT vs WEIGHT -- the distinction that governs utilisation

   cpu.max = 50000 100000   (a LIMIT: 50 ms of every 100 ms = 0.5 CPU)
     idle machine  -> still capped at 0.5 CPU. Predictable; wasteful.
     busy machine  -> capped at 0.5 CPU. Neighbours are protected.

   cpu.weight = 100         (a WEIGHT: a relative share)
     idle machine  -> use ALL the CPUs. Nothing is wasted.
     busy machine  -> proportional share against other weights.

   Kubernetes: requests -> weights;  limits -> ceilings.


   THE ENFORCEMENT ASYMMETRY (the one that surprises people)

   exceed CPU limit    -> THROTTLED. The container runs slower. It lives.
   exceed memory limit -> OOM KILLED. A process is terminated. Exit 137.

   Memory cannot be time-sliced: you either have the page or you do not.


   CPU THROTTLING: SLOW DESPITE LOW AVERAGE UTILISATION

   cpu.max = 100000 100000  (1 CPU), application has 8 threads

   period 1 (100 ms):
   |XXXXXXXXXX|.....................................................|
   |<- 12.5ms ->|<------------ 87.5 ms THROTTLED, doing nothing ---->|
    8 threads burn the 100 ms quota in 12.5 ms of wall time

   average utilisation over the period : 12.5%  <- looks fine!
   p99 latency                         : catastrophic
   cpu.stat: nr_throttled rising       <- THE signal to look at

   Fixes: raise the quota, reduce thread count to match the quota,
          or shorten cpu.cfs_period_us for finer-grained scheduling.
```

```bash
# ---------- Which cgroup version is this system on? ----------
stat -fc %T /sys/fs/cgroup/       # cgroup2fs = v2 (unified), tmpfs = v1
cat /proc/self/cgroup             # "0::/path" means v2

# ---------- Create a cgroup and constrain something ----------
sudo mkdir /sys/fs/cgroup/demo

# CPU: half a core. Format is "QUOTA PERIOD", both in microseconds.
echo "50000 100000" | sudo tee /sys/fs/cgroup/demo/cpu.max

# Memory: a hard ceiling (OOM kill) and a soft one (reclaim/throttle first).
echo "512M" | sudo tee /sys/fs/cgroup/demo/memory.max
echo "400M" | sudo tee /sys/fs/cgroup/demo/memory.high   # throttle BEFORE killing

# Fork-bomb defence -- cheap, and almost always worth setting.
echo "100" | sudo tee /sys/fs/cgroup/demo/pids.max

# I/O: cap a specific device. 8:0 is the major:minor from lsblk.
echo "8:0 rbps=10485760 wiops=500" | sudo tee /sys/fs/cgroup/demo/io.max

# Move a shell into it; everything it spawns inherits the limits.
echo $$ | sudo tee /sys/fs/cgroup/demo/cgroup.procs
stress-ng --cpu 4 --timeout 10s          # 4 threads share 0.5 CPU

# ---------- The two files worth reading ----------
cat /sys/fs/cgroup/demo/cpu.stat
#   usage_usec 5012843
#   nr_periods 100
#   nr_throttled 87           <- throttled in 87 of 100 periods
#   throttled_usec 4310000    <- THIS is why p99 latency is bad, even
#                                though average utilisation looks low

cat /sys/fs/cgroup/demo/memory.current    # actual usage right now
cat /sys/fs/cgroup/demo/memory.events
#   high 1420       <- hit memory.high: reclaim pressure applied
#   max 3           <- hit memory.max
#   oom_kill 1      <- something was killed. Exit code 137 in the container.

# ---------- PSI: saturation, not utilisation ----------
cat /sys/fs/cgroup/demo/cpu.pressure
#   some avg10=41.23 avg60=38.10 avg300=22.4 total=98234211
#        ^ 41% of the last 10s, at least one task was STALLED waiting for CPU.
# 100% utilisation with 0% pressure = healthy and fully used.
#  70% utilisation with 40% pressure = saturated; tasks are queuing.
cat /sys/fs/cgroup/demo/memory.pressure
cat /sys/fs/cgroup/demo/io.pressure

# ---------- The same thing through higher-level tools ----------
docker run --cpus=0.5 --memory=512m --pids-limit=100 nginx
systemd-run --scope -p CPUQuota=50% -p MemoryMax=512M -p TasksMax=100 ./app
systemd-cgtop                       # live per-cgroup resource usage
```

```yaml
# Kubernetes exposes exactly the weight/limit distinction, and the choice
# determines the pod's Quality of Service class.
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: web
spec:
  containers:
    - name: app
      image: nginx
      resources:
        requests:            # -> cpu.weight and scheduling placement.
          cpu: "500m"        #    The scheduler reserves this; under
          memory: "256Mi"    #    contention this is the proportional share.
        limits:              # -> cpu.max and memory.max: hard ceilings.
          cpu: "1000m"       #    Exceeding CPU  -> THROTTLED (slow).
          memory: "512Mi"    #    Exceeding RAM  -> OOMKilled (exit 137).

# QoS classes, derived from the above:
#   Guaranteed  requests == limits for every resource -> evicted last
#   Burstable   requests <  limits                    -> evicted second
#   BestEffort  neither set                           -> evicted first
#
# A common production pattern: set memory requests == limits (so the pod is
# never OOM-killed by overcommit) but leave the CPU limit OFF, so the pod can
# burst into idle capacity instead of being throttled at an arbitrary ceiling.
```

**Key takeaways**

- Namespaces isolate what a process can see; cgroups limit what it can consume, and a container needs both.
- Controllers exist for CPU, memory, I/O, process count, CPU/NUMA placement, and huge pages, arranged in a hierarchy where a child can never exceed its ancestors.
- Limits are absolute ceilings enforced even on an idle machine; weights are proportional shares that apply only under contention, trading predictability against utilisation.
- Exceeding a CPU limit throttles the container; exceeding a memory limit invokes the OOM killer, because memory cannot be time-sliced.
- CPU quota is enforced per 100 ms period, so a multi-threaded process can exhaust it in milliseconds and stall for the rest — producing latency spikes at low average utilisation.
- `cpu.stat`'s `nr_throttled` and `throttled_usec` are the diagnostic for that pathology; average utilisation will not reveal it.
- cgroup v2's unified hierarchy fixed v1's inability to coordinate memory and I/O accounting for the same pages.
- Pressure stall information (PSI) reports stall time rather than utilisation, making it a much better saturation signal.
- `pids.max` is a cheap and effective fork-bomb defence that is frequently left unset.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. Set `cpu.max` to `50000 100000` for a cgroup, run a 4-thread CPU load in it, and explain the `nr_throttled` value you observe.
> 2. Explain why a container exceeding its CPU limit survives while one exceeding its memory limit is killed, and what exit code 137 signifies.
> 3. Compare `cpu.pressure` and average CPU utilisation for a workload of your choice, and explain which one better predicts user-visible latency.
> 4. Interview-style: "A service is reported as slow, but its CPU utilisation averages 30% against a 1-core limit and it has eight worker threads. What do you check?" *Hint: average utilisation is computed over a window much longer than the quota period; ask what happens within a single 100 ms slice.*

#### Container Runtimes

**Theory**

Namespaces and cgroups are kernel mechanisms; a **container runtime** is the software that assembles them into something usable, together with the other half of the story — the filesystem image.

The stack is layered, and the layering is the result of a deliberate standardisation effort:

- **Low-level runtime** (`runc`, `crun`, `youki`). Takes a directory containing a root filesystem plus a JSON `config.json`, and creates the container: `clone()` with namespace flags, set up cgroups, apply seccomp and capabilities, `pivot_root`, and `exec` the entrypoint. It does this once and exits. This behaviour is specified by the **OCI Runtime Specification**, which is why `runc` and `crun` are interchangeable.
- **High-level runtime** (`containerd`, `CRI-O`). Manages image pulls, storage, networking, and container lifecycle, then calls a low-level runtime to do the actual creation. Kubernetes talks to this layer through the **CRI** (Container Runtime Interface).
- **Engine / platform** (Docker, Podman, Kubernetes). User-facing tooling: builds, registries, compose files, orchestration.

The image side is equally important and is where containers get their most valuable property. An **OCI image** is a stack of read-only **layers**, each a tarball of filesystem changes, plus a manifest and a config. A **union filesystem** — normally `overlayfs` — presents the stack as a single tree, with a thin writable layer on top for the running container. Writes to an existing file trigger **copy-up**: the file is copied into the writable layer and modified there, leaving the underlying layer untouched.

This design produces the properties that made containers spread:

- **Sharing.** A hundred containers from the same image share one copy of its layers on disk and in page cache. Starting the hundredth costs only its writable layer.
- **Content addressing.** Layers are identified by SHA-256 digest, so pulls transfer only missing layers and identity is verifiable.
- **Immutability and reproducibility.** An image digest names exactly one bit-identical filesystem, which is what makes "the same artifact in dev and prod" a real guarantee rather than an aspiration.

The layering also explains a security rule that is otherwise mysterious: **deleting a secret in a later layer does not remove it**. A `RUN rm /tmp/credentials` creates a whiteout entry in a new layer; the file remains intact in the earlier layer and anyone who pulls the image can extract it. Secrets must never enter an image layer in the first place.

Runtime architecture has moved in two directions worth knowing. **Daemonless** runtimes (Podman) drop the central root daemon — containers become direct children of the invoking user's shell, managed by systemd, and combined with user namespaces this gives fully rootless containers. And **sandboxed** runtimes replace `runc` under the same OCI interface to strengthen the boundary: **gVisor** interposes a userspace kernel that implements syscalls itself, and **Kata Containers** runs each container inside a lightweight VM. Both plug in where `runc` was, so the orchestration layer above is unchanged.

**Example**

```text
   THE STACK, AND WHERE THE STANDARDS SIT

   kubectl / docker CLI / podman CLI
        |
   +----v-------------------------------+
   |  Kubernetes  /  Docker Engine      |  orchestration, build, registry
   +----|-------------------------------+
        |  CRI (a standard interface)
   +----v-------------------------------+
   |  containerd  /  CRI-O              |  images, storage, networking,
   +----|-------------------------------+  lifecycle
        |  OCI Runtime Spec (config.json + rootfs)
   +----v-------------------------------+
   |  runc / crun / gVisor / Kata       |  actually creates the container
   +----|-------------------------------+
        |  clone(), cgroups, seccomp, capabilities, pivot_root
   +----v-------------------------------+
   |          LINUX KERNEL              |
   +------------------------------------+

   Because the OCI interface is standard, swapping runc for gVisor or Kata
   changes the ISOLATION STRENGTH without changing anything above it.


   OVERLAYFS: WHY THE 100th CONTAINER IS FREE

   container's view (merged)
   +---------------------------------------+
   |  /app/config.yaml   (modified)        |
   |  /app/server                          |
   |  /usr/lib/libc.so                     |
   +---------------------------------------+
            ^ overlayfs merges top-down
   +---------------------------------------+
   |  UPPER (writable, per container)      |  <- only this is per-container
   |    /app/config.yaml   [copied up]     |     typically a few MiB
   +---------------------------------------+
   |  layer 3: COPY app/ /app              |  \
   +---------------------------------------+   |  read-only, SHARED by
   |  layer 2: RUN apt-get install ...     |   |  every container from
   +---------------------------------------+   |  this image -- on disk
   |  layer 1: FROM debian:12              |  /   AND in page cache
   +---------------------------------------+

   100 containers from a 1 GiB image: ~1 GiB total, not 100 GiB.
   Start time is milliseconds because there is nothing to copy.

   COPY-UP: the first write to a lower-layer file copies the WHOLE file
   into the upper layer. Writing one byte of a 2 GiB file copies 2 GiB --
   which is why databases use volumes, not the container filesystem.


   THE LAYER SECURITY TRAP

   Dockerfile:
     RUN curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" ... && rm -f /root/.netrc
                                                       ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
   If the rm is in a LATER layer, the file is still in the earlier one:

     layer 4: whiteout entry for /root/.netrc   <- "deleted"
     layer 3: /root/.netrc  (the actual secret) <- STILL THERE, extractable

     docker save img | tar -x && find . -name '*.tar' -exec tar -tf {} \;

   A secret that ever existed in a layer is IN THE IMAGE, permanently.
   Use BuildKit secret mounts (--mount=type=secret), which are never
   committed to a layer.


   THE THREE RUNTIME STRENGTHS, SAME OCI INTERFACE

   runc    : namespaces + cgroups + seccomp. Shared kernel.
             syscall -> host kernel directly.          fastest, weakest

   gVisor  : a userspace kernel (Sentry) implements ~200 syscalls itself.
             syscall -> Sentry -> (a few) host syscalls
             smaller kernel attack surface; ~10-30% syscall overhead

   Kata    : each container in a microVM with its OWN kernel.
             syscall -> guest kernel -> (rarely) hypervisor
             hardware-enforced boundary; ~100 ms start, ~50 MiB overhead
```

```bash
# ---------- The layers are just tarballs; look inside one ----------
docker history nginx:latest --no-trunc --format '{{.Size}}\t{{.CreatedBy}}'
docker save nginx:latest -o /tmp/nginx.tar && mkdir -p /tmp/x && tar -xf /tmp/nginx.tar -C /tmp/x
cat /tmp/x/manifest.json | jq '.[0].Layers'      # each layer, by digest
# Every layer is extractable by anyone who can pull the image. There is no
# such thing as a "deleted" file in an earlier layer.

# Where overlayfs mounted them for a running container:
docker inspect nginx | jq '.[0].GraphDriver.Data'
#   LowerDir:  /var/lib/docker/overlay2/<a>/diff:/var/lib/docker/overlay2/<b>/diff
#   UpperDir:  /var/lib/docker/overlay2/<c>/diff     <- the only per-container part
#   MergedDir: /var/lib/docker/overlay2/<c>/merged   <- what the container sees
mount | grep overlay

# ---------- Drive the low-level runtime directly ----------
mkdir -p /tmp/ctr/rootfs && cd /tmp/ctr
docker export $(docker create alpine) | tar -C rootfs -xf -
runc spec                                  # generates an OCI config.json
jq '.process.args = ["/bin/sh","-c","hostname; id; ps aux"]' config.json > c.json
mv c.json config.json
sudo runc run demo                         # creates the container and exits
sudo runc list                             # OCI state, no daemon involved

# The config.json IS the container definition -- namespaces, cgroups,
# capabilities and seccomp, all declared:
jq '{namespaces: .linux.namespaces,
     capabilities: .process.capabilities.bounding,
     seccomp: .linux.seccomp.defaultAction}' config.json

# ---------- Swap the runtime to change the isolation strength ----------
docker run --runtime=runsc alpine uname -a        # gVisor
docker run --runtime=kata-runtime alpine uname -r # Kata: a DIFFERENT kernel
# Compare with the host's `uname -r`. Under runc they match, because the
# kernel IS the host's. Under Kata they differ -- that is the whole point.

# ---------- Hardening a container with runc's own mechanisms ----------
docker run \
  --user 10000:10000 \           # never root, even namespaced
  --read-only \                  # immutable root filesystem
  --tmpfs /tmp:rw,noexec,nosuid \
  --cap-drop=ALL \               # drop every capability...
  --cap-add=NET_BIND_SERVICE \   # ...then add back only what is needed
  --security-opt=no-new-privileges \   # setuid binaries cannot escalate
  --security-opt seccomp=profile.json \
  --pids-limit=100 \
  myimage
# Each flag closes one escape route. None of them is implied by "container".

# ---------- Keep secrets out of layers ----------
# BuildKit: the secret is mounted for one RUN and never committed.
#   # syntax=docker/dockerfile:1
#   RUN --mount=type=secret,id=token \
#       curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $(cat /run/secrets/token)" ...
#   DOCKER_BUILDKIT=1 docker build --secret id=token,src=./token .
```

**Key takeaways**

- The runtime stack is layered: an engine or orchestrator calls a high-level runtime (containerd, CRI-O), which calls a low-level runtime (runc, crun) that performs the actual kernel calls.
- The OCI Runtime Specification standardises the low-level interface — a rootfs plus `config.json` — which is why runtimes are interchangeable.
- An OCI image is a stack of content-addressed read-only layers presented as one tree by a union filesystem, usually overlayfs, with a thin per-container writable layer on top.
- Layer sharing is why a hundred containers from one image cost roughly one image on disk and in page cache, and why container start time is measured in milliseconds.
- Copy-up means the first write to a file from a lower layer copies the entire file, which is why write-heavy data belongs in volumes rather than the container filesystem.
- Deleting a file in a later layer only adds a whiteout; the original remains extractable, so secrets must never enter a layer at all.
- Daemonless runtimes such as Podman make containers ordinary child processes and, with user namespaces, allow fully rootless operation.
- gVisor and Kata plug into the same OCI interface to provide a userspace kernel or a per-container microVM, strengthening isolation without changing the layers above.
- Container hardening is a set of explicit choices — non-root user, read-only root, dropped capabilities, seccomp, `no-new-privileges`, pids limit — none of which is implied by using a container.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. Run `docker history` on any image and explain which instructions created layers and why their order affects rebuild speed.
> 2. Extract an image with `docker save` and locate a file that a later layer deleted, then state the correct way to handle build-time secrets.
> 3. Use `runc spec` to generate a `config.json`, modify the entrypoint, and run the container without any daemon; identify which fields correspond to namespaces and which to cgroups.
> 4. Interview-style: "A database container's write throughput is far worse than the same database on the host, though CPU and memory limits are generous. What do you suspect?" *Hint: think about what happens the first time the container writes to a file that came from an image layer, and how large that file is.*

#### Containers vs Virtual Machines

**Theory**

The two technologies are routinely presented as competitors, but they answer different questions. A VM asks "what if this machine were several machines?"; a container asks "what if these processes had the system to themselves?". Choosing between them is mostly a question of where the isolation boundary needs to be.

**Resource cost** favours containers unambiguously. A VM carries an entire guest OS: its own kernel, init system, drivers, page cache, and background daemons — typically 512 MiB to 2 GiB of memory and 10–60 seconds to boot, before the application starts. A container carries only its process tree; the kernel is already running. Memory overhead is a few megabytes and start time is milliseconds. On identical hardware you can run perhaps 10–50 VMs or 100–1,000 containers.

**Isolation strength** favours VMs just as unambiguously, and the reason is structural. Every container on a host shares one kernel. That kernel exposes roughly 350 system calls, plus ioctls, procfs, sysfs, and netlink — an enormous interface reachable directly from inside every container. A single kernel privilege-escalation vulnerability compromises every container on the machine simultaneously. A VM guest's interface to the hypervisor is far narrower: a handful of virtual devices and a hypercall interface, amounting to a few hundred entry points rather than thousands, and the boundary is enforced by hardware (VT-x, EPT, the IOMMU) rather than by kernel code paths.

This is the central trade, and it has a practical corollary: **containers are not a sufficient security boundary between mutually untrusting tenants**. They are an excellent boundary between *your own* workloads. Every public cloud that runs untrusted customer containers puts a VM underneath — AWS Fargate on Firecracker, Google Cloud Run on gVisor, Azure Container Instances on Hyper-V.

| Dimension | Virtual machine | Container |
|---|---|---|
| Isolates | Hardware | Processes (namespaces + cgroups) |
| Kernel | Its own, per VM | Shared with the host |
| Memory overhead | 512 MiB – 2 GiB | A few MiB |
| Start time | 10–60 s (Firecracker: ~125 ms) | 10–200 ms |
| Density per host | 10s | 100s–1000s |
| Guest OS choice | Any, including Windows on Linux | Same kernel only |
| Attack surface from inside | Narrow: virtual devices, hypercalls | Wide: ~350 syscalls, ioctls, /proc, /sys |
| Boundary enforced by | Hardware (VT-x, EPT, IOMMU) | Kernel code |
| Escape blast radius | One VM | Every container on the host |
| Live migration | Mature | Checkpoint/restore (CRIU), limited |
| Image size | GiB | MiB |
| Best for | Multi-tenant isolation, mixed OSes, legacy | Microservices, CI, dense same-OS workloads |

The genuinely interesting development is the middle ground, which has largely dissolved the dichotomy:

- **Firecracker** — a minimal VMM written for exactly this purpose, offering only five emulated devices, booting a microVM in about 125 ms with roughly 5 MiB of overhead. It powers AWS Lambda and Fargate: VM-strength isolation at container-like cost.
- **Kata Containers** — OCI-compatible, so Kubernetes schedules them normally, but each pod runs in its own microVM with its own kernel.
- **gVisor** — no VM at all; a userspace kernel intercepts container syscalls and implements most of them itself, so the host kernel sees a small, constrained set. Weaker than a VM, much stronger than plain `runc`, with a syscall-overhead cost.

The practical decision rule is short: use containers for your own workloads, put a VM boundary under anything untrusted, and reach for a microVM runtime when you need both. And note that in real deployments this is rarely either/or — the overwhelmingly common production shape is containers running inside VMs, with the VM providing the tenant boundary and the container providing packaging and density.

**Example**

```text
   WHERE THE BOUNDARY IS

   VIRTUAL MACHINES                    CONTAINERS
   +---------+ +---------+             +-------+ +-------+ +-------+
   | app     | | app     |             | app   | | app   | | app   |
   | libs    | | libs    |             | libs  | | libs  | | libs  |
   | GUEST   | | GUEST   |             +-------+ +-------+ +-------+
   | KERNEL  | | KERNEL  |             |   namespaces + cgroups      |
   +---------+ +---------+             +-----------------------------+
   |     HYPERVISOR      |             |      SHARED HOST KERNEL     |
   +---------------------+             +-----------------------------+
   |  HARDWARE (VT-x)    |             |          HARDWARE           |
   +---------------------+             +-----------------------------+

   The boundary is HARDWARE-enforced      The boundary is KERNEL CODE.
   and narrow.                            One kernel bug crosses it,
                                          for EVERY container at once.


   THE ATTACK SURFACE, COUNTED

   container -> host kernel
     ~350 system calls, each with many argument combinations
     + ioctl (thousands of device-specific commands)
     + /proc, /sys, netlink, eBPF, io_uring
     -> millions of lines of privileged C, reachable directly

   VM guest -> hypervisor
     a handful of virtual devices (virtio queues)
     + a small hypercall interface
     + instructions that cause VM exits
     -> Firecracker exposes FIVE devices, ~50k lines of Rust

   This ratio is the entire argument. Seccomp narrows the container
   number substantially (a good profile blocks ~250 of the 350), but
   does not change the shape of the problem.


   THE COST, COUNTED

                        VM          container    Firecracker microVM
   memory overhead      ~1 GiB      ~5 MiB       ~5 MiB
   start time           ~30 s       ~50 ms       ~125 ms
   per host             ~30         ~800         ~500
   own kernel           yes         NO           yes
   hardware boundary    yes         no           yes

   Firecracker sits where the table says it cannot: VM isolation at
   container cost, achieved by deleting almost everything a general
   purpose VMM does (no BIOS, no PCI, no USB, no graphics, 5 devices).


   WHAT PRODUCTION ACTUALLY LOOKS LIKE

   +--------------------------------------------------------+
   |  physical host                                         |
   |  +--------------------------+  +---------------------+ |
   |  |  VM (tenant A)           |  |  VM (tenant B)      | |
   |  |  +------+ +------+       |  |  +------+ +------+  | |
   |  |  | ctr  | | ctr  |  ...  |  |  | ctr  | | ctr  |  | |
   |  |  +------+ +------+       |  |  +------+ +------+  | |
   |  +--------------------------+  +---------------------+ |
   +--------------------------------------------------------+

   VM boundary       -> between TENANTS (hardware-enforced)
   container boundary-> between SERVICES of one tenant (packaging,
                        density, deployment)

   This is a Kubernetes node in every managed cloud offering.


   DECISION RULE

   untrusted code / multi-tenant?      -> VM or microVM. Not negotiable.
   different kernel or OS needed?      -> VM. Containers cannot.
   your own microservices, dense?      -> containers.
   need both?                          -> Kata / Firecracker / gVisor.
   compliance requires hardware isolation? -> VM.
```

```bash
# ---------- Measure the difference yourself ----------

# Start time:
time docker run --rm alpine true
#   real 0m0.412s          <- most of it is the daemon, not the container

time (virsh start testvm && until virsh qemu-agent-command testvm \
      '{"execute":"guest-ping"}' 2>/dev/null; do sleep 1; done)
#   real 0m24.8s

# Memory overhead for an idle instance:
docker stats --no-stream alpine-sleeper
#   MEM USAGE: 1.2MiB
virsh dommemstat testvm | grep rss
#   rss 1048576            <- ~1 GiB for an idle VM

# Whose kernel am I using? The clearest single demonstration.
uname -r                               # host:            6.8.0-45-generic
docker run --rm alpine uname -r        # container:       6.8.0-45-generic  <- SAME
docker run --rm --runtime=kata alpine uname -r   # Kata:  5.19.2            <- different
virsh console testvm                   # VM:              whatever it booted

# ---------- The shared-kernel consequence, made concrete ----------
docker run --rm alpine sysctl -w vm.max_map_count=1000000
#   sysctl: error: permission denied on key 'vm.max_map_count'
# Because that sysctl is GLOBAL: there is one kernel, and changing it
# would change it for the host and every other container.

docker run --rm --privileged alpine sysctl -w vm.max_map_count=1000000
#   vm.max_map_count = 1000000
# --privileged just changed the HOST's kernel parameter from inside a
# "container". This is why --privileged is not a container at all.

# ---------- Narrow the container's surface ----------
docker run --rm --security-opt seccomp=/path/default.json alpine true
# Docker's default profile blocks ~44 syscalls outright; a tight
# application-specific profile blocks far more. Generate one by tracing:
strace -c -f -e trace=all ./myapp 2>&1 | awk 'NR>3{print $NF}' | sort -u

# ---------- microVMs: both properties at once ----------
# Firecracker: no BIOS, no PCI, 5 devices, boots in ~125 ms.
firecracker --api-sock /tmp/fc.sock &
curl --unix-socket /tmp/fc.sock -X PUT 'http://localhost/boot-source' \
  -d '{"kernel_image_path":"vmlinux","boot_args":"console=ttyS0 reboot=k panic=1 pci=off"}'
#                                                                       ^^^^^^
#                                        no PCI bus at all: nothing to enumerate
```

**Key takeaways**

- VMs virtualize hardware and carry their own kernel; containers virtualize the system-call interface and share the host's.
- Containers cost a few megabytes and start in milliseconds; VMs cost hundreds of megabytes to gigabytes and start in tens of seconds.
- The isolation argument is about attack surface: a container faces roughly 350 system calls plus ioctls and pseudo-filesystems, while a VM guest faces a handful of virtual devices and hypercalls enforced by hardware.
- One kernel vulnerability compromises every container on a host simultaneously; a hypervisor escape is a much rarer and harder class of bug.
- Containers are an appropriate boundary between your own workloads and an inappropriate one between mutually untrusting tenants.
- Every major cloud that runs untrusted customer containers places a VM or sandboxed runtime underneath.
- Firecracker collapses the trade-off by deleting almost everything a general-purpose VMM does, giving VM-strength isolation at roughly 5 MiB and 125 ms.
- gVisor offers an intermediate point with a userspace kernel and no VM, at the cost of syscall overhead.
- `--privileged` removes the container boundary entirely, which is why it should be treated as "run this as root on the host".
- The dominant production shape is containers inside VMs: the VM is the tenant boundary, the container is the packaging and density mechanism.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. Run `uname -r` on the host and inside a container, explain why they match, and name one consequence for what the container can configure.
> 2. Measure start time and idle memory for a container and a VM on the same machine, and express the density difference for a host with 64 GiB of RAM.
> 3. Explain why a CI system running untrusted pull-request code should not use plain containers, and describe two acceptable alternatives.
> 4. Interview-style: "A team proposes replacing their VM-per-customer architecture with one container per customer to cut costs. What is your response?" *Hint: separate the packaging argument from the isolation argument, and ask what a single kernel CVE would mean under each design.*

#### Unikernels

**Theory**

Every layer this chapter has examined adds isolation and generality at some cost. Unikernels ask what happens if you push in the opposite direction: what if an application did not run *on* an operating system, but *was* one?

The observation motivating them is that a VM running one application carries an enormous amount of machinery it will never use. A general-purpose Linux kernel supports thousands of devices, multiple filesystems, many users, arbitrary process creation, and a full network stack with every protocol — and a containerised microservice uses a tiny fraction of that. All of it must still be loaded, maintained, patched, and is reachable as attack surface.

A **unikernel** is a specialised, single-address-space machine image built by compiling an application together with just the OS functionality it actually calls, using a **library operating system**. Filesystem, network stack, and scheduler are ordinary libraries linked into the binary. The result boots directly on a hypervisor with no separate kernel.

The consequences are dramatic in both directions.

What is gained:

- **Size.** Images of 1–10 MiB rather than hundreds. A minimal web server can be under 1 MiB.
- **Boot time.** Tens of milliseconds — sometimes under 20 ms — because there is no device probing, no init system, and no dynamic linking. Fast enough to boot per request.
- **Attack surface.** If the application never uses a filesystem, no filesystem code is linked in and there is no filesystem to attack. There is no shell to drop into, no `/bin`, no package manager, and typically no way to execute new code at all.
- **Performance.** A single address space with no user/kernel boundary means no system-call transitions: the "syscall" is a function call. No process abstraction means no context switches.

What is given up, and it is a great deal:

- **No process model.** No `fork()`, no `exec()`, often a single address space with cooperative or lightweight threading only.
- **No debugging as you know it.** No shell, no `ps`, no `strace`, no ability to attach to a running instance. Observability must be designed in from the start.
- **Language and library constraints.** MirageOS requires OCaml; other frameworks support specific runtimes. Anything calling an unsupported POSIX interface will not build.
- **Weak internal isolation.** A single address space means a memory-safety bug can reach anything in the image. The argument is that the *external* surface is tiny and the image is often written in a memory-safe language, but there is no internal boundary.
- **Operational immaturity.** Patching means rebuilding and redeploying the whole image, and the tooling ecosystem is nothing like Linux's.

Notable implementations: **MirageOS** (OCaml, the most rigorous realisation of the idea), **IncludeOS** (C++), **OSv** (runs unmodified Linux binaries in a unikernel-like single address space), **Nanos** with the Ops tooling, and **Unikraft**, the most practical current effort — a modular library OS with POSIX compatibility layers that substantially reduces the porting cost.

Unikernels have not displaced containers, and the reason is instructive: the operational cost of losing the entire Linux tooling ecosystem outweighs the gains for most workloads. Their real influence has been indirect — they demonstrated how much of a general-purpose OS a single application does not need, and that argument shaped Firecracker's minimal device model, distroless and scratch container images, and WebAssembly-based runtimes like WASI, which pursue similar goals with far lower migration cost.

**Example**

```text
   THE SPECIALISATION SPECTRUM

   traditional VM     container        microVM        UNIKERNEL
   +-----------+      +---------+      +---------+    +-----------+
   | app       |      | app     |      | app     |    | app       |
   | libs      |      | libs    |      | libs    |    | +only the |
   | full OS   |      | (shared |      | minimal |    |  OS parts |
   | + daemons |      |  kernel)|      | kernel  |    |  it CALLS |
   | + drivers |      +---------+      +---------+    +-----------+
   +-----------+
   ~2 GiB              ~50 MiB          ~50 MiB        ~2 MiB
   ~30 s               ~50 ms           ~125 ms        ~20 ms
   full generality                                     no generality


   ADDRESS SPACE: THE STRUCTURAL DIFFERENCE

   TRADITIONAL                          UNIKERNEL
   +---------------------------+        +---------------------------+
   | user space   (ring 3)     |        |                           |
   |   application             |        |   application             |
   |   libc                    |        |   network stack   (a lib) |
   +---------------------------+        |   filesystem      (a lib) |
   | <<< SYSCALL BOUNDARY >>>  |        |   scheduler       (a lib) |
   +---------------------------+        |                           |
   | kernel space (ring 0)     |        |   ONE address space,      |
   |   scheduler, VFS, TCP/IP, |        |   ONE privilege level     |
   |   drivers, 350 syscalls   |        +---------------------------+
   +---------------------------+        |    HYPERVISOR             |
   |    HARDWARE               |        +---------------------------+
   +---------------------------+

   read() in a unikernel is a FUNCTION CALL, not a mode transition:
     ~1 ns, not ~200 ns. And there is no boundary to attack.


   ATTACK SURFACE BY SUBTRACTION

   what a typical unikernel image DOES NOT CONTAIN:
     no shell            -> nothing to spawn after an RCE
     no /bin, no busybox -> no tools for an attacker to use
     no package manager  -> nothing to install
     no fork/exec        -> a "command injection" has no command to run
     no other users      -> no privilege escalation target
     no unused drivers   -> no vulnerable code path
     no filesystem (if unused) -> no path traversal to exploit

   The classic exploit chain (RCE -> spawn a shell -> pivot) has no
   second step. That is the security argument, and it is a strong one.


   THE HONEST COST

   production incident, Linux VM          production incident, unikernel
   ssh in                                 (no ssh)
   ps aux, top, strace -p                 (none of these exist)
   tcpdump, lsof, /proc                   (none of these exist)
   attach gdb, take a core                (must be designed in)
   patch one package, restart             rebuild the ENTIRE image
   ----------------------------------     ----------------------------
   You have a live system to inspect.      You have logs and metrics you
                                           thought to emit in advance.

   This, not performance, is why unikernels remain niche.
```

```ocaml
(* MirageOS: the entire "operating system" for an HTTP service.
   What is NOT here is the point -- no process model, no filesystem,
   no users, no shell. Only what this service calls gets linked in. *)

open Lwt.Infix

module Main (S : Cohttp_mirage.Server.S) = struct

  let handler _conn request _body =
    (* The network stack is a LIBRARY in this same address space.
       Reading from the socket is a function call, not a syscall:
       no mode transition, no ring change, no TLB implications. *)
    let path = Uri.path (Cohttp.Request.uri request) in
    match path with
    | "/" ->
        S.respond_string ~status:`OK ~body:"hello from a unikernel\n" ()
    | "/health" ->
        S.respond_string ~status:`OK ~body:"ok\n" ()
    | _ ->
        S.respond_string ~status:`Not_found ~body:"not found\n" ()

  (* This IS the whole system. There is no init, no PID 1, no other
     process -- because there is no process abstraction at all. *)
  let start http =
    http (`TCP 8080) (S.make ~callback:handler ())
end
```

```bash
# ---------- Build one and look at what you get ----------
# MirageOS: configure for a hypervisor target, then compile.
mirage configure -t hvt          # hvt = a minimal KVM/Solo5 target
make depend && make
ls -lh dist/httpserver.hvt
#   -rwxr-xr-x  1.8M httpserver.hvt
# 1.8 MiB. The equivalent Linux VM image is 300 MiB to 2 GiB.

solo5-hvt --net:service=tap0 dist/httpserver.hvt
#   Solo5: Bindings version v0.9.0
#   ...
#   boot time: 0.019s          <- 19 ms, cold, from nothing

# ---------- Compare, honestly, across the spectrum ----------
#                      image     boot      idle RAM   has a shell?
#   Ubuntu VM          2.3 GiB   28 s      512 MiB    yes
#   Alpine VM          130 MiB   6 s       48 MiB     yes
#   Docker (alpine)    7 MiB     50 ms     2 MiB      yes
#   Docker (scratch)   4 MiB     40 ms     1 MiB      NO
#   Firecracker microVM 50 MiB   125 ms    5 MiB      yes
#   MirageOS unikernel 1.8 MiB   19 ms     8 MiB      NO

# ---------- Unikraft: the practical modern attempt ----------
kraft pkg update
kraft build --target nginx/qemu-x86_64        # POSIX compat layer means
kraft run nginx                               # real apps can be ported
# Unikraft's contribution is reducing the porting cost, which was the
# single biggest barrier to adoption.

# ---------- The ideas that actually shipped everywhere ----------
# 1. "scratch" and distroless images: no shell, no package manager.
cat <<'EOF' > Dockerfile
FROM golang:1.22 AS build
WORKDIR /src
COPY . .
RUN CGO_ENABLED=0 go build -o /app .

FROM scratch                  # <- NOTHING. Not even libc.
COPY --from=build /app /app
ENTRYPOINT ["/app"]
EOF
# ~4 MiB image, no shell to exec into after an RCE. The unikernel
# security argument, achieved with ordinary container tooling.

# 2. WebAssembly + WASI: a capability-based sandbox, similar goals,
#    far lower migration cost -- arguably where the idea actually landed.
#    wasmtime run --dir=/data app.wasm
```

**Key takeaways**

- A unikernel compiles an application together with only the OS functionality it actually calls, using a library operating system, producing a single-address-space image that boots directly on a hypervisor.
- Images are 1–10 MiB and boot in tens of milliseconds because there is no device probing, no init system, and no dynamic linking.
- With one address space and one privilege level there is no user/kernel boundary, so a system call becomes an ordinary function call.
- The security argument is subtraction: no shell, no `fork`/`exec`, no package manager, and no unused drivers means a remote-code-execution exploit has no second stage.
- The costs are severe: no process model, no conventional debugging, language and library restrictions, and no internal isolation within the single address space.
- Patching requires rebuilding and redeploying the entire image rather than updating a package.
- MirageOS is the most rigorous implementation, while Unikraft is the most practical, reducing porting cost through POSIX compatibility layers.
- Unikernels remain niche because losing the Linux tooling ecosystem outweighs the gains for most workloads — an operational argument, not a technical one.
- Their ideas shipped elsewhere: Firecracker's minimal device model, `scratch` and distroless images, and WebAssembly/WASI all pursue the same specialisation with far lower migration cost.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. List four components of a general-purpose Linux kernel that a stateless HTTP microservice never uses, and explain what each contributes to attack surface.
> 2. Build a Go service into a `FROM scratch` image, compare its size with the `alpine`-based equivalent, and explain which unikernel property you have reproduced and which you have not.
> 3. Explain why a system call in a unikernel costs roughly a function call, and what safety property is given up to achieve that.
> 4. Interview-style: "Unikernels boot in 20 ms, are a hundred times smaller, and have almost no attack surface. Why is essentially nobody running them in production?" *Hint: imagine being paged at 3 a.m. for a latency regression, and list the commands you would normally run first.*
