<a id="14-distributed-and-specialized-systems"></a>
## 14. Distributed and Specialized Systems

Every chapter so far has assumed one machine, one clock, and one memory that all parties can see; this chapter removes those assumptions in three different directions. It looks at systems spread across machines that fail independently and share no clock, at systems where being late is as wrong as being incorrect, and at systems where the battery and the user's attention are the scarcest resources. The common thread is that each specialization changes which OS guarantee is negotiable — consistency, throughput, or average latency — and understanding *which* one is what separates a working design from a plausible-sounding one.

<a id="141-distributed-operating-systems"></a>
### 14.1 Distributed Operating Systems

A distributed system differs from a multiprocessor in one fundamental way: there is no shared memory and no shared clock, and any component can fail while the others keep running. This section builds from the architectural models used to glue machines together, through the ordering and coordination primitives that replace shared memory, to consensus — the algorithm that lets a group of unreliable machines behave like one reliable one.

#### Network Operating System Models

**Theory**

Start with why anyone connects machines at all. A single machine has a hard ceiling on cores, memory, and disk, and — more importantly — it has a single power supply, a single kernel, and a single building. Distribution buys four things: **capacity** beyond one box, **availability** despite one box dying, **locality** so users in Tokyo are not served from Virginia, and **sharing** of resources that physically live somewhere else (a printer, a dataset, a licence server).

The interesting question is how much of the distribution the programmer has to see. There is a spectrum, and the position on it is the single most useful classification.

A **network operating system** is the loosely coupled end. Each machine runs its own independent OS, and remoteness is explicit: you `ssh` to a host, you `scp` a file, you mount `server:/export` at a path you chose. The user knows perfectly well which machine is which, and that knowledge is part of the interface. Nothing migrates, nothing is automatic, and when the remote machine dies you get an error mentioning that machine by name.

A **distributed operating system** is the tightly coupled end. It presents a **single system image**: one process namespace, one filesystem, one scheduler, spread transparently over many machines. You start a process and the system decides where it runs; it may migrate mid-execution. Amoeba, Sprite, Plan 9, and MOSIX all did this, and they worked. They also essentially disappeared from production computing, for reasons worth understanding rather than memorising.

In between — and this is where virtually all real systems live — sits **middleware**: an application-level layer that provides *selective* transparency over ordinary operating systems. Kubernetes, gRPC, Kafka, Spark, and Cassandra are middleware in this sense. They give you some transparency (you address a service, not a host) while leaving the OS boundaries intact and, crucially, leaving failure visible where it matters.

**Transparency** is the property being traded, and it is not one property but several. The ISO/ODP model names eight; these five carry most of the weight:

| Transparency | Hides | Typical mechanism | Cost when it leaks |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Access** | Local vs remote call syntax | RPC stubs, NFS | Remote calls fail and stall in ways local ones do not |
| **Location** | Where a resource physically is | DNS, service discovery | Latency varies by an order of magnitude |
| **Migration** | That a resource moved | Handles instead of addresses | In-flight state must move too |
| **Replication** | That there are several copies | Quorum reads/writes | Copies disagree; you must choose which to believe |
| **Failure** | That a component died | Retries, timeouts | Retries duplicate side effects; "slow" is indistinguishable from "dead" |

The last row is why full transparency failed. **Failure transparency is not achievable**, only approximable, because a node cannot distinguish a crashed peer from a slow peer from a partitioned network — all three look like silence. A system that pretends otherwise does not remove the failure; it removes your ability to handle it.

That insight is captured in the **eight fallacies of distributed computing** (Deutsch and Gosling), each of which is an assumption that is true locally and false remotely:

1. The network is reliable.
2. Latency is zero.
3. Bandwidth is infinite.
4. The network is secure.
5. Topology does not change.
6. There is one administrator.
7. Transport cost is zero.
8. The network is homogeneous.

Every one of these is an assumption an access-transparent RPC layer quietly invites you to make. This is the core critique of "make remote calls look local": the syntax can be made identical, but the *failure semantics* cannot, and the failure semantics are what your error handling is built on.

Finally, the physical arrangement. **Client-server** centralises state at a server (simple, one place to be consistent, one place to fail). **Peer-to-peer** gives every node the same role (no bottleneck, no single failure point, much harder to reason about). A **cluster** is many machines under one administrative domain, presented as one service — and it subdivides usefully into high-availability clusters (a standby takes over, requiring a fencing mechanism so two nodes never both believe they are primary — "split brain") and high-performance clusters (the work is partitioned across nodes, as in MPI or Spark).

**Example**

```text
   THE TRANSPARENCY SPECTRUM

   NETWORK OS                MIDDLEWARE                DISTRIBUTED OS
   (loosely coupled)         (selective)               (single system image)

   +-----------+             +-----------+             +-------------------+
   | OS A      |             | OS A | OS B|            |   one process     |
   | OS B      |             |  middleware |           |   namespace       |
   | OS C      |             |  (k8s,gRPC) |           |   over N machines |
   +-----------+             +-----------+             +-------------------+

   ssh host2 cmd             call svc "cart"           run cmd
   scp f host2:/tmp          k8s picks the pod         system picks the node
   mount srv:/export         retries are YOUR job      process may migrate

   You KNOW the machine      You know it EXISTS        You cannot tell
   Failure names the host    Failure is an error code  Failure is... what?

   NFS, SMB, ssh             Kubernetes, Kafka,        Amoeba, Sprite,
   (everywhere)              Cassandra (everywhere)    Plan 9 (museum)


   WHY THE RIGHT-HAND COLUMN LOST

   Single system image requires hiding failure.
   Hiding failure requires distinguishing:

        crashed node   ---+
        slow node      ---+---> all three look IDENTICAL: silence
        partitioned    ---+

   You cannot. So the abstraction leaks exactly when it matters most,
   and the application -- which has been written as if it cannot leak --
   has no code path for it.

   Middleware won by making failure VISIBLE but MANAGEABLE.


   THE COST OF PRETENDING A REMOTE CALL IS LOCAL

   local function call        remote procedure call
   ------------------------   ---------------------------------
   ~1 ns                      ~0.5 ms LAN, ~150 ms cross-ocean
   never "half-happens"       may execute 0, 1, or MANY times
   fails => exception         may never return at all
   caller/callee same fate    callee may outlive caller, or vice versa
   arguments by reference     arguments serialised (deep copy)

   Same syntax. Entirely different contract.
```

```python
# The fallacies, made concrete. The SAME operation, three ways.

import time, socket, requests

# --- 1. Local call: the baseline contract ----------------------------
def get_user_local(db, uid):
    return db[uid]                       # ~100 ns, cannot partially fail

# --- 2. Network-OS style: remoteness is explicit ----------------------
#    The programmer NAMES the machine. Failure mentions the machine.
def get_user_nos(uid):
    s = socket.create_connection(("users.internal", 9000), timeout=2.0)
    s.sendall(f"GET {uid}\n".encode())
    return s.recv(4096)                  # ConnectionRefused / timeout
    # The error tells you WHICH host failed -- that is the point.

# --- 3. Middleware style: selective transparency ----------------------
#    You address a SERVICE, not a host. But failure stays visible,
#    and handling it is still your job.
def get_user_middleware(uid, attempts=3):
    for n in range(attempts):
        try:
            # "users" resolves via service discovery to SOME instance.
            r = requests.get(f"http://users/v1/{uid}", timeout=2.0)
            r.raise_for_status()
            return r.json()
        except requests.Timeout:
            # A timeout does NOT mean the request did not execute.
            # It means you do not know. Retrying a non-idempotent
            # operation here is how duplicate charges happen.
            time.sleep(2 ** n * 0.1)     # exponential backoff
    raise RuntimeError("users service unreachable")

# --- The trap access transparency sets --------------------------------
#   for uid in all_users:        # 10,000 users
#       get_user_middleware(uid) # looks like a loop over a dict
#   Local:  10,000 * 100 ns  = 1 ms
#   Remote: 10,000 * 0.5 ms  = 5 SECONDS, and any one can fail.
#   The N+1 query problem is fallacy #2 ("latency is zero") in the wild.
```

```bash
# ---- Network OS: remoteness is part of the interface ----
ssh build-07 'make -j32'          # you chose the machine
scp results.tar build-07:/data/   # you chose the direction
mount -t nfs fileserver:/export /mnt/shared
ls /mnt/shared                    # hangs hard if fileserver is down:
                                  # access transparency without failure
                                  # transparency -- the classic NFS hang

# ---- Middleware: you address a service, the system picks a host ----
kubectl run job --image=build:v2   # you did NOT choose the node
kubectl get pods -o wide           # ...but you can still SEE which one
curl http://users/v1/42            # "users" is a name, not a machine

# ---- Measure fallacy #2 for yourself ----
ping -c 5 localhost                # ~0.03 ms
ping -c 5 gateway                  # ~0.5  ms   (LAN: ~15x)
ping -c 5 example.com              # ~120  ms   (WAN: ~4000x)
# Anything that loops over a remote call inherits this multiplier.
```

**Key takeaways**

- Distribution buys capacity, availability, locality, and resource sharing, and pays for it with partial failure and the loss of a shared clock and shared memory.
- A network OS keeps machines independent and makes remoteness explicit; a distributed OS presents a single system image; middleware provides selective transparency over ordinary operating systems and is what real systems use.
- Transparency is several distinct properties — access, location, migration, replication, failure — and they can be adopted independently.
- Failure transparency is unachievable in principle because a crashed node, a slow node, and a partitioned network are indistinguishable from the outside.
- The eight fallacies of distributed computing are each an assumption that holds locally and fails remotely; access-transparent RPC quietly encourages all of them.
- Client-server centralises state and failure, peer-to-peer removes the bottleneck at the cost of reasoning difficulty, and clusters present many machines as one service.
- High-availability clusters require a fencing mechanism to prevent split brain, where two nodes both believe they are the primary.
- A timeout means "unknown", not "did not happen" — which is why retrying non-idempotent operations is a correctness bug, not a robustness feature.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. Classify each of the following as network OS, middleware, or distributed OS, and justify it in one sentence: NFS, Kubernetes, Plan 9, `ssh`, Cassandra, MOSIX.
> 2. Take a loop that fetches 500 records one at a time from a remote service at 0.4 ms RTT. Compute the total time, then explain which of the eight fallacies the code's author assumed and how batching fixes it.
> 3. Mount an NFS share (or simulate one), kill the server, and observe what `ls` does on the mount point. Explain which transparency was provided and which was not.
> 4. Interview-style: "Our RPC framework makes remote calls look exactly like local function calls. Is that good?" *Hint: write down the contract of a local call — timing, failure modes, how many times it executes — and check each line against a remote one.*

#### Distributed Coordination

**Theory**

Once you have several machines that must act as one system, you need them to agree on things: who is in charge, whether a transaction committed, who holds a lock, which nodes are alive. On one machine all of this is trivial — there is a shared memory word, and a mutex protecting it. Distributed coordination is the study of what replaces that word when there is no shared memory.

Begin with the **system model**, because every algorithm's correctness depends on it. Two axes matter.

*Timing.* In a **synchronous** system, message delay and processing time have known upper bounds, so a timeout is proof of failure. In an **asynchronous** system there are no bounds, so a timeout proves nothing. Real networks are **partially synchronous**: usually well-behaved, occasionally arbitrarily slow. Algorithms must be *safe* (never wrong) in the asynchronous model and *live* (eventually make progress) during synchronous periods. This split is the single most important design pattern in the field.

*Failures.* Ordered from benign to malicious:

| Failure model | Node behaviour | Nodes needed to tolerate f | Used by |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Crash-stop** | Halts, never returns | 2f + 1 | Raft, Paxos, etcd |
| **Crash-recovery** | Halts, later returns with stable storage | 2f + 1 | Real Raft implementations |
| **Omission** | Drops some messages | 2f + 1 | Modelled as crash |
| **Byzantine** | Arbitrary, possibly malicious | 3f + 1 | PBFT, blockchains |

Next, **failure detection**, which is the practical form of "is that node alive?". The standard mechanism is a **heartbeat**: each node periodically announces itself, and a peer that has not been heard from within a timeout is *suspected*. Note the word — suspected, not known. Choosing the timeout is a direct trade-off: short timeouts detect real failures fast but generate false positives during a GC pause or a network hiccup, and a false positive that triggers failover is often more damaging than the failure it was guarding against. **Phi-accrual** detectors (used by Cassandra and Akka) improve on this by outputting a continuous suspicion level derived from the observed distribution of heartbeat intervals, letting each consumer pick its own threshold.

A **lease** is the coordination primitive that makes this workable. A lease is a lock with an expiry: the holder gets a resource for a bounded time, and if it does not renew, the lease expires and someone else may take it. The crucial property is that the *granter* can hand the resource on after expiry without contacting the old holder — which matters precisely because the old holder may be unreachable. Leases convert "is it alive?" (unanswerable) into "has its lease expired?" (locally decidable by a clock).

**Leader election** reduces many coordination problems to one: elect a single coordinator, then let it decide sequentially, which restores the single-machine reasoning you are used to. Two classical algorithms:

- **Bully algorithm.** A node that notices the leader is gone sends `ELECTION` to all higher-numbered nodes. If none answer, it declares itself leader. If one answers, it drops out and waits. The highest live node always wins; it costs O(n²) messages in the worst case.
- **Ring algorithm.** Nodes are logically ordered in a ring. An election message circulates carrying the IDs of live nodes; when it returns to the initiator, the highest ID becomes leader. O(n) messages, but requires the ring to be maintained.

Both are correct only in a synchronous model. In a partially synchronous one they can elect two leaders — which is why production systems elect leaders *through* consensus (covered in the last topic of this section) rather than with these algorithms.

Finally, **atomic commit**: making a transaction that spans several nodes either commit everywhere or abort everywhere. **Two-phase commit** (2PC) is the standard protocol. A coordinator asks every participant to *prepare*; a participant that votes yes must be able to commit afterwards no matter what, so it writes the transaction durably and gives up its right to abort. If all vote yes, the coordinator logs `COMMIT` and tells everyone; any no vote means abort.

2PC is atomic but **blocking**. If the coordinator crashes after participants have voted yes but before the decision arrives, those participants are stuck: they cannot commit (maybe someone voted no) and cannot abort (maybe everyone voted yes), and they are holding locks the whole time. **Three-phase commit** adds a pre-commit round to remove the blocking, but is unsafe under network partitions and is essentially unused. The real fix is to make the coordinator itself fault-tolerant by replicating its decision log through consensus — which is what Spanner and modern distributed databases do.

**Example**

```text
   HEARTBEATS AND THE TIMEOUT TRADE-OFF

   node A -- "alive" --> node B    every 1 s
                                   B suspects A after T seconds

   T = 2 s   fast detection, but a 2.5 s GC pause triggers a FALSE
             failover: a healthy leader is deposed, in-flight work lost
   T = 30 s  almost no false positives, but 30 s of downtime on a
             REAL crash

   There is no correct T. There is only the cost of each mistake.
   Phi-accrual: output suspicion LEVEL from observed inter-arrival
   distribution; each consumer picks its own threshold.


   THE BULLY ALGORITHM (highest live ID wins)

   Nodes 1..5, leader was 5, node 5 crashes.

   t0  node 2 notices silence from 5
   t1  2 -> ELECTION -> 3, 4, 5        (only HIGHER ids)
   t2  3 -> OK -> 2                    2 drops out
       4 -> OK -> 2                    2 drops out
       5 -> (silence, it is dead)
   t3  3 -> ELECTION -> 4, 5           3 and 4 now run their own
       4 -> ELECTION -> 5
   t4  4 -> OK -> 3                    3 drops out
       5 -> (silence)
   t5  4 -> COORDINATOR -> 1,2,3       node 4 is leader

   Worst case O(n^2) messages. Correct only if timeouts are RELIABLE.


   TWO-PHASE COMMIT, AND ITS FAILURE MODE

   PHASE 1 (prepare)              PHASE 2 (commit)
   C --prepare--> P1              C --commit--> P1  ack
   C --prepare--> P2              C --commit--> P2  ack
   C --prepare--> P3              C --commit--> P3  ack
        <--YES-- all                   all durable, locks released

   Any NO, or any timeout in phase 1  =>  ABORT everywhere. Fine.

   THE BLOCKING CASE:
   C --prepare--> P1,P2,P3
        <--YES-- all
   C writes COMMIT to its log
   C CRASHES before sending anything
                                  P1,P2,P3: voted YES, holding locks,
                                  cannot commit (was there a NO?),
                                  cannot abort (maybe all said YES).
                                  They BLOCK until C returns. Forever,
                                  if C's disk is gone.

   Fix in practice: replicate C's decision log via consensus,
   so "the coordinator" survives losing any single machine.


   LEASES: TURNING AN UNANSWERABLE QUESTION INTO A LOCAL ONE

   "Is node A alive?"           -> cannot be answered remotely
   "Has A's lease expired?"     -> check your own clock. Done.

   t=0   A acquires lease, TTL 10 s
   t=5   A renews  (TTL now to t=15)
   t=6   A is partitioned away
   t=15  lease expires; B may safely take over
         -- WITHOUT needing to reach A, which is the whole point.

   Caveat: A may not KNOW it lost the lease (its clock, its pause).
   => the resource must reject stale holders. See fencing tokens.
```

```python
# Failure detection and leader election, reduced to their essentials.

import time, threading

# ---------------- Heartbeat failure detector -------------------------
class FailureDetector:
    """Suspects a peer after `timeout` seconds of silence.
    Note: suspect(), never dead(). The distinction is the whole subject."""
    def __init__(self, timeout=5.0):
        self.timeout = timeout
        self.last_seen = {}                     # peer -> monotonic time

    def heartbeat(self, peer):
        self.last_seen[peer] = time.monotonic()

    def suspected(self, peer):
        last = self.last_seen.get(peer, 0)
        return (time.monotonic() - last) > self.timeout

    def alive(self):
        return [p for p in self.last_seen if not self.suspected(p)]

# ---------------- Bully election -------------------------------------
class BullyNode:
    def __init__(self, node_id, peers, transport):
        self.id, self.peers, self.net = node_id, peers, transport
        self.leader = None

    def start_election(self):
        higher = [p for p in self.peers if p > self.id]
        if not higher:                          # nobody above me
            return self.declare_victory()
        responses = [self.net.send(p, "ELECTION", timeout=2.0)
                     for p in higher]
        if not any(r == "OK" for r in responses):
            # Every higher node is silent => treat as dead. This
            # inference is ONLY valid in a synchronous model; a slow
            # higher node here produces TWO leaders.
            return self.declare_victory()
        # Someone higher is alive: stand down and await COORDINATOR.

    def declare_victory(self):
        self.leader = self.id
        for p in self.peers:
            self.net.send(p, f"COORDINATOR {self.id}")

# ---------------- Lease, with the renewal loop -----------------------
class Lease:
    def __init__(self, ttl=10.0):
        self.ttl, self.holder, self.expires = ttl, None, 0.0
        self.lock = threading.Lock()
        self.epoch = 0                          # monotonic fencing token

    def acquire(self, who):
        with self.lock:
            now = time.monotonic()
            if self.holder is None or now > self.expires:
                self.holder, self.expires = who, now + self.ttl
                self.epoch += 1                 # NEW epoch each handover
                return self.epoch               # caller must present this
            return None                         # still held by someone

    def renew(self, who, token):
        with self.lock:
            # Renewal fails if the lease already expired and was regranted.
            if self.holder == who and token == self.epoch \
               and time.monotonic() <= self.expires:
                self.expires = time.monotonic() + self.ttl
                return True
            return False
```

```python
# Two-phase commit, including the blocking window, made explicit.

class Participant:
    def __init__(self, name):
        self.name, self.state = name, "IDLE"

    def prepare(self, txn):
        if not self.can_commit(txn):
            self.state = "ABORTED"
            return "NO"
        self.write_ahead_log(txn)     # MUST be durable before voting YES:
        self.state = "PREPARED"       # after this we have given up the
        return "YES"                  # right to unilaterally abort

    def decide(self, decision):       # phase 2
        self.state = decision         # COMMITTED or ABORTED; locks freed

class Coordinator:
    def commit(self, txn, participants):
        votes = []
        for p in participants:
            try:
                votes.append(p.prepare(txn))
            except TimeoutError:
                votes.append("NO")    # a silent participant means abort:
                                      # phase 1 timeouts are SAFE
        decision = "COMMIT" if all(v == "YES" for v in votes) else "ABORT"
        self.log(decision)            # <-- the point of no return
        # ***  If we crash HERE, every participant that voted YES is    ***
        # ***  blocked: holding locks, unable to decide, until we       ***
        # ***  return. Phase-2 timeouts are NOT safe to resolve locally.***
        for p in participants:
            p.decide(decision)        # retried until acked, forever
        return decision
```

**Key takeaways**

- Coordination algorithms are only correct relative to a system model; assume asynchrony for safety and partial synchrony for liveness.
- Failure models run from crash-stop (tolerate f with 2f + 1 nodes) to Byzantine (3f + 1), and choosing the wrong one is choosing the wrong algorithm.
- Heartbeat detectors suspect rather than know; the timeout trades detection speed against false failovers, and a false failover often costs more than the failure it pre-empts.
- Phi-accrual detectors emit a continuous suspicion level from observed heartbeat statistics instead of a single hard threshold.
- A lease is a lock with an expiry, converting the unanswerable "is it alive?" into the locally decidable "has the lease expired?".
- Bully and ring elections are simple but correct only under synchronous timing; production systems elect leaders through consensus instead.
- Two-phase commit is atomic but blocking: a coordinator crash between the prepare votes and the decision leaves participants holding locks with no safe local resolution.
- Phase-1 timeouts are safe (abort), phase-2 timeouts are not — the asymmetry is the entire weakness of 2PC, and the fix is a consensus-replicated coordinator.

#### Logical Clocks and Ordering

**Theory**

Concurrency on one machine is ordered by a shared clock and shared memory: if A wrote a variable before B read it, hardware and the memory model tell you so. Across machines, neither exists. Two events on two nodes have no inherent order at all, and physical clocks cannot supply one.

Why not? Quartz oscillators drift — a typical server clock drifts by tens of microseconds per second, which is seconds per day. **NTP** corrects this to roughly 1 ms on a LAN and 10-100 ms over the internet, and it corrects by *stepping* or *slewing* the clock, meaning wall-clock time can jump backwards. A leap second can make the same second occur twice. So `if (ts_a < ts_b)` across two machines is not a reliable ordering, and using wall-clock timestamps as version numbers (the "last write wins" of many early distributed stores) silently loses data when a clock is 200 ms fast.

Lamport's insight in 1978 was that most of the time you do not need *when*; you need *whether one thing could have caused another*. Define the **happened-before** relation, written `a -> b`:

1. If `a` and `b` are in the same process and `a` comes first, then `a -> b`.
2. If `a` is the send of a message and `b` is its receipt, then `a -> b`.
3. Transitivity: if `a -> b` and `b -> c` then `a -> c`.

If neither `a -> b` nor `b -> a`, the events are **concurrent** (`a || b`) — not "simultaneous", but *causally independent*: neither could have influenced the other, so the system is free to order them however it likes. This is a partial order, and it is exactly what causality means when there is no clock.

A **Lamport clock** implements it with one integer per process:

- Increment your counter before every local event.
- Send the counter with every message.
- On receipt, set `counter = max(local, received) + 1`.

This guarantees `a -> b  ⟹  L(a) < L(b)`. But the converse fails: `L(a) < L(b)` does *not* imply `a -> b`, because concurrent events also get ordered numbers. Lamport clocks give you a consistent total order (break ties with node ID) but cannot detect concurrency — which is precisely what you need to detect conflicting writes.

**Vector clocks** fix that. Each process keeps a vector of counters, one entry per process:

- Increment your own entry on a local event.
- Send the whole vector.
- On receipt, take the element-wise `max`, then increment your own entry.

Now `V(a) < V(b)` (every element ≤, at least one strictly <) if and only if `a -> b`. If neither vector dominates, the events are genuinely concurrent — a conflict that the application must resolve (Dynamo and Riak surface exactly this as sibling versions). The cost is size: the vector grows with the number of nodes, which is why systems with churn use **version vectors** keyed by replica rather than client, or dotted version vectors to prune.

Finally, the pragmatic hybrid. Physical time is useful (humans and debuggers want it, and it bounds staleness), causality is correct. **Hybrid logical clocks** (HLC) combine them: a timestamp is `(physical, logical)`, where the physical part tracks NTP time and the logical part increments when messages arrive with a timestamp from the same or a future physical instant. HLCs are close to wall time, monotonic, and respect causality — and they are what CockroachDB and MongoDB use. Google's **TrueTime** takes the opposite approach: give every datacentre GPS and atomic clocks, expose time as an *interval* `[earliest, latest]` with a bounded error (typically under 7 ms), and have Spanner simply *wait out the uncertainty* before committing, buying externally consistent global transactions at the cost of a few milliseconds per commit and specialised hardware.

**Example**

```text
   HAPPENED-BEFORE: THREE PROCESSES, TWO MESSAGES

   P1 ---a------------b-------------------- ...
          \            \
           m1           \
            \            \
   P2 -------c---d-------\--------------- ...
                  \       \
                   m2      \
                    \       \
   P3 ---------------e-------f----------- ...

   a -> c   (message m1)
   c -> d   (same process)
   d -> e   (message m2)
   => a -> e by transitivity

   b || e   ?  b is after a on P1; e is after d on P3. No message path
               connects them => CONCURRENT. Neither caused the other.
               The system may order them either way.


   LAMPORT CLOCKS: correct one way only

   P1:  a(1) ----m1----> P2
   P2:  c(max(0,1)+1 = 2)  d(3) ----m2----> P3
   P3:  e(max(0,3)+1 = 4)

   L(a)=1 < L(e)=4  and indeed a -> e.        GOOD
   P1 continues:    b(2)
   L(b)=2 < L(e)=4  but b || e -- NOT causal.  <-- the false implication

   Lamport:  a -> b  IMPLIES  L(a) < L(b)
             L(a) < L(b) does NOT imply a -> b
   Use for: a consistent total order (tie-break on node id).
   Cannot:  detect conflicts.


   VECTOR CLOCKS: an if-and-only-if

   Vectors are [P1, P2, P3].

   P1: a [1,0,0] ---m1---> 
   P2:            c [1,1,0]   d [1,2,0] ---m2--->
   P3:                                    e [1,2,1]
   P1: b [2,0,0]

   a -> e ?  [1,0,0] <= [1,2,1] elementwise, and strictly < somewhere
             => YES, a happened-before e.
   b vs e ?  b=[2,0,0]  e=[1,2,1]
             b[0]=2 > e[0]=1   AND   b[1]=0 < e[1]=2
             neither dominates  =>  CONCURRENT. A genuine conflict.

   This is what a Dynamo-style store reports as "siblings":
   two values, neither newer, application must merge.


   WHY WALL CLOCKS LOSE DATA ("last write wins")

   client A (clock +200 ms fast)   client B (clock correct)
   t_real=10.000  write X=1        
                  stamps 10.200
   t_real=10.100                   write X=2
                                   stamps 10.100

   Store keeps the HIGHEST timestamp => X=1 wins.
   But B wrote LATER in real time. B's write is silently lost,
   with no error, no conflict, no trace. Clock skew ate it.
```

```python
# Lamport and vector clocks side by side, with the crucial comparison.

# ---------------- Lamport clock --------------------------------------
class LamportClock:
    def __init__(self):
        self.t = 0

    def local_event(self):
        self.t += 1
        return self.t

    def send(self):
        self.t += 1
        return self.t                       # piggyback on the message

    def receive(self, ts):
        self.t = max(self.t, ts) + 1        # the whole algorithm
        return self.t

def lamport_total_order(e1, e2):
    """Tie-break on node id to get a TOTAL order from a partial one.
    Consistent (never contradicts causality) but arbitrary for
    concurrent events."""
    return (e1.ts, e1.node) < (e2.ts, e2.node)

# ---------------- Vector clock ---------------------------------------
class VectorClock:
    def __init__(self, node_id, nodes):
        self.id = node_id
        self.v = {n: 0 for n in nodes}

    def local_event(self):
        self.v[self.id] += 1
        return dict(self.v)

    def send(self):
        self.v[self.id] += 1
        return dict(self.v)                 # send the ENTIRE vector

    def receive(self, other):
        for n, t in other.items():          # element-wise max ...
            self.v[n] = max(self.v.get(n, 0), t)
        self.v[self.id] += 1                # ... then count the receipt
        return dict(self.v)

def compare(a, b):
    """Returns 'before', 'after', 'equal', or 'concurrent'.
    Only vector clocks can return 'concurrent' correctly."""
    keys = set(a) | set(b)
    le = all(a.get(k, 0) <= b.get(k, 0) for k in keys)   # a <= b
    ge = all(a.get(k, 0) >= b.get(k, 0) for k in keys)   # a >= b
    if le and ge:   return "equal"
    if le:          return "before"          # a -> b
    if ge:          return "after"           # b -> a
    return "concurrent"                      # CONFLICT: app must merge

# --- Demonstrating the difference ------------------------------------
a = {"P1": 2, "P2": 0, "P3": 0}              # event b in the diagram
e = {"P1": 1, "P2": 2, "P3": 1}              # event e in the diagram
print(compare(a, e))                         # 'concurrent'  <- correct
# Lamport would have said 2 < 4, implying an order that does not exist.
```

```python
# Hybrid logical clock: physical time that never violates causality.

import time

class HybridLogicalClock:
    def __init__(self):
        self.wall = 0          # last physical time used (ms)
        self.logical = 0       # counter for same-millisecond events

    def now(self):
        return int(time.time() * 1000)

    def send_or_local(self):
        pt = self.now()
        if pt > self.wall:
            self.wall, self.logical = pt, 0      # clock advanced normally
        else:
            self.logical += 1                    # clock stalled/went back:
                                                 # stay monotonic anyway
        return (self.wall, self.logical)

    def receive(self, msg_wall, msg_logical):
        pt = self.now()
        # Take the max of: our clock, their clock, and physical time.
        new_wall = max(self.wall, msg_wall, pt)
        if new_wall == self.wall == msg_wall:
            self.logical = max(self.logical, msg_logical) + 1
        elif new_wall == self.wall:
            self.logical += 1
        elif new_wall == msg_wall:
            self.logical = msg_logical + 1
        else:
            self.logical = 0                     # physical time dominates
        self.wall = new_wall
        return (self.wall, self.logical)

# Result: timestamps are within NTP error of real time (so they are
# human-meaningful and bound staleness), strictly monotonic, and
# guarantee a -> b implies HLC(a) < HLC(b). Used by CockroachDB, MongoDB.
```

**Key takeaways**

- Physical clocks drift and can be stepped backwards, so cross-machine wall-clock comparison is not a valid ordering and "last write wins" silently loses data under skew.
- Happened-before (`->`) is the partial order defined by program order plus message send/receive plus transitivity; events unrelated by it are concurrent, meaning causally independent.
- A Lamport clock is one counter updated as `max(local, received) + 1`; it guarantees `a -> b ⟹ L(a) < L(b)` but not the converse, so it cannot detect concurrency.
- Lamport timestamps plus a node-ID tie-break give a consistent total order, which is enough for many algorithms that merely need everyone to agree on *some* order.
- Vector clocks keep one counter per node and give an if-and-only-if test for causality, so they can report genuine conflicts — the "siblings" of Dynamo-style stores.
- Vector clocks cost space proportional to the number of participants, which is why version vectors are keyed by replica rather than client.
- Hybrid logical clocks combine NTP time with a logical counter to get timestamps that are near wall time, monotonic, and causally correct.
- TrueTime exposes time as a bounded interval and has Spanner wait out the uncertainty, converting a clock problem into a latency cost.

#### Distributed Mutual Exclusion

**Theory**

Chapter 5 solved mutual exclusion with an atomic instruction on a shared memory word. Across machines there is no such word, so the lock must be built out of messages — and every message can be delayed, lost, or arrive after the sender has died. This topic is where the theoretical algorithms and the operationally correct answer diverge sharply, and both are worth knowing.

The three classical algorithms:

**Centralised.** One node is the coordinator and holds a queue. To enter the critical section you send `REQUEST` and wait for `GRANT`; to leave you send `RELEASE`. Three messages per entry, easy to reason about, trivially supports FIFO fairness. The coordinator is a bottleneck and a single point of failure — and crucially, if it dies while holding requests, its queue dies with it.

**Distributed (Ricart-Agrawala).** Uses Lamport clocks. To enter, multicast `REQUEST(ts, id)` to all n-1 peers and wait for `REPLY` from every one. A peer replies immediately unless it is in the critical section or wants it with a *smaller* timestamp, in which case it defers the reply until it exits. Timestamp order gives a total order, so exactly one node can be first. Cost is 2(n-1) messages per entry, and — this is the fatal property — it requires *every* node to reply, so a single crashed node blocks everyone forever unless a failure detector is bolted on.

**Token ring.** A token circulates; holding it grants the critical section. One message per entry under saturation, but the token can be lost (requiring regeneration, which risks two tokens) and a node can wait a full ring traversal even when nobody else wants the lock.

| Algorithm | Messages/entry | Latency to enter | Failure of one node | Fairness |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Centralised | 3 | 2 hops | Coordinator fatal; peers harmless | FIFO, easy |
| Ricart-Agrawala | 2(n − 1) | 2 hops | Any node fatal | Timestamp order |
| Maekawa (quorum) | ~3√n | 2 hops | Tolerates some | Needs deadlock handling |
| Token ring | 1 to ∞ | 0 to n hops | Token loss fatal | Ring order |

Now the operationally important part, which textbooks often omit. **A distributed lock is not a mutex; it is a lease, and a lease can expire while its holder still believes it is held.** Consider: a client acquires a 10-second lock, then suffers a 15-second stop-the-world GC pause. The lock expires; another client acquires it and starts writing. The first client wakes up with no idea anything happened and also writes. Two writers, corruption, and no algorithm above prevents it — the failure is *outside* the locking protocol.

The fix is a **fencing token**: the lock service returns a monotonically increasing number with every grant, the client passes it to the protected resource on every operation, and the resource rejects any token lower than the highest it has seen. Now the stale writer's request is refused at the point where it would do damage. This requires the *resource* to participate, which is why "we added a distributed lock" is rarely sufficient on its own.

In practice you do not implement any of the classical algorithms. You use a coordination service — **ZooKeeper**, **etcd**, or **Consul** — which implements a consensus-replicated centralised coordinator: the simplicity of the centralised algorithm, without its single point of failure. The idiom is an ephemeral sequential node (ZooKeeper) or a lease-bound key with a compare-and-swap (etcd); the node's sequence number or the key's revision *is* your fencing token. And the most valuable design move remains avoiding the lock entirely: partition the data so each key has exactly one owner, or use an idempotent operation, or use a compare-and-swap on the resource itself.

**Example**

```text
   RICART-AGRAWALA: EVERY PEER MUST AGREE

   Three nodes. P1 requests at ts=4, P3 requests at ts=6.

   P1 --REQUEST(4,P1)--> P2, P3
   P3 --REQUEST(6,P3)--> P1, P2

   P2: not interested          -> REPLY to both
   P1: wants it, ts 4 < 6      -> DEFER reply to P3
   P3: wants it, ts 6 > 4      -> REPLY to P1 immediately

   P1 has replies from P2 and P3  => ENTERS
   P3 waits (missing P1's reply)
   P1 exits -> sends deferred REPLY to P3 => P3 ENTERS

   Correct, fully symmetric, no coordinator.
   Now crash P2 while P1 is waiting:
      P1 waits for a REPLY that will never come.  DEADLOCK.
      2(n-1) messages also means it scales badly.
   This is why it is taught, not deployed.


   THE FAILURE NO LOCK ALGORITHM PREVENTS

   time --->
   client1: acquire(lock, ttl=10s)
            [====== GC PAUSE, 15 s ======]
                                          write(x) <-- believes it holds
   lock:    |---- held by c1 ----|expired|
   client2:                      acquire()  write(x)

   Both clients write. The lock service did NOTHING wrong: c1's lease
   really did expire. c1 simply could not be told, because it was frozen.

   No consensus algorithm fixes this. The lock is not the problem.


   FENCING TOKENS: MAKE THE RESOURCE THE ENFORCER

   lock service issues a MONOTONIC token with each grant:

   client1: acquire -> token 33
            [GC pause]
   client2: acquire -> token 34
            write(x, token=34)   storage: 34 >= 34, ACCEPT, high=34
   client1: write(x, token=33)   storage: 33 <  34, REJECT
                                 ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
                                 the stale writer is stopped HERE,
                                 at the only place that can stop it.

   Requirement: the RESOURCE must check the token. A lock alone
   cannot give you safety; the write path has to participate.
```

```python
# Ricart-Agrawala, complete enough to see the deferral logic.

import threading

class RicartAgrawala:
    def __init__(self, node_id, peers, net):
        self.id, self.peers, self.net = node_id, peers, net
        self.clock = 0
        self.requesting = False
        self.my_ts = None
        self.deferred = []                  # peers whose REPLY we withheld
        self.replies = 0
        self.cv = threading.Condition()

    def acquire(self):
        with self.cv:
            self.clock += 1
            self.my_ts = self.clock
            self.requesting = True
            self.replies = 0
        for p in self.peers:
            self.net.send(p, ("REQUEST", self.my_ts, self.id))
        with self.cv:
            # Must hear from EVERY peer. One dead peer = wait forever.
            while self.replies < len(self.peers):
                self.cv.wait()

    def on_request(self, ts, sender):
        with self.cv:
            self.clock = max(self.clock, ts) + 1     # Lamport update
            # Defer only if we are ahead in the total order:
            # smaller timestamp wins; equal timestamps break on node id.
            ahead = self.requesting and (self.my_ts, self.id) < (ts, sender)
            if ahead or self.in_cs:
                self.deferred.append(sender)
                return
        self.net.send(sender, ("REPLY", self.id))

    def on_reply(self, _sender):
        with self.cv:
            self.replies += 1
            self.cv.notify_all()

    def release(self):
        with self.cv:
            self.requesting, self.in_cs = False, False
            pending, self.deferred = self.deferred, []
        for p in pending:                   # release the queued waiters
            self.net.send(p, ("REPLY", self.id))
```

```python
# What you actually deploy: a lease-based lock with a fencing token.

import etcd3            # pip install etcd3

def with_distributed_lock(client, name, ttl=10):
    lease = client.lease(ttl)                    # auto-expires if we die
    lock = client.lock(name, ttl=ttl)
    if not lock.acquire(timeout=5):
        raise TimeoutError("lock busy")
    # etcd's mod_revision is monotonic across the whole cluster:
    # it is a ready-made fencing token.
    token = lock.uuid                            # plus key revision
    return lock, lease, token

def protected_write(storage, key, value, token):
    """The RESOURCE enforces the fence. Without this function,
    the lock above still permits two concurrent writers."""
    if token <= storage.highest_token_seen(key):
        raise StaleLockError(                    # the stale writer dies
            f"token {token} <= {storage.highest_token_seen(key)}")
    storage.record_token(key, token)
    storage.put(key, value)
```

```bash
# ZooKeeper's ephemeral-sequential idiom, and etcd's lease idiom.

# --- ZooKeeper: create an ephemeral sequential node under /lock ---
#   /lock/n-0000000017   <- yours; the SEQUENCE NUMBER is your fence
#   You hold the lock iff yours is the LOWEST child.
#   Watch only the node immediately below you (avoids the herd effect).
#   "Ephemeral" means the node vanishes when your session expires --
#   the lease, provided by the service.

# --- etcd: lease + compare-and-swap ---
etcdctl lease grant 10                   # -> lease 694d7d...  ttl 10
etcdctl put /locks/job "owner-A" --lease=694d7d
etcdctl lease keep-alive 694d7d          # renew; stop renewing => expiry
etcdctl get /locks/job -w=json | jq .kvs[0].mod_revision
#   mod_revision is cluster-wide monotonic -> use it as the fencing token

# --- Observe the hazard yourself ---
#   1. take a lock with ttl=5
#   2. SIGSTOP the process for 10 s   (kill -STOP <pid>)
#   3. watch another process take the lock
#   4. SIGCONT the first and watch it write as if nothing happened
```

**Key takeaways**

- Distributed mutual exclusion replaces an atomic memory word with messages, so every algorithm inherits message loss, delay, and node failure.
- The centralised algorithm costs three messages per entry and is easy to reason about, but the coordinator is a bottleneck and a single point of failure.
- Ricart-Agrawala is fully symmetric and orders entries by Lamport timestamp, but requires a reply from every peer, so a single crashed node blocks the system.
- Token-ring schemes cost one message under saturation but suffer token loss and unbounded entry latency at low load.
- A distributed lock is a lease, and a lease can expire while the holder is paused and unaware, producing two simultaneous writers no locking algorithm can prevent.
- Fencing tokens fix this by making the protected resource reject any operation carrying a token lower than the highest it has seen.
- In production, use a consensus-backed coordination service (ZooKeeper, etcd, Consul) whose sequence number or revision serves as the fencing token.
- The cheapest correct answer is usually to avoid the lock: partition so each key has one owner, make the operation idempotent, or compare-and-swap on the resource itself.
