> 2. Replace `xSemaphoreCreateMutex()` with `xSemaphoreCreateBinary()` in the code above and construct a three-task scenario that exhibits priority inversion. Then switch it back and show the inversion is bounded.
> 3. Compare a dual-kernel design and PREEMPT_RT for a system that must run a 20 kHz control loop and also serve a web UI. State which you would pick and what specifically you are giving up.
> 4. Explain why an ARINC 653 major frame uses a static time schedule rather than fixed priorities, given that fixed priorities are the RTOS norm.
> 5. Interview-style: "Can we just use Linux for our hard real-time controller?" *Hint: separate 'can it usually meet the deadline' from 'can anyone prove it always will', and ask what the certification requirement is.*

#### Embedded System Constraints

**Theory**

Real-time software usually runs on hardware that a server programmer would find implausible: a microcontroller with 64 KB of RAM, 512 KB of flash, a 48 MHz clock, no MMU, and a power budget measured in microamps. These constraints are not incidental; they reshape how software is written.

**Memory.** A typical Cortex-M has kilobytes of RAM, so dynamic allocation is usually banned outright. The reason is not just capacity: `malloc` has unbounded worst-case time and fragments over months of uptime until an allocation fails in a system that cannot be restarted. The standard discipline (codified in MISRA C and similar rules) is to allocate everything statically at compile time, so the linker proves at build time that it fits. Where pools are needed, they are fixed-size block pools with O(1) allocation, never a general heap. Stack sizing is its own hazard: each task gets a fixed stack, overflow silently corrupts whatever is adjacent, and the only defences are worst-case stack analysis, guard regions, and an MPU.

**No MMU.** Most microcontrollers have at most a **memory protection unit** — a handful of regions with access permissions, but no address translation. So there is no virtual memory, no demand paging, no `fork()`, and all code shares one address space where a stray pointer can corrupt anything. An MPU still buys a great deal: mark flash read-only and execute, RAM no-execute, and place a guard region below each stack so an overflow faults instead of silently corrupting.

**Flash and execute-in-place.** Code usually runs directly from flash (XIP) rather than being copied to RAM, which saves RAM but makes instruction fetch slower and sometimes less predictable. Flash also wears out (typically 10,000-100,000 erase cycles per block) and erases in large blocks, so logging or configuration storage needs wear levelling and a filesystem designed for it (LittleFS, SPIFFS) rather than a general-purpose one.

**Power.** For a battery device the CPU is asleep almost all the time. The design pattern is the opposite of a server's: do the work in a burst, then return to the deepest sleep state that still preserves what you need. Average current, not peak performance, is the design target — and the arithmetic is brutal. A 220 mAh coin cell powering a device that draws 2 µA asleep and 5 mA awake for 2 ms per second lasts years; raise the sleep current to 20 µA and it lasts months.

**Reliability without an operator.** An embedded device may run for a decade with no one to restart it. Hence the **watchdog timer**: a hardware counter that resets the chip unless the software periodically refreshes it. The subtle part is that a correct watchdog is fed only when *every* critical task has checked in — a naive feed from a timer interrupt will happily keep resetting a system whose main loop is dead. Combined with that: a bootloader supporting **A/B firmware slots** and rollback, so a bad over-the-air update does not brick a device that is physically unreachable.

**Toolchain.** Development is **cross-compiled** on a host, flashed over SWD/JTAG, and debugged with a hardware probe (OpenOCD, Segger). There is often no filesystem, no shell, and no `printf` except over a serial line — so `-Os`, `--gc-sections`, link-time optimisation, and a hard look at the map file are routine parts of the build.

**Example**

```text
   SCALE: SERVER vs MICROCONTROLLER

                    server            Cortex-M4 MCU     ratio
   RAM              64 GB             64 KB             1,000,000x
   storage          2 TB SSD          512 KB flash      4,000,000x
   clock            3.5 GHz x 32      48 MHz x 1        2,000x
   power            200 W             0.0001 - 0.05 W   ~1,000,000x
   MMU              yes               no (MPU only)
   OS               Linux, 30 MB      FreeRTOS, 10 KB
   reboot           whenever          possibly never in 10 years

   Every one of those rows removes a technique you rely on daily.


   THE MEMORY MAP IS THE DESIGN DOCUMENT

   0x0000_0000  +------------------+
                | vector table     |  interrupt handlers, first entry
                |                  |  is the INITIAL STACK POINTER
                +------------------+
                | .text  (code)    |  executed in place from FLASH
                | .rodata          |  constants, lookup tables
   0x0008_0000  +------------------+  <- 512 KB flash ends
                       ...
   0x2000_0000  +------------------+  <- 64 KB RAM begins
                | .data  (init'd)  |  copied from flash at reset
                | .bss   (zeroed)  |  cleared at reset
                +------------------+
                | task stacks      |  FIXED sizes, chosen at build
                |   [guard page]   |  <- MPU region: overflow FAULTS
                |   task A stack   |     instead of silently corrupting
                |   [guard page]   |
                |   task B stack   |
                +------------------+
                | heap (often 0)   |  <- frequently ELIMINATED entirely
   0x2001_0000  +------------------+

   If .data + .bss + stacks exceed RAM, the LINK FAILS. That is the
   point: the proof that it fits happens at build time, not at 3 a.m.


   WHY malloc IS BANNED, IN ONE PICTURE

   fresh heap:      [################ 16 KB free ##################]
   after 6 months:  [##][ ][####][ ][##][  ][#####][ ][###][ ][####]
                        ^    total free = 6 KB
                        request for 2 KB contiguous  ->  FAILS

   Nothing leaked. Fragmentation alone killed it, after the device
   had been in a wall for half a year, and the failure is
   time-dependent and untestable in a 2-hour soak test.

   Fixed-size pools instead: every block the same size, so a free
   block always satisfies any request. O(1), never fragments.


   THE WATCHDOG, DONE WRONG AND RIGHT

   WRONG: feed from a timer ISR
      timer ISR --> WDT_reload()
      Main loop is deadlocked. ISR still fires. Watchdog is happy.
      The device is dead and the watchdog is protecting it.

   RIGHT: every critical task must check in
      task A --> flag A
      task B --> flag B     supervisor: if (A && B && C) WDT_reload();
      task C --> flag C                 else let it EXPIRE -> reset
```

```c
/* Static allocation, pools, and a correct watchdog: the three habits
 * that define embedded C. */
#include <stdint.h>
#include <stdbool.h>
#include <string.h>

/* ---------- 1. Everything static. The linker proves it fits. ------- */
#define MAX_SENSORS   8
#define MSG_POOL_SIZE 16
#define MSG_BYTES     64

static sensor_t  sensors[MAX_SENSORS];        /* .bss, fixed forever */
static uint8_t   msg_pool[MSG_POOL_SIZE][MSG_BYTES];
static uint32_t  pool_free_mask = 0xFFFF;     /* one bit per block   */

/* ---------- 2. O(1) fixed-size pool: cannot fragment -------------- */
void *pool_alloc(void)
{
    if (pool_free_mask == 0) return NULL;     /* exhaustion is a
                                               * DESIGNED, tested path */
    int i = __builtin_ctz(pool_free_mask);    /* lowest free bit: O(1) */
    pool_free_mask &= ~(1u << i);
    return msg_pool[i];
}

void pool_free(void *p)
{
    int i = ((uint8_t (*)[MSG_BYTES])p) - msg_pool;
    pool_free_mask |= (1u << i);
}
/* Every block is the same size, so any free block serves any request.
 * Constant time, no fragmentation, no heap metadata to corrupt.      */

/* ---------- 3. Watchdog: fed only if ALL tasks are alive ---------- */
typedef enum { T_CONTROL, T_SENSOR, T_COMMS, T_COUNT } task_id_t;
static volatile uint32_t checkin_mask = 0;

void task_checkin(task_id_t id)               /* called by each task */
{
    checkin_mask |= (1u << id);
}

void supervisor_tick(void)                    /* runs every 100 ms */
{
    const uint32_t ALL = (1u << T_COUNT) - 1;
    if ((checkin_mask & ALL) == ALL) {
        IWDG->KR = 0xAAAA;                    /* reload the watchdog */
        checkin_mask = 0;                     /* require fresh proof */
    }
    /* Otherwise: do nothing. The watchdog expires and resets the chip.
     * Letting it fire is the CORRECT action -- a device nobody can
     * reach must recover itself.                                     */
}

/* ---------- 4. MPU: protection without an MMU --------------------- */
void mpu_setup(void)
{
    /* Region 0: flash, read-only + executable */
    mpu_region(0, 0x08000000, 512 * 1024, MPU_RO | MPU_EXEC);
    /* Region 1: RAM, read-write + NO EXECUTE (blocks injected code) */
    mpu_region(1, 0x20000000,  64 * 1024, MPU_RW | MPU_NX);
    /* Region 2: a 32-byte guard below task A's stack, NO ACCESS.
     * A stack overflow now takes a MemManage fault at the exact
     * instruction that overflowed, instead of silently corrupting
     * whatever happens to live next door.                            */
    mpu_region(2, (uint32_t)&task_a_stack_bottom - 32, 32, MPU_NONE);
    MPU->CTRL = MPU_CTRL_ENABLE | MPU_CTRL_PRIVDEFENA;
}

/* ---------- 5. The power pattern: burst, then sleep deeply -------- */
void main_loop(void)
{
    for (;;) {
        wake_on_rtc_or_irq();                 /* CPU halted until an
                                               * interrupt: ~2 uA      */
        sample_sensors();                     /* ~2 ms at ~5 mA        */
        if (should_transmit())
            radio_burst();                    /* rare, expensive       */
        enter_stop_mode();                    /* deepest state that
                                               * retains RAM + RTC     */
    }
    /* Average current, not peak MHz, is the design target:
     *   (2 uA * 998 ms + 5 mA * 2 ms) / 1000 ms ~= 12 uA
     *   220 mAh coin cell / 12 uA ~= 2 years.
     *   Raise sleep current to 20 uA and it becomes ~4 months.       */
}
```

```bash
# ---- Cross-compile, then read the map file like a budget ----
arm-none-eabi-gcc -mcpu=cortex-m4 -mthumb -Os \
    -ffunction-sections -fdata-sections \
    -Wl,--gc-sections -Wl,-Map=firmware.map \
    -T stm32f4.ld main.c -o firmware.elf

arm-none-eabi-size firmware.elf
#    text    data     bss     dec     hex filename
#   42184     512    8192   50888    c6c8 firmware.elf
#    ^^^^^    ^^^     ^^^
#    flash    flash->RAM    RAM
#  flash used  = text + data = 42,696 / 512 KB   OK
#  RAM used    = data + bss  =  8,704 /  64 KB   plus STACKS

# What is actually big? Sort the map file's symbols:
arm-none-eabi-nm --size-sort -S firmware.elf | tail -20

# Worst-case stack depth, statically (no measurement, a BOUND):
arm-none-eabi-gcc -fstack-usage ...        # emits .su files per function
# then a call-graph tool sums the deepest path per task.

# ---- Flash and debug over SWD ----
openocd -f interface/stlink.cfg -f target/stm32f4x.cfg \
        -c "program firmware.elf verify reset exit"
arm-none-eabi-gdb firmware.elf -ex "target remote :3333"

# ---- Measure the thing that actually matters ----
# A current probe on the supply rail, not a profiler:
#   sleep current, burst current, burst duration -> average current
#   average current + battery capacity -> years of life
```

**Key takeaways**

- Embedded targets differ from servers by six orders of magnitude in RAM, storage, and power, and each gap removes a technique that general-purpose programming takes for granted.
- Dynamic allocation is avoided because `malloc` has unbounded worst-case time and fragments over long uptimes, failing months later in a device that cannot be restarted.
- Static allocation moves the proof that memory fits from runtime to link time, which is the entire point of the discipline.
- Fixed-size block pools give O(1) allocation that cannot fragment, and are the sanctioned alternative where dynamic behaviour is genuinely needed.
- Most microcontrollers have an MPU rather than an MMU: no translation and no paging, but enough to make flash read-only, RAM non-executable, and stack overflows fault at a guard region.
- Code executes in place from flash, which saves RAM but makes instruction timing less predictable, and flash wear demands purpose-built filesystems.
- Battery life is determined by average current, dominated by sleep current, so the design pattern is a short burst of work followed by the deepest usable sleep state.
- A watchdog must be fed only after every critical task has checked in; feeding it from a timer interrupt protects a dead system.
- A/B firmware slots with rollback are essential for devices that receive over-the-air updates and cannot be physically recovered.
- The map file, `size`, and `-fstack-usage` are routine build outputs, because fitting in memory is a budget that must be checked, not an assumption.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. Compute the battery life of a device on a 220 mAh cell that sleeps at 3 µA and wakes for 5 ms per second at 8 mA. Then recompute with a sleep current of 30 µA and explain which parameter dominates.
> 2. Implement the fixed-size pool above with a free-list instead of a bitmask, and argue which version has the better worst-case time and why that matters more than average time.
> 3. Explain why feeding a watchdog from a periodic timer interrupt is a defect, and rewrite `supervisor_tick` so that a single hung task causes a reset within 500 ms.
> 4. Build any small C program for an ARM target with `-Wl,-Map`, and identify the three largest contributors to `.text` and to `.bss` from the map file.
> 5. Interview-style: "Our firmware works perfectly in testing but a few field units lock up after several months. Where do you look first?" *Hint: think about failure modes whose probability grows with uptime rather than with load — and what a two-hour soak test cannot reveal.*

<a id="143-mobile-operating-systems"></a>
### 14.3 Mobile Operating Systems

A phone runs a full multitasking kernel on hardware comparable to a laptop, yet its operating system makes systematically different choices — because its scarcest resources are battery charge and the user's attention, not cycles. This section covers the three mechanisms that follow from that (aggressive power management, memory reclaim without swap, and OS-controlled application lifetimes) and then examines how Android and iOS each implement them.

#### Mobile Power Management

**Theory**

On a server, power management is a cost optimisation. On a phone it is the primary design constraint, because the device has roughly 10-20 Wh of energy for a full day and the user judges the product by whether it survives until bedtime.

The foundational fact is that a modern SoC's idle power is dramatically lower than its active power — often by three or four orders of magnitude — and that the transition between them costs both time and energy. This produces two competing strategies, and knowing which applies is most of the skill.

**Race to idle** says: run at maximum frequency, finish the work as fast as possible, and get back to the deep sleep state where almost no power is drawn. It wins when static (leakage) power dominates and when the sleep state is much cheaper than any active state. **Frequency scaling** (DVFS) says the opposite: run slower, because dynamic power scales roughly with V²f and voltage can be lowered with frequency, making the energy per instruction lower at low clocks. Real systems do both — the scheduler-driven `schedutil` governor on Android picks a frequency from the scheduler's own utilisation signal, and **Energy Aware Scheduling** on big.LITTLE hardware places each task on the core type whose energy model predicts the lowest cost for that task's demand.

But the CPU is frequently not the problem. The expensive components are the **display** (often the single largest consumer when the screen is on), the **cellular radio**, and **GPS**. The radio in particular behaves in a way that surprises people: an LTE modem transitions through RRC states, and after transmitting it stays in a high-power connected state for a *tail* of 5-15 seconds before stepping down, in case more data arrives. So sending one byte can cost as much energy as sending a megabyte. This makes **batching** the single highest-value optimisation on mobile: ten separate network requests spread over a minute keep the radio hot the whole time, while the same ten requests issued together pay one tail.

The same logic applies to wakeups. If twenty apps each schedule a timer at an arbitrary moment, the CPU never gets a long sleep. **Timer coalescing** (aligning timers to shared boundaries) and **deferred execution** (running work when the device is already awake, charging, or on Wi-Fi) restore long idle periods. This is why modern mobile APIs deliberately refuse to give apps precise periodic timers.

Both platforms enforce this with policy, not just APIs. Android's **wakelock** is an explicit assertion that the CPU must stay awake; an app holding one incorrectly can flatten a battery overnight, which is why holding one is visible in battery statistics and increasingly restricted. **Doze mode** suspends network access and defers jobs when the device has been stationary and unused, batching deferred work into periodic maintenance windows whose frequency decreases the longer the device stays idle. **App Standby Buckets** classify apps by usage frequency (active, working set, frequent, rare, restricted) and tighten their job and alarm quotas accordingly. iOS is stricter still: apps do not generally run in the background at all, and background work is granted through specific entitlements and a scheduler that decides *when* based on the system's own energy and usage model.

**Example**

```text
   THE RADIO TAIL: WHY BATCHING BEATS EVERYTHING

   power
     |    +--------+                   +--------+
     |    | TX/RX  |                   | TX/RX  |
   ~1W|   |        |                   |        |
     |    |        +-----tail-----+    |        +-----tail-----+
   ~0.5W  |        | connected,   |    |        | connected,   |
     |    |        | idle, HOT    |    |        | idle, HOT    |
     |    |        | 5-15 s       |    |        | 5-15 s       |
   ~0.01W +--------+--------------+----+--------+--------------+
     +------------------------------------------------------------> t
          ^ 200 ms of actual data        ^ 200 ms of actual data

   TWO requests 30 s apart  = 2 tails = ~20 s of high power
   TWO requests back to back = 1 tail  = ~10 s of high power

   The energy cost is dominated by the NUMBER of transmission
   episodes, not by the number of BYTES. A 1-byte poll every
   minute can cost more than a 1 MB download.


   WAKEUP ALIGNMENT: WHY THE CPU NEVER SLEEPS PROPERLY

   UNALIGNED (each app picks its own moment)
   app A  |    x       x       x       x      |
   app B  |  x    x      x   x       x        |
   app C  |     x    x     x     x      x     |
   CPU    |__/\_/\__/\_/\_/\__/\_/\__/\_/\____|
             never reaches a deep sleep state; every wake pays
             the entry+exit energy again

   COALESCED (timers snapped to shared boundaries)
   app A  |    x               x              |
   app B  |    x               x              |
   app C  |    x               x              |
   CPU    |____/\______________/\_____________|
             two wakeups, long deep-sleep stretches between

   This is why mobile APIs refuse to give apps exact periodic timers.


   ANDROID DOZE: PROGRESSIVE RESTRICTION

   screen off + stationary + unused
        |
        v
   +----------+   maintenance   +----------+   maintenance
   |  DOZE    |---- window ---->|  DOZE    |---- window --->
   | no net   |  jobs+syncs run | no net   |  (less often)
   | no jobs  |  alarms fire    | no jobs  |
   | no alarms|                 | no alarms|
   +----------+                 +----------+
     ~1 min                       ~2 min      ~4 min  ... up to hours

   The idle windows LENGTHEN the longer the device stays untouched.
   High-priority FCM messages still break through; ordinary
   background work does not.


   WHERE THE ENERGY ACTUALLY GOES (rough, screen-on browsing)

   display        ####################################  ~40%
   cellular/WiFi  ####################                  ~25%
   CPU/GPU        ##############                        ~20%
   GPS (if on)    ########                              ~10%
   other          ###                                    ~5%

   Optimising CPU while polling the network every 5 s is
   optimising the wrong fifth of the problem.
```

```kotlin
// Android: the wrong way and the right way to do periodic work.

// ---------- WRONG: an exact alarm plus a wakelock ----------
// Fires regardless of Doze, wakes the device on its own schedule,
// holds the CPU awake, and cannot be coalesced with anything else.
val am = getSystemService(AlarmManager::class.java)
am.setExactAndAllowWhileIdle(                 // punches through Doze
    AlarmManager.RTC_WAKEUP,
    System.currentTimeMillis() + 60_000,
    pendingIntent
)
val wl = powerManager.newWakeLock(
    PowerManager.PARTIAL_WAKE_LOCK, "app:sync")
wl.acquire()                                  // if a crash skips
doNetworkSync()                               // release(), the battery
wl.release()                                  // is gone by morning

// ---------- RIGHT: describe the CONSTRAINTS, let the OS choose ----
// WorkManager holds the wakelock for you, survives reboots, retries
// with backoff, and coalesces with other apps' deferred work.
val constraints = Constraints.Builder()
    .setRequiredNetworkType(NetworkType.UNMETERED)  // Wi-Fi only
    .setRequiresBatteryNotLow(true)                 // not at 5%
    .setRequiresCharging(true)                      // free energy
    .build()

val sync = PeriodicWorkRequestBuilder<SyncWorker>(
        6, TimeUnit.HOURS)                    // a HINT, not a promise:
    .setConstraints(constraints)              // the OS picks the moment
    .setBackoffCriteria(BackoffPolicy.EXPONENTIAL,
                        30, TimeUnit.SECONDS)
    .build()

WorkManager.getInstance(context)
    .enqueueUniquePeriodicWork("sync", ExistingPeriodicWorkPolicy.KEEP, sync)

class SyncWorker(ctx: Context, params: WorkerParameters)
    : CoroutineWorker(ctx, params) {
    override suspend fun doWork(): Result {
        // Batch everything into ONE radio episode: one tail, not five.
        return try {
            val batch = pendingOperations()          // collect first
            api.sendBatch(batch)                     // then one round trip
            Result.success()
        } catch (e: IOException) {
            Result.retry()                           // backoff handled
        }
    }
}
```

```swift
// iOS: the same principle, enforced more strictly by the platform.

import BackgroundTasks

// Register at launch; the system decides IF and WHEN this ever runs,
// based on how often the user opens the app, battery level, and
// charging state. There is no way to demand a schedule.
BGTaskScheduler.shared.register(
    forTaskWithIdentifier: "com.example.refresh", using: nil
) { task in
    handleRefresh(task: task as! BGAppRefreshTask)
}

func scheduleRefresh() {
    let request = BGAppRefreshTaskRequest(identifier: "com.example.refresh")
    request.earliestBeginDate = Date(timeIntervalSinceNow: 3600)  // a floor,
    try? BGTaskScheduler.shared.submit(request)     // never a guarantee
}

func handleRefresh(task: BGAppRefreshTask) {
    scheduleRefresh()                          // always reschedule first

    // The system may revoke the CPU at any moment; you get seconds.
    task.expirationHandler = {
        operation.cancel()                     // save state, exit cleanly
    }

    operation.completionBlock = {
        // Reporting completion accurately affects whether the system
        // grants you time again: over-running degrades your budget.
        task.setTaskCompleted(success: !operation.isCancelled)
    }
    queue.addOperation(operation)
}

// For large transfers, hand the work to the OS entirely: it runs the
// download out of process, in its own batching window, and wakes the
// app when it is done.
let config = URLSessionConfiguration.background(withIdentifier: "dl")
config.isDiscretionary = true            // "run when it is cheap"
config.allowsCellularAccess = false      // Wi-Fi only
```

```bash
# Inspect and simulate power behaviour on Android.

adb shell dumpsys batterystats --charged com.example.app
#   Wake lock *sync*: 4h 12m 03s partial (12 times)   <- a battery bug
#   Wakeup alarm *walarm*:sync: 1440 times            <- once a minute!

adb shell dumpsys power | grep -A5 "Wake Locks"      # who is holding one now
adb shell dumpsys alarm | grep -B2 -A5 com.example   # scheduled alarms

# Force Doze to test that your app survives it:
adb shell dumpsys deviceidle force-idle
adb shell dumpsys deviceidle step                    # advance the state
adb shell dumpsys deviceidle unforce

# Check and change an app's standby bucket:
adb shell am get-standby-bucket com.example.app      # 10=active .. 45=restricted
adb shell am set-standby-bucket com.example.app rare

# Battery Historian turns a bugreport into a timeline of wakeups,
# radio state, and screen state -- the tool that actually finds drains:
adb bugreport bugreport.zip
```

**Key takeaways**

- Battery energy, not CPU time, is the scarce resource on mobile, and idle power is orders of magnitude below active power, so maximising deep-sleep time dominates every other optimisation.
- Race to idle and DVFS are complementary strategies; scheduler-driven governors and Energy Aware Scheduling choose between them using an energy model of the specific hardware.
- The display, cellular radio, and GPS typically consume more than the CPU, so CPU-focused optimisation often addresses the wrong fifth of the problem.
- The radio's RRC tail keeps the modem in a high-power state for 5-15 seconds after any transmission, making the number of transmission episodes matter more than the bytes sent.
- Batching network requests and coalescing timers restore long idle periods, which is why mobile APIs deliberately withhold precise periodic timers from apps.
- Android wakelocks are explicit assertions that the CPU must stay awake, and a leaked one is a classic overnight battery drain.
- Doze defers network access and jobs during stationary idle periods, with maintenance windows that grow further apart the longer the device is untouched.
- App Standby Buckets tighten quotas for infrequently used apps, so background capability is earned by user engagement.
- The correct API pattern is to declare constraints (charging, unmetered network, battery not low) and let the OS choose the moment, rather than demanding an exact schedule.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. An app polls a server every 30 seconds with a 100-byte request. Given a 10-second radio tail, compute the fraction of each minute the modem spends in a high-power state, then recompute for a single batched poll every 15 minutes.
> 2. Convert the "wrong" `AlarmManager` example above into a `WorkManager` request with constraints, and list every failure mode WorkManager handles that the original does not.
> 3. Run `adb shell dumpsys batterystats` on a device, identify the app holding the most partial wakelock time, and explain what evidence would distinguish a legitimate hold from a leak.
> 4. Explain why iOS gives no guarantee that a `BGAppRefreshTask` will ever run, and what design consequence that has for an app that must display fresh data at launch.
> 5. Interview-style: "Users report our app drains their battery, but our CPU profiler shows almost no usage. Where do you look?" *Hint: profile energy, not cycles — and ask what the device's radio and screen were doing while your code was idle.*

#### Mobile Memory Constraints

**Theory**

The defining memory fact about a phone is what it does *not* have: a swap file backed by a disk. Chapter 8's entire demand-paging machinery assumed anonymous pages could be evicted to secondary storage. On mobile that assumption is removed for two reasons — flash has limited write endurance and would wear out under swap traffic, and reading back from flash while the user is touching the screen produces exactly the stalls mobile design is built to avoid.

So the classic response to memory pressure is unavailable. Clean file-backed pages (code, mapped resources) can still be dropped and re-read, but **anonymous memory — the heap — cannot go anywhere**. Two mechanisms fill the gap.

**Compressed memory.** Rather than writing pages to flash, compress them in RAM. Android uses **zram**, a compressed block device in memory used as swap; iOS has an equivalent compressor in the kernel. A typical 2-3x compression ratio means cold anonymous pages effectively shrink, trading CPU cycles (decompression on access) for capacity. This is strictly better than flash swap on this hardware: decompression costs microseconds, a flash read costs hundreds of microseconds and wears the device.

**Killing whole processes.** When compression is not enough, the OS does something a desktop rarely does: it terminates an entire application. Android's **lmkd** (low memory killer daemon) and iOS's **Jetsam** both maintain a ranking of processes and kill from the least important end until pressure subsides. The ranking is derived from what the user is doing: the foreground app is killed last, a visible app next, then services, then cached background apps, which are killed freely and routinely.

On Android this is expressed as `oom_score_adj`, a per-process value the `ActivityManager` updates as apps change state. The cached-app tier is the key insight: when you press Home, your process usually *stays alive* with its heap intact, purely so that returning to it is instant. Those cached processes are a memory cache, and killing them is a normal, healthy operation — not a failure. Modern Android's lmkd triggers on **PSI** (pressure stall information) rather than raw free-memory thresholds, killing based on how much time processes actually spend stalled on memory rather than on a number that means little on its own.

The consequence for application developers is the central contract of mobile programming: **your process can be killed at any moment, without warning, and without running any cleanup code**. Not an exception, not a callback you can veto — `SIGKILL`. Anything the user would be upset to lose must already be persisted. Both platforms provide pressure callbacks (`onTrimMemory`, `didReceiveMemoryWarning`) as an opportunity to release caches before the killer reaches you, but they are advisory: responding well makes you a less attractive target, and responding badly gets you killed.

There are also hard per-app heap limits. Android gives each app a Dalvik/ART heap cap that varies by device (commonly 128-512 MB), and exceeding it throws `OutOfMemoryError` even when the device has free RAM — a deliberate policy that stops one app from monopolising a shared device. Bitmaps are the usual culprit: a 4000×3000 photo at 4 bytes per pixel is 48 MB decoded, regardless of the JPEG being 3 MB on disk.

**Example**

```text
   NO SWAP CHANGES EVERYTHING

   DESKTOP under memory pressure        MOBILE under memory pressure
   -----------------------------        ---------------------------
   evict clean file pages               evict clean file pages
   swap anonymous pages to disk         COMPRESS anon pages (zram)
   thrash, get slow, stay alive         KILL ENTIRE PROCESSES
   user notices sluggishness            user notices an app "restarted"

   Why no swap: flash write endurance, and a swap-in stall during a
   touch interaction is exactly the jank the whole design avoids.


   ANDROID'S KILL LADDER (oom_score_adj, higher = killed sooner)

   adj    class                          killed
   ----   ----------------------------   ---------------------------
   -1000  native/system critical         never (the kernel itself)
      0   FOREGROUND app (on screen)     last resort only
    100   VISIBLE (behind a dialog)      rarely
    200   PERCEPTIBLE (music playing)    under real pressure
    300   BACKUP / heavy weight
    500   SERVICE (background work)      routinely
    700   CACHED activity (pressed Home) FREELY -- this is by design
    900   CACHED empty process           first, always

   lmkd kills from the BOTTOM UP until memory pressure drops.

   Key point: a cached process is a CACHE. Killing it is normal
   operation, not a failure. Its only purpose is making a return
   to the app instant; when memory is worth more, it goes.


   WHAT THE USER SEES, AND WHY STATE SAVING MATTERS

   user in app A  -> presses Home -> app A becomes CACHED (alive)
                  -> opens B, C, D (camera, maps, game)
                  -> memory pressure -> lmkd kills A
                  -> user returns to A

   If A saved its state:    A restarts, restores scroll position,
                            form contents, selected tab.
                            The user perceives "it was still there".
   If A did not:            A restarts at its home screen with an
                            empty form. The user perceives A CRASH,
                            and blames the app, not the OS.

   Same OS behaviour. Entirely different product.


   THE BITMAP TRAP (the usual cause of OutOfMemoryError)

   file on disk:      photo.jpg          3 MB   (compressed)
   decoded in RAM:    4000 x 3000 x 4 = 48 MB   (ARGB_8888)
   displayed in:      a 400 x 300 thumbnail

   Loading 6 such thumbnails = 288 MB > a 256 MB heap cap -> OOM,
   on a device with 4 GB of free RAM. The cap is per-app POLICY.

   Fix: decode at the size you will actually display
        (inSampleSize / BitmapFactory.Options) -> 400x300x4 = 480 KB,
        a 100x reduction, with no visible difference.
```

```kotlin
// Android: responding to pressure, and the state-saving contract.

class GalleryActivity : AppCompatActivity() {

    // ---- 1. Release caches when asked. This makes you a LESS
    //         attractive kill target, and is the only warning you get.
    override fun onTrimMemory(level: Int) {
        super.onTrimMemory(level)
        when (level) {
            // The process is cached and near the top of the kill list.
            TRIM_MEMORY_COMPLETE,           // about to be killed
            TRIM_MEMORY_MODERATE ->
                imageCache.evictAll()       // drop everything

            TRIM_MEMORY_BACKGROUND ->
                imageCache.trimToSize(imageCache.size() / 2)

            // Still foreground, but the system is under pressure.
            TRIM_MEMORY_RUNNING_LOW,
            TRIM_MEMORY_RUNNING_CRITICAL ->
                imageCache.trimToSize(maxSize / 4)
        }
    }

    // ---- 2. Save state. Your process WILL be killed eventually.
    //         onSaveInstanceState survives process death; onPause does
    //         not save anything by itself.
    override fun onSaveInstanceState(outState: Bundle) {
        super.onSaveInstanceState(outState)
        outState.putInt("scroll", recyclerView.scrollPosition())
        outState.putString("query", searchBox.text.toString())
        // Small UI state only: the Bundle goes through Binder and has
        // a ~1 MB transaction limit. Large data belongs in a database
        // or a file, written as it changes.
    }

    override fun onCreate(saved: Bundle?) {
        super.onCreate(saved)
        // Cannot distinguish "first launch" from "restored after being
        // killed" except by this Bundle -- and that is the point.
        saved?.let {
            recyclerView.scrollTo(it.getInt("scroll"))
            searchBox.setText(it.getString("query"))
        }
    }

    // ---- 3. Never decode more pixels than you will display.
    fun loadThumbnail(path: String, reqW: Int, reqH: Int): Bitmap {
        val opts = BitmapFactory.Options().apply {
            inJustDecodeBounds = true           // measure without allocating
        }
        BitmapFactory.decodeFile(path, opts)

        var sample = 1
        while (opts.outWidth / sample > reqW * 2) sample *= 2
        opts.inSampleSize = sample              // decode 1/sample per axis
        opts.inJustDecodeBounds = false
        opts.inPreferredConfig = Bitmap.Config.RGB_565   // 2 bytes, not 4
        return BitmapFactory.decodeFile(path, opts)!!
    }
}
```

```swift
// iOS: the same contract, different names. Jetsam, not lmkd.

class GalleryViewController: UIViewController {

    override func viewDidLoad() {
        super.viewDidLoad()
        // The warning arrives on the main thread; act immediately.
        NotificationCenter.default.addObserver(
            self,
            selector: #selector(handleMemoryWarning),
            name: UIApplication.didReceiveMemoryWarningNotification,
            object: nil)
    }

    @objc func handleMemoryWarning() {
        imageCache.removeAllObjects()
        // Ignoring this notification does not defer the problem;
        // Jetsam terminates the app with no further notice and
        // the user sees it as a crash.
    }

    // State restoration: iOS may terminate a suspended app at any time.
    func application(_ app: UIApplication,
                     shouldSaveSecureApplicationState c: NSCoder) -> Bool {
        return true      // opt in, then encode state in the coder
    }
}

// NSCache is purge-aware: the system evicts from it automatically
// under pressure. A plain Dictionary does not, and will get you killed.
let imageCache = NSCache<NSString, UIImage>()
imageCache.totalCostLimit = 50 * 1024 * 1024     // a self-imposed budget
```

```bash
adb shell dumpsys meminfo com.example.app
#   Java Heap:  42,180 KB     <- counts against the per-app cap
#   Native Heap: 18,220 KB
#   Graphics:    31,104 KB    <- textures; often the real consumer
#   TOTAL PSS:  104,660 KB    <- proportional set size, the fair metric

# The kill ladder, live:
adb shell cat /proc/$(adb shell pidof com.example.app)/oom_score_adj
#   0     while foreground
#   700   after pressing Home    <- now freely killable

# Who was killed and why:
adb shell dumpsys activity lru
adb logcat | grep -E "lowmemorykiller|lmkd|am_kill"
#   lmkd: Kill 'com.example.app' (12345), adj 700, to free 104660kB
#         because PSI some avg10 = 45.2  <- pressure-based, not
#                                           free-memory-threshold based

# Compressed swap, not flash swap:
adb shell cat /proc/swaps
#   Filename     Type       Size      Used     Priority
#   /dev/block/zram0  partition  2097148  845220   -2
#                     ^^^^^^^^^ in RAM, compressed ~2-3x

# Verify your app survives being killed in the background:
adb shell am kill com.example.app     # simulate lmkd, then reopen it
```

**Key takeaways**

- Mobile devices have no flash-backed swap, because flash wears out and swap-in stalls produce exactly the interaction jank the platform is designed to avoid.
- Clean file-backed pages can still be dropped and re-read, but anonymous heap memory has nowhere to go, so the classic eviction path is unavailable.
- Compressed memory (zram on Android, the kernel compressor on iOS) trades CPU for capacity at roughly 2-3x, and is far cheaper than a flash read.
- When compression is insufficient, the OS terminates entire processes — lmkd on Android, Jetsam on iOS — starting from the least important.
- Android ranks processes by `oom_score_adj`, updated as apps change state, with cached background processes killed freely because they exist only as a fast-resume cache.
- Modern lmkd triggers on pressure stall information rather than free-memory thresholds, reacting to actual stalling rather than an arbitrary number.
- The core mobile contract is that a process can be `SIGKILL`ed with no warning and no cleanup, so anything the user would miss must already be persisted.
- `onTrimMemory` and `didReceiveMemoryWarning` are advisory chances to shed caches; responding well lowers your kill priority and ignoring them does not defer the problem.
- Per-app heap caps cause `OutOfMemoryError` even with free system RAM, and decoded bitmaps — sized by pixels, not by file size — are the usual cause.
- A well-behaved app restores its state so that a kill and restart is indistinguishable from having stayed resident; the OS behaviour is identical, only the perceived quality differs.

#### Application Lifecycle Management

**Theory**

The two previous topics converge on one design decision that most distinguishes mobile from desktop: **the operating system, not the user and not the application, decides how long an application's process lives**.

On a desktop, an application starts when launched and exits when closed or when it crashes. On mobile, neither event maps cleanly. The user "leaves" an app by pressing Home or swiping; they have no concept of quitting it and generally should not need one. Meanwhile the OS must be free to reclaim that memory. So the platform defines a **lifecycle**: a state machine the app is moved through, with callbacks at each transition, and a contract about what it may do in each state.

Android's model is built around components rather than a single main function. An **Activity** (one screen) moves through `onCreate` → `onStart` → `onResume` → *running* → `onPause` → `onStop` → `onDestroy`, and the key discipline is knowing which callback is guaranteed. `onPause` is the last callback guaranteed to run before the app loses foreground; `onStop` usually runs; `onDestroy` may never run at all, because a process kill skips every callback. So the rule is: persist anything important by `onStop` at the latest, and never treat `onDestroy` as a cleanup hook you can rely on. The modern `Lifecycle`-aware components exist so that observers (a location listener, a camera session, a coroutine scope) attach and detach automatically at the right transitions, which eliminated an entire category of leak.

The crucial subtlety is that Activity lifecycle and *process* lifetime are different things. An Activity can be destroyed and recreated — a rotation does exactly that — while the process lives on; or the whole process can be killed while the Activity's saved state survives in the system, to be handed back at relaunch. This is why `onSaveInstanceState` exists separately: it survives process death, whereas fields in your object do not.

iOS uses a simpler, stricter model: Not Running → Inactive → Active → Background → Suspended. The important state is **Suspended**: the app is still in memory, with all of its state intact, but it receives *no CPU time at all*. It is frozen, and it can be terminated from that state without any further notification. Background execution is not a right; it is granted for specific declared purposes (audio playback, location, VoIP, background fetch, processing tasks) and even then is time-limited. `beginBackgroundTask` buys roughly 30 seconds to finish something critical and no more.

The practical consequences are the same on both platforms, and they are worth stating as rules:

- Save state continuously as it changes, not at exit — there may be no exit.
- Any resource held across a transition (camera, GPS, socket, wakelock) must be released when leaving the foreground and reacquired on return, or the OS will hold it against you.
- A cold start after a kill must be fast and must land the user where they were, because to them it was not a restart.
- Never assume a cleanup callback will run.

**Example**

```text
   ANDROID ACTIVITY LIFECYCLE (and which callbacks you can trust)

                    +-------------+
   launch --------> |  onCreate   |  build UI, restore saved state
                    +------+------+
                           v
                    +-------------+
                    |   onStart   |  becoming visible
                    +------+------+
                           v
                    +-------------+
                    |  onResume   |  foreground, interactive
                    +------+------+     acquire camera/GPS HERE
                           |
                    +------v------+
                    |   RUNNING   |
                    +------+------+
                           |  user presses Home / another app opens
                    +------v------+
                    |   onPause   |  <== LAST GUARANTEED CALLBACK
                    +------+------+     release camera/GPS, stop
                           v            animations. Keep it FAST:
                    +-------------+     the next activity waits on it.
                    |   onStop    |  usually runs; persist by here
                    +------+------+
                           v
                    +-------------+
                    |  onDestroy  |  MAY NEVER RUN. Not a cleanup hook.
                    +-------------+
                           |
                     process killed by lmkd  ---> nothing runs at all
                                                   (SIGKILL)

   RETURN PATH:  onRestart -> onStart -> onResume  (process survived)
                 onCreate(savedInstanceState)      (process was killed)
                          ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ the Bundle is how state
                                            crosses process death


   PROCESS LIFETIME vs ACTIVITY LIFETIME -- NOT THE SAME AXIS

   rotation:          Activity destroyed + recreated, process ALIVE
                      -> instance fields lost, static/ViewModel kept
   Home + lmkd kill:  Activity AND process gone
                      -> only the saved Bundle survives
   Home, no pressure: both alive, just cached
                      -> instant resume, nothing to restore

   Your code must produce the SAME user experience in all three.


   iOS APP STATES

   +-------------+   launch    +----------+  becomes  +---------+
   | Not Running |------------>| Inactive |---------->| Active  |
   +-------------+             +----------+   active  +---------+
          ^                         ^                      |
          |                         | interrupted          | home /
          |                         | (call, notification) | app switch
          |                         |                      v
          |                    +----+-----------------+---------+
          |                    |            Background          |
          |                    |  ~30 s, or a declared mode     |
          |                    +---------------+----------------+
          |                                    | time expires
          |    terminated (NO notification)    v
          +---------------------------+  +-----------+
                                         | SUSPENDED |  in memory,
                                         +-----------+  ZERO cpu,
                                                        killable silently

   "Suspended" is the state desktop programmers have no model for:
   the app exists, holds all its state, and executes NOTHING.


   THE RULE THAT FOLLOWS FROM ALL OF IT

   Desktop:  save on exit.          There is an exit.
   Mobile:   save as you go.        There may be no exit, ever.

   text field changed -> persist (debounced)
   item added to cart -> persist immediately
   scroll position    -> save in the state bundle
   "are you sure you want to quit?" -> a category error on mobile
```

```kotlin
// Android: a lifecycle-correct screen.

class MapActivity : AppCompatActivity() {

    private val viewModel: MapViewModel by viewModels()
    // ViewModel survives CONFIGURATION CHANGES (rotation) but NOT
    // process death. Two different survival scopes -- use both.

    override fun onCreate(savedInstanceState: Bundle?) {
        super.onCreate(savedInstanceState)
        setContentView(R.layout.map)

        // Lifecycle-aware: the observer starts and stops itself at the
        // right transitions. This is what removed a whole class of leak
        // where a listener outlived the screen that registered it.
        lifecycle.addObserver(locationTracker)

        // Restore across PROCESS DEATH (the ViewModel cannot do this).
        savedInstanceState?.let {
            viewModel.restoreCamera(it.getParcelable("camera"))
        }
    }

    // Acquire scarce/expensive resources only while interactive.
    override fun onResume() {
        super.onResume()
        mapView.onResume()
        sensorManager.registerListener(compass, rotationSensor, GAME)
    }

    // onPause is the LAST guaranteed callback. Release here, and be
    // quick: the incoming activity's onResume waits for this to return.
    override fun onPause() {
        sensorManager.unregisterListener(compass)   // battery + leak
        mapView.onPause()
        super.onPause()
    }

    // Persist real data by onStop at the latest.
    override fun onStop() {
        super.onStop()
        viewModel.persistDraft()          // to a database or file
    }

    // Small UI state, survives process death via the system.
    override fun onSaveInstanceState(outState: Bundle) {
        super.onSaveInstanceState(outState)
        outState.putParcelable("camera", mapView.cameraPosition)
    }

    // NOT a reliable cleanup hook: a process kill skips it entirely.
    override fun onDestroy() {
        super.onDestroy()
    }
}

// Structured concurrency tied to the lifecycle: this coroutine is
// cancelled automatically when the screen stops, so it cannot leak
// or keep the CPU awake after the user has left.
lifecycleScope.launch {
    repeatOnLifecycle(Lifecycle.State.STARTED) {
        viewModel.locationFlow.collect { updateMarker(it) }
    }
}
```

```swift
// iOS: the scene lifecycle and the 30-second background grace period.

class SceneDelegate: UIResponder, UIWindowSceneDelegate {

    func sceneDidBecomeActive(_ scene: UIScene) {
        resumeTimers(); startLocationUpdates()
    }

    func sceneWillResignActive(_ scene: UIScene) {
        // Called for a phone call or the app switcher too, not just exit.
        pauseTimers()
    }

    func sceneDidEnterBackground(_ scene: UIScene) {
        // This is the realistic last chance to do work. After the grace
        // period the app is SUSPENDED and gets no CPU at all; it may
        // then be terminated with no further callback.
        saveState()
        stopLocationUpdates()      // or the system shows the location
                                   // indicator and blames you for drain
    }
}

// Finishing critical work when leaving the foreground:
func saveOnBackground() {
    var bgTask: UIBackgroundTaskIdentifier = .invalid
    bgTask = UIApplication.shared.beginBackgroundTask(withName: "save") {
        // Expiration handler: the system is reclaiming the time NOW.
        // You must end the task or the app is killed outright.
        UIApplication.shared.endBackgroundTask(bgTask)
        bgTask = .invalid
    }

    DispatchQueue.global().async {
        database.flush()                       // must finish in ~30 s
        UIApplication.shared.endBackgroundTask(bgTask)
        bgTask = .invalid
    }
}
```

```bash
# Drive lifecycle transitions on Android instead of guessing.

# The single most valuable setting during development: "Don't keep
# activities" destroys every activity as soon as it is backgrounded,
# surfacing every state-restoration bug immediately.
adb shell settings put global always_finish_activities 1

adb shell am start -n com.example/.MapActivity
adb shell input keyevent KEYCODE_HOME          # -> onPause, onStop
adb shell am kill com.example                  # simulate lmkd (SIGKILL)
adb shell am start -n com.example/.MapActivity # -> cold start; did the
                                               #    user land where they
                                               #    left off?

adb shell dumpsys activity activities | grep -A3 "mResumedActivity"
adb logcat | grep -E "ActivityManager.*(Start proc|Killing)"

# Rotation: destroys and recreates the activity, process survives.
adb shell settings put system accelerometer_rotation 0
adb shell settings put system user_rotation 1
```

**Key takeaways**

- On mobile the OS decides how long a process lives, because the user has no notion of quitting an app and the system must be free to reclaim memory.
- Android's Activity lifecycle guarantees `onPause`, usually runs `onStop`, and may never run `onDestroy`, so cleanup that matters must happen no later than `onStop`.
- `onPause` must be fast, because the incoming screen's resume waits on it.
- Activity lifetime and process lifetime are independent axes: rotation destroys the Activity while the process lives, and a kill destroys the process while the saved state survives.
- `onSaveInstanceState` is the only channel that crosses process death, and it is limited to small state because it travels over Binder.
- iOS moves apps through Not Running, Inactive, Active, Background, and Suspended, where Suspended means fully resident but receiving zero CPU and terminable without notice.
- iOS background execution is granted for declared purposes and is time-limited; `beginBackgroundTask` buys roughly 30 seconds and requires an expiration handler.
- Exclusive or expensive resources — camera, GPS, sockets, wakelocks — must be released on leaving the foreground and reacquired on return.
- Lifecycle-aware components and lifecycle-scoped coroutines attach and detach observers automatically, eliminating a large category of leaks.
- The governing rule is to save state continuously rather than on exit, because there may be no exit; a correct app makes a kill-and-restart indistinguishable from never having left.

#### Android Architecture

**Theory**

Android is often described as "Linux for phones", which is true of the kernel and misleading about everything else. The kernel is Linux, with significant Android-specific additions; above it sits a stack that shares almost nothing with a desktop GNU/Linux distribution — different libc (Bionic), different IPC (Binder), different init model, different security model, and a managed runtime executing app code.

Working upward:

**The kernel.** Linux, plus additions driven by mobile requirements: **Binder** (the IPC mechanism), **ashmem/memfd** (shared anonymous memory), the low-memory-killer interface used by lmkd, wakelocks, and a strict SELinux policy in enforcing mode. Vendors add device drivers, and **Project Treble** (Android 8) separated the vendor implementation from the framework through a stable **HAL** interface so the OS could be updated without the silicon vendor rebuilding everything — the structural fix for Android's update problem.

**Binder** is the piece worth understanding deeply, because essentially every interesting Android operation is a Binder transaction. It is a kernel driver implementing capability-based object-oriented IPC. Compared with the SysV IPC Android could have used, Binder provides: a single copy (the driver copies directly from sender to a receiver-mapped buffer, rather than user→kernel→user), a per-process thread pool with **priority inheritance** so a high-priority caller is not blocked behind a low-priority server thread, caller credentials (UID/PID) delivered by the kernel so the receiver can authorise reliably rather than trusting a claim, **object references** that the driver refcounts across processes, and **death notifications** when a peer dies. Interfaces are declared in **AIDL** and compiled into proxy/stub code, so `getSystemService(...)` returning a "location manager" actually returns a proxy whose method calls become Binder transactions into `system_server`. The one-megabyte-per-process transaction buffer is the origin of `TransactionTooLargeException`.

**Native layer and runtime.** **Bionic** is a compact libc built for size and licensing rather than POSIX completeness. **ART** (Android Runtime) executes app bytecode using a hybrid strategy: install-time and idle-time **AOT** compilation guided by a **profile** of what actually ran, plus a JIT for what the profile missed, so hot code is native and cold code is not wasting flash. Its concurrent copying collector is tuned for short pauses, because a garbage collection pause during a touch gesture is visible.

**Zygote.** Starting a fresh runtime per app would be slow and would duplicate every framework class. Instead, a single process called Zygote starts at boot, loads the framework classes and resources, and then **forks** for every new app. Thanks to copy-on-write, all those apps share one physical copy of the framework's pages. This is why app startup is fast and why per-app memory overhead is far lower than it would otherwise be.

**system_server** hosts the framework services — ActivityManager, PackageManager, WindowManager, PowerManager and dozens more — each reachable over Binder. It is the policy centre: it decides what starts, what is killed, what permissions apply, and which process is foreground.

**The security model** is the part most different from desktop Linux. Every app gets its own **UID**, so the classic UNIX user-isolation mechanism is repurposed to isolate *applications* from each other; app data directories are simply owned by that UID. On top sit **SELinux** in enforcing mode (mandatory access control constraining even root-owned daemons), **permissions** that are runtime-granted for dangerous categories and increasingly scoped and revocable, **app signing** with update-time signature verification, **Verified Boot** establishing a chain of trust from hardware, and hardware-backed key storage in a **Trusted Execution Environment** or dedicated security chip.

**Example**

```text
   THE ANDROID STACK

   +-----------------------------------------------------------+
   |  APPS (Java/Kotlin bytecode, some native via JNI)         |
   +-----------------------------------------------------------+
   |  JAVA API FRAMEWORK                                        |
   |  Activity/Package/Window/Power managers, View system,      |
   |  Content providers  -- all PROXIES over Binder             |
   +-----------------------------------------------------------+
   |  NATIVE LIBS        |  ANDROID RUNTIME (ART)               |
   |  libc(Bionic), SQLite,  AOT+JIT with profiles,             |
   |  Skia, OpenGL/Vulkan,   concurrent copying GC              |
   |  media codecs           (one ART instance per app)         |
   +-----------------------------------------------------------+
   |  HARDWARE ABSTRACTION LAYER (HAL) -- stable since Treble   |
   |  camera / audio / sensors / GPS ... vendor code lives here |
   +-----------------------------------------------------------+
   |  LINUX KERNEL + Android additions                          |
   |  BINDER | ashmem/memfd | lmkd hooks | wakelocks | SELinux  |
   |  vendor drivers                                            |
   +-----------------------------------------------------------+


   PROCESS MODEL: ZYGOTE AND COPY-ON-WRITE

   boot
     |
     +--> init --> zygote  (loads framework classes + resources ONCE,
     |               |      pre-links them, warms the heap)
     |               |
     |               +-- fork --> com.example.app   (ART + framework
     |               |                               pages SHARED, CoW)
     |               +-- fork --> com.other.app
     |               +-- fork --> system_server
     |
     +--> servicemanager   (the Binder name registry)

   Forking from a pre-warmed template means:
     - fast app start (no class loading or linking)
     - one PHYSICAL copy of the framework across all apps
     - each app still gets its own UID, heap, and address space


   A BINDER TRANSACTION, END TO END

   app process                kernel                 system_server
   -----------                ------                 -------------
   LocationManager
     .getLastLocation()
        |
     proxy marshals args
     into a Parcel
        |
     ioctl(BINDER_WRITE_READ) --->  binder driver
                                    - ONE copy into the target's
                                      pre-mapped buffer (not two)
                                    - attaches REAL caller uid/pid
                                    - priority inheritance: server
                                      thread runs at caller's prio
                                                 |
                                                 v
                                          stub unmarshals
                                          checkPermission(uid) <- uid
                                          came from the KERNEL, so
                                          it cannot be forged
                                                 |
     <--- reply Parcel <------------------------ +
     proxy unmarshals -> Location

   Buffer limit: ~1 MB per process => TransactionTooLargeException
   when an app tries to pass a bitmap through Binder.


   SECURITY: UNIX UIDS, REPURPOSED

   traditional Linux              Android
   ------------------             -------
   uid = a PERSON                 uid = an APP
   /home/alice  (uid 1000)        /data/data/com.example  (uid 10234)
   apps of one user share         two apps CANNOT read each
   everything                     other's files at all

   plus: SELinux enforcing, runtime permissions, app signing,
         Verified Boot, hardware-backed keystore (TEE/StrongBox)

   The oldest mechanism in UNIX, pointed at a problem it was
   never designed for, and fitting remarkably well.
```

```java
// AIDL: the interface definition that becomes a Binder proxy/stub pair.
// File: ILocationService.aidl

interface ILocationService {
    /* Synchronous: the caller BLOCKS in the kernel until the reply
     * arrives. The server thread runs at the caller's priority. */
    Location getLastLocation(String provider);

    /* oneway: fire and forget -- returns as soon as the transaction is
     * queued. Use for notifications; there is no reply and no
     * guarantee the callee even ran. */
    oneway void reportUsage(String tag, long millis);
}
```

```java
/* The service side, running inside system_server. */
public class LocationService extends ILocationService.Stub {

    @Override
    public Location getLastLocation(String provider) {
        /* getCallingUid() is supplied BY THE KERNEL, not by the caller.
         * This is the property that makes Binder an authorisation
         * mechanism rather than just a transport. */
        int uid = Binder.getCallingUid();
        int pid = Binder.getCallingPid();

        if (checkPermission(ACCESS_FINE_LOCATION, pid, uid) != GRANTED)
            throw new SecurityException("no location permission");

        /* When calling further services on the caller's behalf, clear
         * the identity first or the next check uses OUR uid, silently
         * granting the caller system privileges. This is the classic
         * confused-deputy bug in Android services. */
        long token = Binder.clearCallingIdentity();
        try {
            return mProvider.getLast(provider);
        } finally {
            Binder.restoreCallingIdentity(token);   // ALWAYS restore
        }
    }
}

/* The client side: an ordinary-looking method call that is a syscall. */
IBinder b = ServiceManager.getService("location");
ILocationService svc = ILocationService.Stub.asInterface(b);
Location loc = svc.getLastLocation("gps");   // -> ioctl -> system_server

/* Death notification: know when the peer process dies, instead of
 * discovering it on the next failed call. */
b.linkToDeath(() -> reconnectOrDegrade(), 0);
```

```bash
adb shell ps -A -o PID,USER,NAME | head
#   PID   USER      NAME
#   1     root      init
#   xxx   root      zygote64          <- the fork template
#   xxx   system    system_server     <- the framework services
#   xxx   u0_a234   com.example.app   <- one UID per app
#         ^^^^^^^^ "u0_a234" = user 0, app id 234

adb shell service list | head
#   0  activity: [android.app.IActivityManager]
#   1  package:  [android.content.pm.IPackageManager]
#   2  power:    [android.os.IPowerManager]
#   ... every one of these is a Binder object registered by name

# Live Binder traffic and the per-process buffer usage:
adb shell cat /sys/kernel/debug/binder/stats
adb shell cat /sys/kernel/debug/binder/transactions

# App sandbox: UID ownership is the isolation.
adb shell ls -ld /data/data/com.example.app
#   drwx------ u0_a234 u0_a234 ...    <- mode 700, owned by the app's uid

# SELinux domain of a running app:
adb shell ps -AZ | grep com.example
#   u:r:untrusted_app:s0:c234,c256   <- MAC on top of the UID sandbox
adb shell getenforce                 # Enforcing

# ART compilation state (profile-guided):
adb shell dumpsys package dexopt | grep -A2 com.example
#   [status=speed-profile] [reason=bg-dexopt]
#   ^ compiled AOT for the methods the PROFILE says are actually hot

# Verified Boot / update integrity:
adb shell getprop ro.boot.verifiedbootstate      # green = verified
```

**Key takeaways**

- Android uses the Linux kernel with mobile-specific additions — Binder, ashmem/memfd, lmkd hooks, wakelocks, enforcing SELinux — but almost nothing above the kernel resembles a desktop Linux distribution.
- Project Treble separated vendor HAL implementations from the framework behind a stable interface so the OS can be updated without vendor rebuilds.
- Binder is a kernel driver providing single-copy, capability-based IPC with a per-process thread pool, priority inheritance, and kernel-supplied caller credentials.
- Because the kernel supplies the caller's UID, a Binder service can authorise reliably instead of trusting a claim, which makes Binder an authorisation mechanism and not merely a transport.
- The roughly 1 MB per-process Binder buffer is the cause of `TransactionTooLargeException` when large objects are passed through IPC.
- Services calling other services on a caller's behalf must clear and restore the calling identity, or they become a confused deputy that leaks system privilege.
- Zygote preloads framework classes once and forks each app, so startup is fast and framework pages are shared copy-on-write across every process.
- ART combines profile-guided AOT compilation with a JIT and a low-pause concurrent copying collector, because GC pauses during interaction are visible.
- `system_server` hosts the framework services and is the policy centre for what runs, what is killed, and which permissions apply.
- Each app runs under its own UID, repurposing UNIX user isolation to isolate applications, with SELinux, runtime permissions, app signing, Verified Boot, and hardware-backed keys layered above.

#### iOS Architecture

**Theory**

Where Android's design is shaped by running on hardware from hundreds of vendors, iOS's is shaped by running on hardware Apple designs itself. That single difference explains most of the architectural divergence: iOS can rely on specific silicon for its security guarantees and can make restrictions stick because there is no alternative distribution channel.

**The kernel is XNU** ("X is Not Unix"), a **hybrid**: a Mach microkernel core providing tasks, threads, virtual memory, and **Mach ports** for IPC, combined with a BSD layer providing the POSIX API, processes, signals, sockets, and the VFS, plus **IOKit**, a driver framework written in a restricted subset of C++ with an object-oriented device model. Both halves run in one address space, so Mach-style modularity is available without the IPC cost of a true microkernel — the hybrid compromise discussed in Chapter 1.

**Mach ports** are the foundational IPC primitive, and they are capabilities: a port right is unforgeable, can be transferred in a message, and holding one is what grants the ability to send to that port. Higher-level mechanisms (XPC, distributed notifications, much of the frameworks) are built on them. The parallel with Binder is close — both are capability-based, kernel-mediated, credential-carrying object IPC — reached from different lineages.

**launchd** is PID 1 and the ancestor of systemd's design: a single daemon that starts and supervises everything, with on-demand launching driven by property-list job descriptions. **Grand Central Dispatch** (GCD) moves thread management into the OS: applications submit blocks to queues with quality-of-service classes, and the kernel maintains the thread pool, which lets the system make global scheduling and energy decisions that individual apps cannot.

The **layered frameworks** — Cocoa Touch (UIKit/SwiftUI), Media, Core Services, Core OS — are largely Objective-C and Swift, and they are the only supported interface; the BSD layer exists but is heavily restricted from app code by the sandbox.

The security architecture is where iOS is most distinctive, and it is a chain rather than a set of features:

- **Boot ROM** — immutable, fused into silicon at manufacture, containing Apple's root public key. This is the anchor of trust.
- **Secure Boot chain** — each stage verifies the signature of the next, so an unsigned kernel cannot be loaded at all.
- **Secure Enclave** — a separate coprocessor with its own boot ROM, memory, and OS, holding biometric templates and key material. The main CPU never sees these keys; it asks the Enclave to perform operations.
- **Code signing** — every executable page must be signed, enforced at page-in. The practical consequence is that writable-and-executable memory is not available to apps, which eliminates classic code injection and forces JIT engines to use a special, tightly controlled entitlement.
- **Sandbox** (`seatbelt`) — a mandatory access control system applied to every app, with entitlements declaring what an app may do; the default is a private container directory and little else.
- **Data Protection** — files are encrypted with per-file keys wrapped by class keys tied to the passcode, so data in the strongest class is genuinely unreadable while the device is locked.
- **Kernel hardening** — KTRR/KIP (kernel text is made immutable after boot), **PAC** (pointer authentication, signing pointers so a corrupted one fails verification), and Memory Integrity Enforcement on recent silicon.

Memory and lifecycle follow what the previous topics described: no flash swap, a kernel memory compressor, and **Jetsam** terminating apps by priority band under pressure. Finally, distribution itself is part of the security model: App Review plus mandatory signing means the platform controls what can run at all — the principal reason iOS malware is rare, and the principal reason the model is contested.

| Dimension | Android | iOS |
|---|---|---|
| Kernel | Linux + Binder, lmkd, wakelocks | XNU: Mach + BSD + IOKit (hybrid) |
| IPC | Binder (capability, kernel-mediated) | Mach ports / XPC (capability, kernel-mediated) |
| Runtime | ART, profile-guided AOT + JIT, GC | Native compiled Swift/ObjC, ARC (no tracing GC) |
| Process start | Zygote fork, CoW-shared framework | `launchd` spawn, dyld shared cache |
| App isolation | One UNIX UID per app + SELinux | Sandbox profiles + entitlements |
| Memory reclaim | zram, lmkd by `oom_score_adj` | Compressor, Jetsam by priority band |
| Background work | Services, JobScheduler, WorkManager | Declared modes, BGTaskScheduler, strict limits |
| Distribution | Play Store plus sideloading | App Store, signing enforced by the kernel |
| Hardware | Many vendors, HAL via Treble | Apple silicon only, Secure Enclave assumed |

**Example**

```text

                   Mach port                Binder

   IPC must be capability-based and kernel-mediated.


   GCD: THREAD MANAGEMENT AS AN OS SERVICE

   app submits BLOCKS + a QoS class, not threads:

     .userInteractive  -> runs now, highest priority (UI, animation)
     .userInitiated    -> user is waiting on a result
     .default
     .utility          -> progress bar work; may be throttled
     .background       -> may be deferred until charging/idle
                          and runs on efficiency cores

   +------------------------------------------+
   |  queues (serial / concurrent)            |
   +------------------------------------------+
   |  ONE system-wide thread pool, sized and  |  <- the kernel can
   |  placed by the KERNEL                    |     make global energy
   +------------------------------------------+     decisions; an app
                                                    choosing its own
   Apps do not size their own pools, so 20 apps      thread count
   cannot each create 8 threads on a 6-core phone.   cannot.
```

```swift
// GCD: declare intent (QoS), let the OS decide placement and timing.

import Foundation

// High priority: the user is looking at this right now.
DispatchQueue.main.async {
    self.spinner.startAnimating()
}

// Background QoS: the scheduler may run this on efficiency cores and
// may defer it entirely while on battery. That is the POINT --
// energy policy belongs to the OS, not to each app.
DispatchQueue.global(qos: .background).async {
    let thumbnails = self.generateThumbnails()      // slow, not urgent
    DispatchQueue.main.async {
        self.collectionView.reloadData()            // UI on main, always
    }
}

// A serial queue as a lock-free mutual exclusion mechanism: only one
// block runs at a time, so the protected state needs no mutex.
let cacheQueue = DispatchQueue(label: "com.example.cache")
cacheQueue.async { self.cache[key] = value }

// XPC: an out-of-process service over Mach ports. Crash isolation plus
// a smaller sandbox for the risky part (parsing untrusted input).
let connection = NSXPCConnection(serviceName: "com.example.Parser")
connection.remoteObjectInterface = NSXPCInterface(with: ParserProtocol.self)
connection.invalidationHandler = { /* peer died: degrade gracefully */ }
connection.resume()
```

```swift
// Data Protection: the file's protection class decides whether it is
// readable while the device is locked. This is a real cryptographic
// guarantee, not a permission flag.

try data.write(to: url, options: .completeFileProtection)
//   .completeFileProtection            unreadable whenever locked
//   .completeUnlessOpen                readable if already open
//   .completeUntilFirstUserAuthentication  readable after first unlock
//                                          (the usual default)
//   .none                              always readable

// Keychain with Secure Enclave-backed keys: the private key material
// is generated inside the Enclave and cannot be extracted, only used.
let access = SecAccessControlCreateWithFlags(
    nil,
    kSecAttrAccessibleWhenUnlockedThisDeviceOnly,   // no backup, no sync
    [.privateKeyUsage, .biometryCurrentSet],        // Face/Touch ID, and
    nil)                                            // invalidated if the
                                                    // enrolled biometry
                                                    // set changes
let attributes: [String: Any] = [
    kSecAttrTokenID as String: kSecAttrTokenIDSecureEnclave,
    kSecAttrKeyType as String: kSecAttrKeyTypeECSECPrimeRandom,
    kSecPrivateKeyAttrs as String: [kSecAttrAccessControl as String: access]
]
var error: Unmanaged<CFError>?
let key = SecKeyCreateRandomKey(attributes as CFDictionary, &error)
// The app holds a REFERENCE. The key itself never enters app memory,
// so a full compromise of the app does not yield the key.
```

```bash
# Inspecting a Darwin system (macOS shares XNU with iOS; an iOS device
# needs a development setup, so run these on macOS to see the same kernel).

uname -a
#   Darwin ... root:xnu-10063.../RELEASE_ARM64_T6020 arm64
#              ^^^ the XNU build

sysctl kern.osrelease kern.version hw.optional.arm.FEAT_PAuth
#   FEAT_PAuth: 1     <- pointer authentication available

# launchd, PID 1, and the job it supervises:
launchctl list | head
launchctl print system/com.apple.example

# Mach ports held by a process (the IPC primitive, made visible):
lsmp -p $(pgrep -n Safari) | head
#   name      right   flags   boost  reqs  recv  send  ...
#   0x0000010b send    --------        ---     0     1  <- a capability

# Code signature and entitlements -- the sandbox is driven by these:
codesign -dv --entitlements :- /Applications/Safari.app 2>&1 | head -30
#   <key>com.apple.security.app-sandbox</key><true/>
#   <key>com.apple.security.network.client</key><true/>

# Memory compressor, not swap-to-flash (the iOS behaviour, visible here):
vm_stat | grep -i compress
#   Pages occupied by compressor:   412789
#   Pages stored in compressor:     998211    <- ~2.4x compression

# On-device app lifecycle and jetsam events are visible in the log:
log show --predicate 'subsystem == "com.apple.kernel"' --last 5m | grep -i jetsam
```

**Key takeaways**

- iOS runs XNU, a hybrid kernel combining a Mach core (tasks, threads, VM, ports) with a BSD layer (POSIX, processes, sockets, VFS) and IOKit drivers, all in one address space.
- The hybrid design provides Mach's modular structure without paying a microkernel's IPC cost on every service call.
- Mach ports are unforgeable, transferable capabilities carrying kernel-supplied credentials, converging on the same design conclusions as Binder from a different lineage.
- `launchd` is PID 1 and supervises all services with on-demand launching; GCD moves thread-pool management into the OS so energy and scheduling decisions can be made globally.
- Security is a chain anchored in an immutable Boot ROM: each boot stage verifies the next, and every executable page's signature is checked at page-in.
- Mandatory code signing means apps cannot obtain writable-executable memory, which removes the injection step most exploit chains depend on.
- The Secure Enclave is a separate coprocessor holding biometric templates and keys that the main CPU can use but never read.
- Data Protection encrypts files with keys tied to the passcode, so the strongest class is cryptographically unreadable while the device is locked.
- Memory pressure is handled with a kernel compressor and Jetsam terminations by priority band, the same no-swap strategy as Android with different names.
- Controlling both the hardware and the only distribution channel is what makes these restrictions enforceable, which is simultaneously the model's security advantage and its principal criticism.

> 🧪 Practice

> 3. Explain how mandatory code signing prevents a class of exploit that ASLR and DEP only make harder, and state what a JavaScript engine must do to run at all under that restriction.
