<a id="15-case-studies-and-performance"></a>
## 15. Case Studies and Performance

The preceding fourteen chapters examined operating system mechanisms one at a time; this one looks at complete systems that combine them, and at the discipline of measuring whether the combination actually performs. The case studies show that there is no single correct set of trade-offs — Linux, Windows, and the BSDs each resolved the same design questions differently, and each resolution is coherent on its own terms. The performance half then supplies the methodology that turns "the system is slow" into a specific, measured, fixable resource, which is the skill that outlasts any particular kernel.

<a id="151-system-case-studies"></a>
### 15.1 System Case Studies

Reading a real kernel's architecture is the fastest way to see why the abstractions in earlier chapters look the way they do. This section examines the two kernels that run most of the world's computers, the design tradition both descend from, and the research systems whose ideas keep arriving in production a decade after they were published.

#### Linux Kernel Architecture

**Theory**

Linux is the clearest working example of a **monolithic but modular** kernel, the design introduced in Chapter 1. Everything — scheduler, memory manager, filesystems, network stack, drivers — runs in a single address space at the highest privilege level, so a subsystem calls another with an ordinary function call rather than a message. That is what makes it fast, and it is also why a bug in any driver can corrupt any kernel structure.

"Modular" softens this considerably. **Loadable kernel modules** (`.ko` files) can be inserted and removed at runtime, so a distribution ships one kernel that loads only the drivers a machine actually has. Modules are not isolated — once loaded, a module is as privileged as the core — but they give the *deployment* flexibility of a microkernel without its IPC cost.

The kernel is organised into subsystems that map onto the earlier chapters almost one for one:

| Subsystem | Responsibility | Chapter |
|---|---|---|
| Process management | `task_struct`, `fork`/`exec`, signals, namespaces | 2, 13 |
| Scheduler | EEVDF (since 6.6, replacing CFS), RT and deadline classes | 4 |
| Memory management | Page tables, page cache, reclaim, `mmap`, swap | 7, 8 |
| VFS | One interface over every filesystem | 10 |
| Block layer | I/O schedulers, request merging, multi-queue | 9, 11 |
| Network stack | Sockets, TCP/IP, netfilter, qdiscs | — |
| Device drivers | Roughly 60-70% of the source tree | 11 |
| Security | LSM hooks, SELinux/AppArmor, capabilities, seccomp | 12 |

Two design decisions distinguish Linux more than any technical detail.

**Threads are processes.** Linux does not have separate process and thread structures. There is one `task_struct`, and `clone()` chooses how much of it is shared: share the address space and you have made a thread; share nothing and you have made a process; share a namespace subset and you have made a container. `fork()`, `pthread_create()`, and container creation are the same call with different flags — an unusually economical unification, and the reason Chapter 3's "threads vs processes" distinction is blurrier on Linux than on Windows.

**The userspace ABI is sacred; the internal API is not.** Linux guarantees that a binary compiled twenty years ago still runs — "we do not break userspace" is enforced socially and absolutely. Internally, the opposite holds: function signatures, structure layouts, and whole subsystems change between releases without notice. This is deliberate. It is why out-of-tree drivers are painful to maintain and why the project pressures vendors to upstream code, and it is why Linux can refactor its internals in ways a stable-internal-ABI kernel like Windows cannot.

The development model is itself an architectural force: a merge window of roughly two weeks, then seven or eight release candidates, a release every 9-10 weeks, and selected releases marked **LTS** for multi-year maintenance. Thousands of developers from competing companies merge tens of thousands of commits per release under the GPLv2, which requires derivative kernels to be published — the licensing choice that shaped the ecosystem more than any code.

The most significant recent addition is **eBPF**: a verified, JIT-compiled virtual machine inside the kernel. Programs are checked before loading to prove they terminate and cannot access memory out of bounds, then run at hook points across the kernel. It lets you extend kernel behaviour — tracing, networking, security policy — without writing a module or rebooting, and it is the closest thing Linux has to the extensibility an exokernel promised.

**Example**

```text
   LINUX: MONOLITHIC, BUT MODULAR

   USER SPACE
   +------------------------------------------------------------+
   |  applications  |  glibc / musl  |  systemd  |  containers   |
   +------------------------------------------------------------+
              |  system call interface (~350 stable syscalls)
   ===========v================================================== 
   KERNEL SPACE -- ONE address space, ONE privilege level
   +------------------------------------------------------------+
   |  PROCESS   |  MEMORY   |   VFS     |  NETWORK  |  eBPF VM   |
   |  task_struct  page      +--------+   sockets     verified,  |
   |  scheduler    tables    | ext4   |   TCP/IP      JIT'd,     |
   |  (EEVDF)      reclaim   | xfs    |   netfilter   sandboxed  |
   |  signals      page      | btrfs  |   qdiscs      programs   |
   |  namespaces   cache     | overlay|                          |
   +------------+-----------+----+----+-----------+--------------+
   |              BLOCK LAYER (multi-queue, I/O sched)           |
   +-------------------------------------------------------------+
   |  DEVICE DRIVERS  (~65% of the source tree)  [loadable .ko]  |
   +-------------------------------------------------------------+
                             |
                          HARDWARE

   Calls between boxes are FUNCTION CALLS, not messages.
   Fast (ns, not us) -- and a fault in any box can corrupt any other.


   ONE STRUCTURE, THREE ABSTRACTIONS: clone() FLAGS

   fork()            clone(SIGCHLD)
                     -> shares NOTHING: a new process

   pthread_create()  clone(CLONE_VM | CLONE_FS | CLONE_FILES |
                           CLONE_SIGHAND | CLONE_THREAD)
                     -> shares address space, fds, signals: a THREAD

   container start   clone(CLONE_NEWPID | CLONE_NEWNS | CLONE_NEWNET
                           | CLONE_NEWUSER | ...)
                     -> shares the kernel, isolates the VIEW

   Same syscall. Same task_struct. The "kind" of thing you created
   is just which pointers it shares with its parent.

        parent task_struct              child task_struct
        +----------------+              +----------------+
        | mm      -------|---+      +---|------ mm       |
        | files   -------|--+|      |+--|------ files    |
        | fs             |  ||      ||  | ...            |
        +----------------+  ||      ||  +----------------+
                            vv      vv
                   CLONE_VM: both point at the SAME mm_struct
                   no CLONE_VM: child gets a COPY (copy-on-write)


   THE TWO ABI PROMISES

   USERSPACE ABI            INTERNAL KERNEL API
   -------------            -------------------
   NEVER broken.            Broken constantly, on purpose.
   A 2004 binary runs       Function signatures, struct layouts,
   on a 2026 kernel.        whole subsystems change per release.

   consequence:             consequence:
   distros can upgrade      out-of-tree drivers rot fast
   the kernel freely        -> strong pressure to UPSTREAM
                            -> the kernel can refactor internals
                               that Windows, with a stable driver
                               ABI, must keep supporting forever
```

```c
/* The unification, in code: one syscall, three meanings. */
#define _GNU_SOURCE
#include <sched.h>
#include <sys/wait.h>
#include <unistd.h>
#include <stdio.h>

static char stack[1024 * 1024];
static int shared_counter = 0;

static int child(void *arg)
{
    shared_counter++;                 /* visible to the parent ONLY if
                                       * CLONE_VM was set */
    printf("  child: pid=%d counter=%d\n", getpid(), shared_counter);
    return 0;
}

int main(void)
{
    /* 1. A PROCESS: no sharing. The child gets a copy-on-write copy
     *    of the address space, so its increment is invisible here. */
    pid_t p = clone(child, stack + sizeof stack, SIGCHLD, NULL);
    waitpid(p, NULL, 0);
    printf("after process clone: counter=%d\n", shared_counter);   /* 0 */

    /* 2. A THREAD: CLONE_VM means one shared mm_struct, so the
     *    increment IS visible. This is what pthread_create() does. */
    p = clone(child, stack + sizeof stack,
              CLONE_VM | CLONE_FS | CLONE_FILES | CLONE_SIGHAND
              | CLONE_THREAD | SIGCHLD, NULL);
    /* ... */
    printf("after thread clone: counter=%d\n", shared_counter);    /* 1 */

    /* 3. A CONTAINER: same call again, isolating the VIEW instead
     *    of the memory (Chapter 13). */
    p = clone(child, stack + sizeof stack,
              CLONE_NEWPID | CLONE_NEWNS | CLONE_NEWNET | SIGCHLD, NULL);
    return 0;
}
```

```c
/* A minimal loadable module: privileged code, inserted at runtime.
 * Note there is no isolation -- once loaded this IS the kernel. */
#include <linux/module.h>
#include <linux/kernel.h>
#include <linux/init.h>

static int __init hello_init(void)
{
    pr_info("module: loaded, running in kernel mode\n");
    return 0;                      /* non-zero aborts the insertion */
}

static void __exit hello_exit(void)
{
    pr_info("module: unloaded\n"); /* must undo EVERYTHING: a leaked
                                    * allocation here leaks until reboot */
}

module_init(hello_init);
module_exit(hello_exit);
MODULE_LICENSE("GPL");             /* non-GPL modules are denied access
                                    * to many symbols ("tainting") */
```

```bash
# ---- Read the architecture off a running system ----
uname -r                                  # 6.12.1-arch1-1
ls /usr/src/linux/                        # arch/ drivers/ fs/ kernel/ mm/
                                          # net/ include/ security/
du -sh /usr/src/linux/drivers             # ~65% of the tree is drivers

# Loaded modules = the modular half of "monolithic but modular":
lsmod | head
#   Module        Size   Used by
#   nvme          49152  3
#   ext4         987136  1
modinfo ext4 | head -5
sudo modprobe -r some_module              # unload at runtime

# The stable interface, enumerated:
ausyscall --dump | wc -l                  # ~350 syscalls, ~never removed
man 2 syscalls

# Threads really are tasks:
ps -eLf | head                            # -L shows LWPs (threads)
ls /proc/$$/task/                         # one directory per thread
cat /proc/$$/status | grep -E 'Threads|Pid|TracerPid'

# Scheduler class in use (Chapter 4):
cat /sys/kernel/debug/sched/features 2>/dev/null | head -3
chrt -p 1                                 # pid 1 scheduling policy

# eBPF: extend the kernel without a module or a reboot
sudo bpftool prog list | head
sudo bpftrace -e 'tracepoint:syscalls:sys_enter_openat {
    @[comm] = count(); }'                 # count opens by process name
```

**Key takeaways**

- Linux is monolithic — all subsystems share one address space and call each other directly — but modular, since drivers load and unload at runtime without the isolation a microkernel would provide.
- Loadable modules give deployment flexibility without IPC cost; a loaded module is as privileged as the core kernel, so it is not a security boundary.
- Linux has a single `task_struct` for processes and threads, and `clone()` flags decide what is shared, unifying `fork`, thread creation, and container creation into one mechanism.
- The userspace ABI is never broken, which lets distributions upgrade kernels freely and keeps decades-old binaries running.
- The internal kernel API is broken deliberately and often, which forces drivers upstream and lets the kernel refactor internals that a stable-internal-ABI system could never change.
- Drivers are roughly two thirds of the source tree, which is the practical reason the monolithic design persists: in-tree drivers get refactored along with the interfaces they use.
- Development runs on a fixed cadence — a two-week merge window, release candidates, a release every 9-10 weeks — with selected LTS releases maintained for years.
- GPLv2 requires derivative kernels to be published, which shaped the ecosystem more than any individual technical decision.
- eBPF adds verified, JIT-compiled, sandboxed programs at kernel hook points, delivering safe runtime extensibility for tracing, networking, and security policy.

> 🧪 Practice

> 2. Compare the flags Linux uses for `fork()`, `pthread_create()`, and a container start. For each, state which resource is shared and which is copied.
> 3. Use `lsmod` and `modinfo` to identify three loaded modules and what hardware or filesystem each supports. Explain why unloading one is possible while unloading the scheduler is not.

#### Windows Kernel Architecture

**Theory**

Windows NT was designed from a blank sheet in 1989 by a team led by Dave Cutler, who had built VMS at DEC — and it shows. Where Linux grew organically from a UNIX-like kernel, NT was specified up front with goals that Linux never had: run multiple OS personalities simultaneously, be portable across processor architectures, and meet a formal security specification. Every architectural oddity follows from those goals.

The result is a **hybrid** kernel (Chapter 1). A layered, modular structure resembling a microkernel, but with the components that would be separate servers pulled into kernel mode for speed.

From the bottom:

- The **HAL** (Hardware Abstraction Layer) isolates processor and platform specifics — interrupt controllers, timers, DMA, SMP details — so the kernel above it is largely platform-independent. This is what made NT portable to MIPS, Alpha, PowerPC, Itanium, x86-64, and ARM64.
- The **kernel** proper (`ntoskrnl`'s lowest layer) handles thread scheduling, interrupt and exception dispatch, and multiprocessor synchronisation. It is deliberately small and never paged out.
- The **Executive** contains the real subsystems: Object Manager, Process/Thread Manager, Virtual Memory Manager, I/O Manager, Cache Manager, Security Reference Monitor, Configuration Manager (the registry), and more. These call one another directly, like Linux subsystems.
- **Environment subsystems** run in user mode and implement OS personalities. Win32 is the survivor; POSIX and OS/2 subsystems existed and were removed. **WSL1** revived the idea by implementing Linux syscalls as a subsystem; **WSL2** abandoned it and runs a real Linux kernel in a lightweight VM — an admission that emulating a syscall surface faithfully is harder than virtualising hardware.

Three features are genuinely distinctive.

**Everything is an object.** Where UNIX says everything is a file, NT says everything is an object managed by the **Object Manager**: processes, threads, files, events, mutexes, semaphores, registry keys, devices, and desktops are all objects in a single hierarchical namespace with uniform naming, security descriptors, and reference counting. A **handle** is a per-process index into a handle table pointing at an object, with an access mask recorded at open time. The consequence is uniformity: one security model, one lifetime model, and one set of wait primitives covering every resource type — `WaitForMultipleObjects` can wait on a thread, a file operation, a mutex, and a timer in a single call, which UNIX historically could not do (hence `select`/`poll` covering only descriptors).

**I/O is asynchronous and packet-based.** The I/O Manager builds an **IRP** (I/O Request Packet) and passes it down a *stack* of layered drivers — a filter driver, a filesystem driver, a volume manager, a disk driver — each of which may handle, modify, or forward it. Asynchronous completion (**overlapped I/O**, with **I/O Completion Ports** for scalable event handling) was designed in from the start, whereas UNIX bolted async I/O on repeatedly (`aio`, `epoll`, and finally `io_uring`).

**The scheduler is strictly priority-based.** Thirty-two priority levels: 0-15 dynamic (normal applications, with priority boosts on I/O completion and for the foreground window) and 16-31 real-time (no boosting, fixed). The dispatcher always runs the highest-priority ready thread. Compare Linux's CFS/EEVDF, which is fair-share by design — a philosophical difference, not just an algorithmic one.

| Dimension | Linux | Windows NT |
|---|---|---|
| Structure | Monolithic + modules | Hybrid: HAL, kernel, Executive, user-mode subsystems |
| Core abstraction | Everything is a file (fd) | Everything is an object (handle) |
| Process/thread | One `task_struct`, `clone()` flags | Distinct process and thread objects; `CreateProcess` is heavy |
| Process creation | `fork()` + `exec()`, cheap, CoW | `CreateProcess()` — no fork equivalent |
| Scheduling | Fair-share (EEVDF) + RT classes | 32 strict priority levels, with boosts |
| I/O model | Synchronous by default; `epoll`, `io_uring` | Asynchronous by design; IRPs, completion ports |
| Driver ABI | Unstable internally | Stable — decades-old drivers still load |
| Config | Text files in `/etc` | Registry (Configuration Manager) |
| Source | Open, GPLv2 | Proprietary (partial source programs) |

**Example**

```text

   USER MODE
   +-------------------------------------------------------------+
   | applications                                                |
   +-------------------------------------------------------------+

   | Object Mgr | Process/Thread | Virtual Memory | I/O Manager   |
   | Security Reference Monitor  | Cache Mgr | Config Mgr (registry)|
   | Plug&Play | Power | ALPC                                    |
   +-------------------------------------------------------------+
   |  KERNEL: scheduling, interrupts, DPC/APC, SMP sync          |
   +-------------------------------------------------------------+
   |  HAL: interrupt controller, timers, DMA, bus, SMP specifics |
   +-------------------------------------------------------------+
   |  DRIVERS (layered stacks, IRP-based)   |  Win32k (GUI)      |
   +-------------------------------------------------------------+
                             |

   "Hybrid": the STRUCTURE of a microkernel, with the servers
   pulled into kernel mode so calls stay cheap.


   HANDLES AND THE OBJECT MANAGER

   process A handle table          Object Manager namespace
   +----+-------------------+      \Device\HarddiskVolume1
   | 4  | -> File object    |      \BaseNamedObjects\MyMutex
   | 8  | -> Mutex object   |      \Processes\...
   | 12 | -> Process object |      \Registry\Machine\...
   +----+-------------------+
          |     |     |
          v     v     v
   +--------------------------------+
   |  OBJECT (one per resource)     |
   |  header: name, type,           |   ONE security model,
   |          security descriptor,  |   ONE lifetime model,
   |          HANDLE COUNT,         |   ONE wait model --
   |          POINTER COUNT         |   for files, threads,
   |  body:   type-specific data    |   mutexes, registry keys.
   +--------------------------------+
        freed when both counts hit 0

   Because everything is a waitable object:
     WaitForMultipleObjects(4, {thread, file_event, mutex, timer}, ...)
   One call, four DIFFERENT resource types. UNIX's select()/poll()
   only ever covered file descriptors.


   AN IRP TRAVELLING DOWN A DRIVER STACK

   ReadFile()  -> I/O Manager builds an IRP
                        |
                        v
            +-----------------------+
            | filter (antivirus,    |  may inspect, block, or pass on
            | encryption)           |
            +-----------+-----------+
                        v
            | filesystem (NTFS)     |  maps file offset -> volume LBA
            +-----------+-----------+
                        v
            | volume manager (RAID) |  maps volume LBA -> disk LBA
            +-----------+-----------+
                        v
            | disk / storport       |  issues the hardware command
            +-----------+-----------+
                        v
                     hardware
                        |
            completion travels back UP the stack, each layer
            getting a chance to post-process (an "IoCompletion routine")

   This layering is why a filesystem filter can be a separate,
   independently shipped driver -- and why a bad one hangs every
   read on the machine.


   SCHEDULING PHILOSOPHIES, SIDE BY SIDE

   WINDOWS                          LINUX (CFS/EEVDF)
   31 +-- real-time (no boost) --+  strict priority is the EXCEPTION
   ...|                          |  (SCHED_FIFO/RR/DEADLINE)
   16 +--------------------------+
   15 |                          |  the NORM is fair share:
   ...| dynamic: boosted on I/O  |  every runnable task gets a
    8 | completion and for the   |  proportional slice, nice values
   ...| foreground window        |  adjust the proportion
    0 +--------------------------+

   "Highest priority ready thread runs"   vs   "everyone advances"
   Neither is wrong; they optimise different things.
```

```c
/* The Win32 view: handles, objects, and unified waiting. */
#include <windows.h>
#include <stdio.h>

int main(void)
{
    /* A file is an object; CreateFile returns a HANDLE, not an int fd.
     * FILE_FLAG_OVERLAPPED opts into asynchronous I/O -- the native
     * model, not an add-on. */
    HANDLE hFile = CreateFile(L"data.bin", GENERIC_READ, FILE_SHARE_READ,
                              NULL, OPEN_EXISTING,
                              FILE_FLAG_OVERLAPPED, NULL);

    /* A mutex is an object too, and it can be NAMED in the global
     * namespace so unrelated processes can find it by name. */
    HANDLE hMutex = CreateMutex(NULL, FALSE, L"Global\\MyAppMutex");

    /* So is a timer, and so is a thread. */
    HANDLE hTimer  = CreateWaitableTimer(NULL, TRUE, NULL);
    HANDLE hThread = CreateThread(NULL, 0, worker, NULL, 0, NULL);

    /* THE distinctive primitive: wait on FOUR DIFFERENT KINDS of
     * object in one call. There is no UNIX equivalent -- select()
     * and epoll() handle descriptors only, never threads or mutexes. */
    HANDLE objs[] = { hThread, hMutex, hTimer, hFile };
    DWORD r = WaitForMultipleObjects(4, objs, FALSE /* any */, INFINITE);
    printf("object %lu signalled\n", r - WAIT_OBJECT_0);

    /* Overlapped read: returns IMMEDIATELY, completion arrives later. */
    OVERLAPPED ov = { .Offset = 0 };
    ov.hEvent = CreateEvent(NULL, TRUE, FALSE, NULL);
    char buf[4096];
    ReadFile(hFile, buf, sizeof buf, NULL, &ov);   /* async */
    /* ... do other work while the IRP travels the driver stack ... */
    DWORD got;
    GetOverlappedResult(hFile, &ov, &got, TRUE);   /* now collect it */

    /* CloseHandle decrements the object's handle count; the object
     * itself is freed only when handle AND pointer counts reach zero. */
    CloseHandle(hFile); CloseHandle(hMutex);
    CloseHandle(hTimer); CloseHandle(hThread);
    return 0;
}
```

```c
/* Process creation: the deepest API difference from UNIX.
 * Windows has no fork(). CreateProcess does load+start in one call,
 * and customisation happens through a parameter block rather than
 * through code running between fork and exec (Chapter 2). */
STARTUPINFO si = { .cb = sizeof si };
PROCESS_INFORMATION pi;

si.dwFlags    = STARTF_USESTDHANDLES;
si.hStdOutput = hPipeWrite;        /* redirection is set up HERE,
                                    * not by dup2() in a child */

BOOL ok = CreateProcess(
    L"C:\\Windows\\System32\\cmd.exe",  /* image                     */
    L"cmd.exe /c dir",                  /* command line              */
    NULL, NULL,                         /* security descriptors      */
    TRUE,                               /* inherit handles           */
    CREATE_NEW_CONSOLE,                 /* creation flags            */
    NULL, NULL, &si, &pi);

WaitForSingleObject(pi.hProcess, INFINITE);   /* a process IS an object */
DWORD code; GetExitCodeProcess(pi.hProcess, &code);
CloseHandle(pi.hProcess); CloseHandle(pi.hThread);

/* UNIX equivalent needs fork() + dup2() + execve() -- three calls and
 * a window of arbitrary child code. Windows needs one call and a
 * struct. The UNIX version is more flexible; the Windows version
 * avoids ever duplicating an address space it is about to discard. */
```

```powershell
# Inspect the architecture on a live Windows system.

Get-Process | Sort-Object -Property Handles -Descending |
    Select-Object -First 5 Name, Handles, Threads
#   Name          Handles Threads     <- handle count IS the object count

# Scheduling priority classes (the 32-level scheme, named):
Get-Process notepad | Select-Object Name, PriorityClass
(Get-Process notepad).PriorityClass = "AboveNormal"
#   Idle / BelowNormal / Normal / AboveNormal / High / RealTime

# Loaded kernel drivers -- the layered stacks:
Get-WmiObject Win32_SystemDriver | Where-Object State -eq "Running" |
    Select-Object -First 5 Name, PathName

# The Object Manager namespace is browsable with Sysinternals WinObj;
# from the CLI, the registry (Configuration Manager) is a namespace too:
Get-ChildItem HKLM:\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services | Select -First 5

# WSL: subsystem (WSL1) vs real kernel in a VM (WSL2)
wsl --list --verbose
#   NAME      STATE     VERSION
#   Ubuntu    Running   2        <- VERSION 2 = a genuine Linux kernel
wsl --system -d Ubuntu uname -r  # shows a Microsoft-built Linux kernel
```

**Key takeaways**

- Windows NT was specified up front for portability, multiple OS personalities, and a formal security model, and its architecture follows from those goals rather than from UNIX tradition.
- It is a hybrid kernel: microkernel-like layering with the Executive's subsystems placed in kernel mode so inter-component calls stay cheap.
- The HAL isolates platform specifics and is why NT ported across MIPS, Alpha, PowerPC, Itanium, x86-64, and ARM64.
- Everything is an object managed by the Object Manager, giving one naming, security, lifetime, and wait model across files, threads, mutexes, registry keys, and devices.
- A handle is a per-process table index with an access mask fixed at open time, and objects are freed only when both handle and pointer counts reach zero.
- `WaitForMultipleObjects` can wait on heterogeneous object types in a single call, which UNIX's descriptor-only `select`/`poll` could not do.
- I/O is asynchronous and packet-based: the I/O Manager sends IRPs down layered driver stacks, with completion travelling back up.
- Scheduling is strict priority across 32 levels with boosts for I/O completion and the foreground window, contrasting with Linux's fair-share default.
- Windows guarantees a stable driver ABI, which keeps old drivers working but constrains internal evolution — the opposite of Linux's trade.
- Windows has no `fork()`; `CreateProcess` loads and starts in one call with customisation supplied through a parameter block rather than by code between fork and exec.

#### UNIX and BSD Design

**Theory**

Nearly everything in this book descends from a system built in 1969 by a small group at Bell Labs on a machine nobody else wanted. Understanding UNIX's design principles explains why modern systems look the way they do — and understanding the BSD branch explains why "UNIX-like" is not one thing.

The **UNIX philosophy** is a set of design commitments, not a feature list:

- **Everything is a file.** Devices, pipes, sockets (eventually), and in Linux kernel state itself (`/proc`, `/sys`) are all reached through `open`/`read`/`write`/`close`. One interface, one set of tools, one permission model.
- **Small programs that do one thing well**, composed through **pipes**. The pipe made composition the primary mode of use, which is why the shell became a programming environment rather than a launcher.
- **Text as the universal interface.** If every program's output is lines of text, every program can be the input to every other, without agreeing on anything.
- **Mechanism, not policy.** The kernel supplies primitives; userspace decides how to use them. This is why the same kernel runs a phone and a supercomputer.
- **Portability through C.** Rewriting UNIX in C around 1973 was the decisive move — it made the OS a portable artifact, which nothing else was.

The genealogy matters because the splits still shape the landscape. AT&T's research UNIX forked into **System V** (commercial) and **BSD** (the Berkeley Software Distribution, from university work). BSD contributed an astonishing share of what people think of as UNIX: **sockets** and the TCP/IP stack, the **Fast File System** (cylinder groups, long filenames), virtual memory with `mmap`, job control, `vi`, and the C shell. The two lineages diverged enough that **POSIX** was created to standardise a common core, which is the reason portable code is possible at all.

Legal history then produced the outcome everyone lives with. The USL v. BSDi lawsuit (1992-94) left BSD's future uncertain at precisely the moment Linux appeared with an unambiguous licence, and by the time BSD was clear, Linux had the developers. A timing accident, not a technical verdict.

The **licensing** difference persists and is genuinely consequential:

| | GPL (Linux) | BSD/MIT licence (BSDs) |
|---|---|---|
| Derivative works | Must publish source | May stay proprietary |
| Commercial embedding | Requires releasing changes | No obligation |
| Practical result | Vendors upstream their work | Code appears in closed products |
| Visible outcome | One dominant shared kernel | BSD code inside macOS, PlayStation, Junos, Netflix's CDN, Windows' TCP utilities |

The other structural difference is **whole-system versus kernel-only** development. Linux is a kernel; a distribution assembles it with GNU userland, an init system, and packaging chosen by different groups. A BSD is a **complete operating system** developed in one repository — kernel, libc, userland, documentation, and build system evolve together. This yields notable coherence (the man pages are genuinely authoritative, `make buildworld` rebuilds everything from source) at the cost of a smaller ecosystem.

The three main BSDs each optimise something different, and each has produced technology the rest of the world adopted: **FreeBSD** (performance and server use; ZFS integration, jails, DTrace, `kqueue`, the network stack Netflix uses to serve a large fraction of internet video from single machines), **OpenBSD** (correctness and security; OpenSSH, `pf`, LibreSSL, and a long series of exploit mitigations later adopted elsewhere), and **NetBSD** (portability; it runs on an almost absurd range of architectures). And **macOS** is a certified UNIX whose userland and much of whose kernel personality are BSD, sitting on the XNU hybrid kernel from Chapter 14.

**Example**

```bash
# The philosophy, demonstrated rather than described.

# 1. One interface for everything -- the same syscalls throughout.
exec 3< /dev/urandom            # a driver as a file descriptor
exec 4< /proc/cpuinfo           # kernel state as a file descriptor
head -c 16 <&3 | xxd            # read() from a device
grep -m1 'model name' <&4       # read() from a kernel structure

# 2. Mechanism, not policy: the kernel supplies primitives, the shell
#    composes them. Nothing here was designed as a "log analyser".
grep -h 'ERROR' /var/log/*.log \
  | awk '{print $5}' \
  | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -20

# 3. Text as the universal interface: every stage speaks lines.
#    Compare to an API where each tool needs a binding for every other.

# ---- BSD vs Linux: the same task, different toolchains ----
#          Linux                        FreeBSD
# init     systemd                      rc.d scripts
# fw       nftables/iptables            pf
# fs       ext4/xfs/btrfs               UFS2/ZFS (ZFS integrated)
# pkg      apt/dnf/pacman               pkg + ports
# trace    eBPF/bpftrace                DTrace
# jail     namespaces+cgroups           jails (one primitive, 2000)
# async    epoll / io_uring             kqueue (1999, one API for
#                                        fds, signals, timers, vnodes)

# Rebuild an ENTIRE BSD operating system from source -- kernel and
# userland together. There is no Linux equivalent of this command,
# because on Linux those pieces belong to different projects.
cd /usr/src && make -j8 buildworld && make -j8 buildkernel

# See POSIX conformance in action -- the same C compiles on all of them:
getconf _POSIX_VERSION           # 200809
man 7 standards                  # what your system claims to conform to
```

```c
/* Portability through POSIX: this compiles unmodified on Linux, the
 * BSDs, macOS, and AIX, because POSIX standardised the common core
 * that survived the System V / BSD split. */
#define _POSIX_C_SOURCE 200809L
#include <fcntl.h>
#include <unistd.h>
#include <stdio.h>

int main(void)
{
    /* open/read/write/close: the universal interface. The path can be
     * a regular file, a device, a pipe, or a kernel pseudo-file, and
     * this code does not change. */
    int fd = open("/etc/hostname", O_RDONLY);
    if (fd < 0) { perror("open"); return 1; }

    char buf[256];
    ssize_t n = read(fd, buf, sizeof buf - 1);
    if (n > 0) { buf[n] = '\0'; printf("host: %s", buf); }
    close(fd);
    return 0;
}

/* The non-portable parts are exactly where the branches diverged:
 *   Linux:   epoll_create1/epoll_wait, inotify, io_uring
 *   BSD:     kqueue/kevent (one API for fds, signals, timers, and
 *            filesystem events -- a cleaner design that arrived first)
 * Portable code either restricts itself to poll(), or abstracts both
 * behind a library (libevent, libuv) -- which is what everyone does. */
```

**Key takeaways**

- The UNIX philosophy is a set of commitments — everything is a file, small composable programs, text as the universal interface, mechanism over policy, portability through C — and each is visible in systems built fifty years later.
- Rewriting UNIX in C made an operating system a portable artifact for the first time, which mattered more than any single feature.
- The pipe made composition the primary mode of use, letting users create workflows from programs whose authors never coordinated.
- BSD contributed sockets and TCP/IP, the Fast File System, `mmap`-based virtual memory, and job control, so much of what is called "UNIX" is specifically Berkeley's work.
- POSIX exists to standardise a common core across the System V and BSD lineages, and is the reason portable C is possible.
- The USL v. BSDi lawsuit left BSD's legal status uncertain exactly when Linux appeared with a clear licence, which decided the outcome on timing rather than technical merit.
- GPL forces derivative kernels to be published while BSD licences do not, which is why Linux consolidated contributions and why BSD code appears inside macOS, PlayStation, Junos, and Netflix's CDN.
- Linux is a kernel assembled into distributions by others; a BSD is a complete OS whose kernel, libc, userland, and docs are versioned together and rebuilt with one command.
- FreeBSD optimises server performance, OpenBSD correctness and security, and NetBSD portability, and each has exported technology — jails, `pf`, OpenSSH, `kqueue`, DTrace integration — that the wider world adopted.

#### Research Operating Systems

**Theory**

Very few research operating systems are deployed, and that is the wrong measure of their worth. Their ideas migrate: virtual memory, the microkernel, capability security, and per-process namespaces were all research results long before they were ordinary. Reading them is how you tell which of today's constraints are fundamental and which are merely habitual.

**Mach** (CMU, 1985) tried to reduce the kernel to tasks, threads, virtual memory, and message-passing ports, with everything else in user-mode servers. It was influential enough that its DNA is in macOS and iOS to this day (Chapter 14), but pure Mach's performance disappointed — IPC cost dominated — which produced the hybrid compromise instead of the pure design. Its real legacy is the lesson: *the microkernel's problem was never the concept, it was the cost of crossing the boundary*.

**L4 and seL4** answered that directly. Jochen Liedtke's L4 (1993) made IPC 10-20x faster than Mach by ruthless minimality and careful attention to cache behaviour, proving the cost was an implementation property rather than an inherent one. **seL4** (2009) went further and produced a **formally verified** kernel: a machine-checked mathematical proof that the C implementation matches its specification, with no buffer overflows, no null dereferences, and correct enforcement of its security properties. It is around 10,000 lines of C — small enough to prove things about, which is the entire argument — and it ships today in defence, automotive, and aviation systems where the proof justifies the constraints.

**Exokernel** (MIT, 1995) attacked a different assumption: that the kernel should provide abstractions at all. It argued the kernel should only *securely multiplex* hardware and let applications implement their own abstractions in library operating systems, so a database could implement paging policy suited to a database rather than fighting the kernel's. The idea reappears constantly — in `io_uring`'s bypass of traditional syscall paths, in DPDK and SPDK doing userspace networking and storage, in eBPF letting applications inject policy into the kernel, and in unikernels (Chapter 13).

**Plan 9** (Bell Labs, late 1980s) is what happens when UNIX's own principles are applied without compromise. If everything is a file, then *everything* is a file: the network stack, the window system, process state, and remote machines' resources all appear in the filesystem. Each process gets its own **namespace** it can modify, and the **9P** protocol makes any resource accessible over the network identically to a local one. Plan 9 never took over — but per-process namespaces are now the foundation of Linux containers, `/proc` grew from it, and UTF-8 was invented for it and is now universal.

Two more worth knowing. **Singularity** (Microsoft Research, 2004) built an OS where isolation came from *type safety* rather than hardware: processes are sealed, written in a managed language, verified before running, and communicate over statically checked channels — so isolation costs no page-table switch and everything can share one address space. **Barrelfish** (ETH/Microsoft, 2009) treated a many-core machine as a distributed system, running a separate kernel per core communicating by message passing, on the argument that cache-coherent shared memory does not scale indefinitely and the OS should stop pretending it does.

Modern efforts continue: **Fuchsia** (Google) with its Zircon microkernel and capability-based security, and **Redox**, a microkernel OS in Rust. Whether either ships broadly matters less than what they are testing.

| System | Central question | Idea that escaped into production |
|---|---|---|
| Mach | Can services live outside the kernel? | XNU's hybrid core; the microkernel vocabulary |
| L4 / seL4 | Can IPC be cheap? Can a kernel be *proven*? | Fast IPC design; formal verification in safety-critical use |
| Exokernel | Should the kernel abstract at all? | io_uring, DPDK/SPDK, eBPF, unikernels |
| Plan 9 | What if everything really were a file? | Per-process namespaces (containers), `/proc`, UTF-8 |
| Singularity | Can isolation come from types, not hardware? | Language-based sandboxing; WebAssembly's model |
| Barrelfish | Is shared memory the right model for many cores? | NUMA-aware and message-passing kernel designs |

**Example**

```text
   THE PIPELINE FROM RESEARCH TO YOUR LAPTOP

   Mach (1985)         --> XNU hybrid kernel --> every Mac and iPhone
   L4 IPC (1993)       --> fast-IPC designs  --> seL4 in avionics/auto
   Exokernel (1995)    --> "let apps bypass the kernel"
                           --> DPDK, SPDK, io_uring, eBPF, unikernels
   Plan 9 namespaces   --> per-process namespaces --> DOCKER
   Plan 9's UTF-8      --> literally every text file you own
   Singularity (2004)  --> language-based isolation --> WebAssembly
   Barrelfish (2009)   --> per-core kernels --> NUMA-aware scheduling

   Typical lag: 10-25 years. The research was not "unsuccessful";
   it was early.


   THE MICROKERNEL STORY, IN THREE ACTS

   ACT 1 -- Mach: the idea
      +---------+  +--------+  +-------+
      | FS srv  |  | net srv|  | pager |   user mode
      +----+----+  +---+----+  +---+---+
           |  IPC     |  IPC      |  IPC      <- and here is the problem:
      +----v----------v-----------v-------+      every service call is
      |  microkernel: tasks, threads, VM  |      now TWO context switches
      +-----------------------------------+      plus message copying
      Verdict: beautiful, and too slow as built.

   ACT 2 -- L4: the measurement
      Liedtke: Mach's IPC is slow because of HOW IT WAS WRITTEN,
      not because IPC is inherently slow.
         Mach IPC:  ~100 us        L4 IPC:  ~5 us
      Minimal kernel, registers instead of memory for small messages,
      cache-conscious layout. 10-20x, same hardware.

   ACT 3 -- seL4: the proof
      ~10,000 lines of C, and a machine-checked proof that:
         - the C code refines the formal specification
         - no buffer overflow, no null deref, no arithmetic overflow
         - the security properties (confidentiality, integrity,
           availability of the isolation mechanism) actually hold
      Cost: years of proof effort, ~20 person-years, and every
            change must re-verify.
      Payoff: "this kernel has no bugs" is a THEOREM, not a claim.

      Linux: ~30,000,000 lines. Proving it is not a funding problem;
      it is a category problem. That size difference IS the argument.


   EXOKERNEL: REMOVE THE ABSTRACTION, NOT JUST THE POLICY

   CONVENTIONAL                     EXOKERNEL
   +---------------------+          +---------------------+
   | app                 |          | app + libOS         |  app picks
   +---------------------+          | (its own paging,    |  its OWN
   | OS abstractions:    |          |  its own fs layout, |  abstractions
   | files, processes,   |          |  its own scheduling)|
   | sockets, VM policy  |          +---------------------+
   +---------------------+          | exokernel: securely |
   | hardware            |          | MULTIPLEX hardware  |  nothing else
   +---------------------+          +---------------------+
                                    | hardware            |
   one policy for everyone          +---------------------+
   (a database fights the
    page cache constantly)          each app gets the policy it wants

   Where this actually shipped:
     io_uring   -- bypass per-syscall overhead, app drives the queue
     DPDK/SPDK  -- userspace owns the NIC/SSD queues entirely
     eBPF       -- app-supplied policy, verified, run IN the kernel
     unikernels -- the libOS idea, taken literally (Chapter 13)


   PLAN 9: "EVERYTHING IS A FILE" WITHOUT EXCEPTIONS

   UNIX stopped halfway.            Plan 9 did not.
   /dev/sda        a disk           /net/tcp/0/ctl     open a connection
   /proc/1/status  a process        /net/tcp/0/data    read/write it
   BUT:                             /dev/draw/...      the WINDOW SYSTEM
     sockets need socket()          /mnt/wsys/...      the GUI, as files
     GUI needs X protocol           /proc/1/mem        another process
     no per-process view            per-process NAMESPACE, mutable

   Networking with no networking API:
     % cat /net/tcp/clone           -> allocates a connection, says "3"
     % echo 'connect 10.0.0.1!80' > /net/tcp/3/ctl
     % echo 'GET / HTTP/1.0' > /net/tcp/3/data
     % cat /net/tcp/3/data
   No sockets. No new syscalls. open/read/write, all the way down.

   And because 9P makes remote resources mount identically:
     mount a REMOTE machine's /net and use ITS network stack
     as if it were local. Distribution for free.

   Every container on earth uses the namespace idea. Almost nobody
   remembers where it came from.
```

```c
/* seL4: capabilities instead of ambient authority. A thread can do
 * exactly what its capability space contains -- there is no "root",
 * and no way to name an object you were not given. */

/* Send a message on an endpoint. The capability IS the permission:
 * possessing ep_cap is the only way to send here. */
seL4_MessageInfo_t info = seL4_MessageInfo_new(
        0,      /* label: application-defined operation code */
        0,      /* capsUnwrapped */
        0,      /* extraCaps: capabilities to transfer with the message */
        1);     /* length: one machine word of payload */

seL4_SetMR(0, 42);                   /* message register 0 = payload.
                                      * Small messages travel in CPU
                                      * REGISTERS -- this is the trick
                                      * that made L4-family IPC fast. */
seL4_Call(ep_cap, info);             /* send + block for the reply */

/* Grant a subset of authority to a child: derive a WEAKER capability.
 * Authority can only ever be narrowed, never widened, so there is no
 * privilege-escalation path of the setuid kind (Chapter 12). */
seL4_CNode_Mint(
    dest_root, dest_index, dest_depth,
    src_root,  src_index,  src_depth,
    seL4_CanWrite,                   /* strictly fewer rights than ours */
    badge);                          /* the receiver sees this badge, so
                                      * it can tell callers apart */
```

```bash
# Research ideas you can run today.

# --- Exokernel descendants: the app drives the hardware queues ---
# io_uring: submit and complete without a syscall per operation
#   (the exokernel argument, applied to the syscall boundary)
grep io_uring_setup /proc/kallsyms | head -1
sudo fio --ioengine=io_uring --name=t --rw=randread --bs=4k \
         --filename=/dev/nvme0n1 --runtime=10 --numjobs=4
# compare --ioengine=psync: same hardware, different kernel involvement

# --- eBPF: app-supplied, VERIFIED policy running inside the kernel ---
sudo bpftrace -e 'kprobe:vfs_read { @[comm] = count(); }'
#   The verifier proves termination and memory safety BEFORE loading --
#   the same "prove it, then trust it" idea as seL4, at a smaller scale.

# --- Plan 9 namespaces, which you already use as containers ---
sudo unshare --mount --pid --fork --mount-proc bash
#   You now have your own namespace -- Plan 9's central idea, arriving
#   in Linux roughly 20 years later (Chapter 13).

# --- Plan 9 itself, and 9P, are still runnable ---
#   9P is a supported Linux filesystem: it is how many VMs share
#   directories with the host.
grep 9p /proc/filesystems
#   nodev   9p            <- Plan 9's protocol, in your kernel, today

# --- seL4 and modern microkernels ---
#   seL4: https://sel4.systems -- builds and runs under QEMU
#   Fuchsia (Zircon): capability-based, ships on Nest Hub devices
#   Redox: a Rust microkernel OS, boots under QEMU
```

**Key takeaways**

- Research operating systems are judged by which ideas migrate, not by deployment share, and the typical lag from paper to production is 10-25 years.
- Mach showed that services can live outside the kernel but that IPC cost dominates, which produced hybrid kernels like XNU rather than pure microkernels.
- L4 demonstrated that microkernel IPC was slow by implementation rather than by nature, achieving a 10-20x improvement through minimality and cache-conscious design.
- seL4 is formally verified: a machine-checked proof that its 10,000 lines of C match a specification and enforce its isolation properties, which is feasible only because it is small.
- Exokernel argued the kernel should securely multiplex hardware and let applications supply their own abstractions, an idea now visible in io_uring, DPDK/SPDK, eBPF, and unikernels.
- Plan 9 applied "everything is a file" without exception, giving each process a mutable namespace and exposing the network and window system as files.
- Per-process namespaces, `/proc`, 9P, and UTF-8 all came from Plan 9, and namespaces are the foundation of every Linux container.
- Singularity explored isolation through type safety and verified managed code rather than hardware protection, an approach WebAssembly now echoes.
- Barrelfish modelled a many-core machine as a distributed system with one kernel per core, anticipating that cache coherence would not scale indefinitely.
- Reading research systems is how you distinguish constraints that are fundamental from ones that are merely conventional.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. For each of Mach, Exokernel, and Plan 9, name one mechanism in a system you use daily that descends from it, and explain the connection in a sentence.
> 2. Explain why seL4 can be formally verified while Linux cannot, in terms of a specific quantitative property rather than effort or funding.
> 3. Use `unshare` to create a private mount and PID namespace, then describe what Plan 9 idea you have just reproduced and what Plan 9 additionally offered that Linux does not.
> 4. Benchmark the same random-read workload with `fio` using the `psync` and `io_uring` engines. Explain the difference in exokernel terms.
> 5. Interview-style: "Microkernels were supposed to win and did not. Was the idea wrong?" *Hint: separate the concept from a single 1980s implementation, and ask where microkernels are in fact deployed today and why those domains chose them.*

<a id="152-performance-analysis"></a>
### 15.2 Performance Analysis

Knowing how an operating system works is only half of the skill; the other half is determining, from a running system, which of its mechanisms is currently the limit. This section covers the metrics worth trusting, the tracing tools that answer questions profiling cannot, a repeatable method for finding bottlenecks, the arithmetic of planning capacity before the system saturates, and the tunable parameters worth touching once you have evidence.

#### System Metrics and Profiling

**Theory**

"The system is slow" is not a measurement. Turning it into one requires knowing which numbers mean something, and — more importantly — which popular numbers do not.

Start with the most misleading metric of all. **CPU utilisation** does not measure work done; it measures time not idle. A CPU stalled waiting for DRAM is counted 100% busy while retiring almost no instructions. On a memory-bound workload, "100% CPU" frequently means "100% waiting for memory", and adding CPUs will not help. The metric worth using alongside it is **IPC** (instructions per cycle): below roughly 1.0 suggests a stall-bound workload, above roughly 2.0 suggests genuine compute.

**Load average** is misunderstood almost as often. On Linux it counts processes that are running *or in uninterruptible sleep* (disk wait), averaged over 1, 5, and 15 minutes — so heavy disk I/O inflates it with no CPU shortage at all. A load of 8 on an 8-core machine may be perfect saturation or may be one runnable process and seven blocked on a failing disk.

Two frameworks organise the rest and are worth memorising.

**The USE method** (Brendan Gregg), for *resources*: for every resource, check **Utilisation**, **Saturation**, and **Errors**. Utilisation is the fraction of time busy; saturation is the degree of queued extra work; errors are failed operations. Saturation is the one people skip and the one that matters — a disk at 100% utilisation with no queue is fine, while a disk at 60% utilisation with a deep queue is not.

**The RED method**, for *services*: **Rate** (requests per second), **Errors** (failed requests), **Duration** (the latency distribution). USE tells you which resource hurts; RED tells you whether users notice.

For latency, **averages are nearly useless**. Latency distributions are right-skewed and often multi-modal (cache hit versus cache miss), so the mean describes nobody's experience. Use percentiles — p50, p95, p99, p99.9 — and remember that tail latency compounds: a page making 20 backend calls sees its p99 with probability roughly 1 − 0.99²⁰ ≈ 18% of requests. The tail *is* the user experience at scale.

One measurement bug deserves naming: **coordinated omission**. A load generator that waits for each response before sending the next stops sending requests exactly when the system stalls, so the stall is never measured. The results look excellent precisely because the worst behaviour was omitted. Fix it by sending at a fixed rate and measuring latency from *intended* send time (`wrk2`, and Gil Tene's work on this, exist for exactly this reason).

Finally, **profiling**. **Sampling profilers** (`perf record`) interrupt periodically and record the stack, giving statistical coverage at low overhead — the default choice. **Instrumenting profilers** insert counters at every function, giving exact counts but distorting timing and often changing the behaviour they measure. **Flame graphs** are the standard visualisation: stacks are collapsed, sorted alphabetically, and drawn as nested rectangles whose *width is time spent* — a wide plateau is where the CPU actually is. And a crucial complement: a normal profiler shows only **on-CPU** time, so a process blocked on a lock or disk is invisible. **Off-CPU analysis** samples what threads block on and is how you find the other half of the latency.

**Example**

```text
   THE FOUR METRICS THAT MISLEAD

   1. CPU UTILISATION: "busy" != "working"
      +--------------------------------------------+
      | 100% CPU, IPC = 0.3   -> stalled on MEMORY  |
      | 100% CPU, IPC = 2.4   -> actually computing |
      +--------------------------------------------+
      Same top(1) output. Completely different fix:
      the first needs better data layout, NOT more cores.

   2. LOAD AVERAGE (Linux): running + UNINTERRUPTIBLE SLEEP
      load 8.0 on 8 cores could be:
        - 8 CPU-bound threads      -> perfect saturation
        - 1 thread + 7 stuck on a dying disk -> a storage incident
      The number cannot distinguish them. Look at run queue vs iowait.

   3. AVERAGE LATENCY: describes nobody
      requests: 90 x 10ms, 9 x 100ms, 1 x 2000ms
      mean = 30 ms      <- no request took 30 ms
      p50  = 10 ms   p99 = 2000 ms
      The mean hid a 2-second outlier completely.

   4. "AVAILABILITY 99.9%": over what window, measured by whom?
      99.9% monthly = 43 minutes down. In one outage or 43 one-minute
      blips? Users experience those very differently.


   USE METHOD: A CHECKLIST, NOT AN INTUITION

   for EVERY resource:  Utilisation | Saturation | Errors
   ------------------------------------------------------------
   CPU        %busy, IPC    | runqueue len, PSI  | throttles, MCE
   Memory     %used         | swap/compress rate,| OOM kills
                            | PSI, page scanning |
   Disk       %util         | avgqu-sz, await    | I/O errors, SMART
   Network    bytes/s vs    | dropped, retrans,  | errors, CRC
              link speed    | backlog
   ------------------------------------------------------------
   SATURATION is the column people skip and the one that predicts pain:
     disk 100% util, queue depth 1  -> fine, just always busy
     disk  60% util, queue depth 40 -> everyone is waiting

   RED METHOD (per service): Rate | Errors | Duration(p50/p99/p999)
   USE finds the sick RESOURCE; RED says whether USERS feel it.


   FLAME GRAPH: WIDTH IS TIME, NOT CALL COUNT

                              [all]
        +----------------------+--------------------------+
        |      http_handler (62%)          | gc (21%)| ...|
     +--+-----------+-----------+           +--------+
     | parse_json(41%)          | db_query  |
     +-------+--------+         +-----------+
     | utf8  | alloc  |
     +-------+--------+
             ^^^^^^^^
     Read it BOTTOM-UP for ancestry, and look for the widest
     PLATEAU: parse_json at 41% of all CPU time is the answer.
     x-axis is alphabetical, NOT time -- do not read it left to right.


   COORDINATED OMISSION: THE BUG IN YOUR BENCHMARK

   BAD (closed loop): send -> wait for reply -> send -> ...
     t=0    send req1
     t=0.01 reply. send req2
     t=0.02 SERVER STALLS FOR 5 SECONDS
     t=5.02 reply to req2 (5 s). send req3...
     Recorded: 1 slow request.
     Reality:  during those 5 s a real user base would have sent
               500 requests, ALL of which would have been slow.
     The generator stopped sending exactly when it mattered.

   GOOD (open loop, fixed rate): send at 100/s REGARDLESS of replies,
     and measure latency from the INTENDED send time.
     Recorded: 500 slow requests. Which is the truth.


   ON-CPU vs OFF-CPU: TWO HALVES OF THE SAME LATENCY

   request latency = 200 ms
     on-CPU  |###|                       30 ms  <- what perf shows
     off-CPU     |####################|  170 ms <- INVISIBLE to perf
                  waiting on: lock 120 ms, disk 50 ms

   Profiling alone would send you optimising the 30 ms.
```

```bash
# ---- The 60-second first pass (Netflix's checklist) ----
uptime                    # load averages: trend over 1/5/15 min
dmesg -T | tail -20       # OOM kills, disk errors, TCP drops
vmstat 1 5                # r (runqueue), si/so (swap), us/sy/id/wa
mpstat -P ALL 1 3         # per-CPU: is ONE core pinned? (single-threaded)
pidstat 1 3               # which processes, on/off CPU
iostat -xz 1 3            # per-disk: %util, avgqu-sz, await
free -m                   # memory and, critically, buff/cache
sar -n DEV 1 3            # network throughput vs link capacity
sar -n TCP,ETCP 1 3       # retransmits, connection failures
top                       # the overview, read LAST not first

# ---- Utilisation is not work: check IPC ----
perf stat -a sleep 10
#   12,345,678,901  cycles
#    3,456,789,012  instructions   #  0.28 insn per cycle  <-- STALLED
#   ^ IPC 0.28 means ~3.5 cycles per instruction: memory-bound.
#     More cores will not help; better locality will.

# ---- Saturation, the column that predicts pain ----
cat /proc/pressure/cpu /proc/pressure/io /proc/pressure/memory
#   some avg10=42.11 avg60=38.05 ...   <- PSI: % of time tasks STALLED
#   full avg10=12.00 ...               <- ALL tasks stalled
#   PSI is a far better saturation signal than utilisation (Chapter 13).

# ---- Sampling profile + flame graph ----
sudo perf record -F 99 -a -g -- sleep 30     # 99 Hz, all CPUs, callgraphs
sudo perf script | stackcollapse-perf.pl | flamegraph.pl > cpu.svg
#   -F 99 (not 100) avoids sampling in lockstep with periodic timers

# ---- The other half: OFF-CPU time ----
sudo offcputime-bpfcc -df 30 | flamegraph.pl --color=io > offcpu.svg
#   Shows WHERE threads blocked and for how long: locks, disk, network.
sudo wakeuptime-bpfcc 10      # who WOKE the blocked thread (the culprit)
```

```python
# Why percentiles, and why the tail dominates at scale.

import random, statistics

def simulate(n=100_000):
    out = []
    for _ in range(n):
        r = random.random()
        if   r < 0.90: out.append(random.gauss(10, 2))    # cache hit
        elif r < 0.99: out.append(random.gauss(100, 20))  # cache miss
        else:          out.append(random.gauss(1500, 300))# lock + retry
    return sorted(x for x in out if x > 0)

lat = simulate()
pct = lambda q: lat[int(len(lat) * q)]
print(f"mean {statistics.mean(lat):7.1f} ms   <- describes NOBODY")
print(f"p50  {pct(0.50):7.1f}   p95 {pct(0.95):7.1f}")
print(f"p99  {pct(0.99):7.1f}   p999 {pct(0.999):7.1f}")
# mean   35.0 ms  <- between the modes: a value no request ever had
# p50    10.0     p95   103.2
# p99  1436.8     p999 2107.4

# TAIL AMPLIFICATION: one page = many backend calls.
for calls in (1, 10, 20, 100):
    p = 1 - 0.99 ** calls          # chance at least one call is p99-slow
    print(f"{calls:3d} backend calls -> {p:5.1%} of PAGES hit the p99 tail")
#   1 ->  1.0%    10 -> 9.6%    20 -> 18.2%    100 -> 63.4%
#
# At 100 fan-out, nearly two thirds of page loads contain a p99 call.
# This is why the p99 of a backend IS the p50 experience of a product,
# and why "only 1% are slow" is not a reassuring sentence.

# COORDINATED OMISSION, demonstrated:
def closed_loop(stall_s=5.0, rate=100):
    # Waits for each reply, so during the stall it sends NOTHING.
    return [stall_s * 1000]                       # 1 slow sample
def open_loop(stall_s=5.0, rate=100):
    # Keeps sending at a fixed rate; every request queued behind the
    # stall is also slow, measured from its INTENDED send time.
    return [(stall_s - i / rate) * 1000 for i in range(int(stall_s * rate))]
print(len(closed_loop()), "vs", len(open_loop()), "slow samples recorded")
# 1 vs 500 -- the same outage, two benchmarks, opposite conclusions.
```

**Key takeaways**

- CPU utilisation measures time not idle, not work performed; pair it with IPC, where below roughly 1.0 indicates a stall-bound workload that more cores will not fix.
- Linux load average counts uninterruptible sleep as well as runnable tasks, so disk problems inflate it without any CPU shortage.
- The USE method checks utilisation, saturation, and errors for every resource, and saturation is both the most skipped and the most predictive column.
- The RED method checks rate, errors, and duration per service; USE identifies the sick resource while RED shows whether users feel it.
- Latency distributions are skewed and often multi-modal, so averages describe no real request and percentiles are required.
- Tail latency amplifies with fan-out: at 20 backend calls roughly 18% of requests encounter a p99-slow call, so a backend's p99 becomes the product's typical experience.
- Coordinated omission makes closed-loop benchmarks stop sending exactly during a stall, hiding the worst behaviour; fixed-rate load with latency measured from intended send time fixes it.
- Sampling profilers are the low-overhead default; instrumenting profilers give exact counts but distort the timing they measure.
- Flame graph width is time spent and the x-axis is alphabetical, so the widest plateau — not the leftmost stack — is the target.
- On-CPU profiling misses time spent blocked, so off-CPU analysis is required to find latency caused by locks, disk, and network waits.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. Run `perf stat -a sleep 10` on an idle machine and again under a CPU-heavy workload. Report the IPC in each case and say whether the workload is stall-bound or compute-bound.
> 2. Generate a bimodal latency distribution in a script, then compute the mean, p50, p99, and p99.9. Explain in one sentence why reporting the mean to a stakeholder would be misleading.
> 3. Record a flame graph of any CPU-heavy process on your machine, identify the widest plateau, and explain why the x-axis ordering carries no meaning.
> 4. A page makes 30 backend calls, each with a 99.5th-percentile latency of 400 ms. Compute the fraction of page loads containing at least one such call.
> 5. Interview-style: "Our dashboard shows CPU at 100%, so we are scaling out. Reasonable?" *Hint: ask what the IPC and run-queue length are, and what would happen to both if you doubled the core count.*

#### Tracing and Instrumentation

**Theory**

Profiling answers "where is time being spent?" statistically. Tracing answers the questions profiling cannot: *which* file was slow, *which* process issued that syscall, *why* did this one request take 4 seconds when the average is 8 ms. A profiler samples; a tracer records events with their arguments and timestamps.

The distinction that organises everything is **static versus dynamic** instrumentation.

**Static tracepoints** are put in the source by its authors at points deemed interesting — Linux has thousands (`sched:sched_switch`, `block:block_rq_issue`, `syscalls:sys_enter_*`), and userspace can add **USDT** probes. They are stable across versions, documented, and nearly free when disabled, but you only get the points someone chose to expose.

**Dynamic instrumentation** (`kprobes` for the kernel, `uprobes` for userspace) can attach to *almost any instruction address* at runtime by patching in a breakpoint. Total freedom, at the cost of stability: you are attaching to internal functions whose names and arguments change between releases.

The historical arc is worth knowing because it explains today's tooling. **DTrace** (Sun, 2005) was the breakthrough — safe, production-grade, dynamic, whole-system tracing with a small language — and it was the first to make "just instrument production" a reasonable sentence. Linux's answer arrived piecemeal (`ftrace`, `perf`, SystemTap) until **eBPF** unified it: a verified, JIT-compiled VM in the kernel that attaches programs to tracepoints, kprobes, uprobes, and more, and aggregates *in the kernel* rather than shipping every event to userspace. That last property is the important one — computing a histogram in kernel space costs a fraction of emitting a million events for userspace to parse.

Overhead is the governing constraint, and the difference between tools is enormous:

| Tool | Mechanism | Typical overhead | Production safe |
|---|---|---|---|
| `strace` | `ptrace`, two stops per syscall | 100-500x on syscall-heavy code | No |
| `ltrace` | Library call interception | Similarly severe | No |
| `perf record` | Sampling interrupts | 1-5% at 99 Hz | Yes |
| `ftrace` | In-kernel ring buffer | 1-5% | Yes |
| `bpftrace`/BCC | eBPF, in-kernel aggregation | Under 1% for most probes | Yes |

`strace` deserves the warning explicitly: it stops the traced process twice per syscall, and on a syscall-heavy program it can slow execution by two orders of magnitude — enough to change the behaviour you were investigating, and enough to cause an outage if applied to a production database. Use it on a test instance or use eBPF instead.

The other major use is **distributed tracing**, which extends the idea across machines. A request is given a **trace ID** at entry, each service records **spans** (start, end, parent, attributes), and a collector reassembles the causal tree. This is the only practical way to answer "which of these 40 services made that request slow", and it exists because a single machine's profile cannot see a call it made to another machine. **OpenTelemetry** is the current standard for the instrumentation API and wire format.

**Example**

```text
   PROFILING vs TRACING: DIFFERENT QUESTIONS

   PROFILER (sampling)                TRACER (events)
   "44% of CPU is in parse_json"      "THIS request called parse_json
   statistical, cheap, lossy           3,412 times, 2 of which took
   answers WHERE                       800 ms, on file X, from pid Y"
                                       exact, per-event, answers WHICH
                                       and WHY

   Use a profiler for: steady-state CPU cost.
   Use a tracer for:   rare events, outliers, causality, arguments.
   The 4-second request in a system with an 8 ms average is a
   TRACING problem -- it will never show up in a profile.


   THE INSTRUMENTATION POINTS AVAILABLE TO YOU

   USER SPACE
     application  --- USDT probes (author-placed, stable)
                  --- uprobes    (any function, any address; unstable)
     libraries    --- uprobes on libc: malloc, read, ...
   ------------------------------------------------ syscall boundary
   KERNEL
     syscalls     --- tracepoints: syscalls:sys_enter_openat  (STABLE)
     scheduler    --- tracepoints: sched:sched_switch, sched_wakeup
     block layer  --- tracepoints: block:block_rq_issue/complete
     network      --- tracepoints + kprobes: tcp_retransmit_skb
     ANY function --- kprobes (attach to ~any address; UNSTABLE)
   ------------------------------------------------
   HARDWARE
     PMU counters --- cycles, instructions, cache-misses, LLC-load-miss

   STATIC (tracepoints/USDT)     DYNAMIC (kprobes/uprobes)
   stable across releases        may break on any kernel update
   documented arguments          you must read the source for args
   only what authors exposed     anything you can name
   ~zero cost when off           ~zero cost when off


   WHY eBPF AGGREGATES IN THE KERNEL

   OLD WAY (strace / naive tracing)
     kernel event -> copy to userspace -> parse -> count
     1,000,000 events/s x (context switch + copy + parse)
     = the tool costs more than the workload

   eBPF WAY
     kernel event -> eBPF program runs IN KERNEL -> increments a
                     map entry (a histogram bucket)
     userspace reads the finished HISTOGRAM once per second
     = 1,000,000 events cost ~1,000,000 map increments, and
       userspace sees ~50 numbers

   This is the entire reason eBPF tracing is production-safe
   and strace is not.


   DISTRIBUTED TRACING: THE ONLY VIEW THAT CROSSES MACHINES

   trace_id = 7f3a...   (generated at the edge, propagated in headers)

   |------------------------ gateway 840 ms -----------------------|
      |--- auth 12 ms ---|
      |------------------ cart 810 ms -----------------------|
           |-- db query 30 ms --|
           |------------- inventory 760 ms ------------|
                 |-- redis 2 ms --|
                 |---------- db: LOCK WAIT 740 ms ----------|
                                  ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
                                  the answer, four services deep

   No single machine's profile could have found this: from the
   gateway's view it is "cart was slow", and cart's own CPU profile
   shows it doing nothing at all -- it was BLOCKED (off-CPU).
```

```bash
# ---- bpftrace: a tracing language in one line ----

# 1. Which processes are opening which files?
sudo bpftrace -e 'tracepoint:syscalls:sys_enter_openat {
    printf("%-16s %s\n", comm, str(args->filename)); }'

# 2. Syscall latency as an in-kernel HISTOGRAM (log2 buckets).
#    Note: no per-event data ever crosses to userspace.
sudo bpftrace -e '
  tracepoint:syscalls:sys_enter_read  { @start[tid] = nsecs; }
  tracepoint:syscalls:sys_exit_read /@start[tid]/ {
      @us = hist((nsecs - @start[tid]) / 1000);   // aggregate in kernel
      delete(@start[tid]);
  }'
#   @us:
#   [1]        4213 |@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@|
#   [2, 4)     1102 |@@@@@@@@@@                              |
#   [1K, 2K)     18 |                                        |  <- the tail
#   [8K, 16K)     3 |                                        |  <- outliers
#   The shape is the answer: bimodal means two different code paths.

# 3. Who is causing disk I/O, with size and latency?
sudo biolatency-bpfcc 10 1        # block I/O latency histogram
sudo biosnoop-bpfcc               # per-I/O: pid, disk, sector, ms
sudo ext4slower-bpfcc 10          # only ext4 ops slower than 10 ms
                                  # ^ the "show me only outliers" idiom

# 4. Off-CPU: why is a thread not running?
sudo offcputime-bpfcc -p $(pgrep -n myapp) 30

# 5. Dynamic instrumentation of an arbitrary kernel function:
sudo bpftrace -e 'kprobe:vfs_read { @[kstack] = count(); }'
sudo bpftrace -l 'tracepoint:*' | wc -l     # thousands of stable points
sudo bpftrace -l 'kprobe:tcp_*' | head      # everything attachable

# 6. Userspace dynamic tracing (uprobes) -- no recompilation needed:
sudo bpftrace -e 'uprobe:/usr/lib/libssl.so:SSL_write {
    printf("%s wrote %d bytes\n", comm, arg2); }'
```

```bash

cd /sys/kernel/tracing

# Function graph: see the call tree WITH durations.
echo function_graph > current_tracer
echo vfs_read > set_graph_function
echo 1 > tracing_on; sleep 1; echo 0 > tracing_on
head -30 trace
#   CPU  DURATION      FUNCTION CALLS
#   0)               |  vfs_read() {
#   0)   0.213 us    |    rw_verify_area();
#   0) + 18.442 us   |    ext4_file_read_iter();   <- '+' = over 10 us
#   0) ! 142.881 us  |  }                          <- '!' = over 100 us

echo nop > current_tracer          # ALWAYS turn it off afterwards

# ---- strace: correct, and dangerous ----
strace -c -p 1234        # SUMMARY mode: counts and time per syscall
#   % time  seconds  usecs/call  calls  errors syscall
#   62.11  0.451200        112   4028      12 futex     <- lock contention
#   21.34  0.155000          9  17222         read
strace -T -e trace=openat,read ./app 2>&1 | head
#   -T shows time spent IN each call

#   WARNING: ptrace stops the process TWICE per syscall. On a busy
#   server this is a 100-500x slowdown and can cause an outage.
#   The eBPF equivalent, at <1% overhead:
sudo syscount-bpfcc -p 1234        # same summary, production-safe
```

```python
# Distributed tracing: propagate context, record spans.
from opentelemetry import trace
from opentelemetry.propagate import inject, extract
import requests

tracer = trace.get_tracer(__name__)

def handle_checkout(request):
    # Continue the trace the caller started (context arrives in headers),
    # rather than starting a new, disconnected one.
    ctx = extract(request.headers)

    with tracer.start_as_current_span("checkout", context=ctx) as span:
        # Attributes make spans searchable: "show me slow spans where
        # cart_size > 50" is the query that finds real bugs.
        span.set_attribute("user.tier", request.user.tier)
        span.set_attribute("cart.size", len(request.cart))

        with tracer.start_as_current_span("inventory.check"):
            headers = {}
            inject(headers)          # propagate trace_id + span_id
            r = requests.get("http://inventory/check",
                             headers=headers, timeout=2.0)

        with tracer.start_as_current_span("payment.charge") as pay:
            try:
                charge(request.cart)
            except PaymentError as e:
                pay.record_exception(e)
                pay.set_status(trace.StatusCode.ERROR)   # errors are
                raise                                    # searchable too

# Sampling matters: tracing every request at scale is unaffordable.
# Head sampling (decide at entry, e.g. 1%) is cheap but may miss the
# rare slow request entirely. TAIL sampling buffers spans and keeps
# traces that were slow or errored -- more expensive, far more useful,
# because the interesting traces are by definition the rare ones.
```

**Key takeaways**

- Profiling answers where time goes statistically; tracing records individual events with arguments and timestamps, which is the only way to explain a rare outlier.
- Static tracepoints and USDT probes are author-placed, stable, and documented; kprobes and uprobes attach dynamically to almost any address but break across releases.
- DTrace established safe production-wide dynamic tracing, and eBPF is the Linux realisation of the same idea with a verifier and a JIT.
- eBPF aggregates inside the kernel, so a million events become a histogram rather than a million userspace copies, which is precisely why it is production-safe.
- `strace` stops the process twice per syscall and can slow it by 100-500x, changing the behaviour under investigation and risking an outage.
- `perf record`, `ftrace`, and eBPF tools run at a few percent or less and are appropriate on production systems.
- Histogram shape carries information: a bimodal latency distribution usually means two distinct code paths, such as cache hit versus miss.
- Filtering tools that emit only outliers (`ext4slower`, `biosnoop`) are the practical way to catch rare slow events without recording everything.
- Distributed tracing propagates a trace ID and records parent-linked spans, which is the only way to attribute latency across service boundaries.
- Tail-based sampling retains slow and errored traces rather than a uniform fraction, which matters because the interesting traces are by definition rare.
