#### Bottleneck Identification

**Theory**

A system has exactly one bottleneck at a time — the resource that, if improved, improves the whole. Everything else is slack. The discipline is finding it rather than guessing, because intuition is reliably wrong: the code you suspect is rarely the code that is slow, and the resource showing the most alarming number is often a symptom of a different one.

The most common error is **optimising the wrong thing**, which **Amdahl's law** quantifies. If a fraction *p* of the runtime is improved by factor *s*, overall speedup is `1 / ((1 − p) + p/s)`. Make a component that is 5% of runtime infinitely fast and you gain 5.3%. Halve a component that is 80% and you gain 67%. The corollary: measure the proportion before you optimise, because the ceiling is set by the proportion, not by how clever the optimisation is.

The second error is confusing symptoms with causes. High CPU can be caused by a memory problem (cache misses stalling execution), by a disk problem (a busy-wait retry loop), by a lock problem (spinning), or by genuine compute. High iowait can be caused by a memory problem (reclaim pressure forcing page-outs). The USE method resists this by making you check every resource rather than following the first alarming number.

A practical taxonomy, with the signature of each:

| Bottleneck | Signature | Confirm with | Typical fix |
|---|---|---|---|
| **CPU-bound (compute)** | High %usr, IPC > 1.5, run queue > cores | `perf stat`, flame graph | Better algorithm; parallelise |
| **CPU-bound (stalled)** | High %usr, IPC < 1.0, high cache-miss | `perf stat -e cache-misses` | Data layout, locality, prefetch |
| **Memory-capacity** | Swap/compression activity, high PSI memory, page scanning | `vmstat`, `/proc/pressure/memory` | Add RAM; reduce footprint |
| **Disk-bound** | High `await`, deep `avgqu-sz`, high %iowait | `iostat -xz`, `biolatency` | Caching, batching, faster device |
| **Network-bound** | Throughput at link ceiling, retransmits | `sar -n DEV,ETCP`, `ss -ti` | Compression, batching, locality |
| **Lock-bound** | Low CPU, low disk, high latency, `futex` time | `offcputime`, `strace -c` | Shrink critical sections; shard |
| **Single-threaded** | One core at 100%, others idle | `mpstat -P ALL` | Parallelise; shard the work |

The last two are the ones people miss, because they look like *nothing* is wrong: the machine is mostly idle and everything is slow. That combination — low utilisation everywhere plus high latency — almost always means waiting, and off-CPU analysis is the tool.

Two laws structure the reasoning. **Little's law**: `L = λW` (items in system = arrival rate × time in system). It is remarkably useful for sanity-checking — if a service handles 1,000 req/s with 50 ms average latency, there are on average 50 requests in flight, so a connection pool of 20 is itself the bottleneck. And the **queueing response-time curve**: as utilisation ρ approaches 1, waiting time grows as roughly `1/(1 − ρ)`. At 50% utilisation the queue adds 1x the service time; at 90% it adds 9x; at 99%, 99x. This is why systems appear to fall off a cliff — they do not; the curve was always a hyperbola, and load merely walked up it.

The method itself, in order: characterise the workload (what is it actually doing?), apply USE across all resources, form a hypothesis, test it by changing *one* thing, and measure again. Then repeat — because fixing a bottleneck does not eliminate bottlenecks, it moves them.

**Example**

```text
   AMDAHL'S LAW: THE CEILING IS SET BY THE PROPORTION

   speedup = 1 / ((1 - p) + p/s)

   optimise a part that is...   make it 2x     make it INFINITE
   ---------------------------------------------------------------
    5% of runtime                1.03x          1.05x   <- pointless
   20% of runtime                1.11x          1.25x
   50% of runtime                1.33x          2.00x
   80% of runtime                1.67x          5.00x   <- the target
   95% of runtime                1.90x         20.00x

   The lesson is not "optimise more", it is "MEASURE THE PROPORTION
   FIRST". A brilliant 100x optimisation of 5% of runtime is worth
   less than a lazy 2x of 80%.


   THE RESPONSE-TIME CURVE: WHY SYSTEMS "SUDDENLY" COLLAPSE

   response
   time
     |                                            *
     |                                          *
     |                                        *
     |                                     *
     |                                 *
     |                           *
     |                  *
     |        *  *  *
     +----------------------------------------------> utilisation
     0%      50%       70%    80%   90%  95%  99%

   W = S / (1 - rho)      (M/M/1, service time S)
     rho=0.5 -> 2x S       rho=0.9 -> 10x S
     rho=0.7 -> 3.3x S     rho=0.95-> 20x S
     rho=0.8 -> 5x S       rho=0.99-> 100x S

   Going 90% -> 99% utilisation is "10% more work" and 10x the
   latency. Nothing broke. The curve was always this shape.
   This is WHY the operational rule is to stay near 70%.


   SYMPTOM vs CAUSE: THE SAME SIGNAL, FOUR DISEASES

   "CPU is at 100%"
     |
     +-- IPC 2.4, high %usr      -> genuinely computing       -> algorithm
     +-- IPC 0.3, cache-misses   -> STALLED ON MEMORY         -> layout
     +-- high %sys, futex calls  -> SPINNING ON A LOCK        -> shard it
     +-- high %sys, many reads   -> syscall overhead          -> batch it

   Same top(1). Four different fixes. Three of them do not
   involve making the code "faster" at all.


   THE BOTTLENECK NOBODY SEES: EVERYTHING IDLE, EVERYTHING SLOW

   CPU  ~8% busy        disk ~2% util       net ~1%
   latency p99 = 3.2 s

   No resource is saturated, so USE finds nothing. The work is
   not RUNNING -- it is WAITING:

   sudo offcputime-bpfcc -df 30 | flamegraph.pl
     futex_wait  ############################  2.9 s   <- a lock
     io_schedule ###                           0.2 s

   Low utilisation + high latency == waiting. Always go off-CPU.


   LITTLE'S LAW AS A SANITY CHECK:  L = lambda * W

   service does 1,000 req/s, average latency 50 ms
   L = 1000 * 0.050 = 50 requests IN FLIGHT on average

   connection pool size = 20   ->  the POOL is the bottleneck;
                                   requests queue for a connection
                                   before the server is even involved
   thread pool = 200           ->  fine
   db connections = 10         ->  the database link is the limit

   One multiplication finds capacity bugs that load tests take
   hours to reproduce.
```

```bash
# ---- A worked bottleneck hunt, in the order you should do it ----

# STEP 1: characterise. What is the system actually doing?
uptime; vmstat 1 5; mpstat -P ALL 1 3
#   r  b   swpd  free  buff  cache   si so   bi   bo  in   cs us sy id wa
#   1  9      0  2.1G   80M   9.8G    0  0  142  980 4.2k 18k  9  4 12 75
#      ^                                                          ^^^^^
#      9 blocked                                                  75% iowait
#   Hypothesis: disk-bound, not CPU-bound. us+sy = 13%.

# STEP 2: USE the suspected resource.
iostat -xz 1 3
#   Device  r/s    w/s   rkB/s  %util  aqu-sz  r_await  w_await
#   nvme0n1 180   2400   720    99.2    38.4     2.1     41.7
#                                ^^^^    ^^^^              ^^^^
#            utilisation 99%, QUEUE DEPTH 38, writes waiting 42 ms
#   Saturation confirmed: it is not merely busy, work is QUEUED.

# STEP 3: attribute it. WHO is issuing the I/O?
sudo biosnoop-bpfcc | head -20
#   TIME     COMM        PID    DISK   T SECTOR    BYTES  LAT(ms)
#   0.000    postgres    8812   nvme0n1 W 41288    8192   38.42
#   0.004    postgres    8812   nvme0n1 W 41304    8192   41.10
sudo biolatency-bpfcc 10 1       # is the device slow, or overloaded?
#   [16K, 32K) us  ####  -> the DEVICE is fine; the QUEUE is the delay

# STEP 4: is it really the disk, or memory pushing on the disk?
cat /proc/pressure/io /proc/pressure/memory
free -m; vmstat 1 3 | awk '{print $7, $8}'   # si/so: swap activity
#   If si/so are non-zero, the "disk problem" is a MEMORY problem
#   wearing a disk costume.

# STEP 5: the low-utilisation case -- everything idle, still slow.
sudo offcputime-bpfcc -df 30 > off.stacks
flamegraph.pl --color=io --title="Off-CPU" off.stacks > off.svg
sudo wakeuptime-bpfcc 10        # who WOKE the blocked thread = culprit

# STEP 6: change ONE thing, measure again, repeat.
#   Fixing a bottleneck does not remove bottlenecks -- it MOVES them.
#   Expect the next run to be limited by something else. That is
#   success, not failure.
```

```python
# The two laws, as tools you can actually run.

def amdahl(fraction_improved, speedup):
    """Ceiling on overall gain. Run this BEFORE starting the work."""
    p, s = fraction_improved, speedup
    return 1 / ((1 - p) + p / s)

print(f"{amdahl(0.05, 1e9):.2f}x")   # 1.05x  -- 5% of runtime, infinite
print(f"{amdahl(0.80, 2):.2f}x")     # 1.67x  -- 80% of runtime, merely 2x
# The lazy optimisation of the big thing beats the heroic one
# of the small thing. Every time.

def queue_wait(service_time_ms, utilisation):
    """M/M/1 response time. Shows the cliff that is not a cliff."""
    if utilisation >= 1: return float("inf")
    return service_time_ms / (1 - utilisation)

for rho in (0.5, 0.7, 0.8, 0.9, 0.95, 0.99):
    print(f"rho={rho:4.2f} -> {queue_wait(10, rho):7.1f} ms")
# rho=0.50 ->    20.0 ms
# rho=0.90 ->   100.0 ms      <- 10x the service time
# rho=0.99 ->  1000.0 ms      <- 100x. "10% more load" = 10x latency.

def littles_law(rate_per_s, latency_s):
    """L = lambda * W: how many requests are in flight right now?"""
    return rate_per_s * latency_s

in_flight = littles_law(1000, 0.050)          # 50 concurrent requests
print(f"in flight: {in_flight:.0f}")
for pool in (10, 20, 50, 100):
    verdict = "BOTTLENECK" if pool < in_flight else "adequate"
    print(f"  pool={pool:3d}: {verdict}")
# pool=10  BOTTLENECK    <- requests queue before reaching the server
# pool=20  BOTTLENECK
# pool=50  adequate      <- exactly at the limit: no headroom for spikes
# pool=100 adequate
```

**Key takeaways**

- A system has one bottleneck at a time, and fixing it moves the limit elsewhere rather than removing it — expect the next measurement to show a different constraint.
- Amdahl's law sets a ceiling from the proportion of runtime affected, so measuring the proportion must precede optimising; an infinite speedup of 5% of runtime yields 5%.
- High CPU can be genuine compute, memory stalls, lock spinning, or syscall overhead, and IPC plus cache-miss counters distinguish them.
- The signature of a lock or dependency bottleneck is low utilisation everywhere combined with high latency, which USE alone will not reveal.
- Off-CPU analysis is the tool for that case, and wakeup tracing identifies which thread caused the blocking.
- Little's law (`L = λW`) converts throughput and latency into concurrency, immediately exposing undersized connection and thread pools.
- The queueing response-time curve grows as `1/(1 − ρ)`, so 90% to 99% utilisation multiplies waiting time by ten for 10% more work.
- Systems do not suddenly collapse; the hyperbola was always there, and load merely moved along it, which is why 70% is the usual operational target.
- High iowait can be a memory problem, since reclaim pressure generates disk traffic — always check swap and memory pressure before blaming storage.
- The method is: characterise the workload, apply USE to every resource, hypothesise, change one thing, measure, repeat.

#### Capacity Planning

**Theory**

Capacity planning is the discipline of knowing, before it happens, when a system will run out of room — and deciding in advance what to do about it. The alternative is discovering it during an incident, which is both more expensive and much less pleasant.

The foundation is the queueing arithmetic from the previous topic, applied forward in time. Because response time rises as `1/(1 − ρ)`, **the usable capacity of a system is not 100% of its theoretical capacity**. A resource at 95% utilisation is technically working and practically unusable, since latency is 20x service time and any burst tips it over. The standard operating target is **70-80%**, which leaves the headroom that absorbs traffic spikes, tolerates the loss of an instance, and leaves time to react.

Planning proceeds in four steps.

**1. Characterise the workload.** What is a "request" here, and what does one cost? Requests are rarely uniform: a search query and an image upload are both requests and differ by orders of magnitude in cost. Useful characterisation records the mix, the rate, the variability (peak-to-mean ratio is often 3-10x for consumer traffic, with weekly and seasonal cycles), and the growth trend.

**2. Measure the cost per unit of work.** From production or a load test: CPU-seconds per request, bytes of memory per session, IOPS per transaction, bytes per response. This converts a business forecast ("we expect 3x users") into a resource forecast ("we will need 2.4x the IOPS").

**3. Model the limit.** Find which resource saturates first at the projected rate. The answer is frequently not the obvious one — memory per connection, file descriptors, database connections, a single-threaded component, or a network link often bind before CPU does. Little's law is the fastest way to check concurrency limits.

**4. Decide the scaling strategy.** **Vertical** scaling (a bigger machine) is simple, requires no code changes, and has a hard ceiling with poor failure characteristics. **Horizontal** scaling (more machines) has no ceiling but demands statelessness or partitioning, and introduces the coordination problems of Chapter 14. The **Universal Scalability Law** refines Amdahl by adding a *coherency* term: throughput rises, flattens, and then **falls** as more nodes are added, because cross-node coordination grows quadratically. That the curve turns downward is the important part — beyond some point, adding capacity actively reduces throughput.

Then there is the part that is not arithmetic. **Failure domains**: if you run three instances at 70% and lose one, the survivors need 105% — so N+1 planning means sizing for the post-failure load, not the steady state. Load tests must be **open-loop** (fixed arrival rate) to avoid coordinated omission, and must use realistic data, because a benchmark against an empty database measures nothing. And the result of all this should be written down as explicit thresholds — the utilisation at which you order hardware, the latency at which you page someone — because a plan nobody wrote down is a plan that will be improvised at 3 a.m.

**Example**

```text
   USABLE CAPACITY IS NOT TOTAL CAPACITY

   utilisation   latency vs service time   usable?
   ------------------------------------------------------
     50%              2.0x                 lots of headroom
     70%              3.3x                 <-- TARGET
     80%              5.0x                 acceptable, watch it
     90%             10.0x                 no burst tolerance
     95%             20.0x                 effectively saturated
     99%            100.0x                 an outage with a heartbeat

   A machine at 95% is "working" the way a motorway at 95% density
   is "moving". Both are one small perturbation from a jam.


   N+1: SIZE FOR THE FAILURE, NOT THE STEADY STATE

   3 instances, each at 70% -> total load = 210% of one instance
   one dies:
        210% / 2 survivors = 105% each  -> CASCADE
        (each survivor saturates, latency explodes, health checks
         fail, they get killed, the remaining one gets 210%...)

   Correct sizing for N+1 at a 70% post-failure target:
        need: total_load / 0.70 + 1 instance
        210% / 0.70 = 3 instances of capacity, + 1 spare = 4
        steady state: each at 52.5%, after a failure: 70%. Survivable.

   The cascade is why "we had redundancy" and "we had an outage"
   are compatible statements.


   UNIVERSAL SCALABILITY LAW: MORE NODES CAN MEAN LESS THROUGHPUT

   C(N) = N / (1 + a(N-1) + bN(N-1))
                    ^           ^
            contention      COHERENCY (crosstalk): grows as N^2

   throughput
      |            ....*....
      |         ..*         *..            <- the peak
      |      .*                 *..
      |    .*                       *..    <- adding nodes now
      |  .*                             *     REDUCES throughput
      |.*
      +------------------------------------> nodes
       1   4   8   16   32   64   128

   Amdahl's curve flattens. The USL curve TURNS DOWN, because every
   new node must coordinate with every existing one.
   Practical reading: find your peak empirically, then stay left of it.


   FROM BUSINESS FORECAST TO HARDWARE ORDER

   measured today:
     4,000 req/s peak, 12 cores at 70%, 48 GB at 60%, 9k IOPS
     cost per request: 0.0021 CPU-s, 12 MB session, 2.25 IOPS

   forecast: 3x traffic in 12 months -> 12,000 req/s peak

     CPU:    12000 * 0.0021 = 25.2 cores of work
             / 0.70 target  = 36 cores needed        (have 12)
     memory: 12000 * 0.012 GB concurrent sessions...
             -> compute via Little's law, not per-request
     IOPS:   12000 * 2.25   = 27,000 IOPS
             / 0.70         = 38,571 provisioned     (have 9k)
                                ^^^^^^ STORAGE binds first, not CPU

   The point of the exercise: the first thing to saturate was not
   the thing anyone was watching.
```

```python
# Capacity planning as arithmetic you can re-run when the forecast changes.

import math

def usable_capacity(total, target_util=0.70):
    """Never plan against 100%: the response-time curve forbids it."""
    return total * target_util

def response_multiplier(rho):
    """How many service times a request takes at utilisation rho."""
    return float("inf") if rho >= 1 else 1 / (1 - rho)

def instances_needed(load_units, target_util=0.70, tolerate_failures=1):
    """Size for the POST-FAILURE state, which is the state that matters."""
    active = math.ceil(load_units / target_util)
    return active + tolerate_failures          # N+1 (or N+2)

def usl(n, contention=0.03, coherency=0.0005):
    """Universal Scalability Law: returns SPEEDUP at n nodes.
    Note that it eventually DECREASES -- Amdahl's never does."""
    return n / (1 + contention * (n - 1) + coherency * n * (n - 1))

# --- Where does adding nodes stop helping? ---
best = max(range(1, 257), key=usl)
print(f"peak throughput at {best} nodes -> {usl(best):.1f}x")
print(f"at {best*2} nodes -> {usl(best*2):.1f}x   (WORSE, and costs 2x)")
# peak throughput at 41 nodes -> 13.5x
# at 82 nodes -> 12.7x   (WORSE, and costs 2x)

# --- A full forecast ---
current = {"rps": 4000, "cpu_s_per_req": 0.0021,
           "iops_per_req": 2.25, "mb_per_session": 12}
growth = 3.0
future_rps = current["rps"] * growth

cpu_work   = future_rps * current["cpu_s_per_req"]        # cores of work
cpu_needed = math.ceil(cpu_work / 0.70)
iops_need  = math.ceil(future_rps * current["iops_per_req"] / 0.70)

print(f"at {future_rps:.0f} rps: {cpu_needed} cores, {iops_need:,} IOPS")
# at 12000 rps: 36 cores, 38,572 IOPS

# --- N+1 sizing, and the cascade it prevents ---
load = 2.1                                    # 3 instances at 70%
print(f"instances required: {instances_needed(load)}")      # 4
survivors = 3 - 1
print(f"naive 3-instance design after 1 failure: "
      f"{load / survivors:.0%} each -> "
      f"{response_multiplier(min(load/survivors, 0.999)):.0f}x latency")
# naive 3-instance design after 1 failure: 105% each -> inf x latency
```

```bash
# ---- Load testing WITHOUT coordinated omission ----

# wrk2: fixed ARRIVAL RATE (-R), latency measured from intended send
# time. This is the property that makes the numbers honest.
wrk2 -t8 -c200 -d5m -R2000 --latency http://svc/api
#   Latency Distribution (HdrHistogram - Recorded Latency)
#    50.000%   12.31ms
#    90.000%   28.94ms
#    99.000%  145.22ms
#    99.990%  892.11ms      <- the number that sizes your headroom
#
# Compare with a closed-loop tool (ab, plain wrk) on the SAME service:
# it will report a far better tail, because it stopped sending during
# every stall. Same system, flattering numbers.

# Find the knee: step the rate up and watch where latency departs
# from flat. That inflection is your real capacity, not the rate at
# which errors start.
for rate in 500 1000 1500 2000 2500 3000 4000; do
  echo "=== ${rate} rps ==="
  wrk2 -t8 -c200 -d60s -R$rate --latency http://svc/api \
    | grep -E '99.000%|Requests/sec'
done
#   1000 rps -> p99  18 ms   flat
#   2000 rps -> p99  31 ms   flat-ish
#   2500 rps -> p99  96 ms   <- the KNEE: plan to run below this
#   3000 rps -> p99 890 ms   past the knee, on the hyperbola
#   4000 rps -> errors

# ---- Trend the resources you will run out of ----
sar -u -f /var/log/sa/sa$(date +%d) | tail -20      # CPU history
sar -r -f /var/log/sa/sa$(date +%d) | tail -20      # memory history
sar -d -f /var/log/sa/sa$(date +%d) | tail          # disk history
#   Fit a line to weekly peaks, not to averages: you run out of
#   capacity at the PEAK, and averages hide it entirely.

df -h; df -i                       # both blocks AND inodes (Chapter 10)
ss -s                              # socket counts vs limits
cat /proc/sys/fs/file-nr           # open fds: allocated / free / max
```

**Key takeaways**

- Usable capacity is well below total capacity because response time grows as `1/(1 − ρ)`; 70-80% utilisation is the standard target and 95% is effectively saturated.
- Capacity planning proceeds by characterising the workload, measuring cost per unit of work, modelling which resource saturates first, and choosing a scaling strategy.
- Requests are not uniform, and peak-to-mean ratios of 3-10x with weekly and seasonal cycles mean planning must target peaks, not averages.
- The first resource to saturate is often not CPU — memory per session, IOPS, file descriptors, database connections, or a single-threaded component frequently bind first.
- Vertical scaling is simple with a hard ceiling; horizontal scaling has no ceiling but requires statelessness or partitioning and introduces distributed coordination.
- The Universal Scalability Law adds a coherency term to Amdahl, so throughput peaks and then declines as coordination costs grow quadratically with node count.
- N+1 sizing must target the post-failure utilisation, or losing one instance pushes survivors past saturation and triggers a cascade.
- Load tests must be open-loop with a fixed arrival rate, or coordinated omission will hide exactly the stalls that determine required headroom.
- The knee of the latency curve, found by stepping the offered rate, is the real capacity limit — not the rate at which errors begin.
- Capacity thresholds should be written down in advance, because the alternative is improvising the decision during an incident.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. A service uses 0.004 CPU-seconds per request and currently peaks at 1,500 requests per second. Compute the cores required to serve 4x that traffic at 70% utilisation.
> 2. Four instances each run at 65%. Compute the per-instance utilisation after one fails, and determine the minimum instance count that keeps survivors at or below 75%.
> 3. Use `wrk2` (or any fixed-rate tool) to step the offered load against a local service and identify the knee of the latency curve. Explain why a closed-loop tool would report a different answer.
> 4. Plot the Universal Scalability Law for contention 0.05 and coherency 0.001, find the node count with peak throughput, and explain what is happening past that peak.
> 5. Interview-style: "We run at 45% CPU and want to save money, so we are halving the fleet. Any concerns?" *Hint: compute the post-change utilisation, then the post-change utilisation after one instance fails — and locate both on the response-time curve.*

#### Kernel Tuning Parameters

**Theory**

Every kernel ships with defaults chosen to be reasonable across an enormous range of machines and workloads. That generality is exactly why tuning sometimes helps: your machine is not the average of all machines. But it is also why most tuning advice found online is harmful — a value that helped someone's write-heavy database in 2014 is not a value that helps your latency-sensitive web server on hardware that did not then exist.

So the rule comes before the knobs: **measure, change one parameter, measure again, and keep the record.** A tuning change with no before-and-after measurement is not tuning; it is superstition with root privileges. Most real performance problems are in the application, and the kernel's defaults are usually fine.

The parameters worth knowing, grouped by the subsystem they belong to:

**Memory (Chapter 8).** `vm.swappiness` (0-200, default 60) trades anonymous-page swapping against page-cache eviction — lower it for databases that manage their own caching, but 0 does not disable swap and can make OOM kills more likely. `vm.dirty_ratio` and `vm.dirty_background_ratio` bound how much modified page cache accumulates before writeback; large values on a big-memory machine create multi-gigabyte write storms that stall everything. `vm.overcommit_memory` decides whether the kernel permits allocations exceeding RAM plus swap. **Transparent huge pages** reduce TLB misses but their compaction can cause latency spikes, which is why most database vendors recommend `madvise` rather than `always`.

**Storage (Chapters 9 and 11).** The I/O scheduler choice matters far more than any single parameter: `none` (or `mq-deadline`) for NVMe, where the device reorders better than the kernel can, and `bfq` for desktop interactivity. `nr_requests` sets queue depth, and `read_ahead_kb` helps sequential scans while wasting bandwidth on random access.

**Network.** `net.core.somaxconn` caps the accept backlog and is a classic cause of dropped connections under bursty load — the default has been raised repeatedly precisely because so many people hit it. `tcp_rmem`/`tcp_wmem` size the socket buffers that determine achievable throughput on high bandwidth-delay-product links; `tcp_max_syn_backlog` and `tcp_syncookies` govern behaviour under connection floods; and the congestion control algorithm (`bbr` versus `cubic`) can matter significantly on lossy or long-haul paths.

**Scheduler and limits (Chapters 3 and 4).** `sched_min_granularity_ns` and `sched_latency_ns` trade context-switch overhead against responsiveness. `fs.file-max` and per-process `RLIMIT_NOFILE` bound open descriptors — "too many open files" is one of the most common production failures and is almost always a limit, not a resource shortage. `kernel.pid_max` matters on container hosts running thousands of processes.

Three cautions. First, **many limits are per-cgroup now**, so a container's effective limits come from its cgroup rather than from the host `sysctl` (Chapter 13) — tuning the host and wondering why nothing changed is a common waste of an afternoon. Second, **NUMA placement usually beats parameter tuning** on multi-socket machines: remote memory access can cost 1.5-2x, which dwarfs most knob adjustments. Third, **make changes persistent and documented**: a `sysctl` applied by hand disappears at reboot, and an undocumented one becomes a mystery the next person cannot safely remove.

**Example**

```text
   THE TUNING METHOD (the part that is not a parameter list)

   1. MEASURE the problem          (USE/RED, a number you can compare)
   2. FORM a hypothesis            ("writeback stalls cause the p99")
   3. CHANGE ONE PARAMETER         (one, so causality survives)
   4. MEASURE again                (same workload, same duration)
   5. KEEP or REVERT               (and WRITE DOWN which, and why)
   6. Make it persistent           (sysctl.d, with a comment)

   Skipping step 1 produces "we set 40 sysctls from a blog post and
   things feel better" -- unreproducible, unremovable, and untestable.


   THE KNOBS THAT MATTER, BY SUBSYSTEM

   MEMORY                          default   consider              ch.
   vm.swappiness                   60        1-10 for databases     8
   vm.dirty_ratio                  20        5-10 on big-RAM boxes  8
   vm.dirty_background_ratio       10        3-5                    8
   vm.overcommit_memory            0         2 for strict accounting 7
   THP /sys/.../enabled            always    madvise (databases)    7

   STORAGE
   .../queue/scheduler             mq-deadline  none for NVMe       9
   .../queue/nr_requests           256       higher for deep queues 9
   .../queue/read_ahead_kb         128       higher: seq; lower: rnd 9

   NETWORK
   net.core.somaxconn              4096      raise for bursty accept -
   net.ipv4.tcp_rmem/wmem          auto      raise for high BDP      -
   net.ipv4.tcp_congestion_control cubic     bbr on lossy/long paths -
   net.ipv4.tcp_syncookies         1         keep at 1              12

   SCHED / LIMITS
   kernel.sched_latency_ns         ~24ms     lower = responsive      4
   fs.file-max / RLIMIT_NOFILE     varies    raise; the #1 prod bug 10
   kernel.pid_max                  32768     raise on container hosts 2


   WHY vm.dirty_ratio MATTERS ON A LARGE MACHINE

   256 GB RAM, dirty_ratio = 20 (the default)
     -> up to 51 GB of dirty pages may accumulate before a writer
        is forced to block
     -> then the kernel flushes 51 GB to a device doing 500 MB/s
     -> 100 SECONDS of writeback, during which unrelated processes
        stall on the same device

   dirty                                          forced writeback
   pages  |                                  /|   everything stalls
          |                             /----  |
          |                     /------        |
          |             /------                v
          +-------------------------------------- time
                                          ^ dirty_ratio reached

   Lowering it to 5% (12.8 GB) makes writeback smaller and more
   frequent: worse peak throughput, FAR better worst-case latency.
   That is the same trade as every other real-time decision (Ch. 14).


   THE TRAP: TUNING THE HOST, RUNNING IN A CONTAINER

   host:      sysctl fs.file-max = 2000000       you set this
   container: cgroup pids.max = 4096             this is what applies
              RLIMIT_NOFILE   = 1024             and this
   result:    "too many open files" at 1024, while the host says 2M

   Since Chapter 13, the effective limit is the MOST RESTRICTIVE of:
     host sysctl -> cgroup limit -> rlimit -> application config
   Check all four before concluding the kernel is at fault.
```

```bash
# ---- Inspect before you change anything ----
sysctl -a | wc -l                    # ~1000 parameters exist
sysctl vm.swappiness vm.dirty_ratio net.core.somaxconn
sysctl -a --pattern 'net.ipv4.tcp_(r|w)mem'

# ---- Change ONE thing, temporarily, and measure ----
sysctl -w vm.swappiness=10           # runtime only; gone on reboot
# ... run the SAME workload, for the SAME duration, and compare ...
sysctl -w vm.swappiness=60           # revert if it did not help

# ---- Make it persistent, WITH A REASON ----
cat > /etc/sysctl.d/99-db-tuning.conf <<'EOF'
# 2026-09-11: postgres manages its own cache; swapping shared_buffers
# caused p99 spikes (see incident 4417). Measured: p99 820ms -> 95ms.
vm.swappiness = 10

# 256 GB RAM: default dirty_ratio=20 allowed ~51 GB of dirty pages and
# 100 s writeback storms. 5% = ~12.8 GB. Throughput -3%, p99 -85%.
vm.dirty_ratio = 5
vm.dirty_background_ratio = 2
EOF
sysctl --system                      # apply all sysctl.d files

# ---- Storage: the scheduler choice outweighs the knobs ----
cat /sys/block/nvme0n1/queue/scheduler
#   [none] mq-deadline kyber bfq      <- NVMe: 'none' is usually right
echo none > /sys/block/nvme0n1/queue/scheduler
cat /sys/block/sda/queue/rotational   # 1 = spinning: scheduling helps

# ---- The single most common production failure ----
ulimit -n                            # per-shell soft limit
cat /proc/sys/fs/file-nr             # allocated / unused / max
cat /proc/$(pgrep -n myapp)/limits | grep 'open files'
#   Max open files   1024   4096   files      <- soft / hard
# systemd services ignore /etc/security/limits.conf; set it here:
#   [Service]
#   LimitNOFILE=65535

# ---- In a container, check the cgroup, not the host ----
cat /sys/fs/cgroup/pids.max
cat /sys/fs/cgroup/memory.max
cat /sys/fs/cgroup/cpu.max
cat /sys/fs/cgroup/memory.pressure    # PSI per cgroup (Chapter 13)

# ---- NUMA placement often beats every sysctl on this list ----
numactl --hardware
#   node distances:  node 0  1
#            0:      10     21     <- remote memory ~2x the latency
lscpu | grep -i numa
numactl --cpunodebind=0 --membind=0 ./workload     # pin CPU and memory
numastat -p $(pgrep -n myapp)       # numa_miss > 0 means remote access
```

```python
# Tuning without measurement is superstition. This is the minimum
# honest harness: same workload, same duration, one variable changed.

import subprocess, statistics, json, time

def get(param):
    return subprocess.check_output(["sysctl", "-n", param]).decode().strip()

def set_(param, value):
    subprocess.run(["sysctl", "-w", f"{param}={value}"], check=True)

def benchmark(runs=5):
    """Return p99 latency in ms. Must be the REAL workload -- a
    synthetic loop measures the synthetic loop."""
    samples = []
    for _ in range(runs):
        out = subprocess.check_output([
            "wrk2", "-t4", "-c100", "-d60s", "-R1000",
            "--latency", "http://localhost:8080/api"])
        samples.append(parse_p99(out))
    return statistics.median(samples)      # median of runs: resists
                                           # one noisy outlier

def try_parameter(param, new_value):
    old = get(param)
    before = benchmark()
    set_(param, new_value)
    time.sleep(30)                         # let the system settle:
                                           # caches and writeback lag
    after = benchmark()

    delta = (after - before) / before * 100
    verdict = "KEEP" if after < before * 0.95 else "REVERT"
    if verdict == "REVERT":
        set_(param, old)                   # leave no undocumented state

    return {"param": param, "old": old, "new": new_value,
            "p99_before_ms": before, "p99_after_ms": after,
            "change_pct": round(delta, 1), "verdict": verdict}

results = [try_parameter("vm.swappiness", 10),
           try_parameter("vm.dirty_ratio", 5),
           try_parameter("net.core.somaxconn", 8192)]
print(json.dumps(results, indent=2))
# Keep this output. It is the justification the next engineer needs
# in order to remove the setting safely when the workload changes.
```

**Key takeaways**

- Kernel defaults are chosen to be reasonable across all machines, which is both why tuning can help a specific workload and why copied advice usually does not.
- The method is to measure, change one parameter, measure again with the same workload, and record the result; an unmeasured change is superstition with root access.
- Most performance problems are in the application, so kernel tuning should follow application profiling, not precede it.
- `vm.swappiness` trades anonymous swapping against page-cache eviction and is commonly lowered for databases that manage their own caching, but 0 does not disable swap.
- `vm.dirty_ratio` bounds accumulated dirty pages, and the default on a large-memory machine can permit tens of gigabytes and multi-second writeback stalls.
- Transparent huge pages reduce TLB misses but their compaction causes latency spikes, which is why `madvise` is the common database recommendation.
- Choosing the I/O scheduler — `none` for NVMe, `bfq` for desktop interactivity — matters more than any individual queue parameter.
- `net.core.somaxconn` and socket buffer sizes are frequent causes of dropped connections and throughput ceilings on bursty or high bandwidth-delay-product links.
- "Too many open files" is among the most common production failures and is a limit problem, resolved at the systemd unit or rlimit level rather than by adding resources.
- In containers the effective limit is the most restrictive of host sysctl, cgroup limit, rlimit, and application config, so tuning the host alone often changes nothing.
- NUMA placement frequently outweighs every sysctl on a multi-socket machine, since remote memory access can cost 1.5-2x.
- Persist changes in `sysctl.d` with a comment explaining the measurement that justified them, so a future engineer can safely remove them.
